fields.result: Quantum-assisted interferometers retain direct-detection weak-light sensitivity $\mathrm{SNR}\propto|V|\sqrt{\eta_q M\overline{n}}$ while avoiding physical optical delay lines across baselines $>1\text{ km}$, but cannot beat direct detection on ground arrays up to a few kilometers.
fields.question: Can quantum networking and quantum memory architectures overcome classical beam-transport limits in optical and infrared astronomical interferometry?
fields.prior: Classical direct detection spans baselines up to 330 m but is limited by optical transport losses, while HBT and heterodyne detection scale unfavorably as $\mathrm{SNR}\propto\overline{n}$ when $\overline{n}\ll 1$.
fields.limits: Broadband astronomical light is photon-starved ($\overline{n}\ll 1$), single-mode, and degraded by atmospheric turbulence; no on-sky stellar fringe verification yet reported.
tools: quantum memories (diamond color centers and cold atoms)

fields.result: Dynamic programming qubit routing reduces inter-node EPR pair consumption by an average of 24.40% and up to 85.06% across 80 circuit configurations.
fields.question: How to minimize inter-node communication across collective communication blocks in distributed quantum circuits by accounting for global inter-block dependencies?
fields.prior: QuComm compiler, which uses greedy block-level routing.
fields.limits: Evaluated on 4 benchmark circuits (QAOA, RCA, BV, VQE) up to 200 qubits in simulation across 3 network topologies (mesh-grid, ring, fully-connected).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2. Cost comparison of DPRQ and QuComm on the 4 benchmark circuits as total number of qubits increases from 50 to 200. The top-left graph displays data for QAOA, the top-right graph displays data for RCA, the bottom-left graph displays data for BV, and the bottom-right graph displays data for VQE. \alpha|^2 = 2$ dark-to-bright threshold in single-phase CCF regime (Ref. [30])

fields.result: Stabilizer generators of an unknown stabilizer code can be reconstructed from $N \ge A\ln g + A\ln(1/\delta)$ states using single-qubit product measurements, requiring polylogarithmically many copies in physical qubit count $n$ for qLDPC codes.
fields.question: Can stabilizer generators of an unknown quantum error-correcting code be learned using only local single-qubit measurements on codewords without prior structural knowledge?
fields.limits: Bounded stabilizer generator weight $w$, code defined in stabilizer formalism, failure probability $\delta$, bit-flip error rate per qubit $p$.

fields.result: 3D neutral-atom embedding of the $[[144,12,12]]$ bivariate bicycle code achieves approximately $4\times$ higher areal logical-qubit density than planar layout and $42\times$ higher than distance-11 surface codes, while halving syndrome-extraction round duration.
fields.question: How does native 3D qubit control affect the routing overhead, footprint, and temporal execution cost of nonlocal qLDPC syndrome extraction?
fields.prior: Planar 2D atom-array embeddings of the $[[144,12,12]]$ code.
fields.limits: Numerical simulation rather than physical hardware implementation. Assumes single-shot multi-layer readout and collision-free parallel 3D transport.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Syndrome-extraction schedule comparison for twelve planar distance-11 surface-code patches and three implementations of the $[[144,12,12]]$ bivariate bicycle (BB) code: LR-triangular, LR-planar, and systolic. (a) Cycle-time decomposition for one syndrome-extraction round. The surface-code baseline is fastest because its stabilizer interactions are geometrically local and require no atom transport. Among the BB implementations, the LR-triangular layout has the shortest cycle time, primarily because of its reduced routing overhead. (b) Operation counts. All BB implementations require the same number of entangling gates, $864$ , but differ in the number of movement operations required by their physical schedules. The surface code requires no movement since all entangling operations are local. (c) Total atom-transport distance. The LR-triangular layout requires the shortest total movement distance, $404\penalty\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ , compared with $1512\penalty\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ for LR-planar and $704\penalty\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ for the systolic implementation, illustrating that the cycle-time reduction arises from the physical realization of the nonlocal interactions rather than a reduction in entangling-gate count.
fields.figure_gloss: Syndrome-extraction round cycle time broken down by operation (readout, transport, transfer, and gates) across surface-code, systolic planar, LR-planar, and LR-triangular 3D architectures, showing total time halved in 3D relative to the planar baseline.

fields.result: Combining substrate phonon barrier tiling with QEC interleaving reduces peak logical error rate by over $99.8\%$ and shortens transient duration by $80\%$ under simulated radiation strikes. Sparser multi-qubit tiling cuts barrier fabrication perimeter cost by up to $87\%$ with minimal performance loss.
fields.question: Can substrate-level phonon barrier tiling and quantum error correction code interleaving mitigate radiation-induced spatially correlated faults in superconducting quantum chips without execution overhead?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation only (51 million circuit simulations) using rotated surface codes under a parametrizable barrier permeability model ($b_p$).
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 8 : Average logical error rate of a distance-7 rotated surface code with respect to the number of interleaved independent surface codes (rows) and the number of qubits enclosed in each phonon barrier (columns) with a constant barrier permeability $b_{p}=0.1$ , averaged over the total duration of identical radiation-induced faults.
fields.figure_gloss: Heatmap of average logical error rate for a distance-7 rotated surface code across tile sizes (1 to 16 qubits) and numbers of interleaved codes (1 to 9) at barrier permeability $b_p = 0.1$.

fields.result: Active-volume-aware compilation cuts the active volume of 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy estimation by up to $3.9\times$ across $L\times L$ square lattices with $L=4$ to $20$. Also cuts Toffoli count by $\sim 2\times$ at $L=20$.
fields.question: How much can the execution cost and runtime of quantum phase estimation for 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy be reduced by compiling directly for active-volume architectures instead of non-Clifford proxies?
fields.prior: Baseline compilation optimized for non-Clifford cost, as analyzed by Campbell (2022) and Kan et al. (2024).
fields.limits: Evaluated for $t=1$, $u=8$ with periodic boundary conditions and extensive energy error budget $0.0051t L_{x} L_{y}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : Comparison of computational volume of 2D square Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy estimation for the baseline and improved implementations against the logical qubit count. The logical qubit count includes both the system qubits and the auxiliary qubits required to implement a single batch of Hamming-weight phasing. The numbers above the baseline active volume data points indicate the lattice size. Top : Absolute circuit volume (as defined in Ref. [ 62 ] ) and active volume resource estimates for the total cost of QPE algorithm achieving a $0.0051tL^{2}$ error. Bottom : Relative speedups obtained by first replacing circuit volume with active volume as the resource metric (orange), and then by applying the compilation techniques proposed in this work (green). Circuit volume (CV) exceeds the baseline active volume (AV) by up to $12.1\times$ for the $20\times 20$ lattice. The proposed compilation provides a further reduction in active volume of up to $3.9\times$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Active volume and conventional computational spacetime volume plotted against logical qubit count across square lattice sizes $L=4$ to $20$, comparing baseline against improved compilation.

fields.result: Centralized repetition code storage lifetime scales exponentially with qubit count $n$ at any finite temperature $T < \infty$, avoiding the thermal instability of a 1D Ising chain despite having only 1 Ising bond per qubit.
fields.question: Does a star-graph centralized repetition code behave thermodynamically like an unstable 1D Ising chain or a stable complete-graph repetition code under thermal noise?
fields.limits: Local bit-flip error model only (does not suppress phase errors). Assumes Born-Markov bath coupling and odd physical qubit number $n$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Plot of bound ( 21 ) on $\lambda_{1}$ as a function of $n$ for the particular choice $\beta J=0.8$ . As $n$ increases to $\infty$ , the code becomes increasingly stable despite the fact that the temperature $k_{B}T$ exceeds $J$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Upper bound on the transition rate eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ plotted against qubit number $n$ at inverse temperature $\beta J = 0.8$. The decay toward zero illustrates exponentially increasing stability with system size even when thermal energy $k_B T$ exceeds coupling $J$.

fields.result: Proves optimal root-influence inequality $\|p\|_{\mathrm{cb}}\ge \sum_i \sqrt{\mathrm{Inf}_i[p]}/t$ for degree-$t$ block-multilinear polynomials, and tight top-level Fourier growth $\|\widehat{p}_{2t}\|_{\ell_1} \le (en/(2t-1))^{\frac{2t-1}{2}} \|p\|_{\mathrm{cb}}$ for degree-$2t$ polynomials.
fields.question: Can inequalities for completely bounded polynomials establish improved upper limits on the computational power and Fourier growth of quantum query algorithms?
fields.prior: Root-influence bound was $\|p\|_{\mathrm{cb}}\ge \sum_i \sqrt{\mathrm{Inf}_i[p]}/t^2$ (Bansal, Sinha, and de Wolf 2022).
fields.limits: Applies to quantum query algorithms whose acceptance probabilities or amplitudes map to completely bounded polynomials (e.g. block-multilinear architectures, parallel query models).

operator norm bounds on tensor forms

fields.result: Introduced chameleon gates $\mathcal{C}_{\rho}$ parametrized by a quantum state knob $\rho$, constructible via a controlled-$\mathrm{swap}$ and partial trace to implement state-based quantum computation and simulate nonlinear Hamiltonians.
fields.question: How can quantum controlled-gates be generalized to adapt their transformations dynamically based on arbitrary input quantum states without prior knowledge of those states?
fields.limits: Requires ancilla control qubit initialized with small parameter $|δ| \ll 1$; valid up to $O(\delta^2)$ error; requires post-selection on the $|+\rangle$ measurement outcome.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: [Left] Quantum-circuit schematic of a state-based controlled-gate $\mathcal{C}_{\rho}$ , which we refer to as the chameleon gate [Eq. ( 6 )]. [Right] An equivalent standard gate-based construction is also shown for this gate, which uses a specific combination of quantum states, quantum controlled- swap gate, and partial tracing. Note that basically the control qubit can be any state. But when the control qubit is chosen as $\psi_{\delta}$ with $|\delta|\ll 1$ , this also yields an implementation for $\mathpzc{U}_{\rho}$ [Eq. ( 1 )] to an $O(\delta^{2})$ error.

fields.result: Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas (L-MPF) combine classically computed linear coefficients with noisy quantum expectation values to outperform low-bond-dimension classical tensor network simulations and unmitigated quantum results on 65 qubits, achieving classical GPU speedups up to $5.6\times$.
fields.question: Can high-dimensional tensor network contractions be integrated directly into a quantum error mitigation workflow to estimate noiseless expectation values with rigorous error bars?
fields.limits: Demonstrated on a 2D discrete time crystal model on a $3\times 3$ heavy-hexagonal lattice up to 10 Floquet cycles; non-ergodic amplification settings require PEA and higher sample counts to prevent large error bars.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Comparison of dimensionless expectation values obtained with three methods: (i) purely classical high bond dimension simulations, (ii) purely classical low bond dimension simulations that have been extrapolated to the zero truncation error limit, and (iii) quantum hardware results on ibm_basquecountry that have been mitigated with the L-MPF method, where the expectation values in the sum $c_{i}\langle O\rangle_{\lambda_{i}}$ have been obtained with ergodic amplification. a) Expectation values of the target observable, with corresponding $1\sigma$ error bars, shown as a function of the Floquet cycles. The reference expectation values (black) are obtained from Schrödinger-picture tensor network simulations with a truncation error of $10^{-8}$ . The red markers correspond to the application of the L-MPF workflow to the raw hardware measurements, while the noiseless expectation values (blue) are extrapolated from Heisenberg-picture tensor network simulations. b) Deviation from the Schrödinger-picture belief propagation expectation values for both Heisenberg-picture simulation and hardware values, shown as a function of the Floquet cycles. The blue and red markers correspond to the same datasets shown in plot a), and the shaded regions indicate the associated $1\sigma$ error bands. Details regarding the calculation of these uncertainties are discussed in the main text.
fields.figure_gloss: Expectation value vs. Floquet cycle number, comparing purely classical low-bond simulations, unmitigated hardware measurements, and L-MPF error-mitigated results against high-bond-dimension classical ground truth.

fields.result: Residual $ZZ$ interaction cancels completely outside straddling regime without direct qubit-qubit capacitive coupling using single-junction double-resonator coupler. Provides $\sim 70\,\mathrm{MHz}$ activated $ZZ$ interaction, enabling $20\,\mathrm{ns}$ CZ gate with simulated coherent infidelity below $10^{-5}$.
fields.question: How to completely suppress residual $ZZ$ interactions across flexible qubit-qubit frequency detunings without requiring multi-junction couplers or direct capacitive layout constraints?
fields.prior: Single-transmon couplers require qubit detuning within straddling regime and direct qubit capacitance balancing; double-transmon and fluxonium couplers require multiple Josephson junctions.
fields.limits: Numerical simulation only. Evaluated using a 20-state basis with perturbative leakage corrections; dephasing assumes $1/f$ flux-noise amplitude $A_{\varphi_{\mathrm{ex}}}=2\pi\times 10^{-6}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: (a) Circuit diagram of the proposed architecture. Two transmon qubits, $\mathrm{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{Q}_{2}$ (purple), are capacitively coupled to a double-resonator coupler (DRC, blue). (b) False-color rendering of the device layout, with colors matching the circuit elements in (a). The scale bar denotes $200\,\mu$ m. (c) Mode-coupling diagram of the qubit–DRC system, with arrow colors indicating the coupling signs: red (blue) denotes positive (negative) coupling. The common mode $\Sigma$ couples positively to both qubits, whereas the differential mode $\Delta$ couples negatively to Q 1 and positively to Q 2 . Asymmetric inductance values ( $L_{\ell}\neq L_{r}$ ) introduce an inter-mode coupling $g_{L}$ between the $\Sigma$ and $\Delta$ modes. (d) Single-excitation spectrum of the qubit–DRC system versus reduced external flux $\varphi{\mathrm{ex}}$ . Dotted curves show the coupler eigenenergies in the symmetric limit $\Delta E_{L}=0$ ( $g_{L}=0$ ), dashed curves show the bare eigenenergies of $\hat{H}{\mathrm{q}}+\hat{H}{\mathrm{c}}$ for $\Delta E_{L}/h=-16~\mathrm{GHz}$ , and solid curves show the dressed eigenenergies of the full Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$ . The labels $\ket{n_{1}n_{2};n_{\Sigma}n_{\Delta}}$ denote bare states with occupations $n_{1},n_{2}$ in the qubits and $n_{\Sigma},n_{\Delta}$ in the common and differential modes. (e) Differential-mode potential and wavefunctions at selected external flux biases $\varphi_{\mathrm{ex}}/2\pi=0$ , $0.3$ , and $0.5$ . The gray-to-black curves show the potential energy as a function of $\varphi_{\Delta}$ , and the colored curves show the wavefunctions of the three lowest eigenstates $\ket{n}_{\Delta}$ ( $n=0,1,2$ ), each offset vertically by its eigenenergy. (f) Schematic of the coupler-mediated exchange interaction. Tuning the differential-mode frequency $\omega\Delta$ through the common-mode frequency $\omega_{\Sigma}$ changes the relative strengths of the two virtual exchange paths, tuning the effective qubit–qubit coupling $\tilde{g}_{12}$ from positive to negative and producing cancellation near $\omega_{\Delta}\simeq\omega_{\Sigma}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Circuit and layout of transmon qubits coupled via the double-resonator coupler (a, b), mode coupling and flux-dependent single-excitation spectra (c, d), differential-mode potential wells (e), and mechanism of virtual-exchange path cancellation (f).

fields.result: Electrostatic splitting of an edge magnetoplasmon resonator yields RF transmission signatures for integer ($\nu=1, 2$) and fractional ($\nu=4/3, 2/3$) quantum Hall states, with cavity perimeter dropping to $17.5\text{ }\mathrm{\mu m}$ past QPC pinch-off.
fields.question: How does polarizing an embedded quantum point contact influence edge magnetoplasmon modes and cavity geometry in a quantum Hall resonator?

fields.result: Single-qubit average Clifford fidelity reaches $99.61\% \pm 0.03\%$ and two-qubit Mølmer-Sørensen Bell-state fidelity reaches $92.35\% \pm 1.50\%$ using a chip-scale Brillouin laser locked to an integrated coil resonator.

fields.question: Can an on-chip optomechanical resonator achieve absorptive quantum memory for telecom photons near the mechanical ground state with flexible on-demand retrieval?

fields.result: Surveys quantum data encoding methods across state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM, and block-encoding, synthesizing circuit size, depth, and fault-tolerant gate counts.
fields.question: How can deterministic classical data be compiled into quantum representations under minimal circuit depth, gate counts, and non-Clifford resources?
fields.limits: Restricted to deterministic, fully known classical data in the standard qubit circuit model with all-to-all or binary-tree connectivity; excludes sampled distributions and continuous variables.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: From bit (classical data) to qubit (quantum data). Quantum algorithm and corresponding problem inputs are compiled to concrete quantum circuits. Quantum state preparation: for classical vector $\bm{v}$ , the task is to prepare a quantum state $|\psi\rangle=\|\bm{v}\|^{-1}\sum_{j}v_{j}|j\rangle$ . QRAM: For binary vector $\bm{v}$ , the task is to construct a unitary transformation that $|j\rangle|0\rangle\rightarrow|j\rangle|v_{j}\rangle$ . Block-encoding: for matrix $A$ , the task is to construct a unitary $U_{A}$ such that $(\left\langle{0}\right|^{\otimes a}\otimes I_{n})U_{A}(\left|{0}\right\rangle^{\otimes a}\otimes I_{n})=A/\alpha$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Three core access models mapping classical vectors and matrices to quantum operations: quantum state preparation, QRAM, and block-encoding.

fields.result: Non-reciprocal three-cavity system exhibits a third-order exceptional point from the coalescence of two second-order exceptional points, speeding up entanglement generation time to $t_m \approx 15$ ns with an enhancement factor scaling as $J^{-4/5}$.

fields.limits: Single-excitation subspace under post-selection against decay to ground state $|0,0,0\rangle$; assumes cavity dissipation rates are matched ($\Delta\gamma/\gamma \ll 1$).

fields.limits: Coefficient truncation threshold of $10^{-6}$; benchmarks evaluated on 64 AMD EPYC 7H12 cores for Trotterized 2D TFIM and 2D Hubbard models.

fields.result: Cavity magnonics can be driven into non-Hermitian and quantum regimes via reservoir-mediated dissipative coupling, Floquet frequency modulation, and parametric squeezing transfer. Long-lived subradiant modes near anti-$\mathcal{PT}$ exceptional points lower the bistability threshold as $|\Omega_{\rm th}|^{2}\propto(\gamma-\Gamma)^{3}/K$, scaling quantum Fisher information as $\mathcal{F}_{Q}\propto\varepsilon^{-4}$.
fields.question: How do engineered dissipative coupling, Floquet modulation, and parametric driving enable quantum state generation, nonreciprocal transport, and enhanced sensing in cavity magnonics?
fields.limits: Dynamical stability requires parametric drive strength $x < 1$. Bright-magnon quadrature squeezing persists only below critical thermal occupation $\bar{n}_{m}^{\rm crit}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Characteristic eigenspectrum of a dissipatively coupled anti- $\mathcal{PT}$ -symmetric system. (a) Real and (b) imaginary parts of the eigenvalues as functions of the relative detuning $\delta$ . The EPs at $|\delta|=\Gamma$ separate the spectrally split regime from the regime of frequency coalescence and linewidth bifurcation into superradiant and subradiant branches. Adapted from Ref. [ 27 ] .
fields.figure_gloss: Real and imaginary eigenspectrum parts plotted versus relative detuning $\delta$. At exceptional points $|\delta|=\Gamma$, real frequencies coalesce while imaginary damping rates bifurcate into superradiant and subradiant branches.

fields.result: Amplifies cross-Kerr interaction between two microwave cavity modes via single-frequency transmon drive near intermediate-state divergences, achieving on-demand $\textsc{crot}$ gate for rotation-symmetric bosonic error correction without requiring multiple frequencies or frequency-tunable elements.
fields.question: How can a direct, code-agnostic $\textsc{crot}$ gate between bosonic cavity modes be implemented in circuit QED without multi-tone driving or gigahertz frequency tuning?
fields.prior: Prior direct implementations required $>1$ GHz frequency tunability or multi-tone drives scaling with logical state size.
fields.limits: Numerical and analytical modeling. Assumes perfect cancellation of self-Kerr from auxiliary side transmons, neglecting higher-order mode distortions and unmodeled side-transmon Hilbert spaces.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: (a) Kerr spectrum (in units of the no-drive cross-Kerr) in the weak-coupling regime at fixed effective amplitude $\left|\frac{\Omega_{d}}{\delta_{d}}\right|=1$ . Dispersive structures arise from drive-induced resonances. The dashed green and blue vertical lines mark single-cavity resonances where both cross- and (unwanted) self-Kerr effects are amplified. The desired working point lies near the two-cavity resonance marked by the dashed magenta vertical line. (b) The immediate vicinity of the chosen resonance, overlaid with the numerical sixth-order terms $K_{\textrm{dis}}$ $\propto N_{a}^{2}N_{b}$ (purple) and $N_{a}N_{b}^{2}$ (brown) that lead to distortions. The gray shaded region identifies a range of drive detuning for which the higher-order distortions are mild, while the cross-Kerr coefficient already experiences significant growth close to the resonance. Our chosen crot working point is at $\delta_{d}/\alpha=0.835$ (gray vertical line). (c) Teleportation-based error-correction (EC) circuit for rotation-symmetric bosonic (RSB) codes, employing two crot gates [ crot $(2\pi/NM)$ and crot $(\pi/N^{2})$ , with $M$ and $N$ as the RSB code orders], two measurements (DP $=$ discrete-phase measurement; $\overline{X}=$ logical- $X$ measurement), and a final classically controlled single-mode gate to complete the teleportation. (Figure adapted from Ref. [ 24 ] .) (d) Wigner diagrams of input and output [after crot $(2\pi/NM)$ ] states at our chosen working point, for different loss error $k$ and phase error $\theta$ values. (e) Memory task: Ratio $R$ of the average fidelities, after EC with actual crot gates versus the unencoded physical qubit, for different loss and dephasing rates $\kappa$ and $\kappa_{\text{ph}}$ . The small black circles are numerically simulated data points; the contour plot interpolates across those points. The solid white line marks $R=1$ for EC with actual crot gates; the dashed white line gives the analogous line for EC with ideal crot s.
fields.figure_gloss: Effective self- and cross-Kerr nonlinearities plotted against drive detuning at fixed drive strength $\left|\Omega_d/\delta_d\right|=1$, showing resonant divergences that enhance cross-Kerr interaction while distinguishing two-cavity from single-cavity resonances.

fields.result: Constructs bosonic four-body matrix-quantum-mechanics potentials via Floquet-engineered oscillating two-body spin interactions with a constant number of unitaries per cycle. Control-frequency bandwidth scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^{3})$ with matrix size $N$, reaching non-perturbative couplings $\lambda \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$ at driving frequencies $\omega \sim \mathcal{O}(\text{MHz})$.
fields.question: Can four-body potentials of bosonic matrix quantum mechanics be simulated on an analog optical-lattice platform without the deep circuits of digital implementations?
fields.limits: Requires non-spin-conserving spin-spin interactions and large-spin ferromagnetic regime ($m \sim j$). Bosonic Hilbert space must be truncated.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : This plot shows the convergence of the spin model to the truncated $SU(2)\times SO(2)$ bosonic matrix model (with $\lambda=2$ ) for the ground state energy. For both models, we have chosen the truncation $\Lambda=6$ . The relative error for $j=3$ is $0.5\,\%$ and improves to $0.007\,\%$ for $j=200$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Ground-state energy convergence as a function of spin size $j$ comparing the large-spin model against the truncated $SU(2) \times SO(2)$ bosonic matrix model with $\lambda=2$ and cutoff $\Lambda=6$. Relative error is $0.5\,\%$ at $j=3$ and drops to $0.007\,\%$.

fields.result: Constructs transversal distributed logical fanout and global controlled-$Z$ ($GCZ$) operations across encoded code blocks to minimize non-local communication and entanglement overhead.
fields.question: How can logical fanout operations across remote nodes in distributed quantum computers be implemented fault-tolerantly with reduced non-local communication overhead?
fields.limits: Theoretical and architectural analysis; illustrated specifically on Bivariate Bicycle code blocks.

fields.result: Even-distance Generalized Superfast Encoding maintains constant stabilizer weights of 4 or 6, exhibiting a quantum memory pseudo-threshold crossing near physical depolarizing error rate $p \approx 4\times 10^{-3}$.
fields.question: Can a fermion-to-qubit mapping achieve fault-tolerant quantum memory with threshold-like error suppression under circuit-level noise?
fields.prior: Generalized Superfast Encoding was restricted to error detection or odd-distance constructions with weight-6 stabilizers (Brown et al. 2024), with no fault-tolerant quantum memory threshold observed.
fields.limits: Circuit-level depolarizing noise simulations only; evaluated on two code instances ($[[48,8,6]]$ and $[[64,8,8]]$); requires $N > d$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Logical error rate per round per logical qubit versus physical depolarizing error rate $p$ , for the $[\![48,8,6]\!]$ and $[\![64,8,8]\!]$ even-weight GSE codes, decoded with Relay-BP using AlphaSyndrome-scheduled syndrome extraction. Solid curves are log-log power-law fits to each code’s data. The dashed line is the unencoded (physical) error rate for reference. The higher-distance code suppresses logical error more strongly at low $p$ with the two curves approaching each other near $p\approx 4\times 10^{-3}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate per round per logical qubit versus physical error rate $p$. The $[[64,8,8]]$ code suppresses errors faster than the $[[48,8,6]]$ code below their projected crossing point near $p \approx 4\times 10^{-3}$.

fields.result: Asymmetric $(5,3)$ quantum parity code with 15 physical qubits matches the optimization performance of the symmetric $(5,5)$ code requiring 25 qubits because QAOA objective degrades significantly more under bit flips than phase flips.
fields.question: How do asymmetric bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise channels affect QAOA performance across different circuit decompositions, and can asymmetric quantum error correction exploit this asymmetry?
fields.limits: Simulated on a 6-qubit flight-gate assignment problem; syndrome extraction circuit noise and gate-level QEC fault-tolerance overhead not directly modeled in the QEC evaluation.
tools: Layer-level and gate-level Pauli noise models
fields.figure_caption: Figure 9: The performance of the QAOA algorithm when using different sizes of the outer and inner repetition code of the quantum parity code, $(m_{1},m_{2})$ . The lower $\Delta$ the better. The shown plot corresponds to layer level noise for $d=2$ layers and similar plots can be drawn for the other cases considered above. The (5, 5) code beats the standard 9-qubit Shor code (3, 3) , but due to the asymmetric effect of the noise on the cost function, the (5, 3) code suffices to achieve the same results. Lines only guide the eye. The visible numerical inaccuracies are inherited from our numerical simulation, see section IV.3 .
fields.figure_gloss: Residual cost deviation $\Delta$ plotted against physical error probability $p$ under $d=2$ layer-level noise for uncoded QAOA and various quantum parity code configurations $(n_1,n_2)$.

fields.result: Solving the ECDLP on $\mathtt{secp256k1}$ requires 19,397 physical trapped-ion qubits and 25.7 days for a 63% success probability per attempt, executing $40\cdot 10^6$ Toffoli gates over 1457 logical qubits.
fields.question: How many physical qubits and how much runtime does a fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computer need to compute 256-bit elliptic curve discrete logarithms under realistic noise, transport, and loss constraints?
fields.prior: Prior trapped-ion estimates required 1.2 million to 9.4 million physical qubits; recent generic-architecture estimates needed $60\cdot 10^6$ Toffolis (Schrottenloher 2026).
fields.limits: Assumes physical two-qubit gate error rate $p = 10^{-4}$, single-qubit error rate $10^{-5}$, swap-loss with $p_{\mathrm{leak}} = p/10$ and $p_{\mathrm{loss}} = p/1000$. Success probability lower-bounded assuming all 69 memory blocks remain active throughout full runtime.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5 : Full-scale $\mathtt{secp256k1}$ device. Purple blocks are magic-state factories required for $\mathrm{CCZ}$ state generation, green blocks are memory blocks, orange blocks are cat-state factories, and blue blocks are Bell-state bundles for LM2 measurements. Each group of four orange blocks forms a mobile cat-state bundle pair. The two cyan sites inside each magic-factory group are local six-qubit C6 Bell-state sources. The cobalt and crimson blocks are reserved for two Logical CliNR instances used for Clifford-frame clearing. The small gray box attached to each code block is its local ion reservoir, while the full loading reservoir runs along the right edge of the device.
fields.figure_gloss: Physical layout of the 19,397-qubit $\mathtt{secp256k1}$ processor, showing 69 memory blocks, 4 CCZ magic-state factories, edge-packed cat-state factories, and Bell-state routing channels.

fields.result: Compiling Parity Twine to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits reduces the physical exchange-pulse count by more than 22% for QFT and up to 34% for QAOA compared to baseline compilation schemes.
fields.question: How do algorithmic benchmarks and simulation routines scale from NISQ to fault-tolerance when mapped directly to physical exchange-pulse sequences on exchange-only spin qubit QPUs?
fields.limits: Analytical and numerical compilation models; assumes single-pulse error rates $p \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-4}$, readout error $p_m \approx 0.01$, and $T_2 \approx 19.3\ \mu\text{s}$.
tools: surface code QEC / lattice surgery error modeling
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: QFT resource estimate. (a) Pulse count scaling comparing linear Parity Twine QFT (red) with the reference Fowler QFT implementation (blue) as a function of device length $L$ . Both implementations scale quadratically. The inset shows the pulse count ratio of Twine/Fowler with more than 22% asymptotic reduction in pulse count for Parity Twine QFT. (b) Circuit depth scaling comparing both QFT implementations for increasing exclusion radii $r$ . (c) Depth ratio of Twine/Fowler indicating more than 50% reduction for parallel pulse operation while the reduction is less pronounced for finite exclusion radii.

fields.result: Ancilla-mediated inter-block logical $R_{ZZ}$ gate enables multi-block $[[4,2,2]]$ error detection for QAOA Max-Cut. Encoded circuits maintain higher ground-state probability than unencoded baselines up to noise rate $p = 0.03$ under grid-routed two-qubit depolarizing noise and up to $p = 0.04$ with all-to-all connectivity.
fields.question: How can multi-block $[[4,2,2]]$ error detection be implemented for QAOA Max-Cut circuits using non-transversal inter-block two-qubit rotations?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation on a single 4-vertex cycle graph $C_4$. Post-selection acceptance rate drops exponentially with circuit depth and error rates.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Post-selection rate (left) and ground state probability of post-selected samples (right) as a function of noise strength $p$ , for single-qubit (top) and two-qubit (bottom) depolarizing noise. Line colour denotes encoding: orange for the [[4,2,2]]-encoded circuit, blue for the unencoded baseline. Line style denotes topology: solid for the all-to-all connectivity, dashed for the grid-routed circuit. Shaded bands represent $\pm 1$ standard deviation across the 10 experimental runs.
fields.figure_gloss: Post-selection rate (left) and post-selected ground-state probability (right) versus noise error probability $p$ for single-qubit (top) and two-qubit (bottom) depolarizing noise channels under all-to-all and grid-routed topologies.

fields.result: Weight-8 bivariate bicycle codes yield $[[144,6,d\ge 15]]$, $[[144,10,12]]$, $[[144,16,10]]$, and $[[72,14,8]]$ with $kd^2/n=12.44$. All have exact even dimension $k=2\dim R/(A,B)$ and $d_X=d_Z$.
fields.question: Can bivariate bicycle codes with weight-8 checks be constructed and certified systematically to surpass the $(n,k,d)$ performance of standard weight-6 bivariate bicycle codes?
fields.prior: Flagship weight-6 bivariate bicycle code reached $[[144,12,12]]$ with $kd^2/n=12$, and length-72 reference was $[[72,12,6]]$ with $kd^2/n=6$ (Bravyi et al. 2024).
fields.limits: Circuit-level memory simulations assume gate-level bit-flip noise over 6 rounds without flag fault-tolerance, incurring deeper depth-10 syndrome circuits and thickness 3 embeddings.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Circuit-level BP-OSD memory experiment (gate-level bit-flip noise, rounds $=6$ ): logical error rate $p_{L}$ vs. physical error rate $p$ . The weight- $6$ BB references (black/gray, dashed) attain higher pseudo-thresholds ( $\approx 0.4\%$ , $0.2\%$ ) than our weight- $8$ codes (red/orange, $\approx 0.1\%$ ), illustrating the threshold-for-parameters trade-off.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate $p_L$ versus physical error rate $p$ in a 6-round circuit-level memory experiment with BP-OSD decoding. Weight-8 codes exhibit a pseudo-threshold of $\approx 0.1\%$, compared to $\approx 0.4\%$ and $\approx 0.2\%$ for weight-6 reference codes.

fields.result: Grover search implemented in a bosonic mode resolves 11 frequency candidates with 2.40 bits of extracted mutual information at $m=2$ sensing iterations across a Hilbert space exceeding 128 photons.
fields.question: Can the computational advantage of quantum algorithms be directly converted into an advantage for quantum frequency sensing using an unknown physical signal as an oracle?
fields.prior: Classical sequential search resolves $N=3$ candidates with 1.58 bits of mutual information for $m=2$ iterations.
fields.limits: Known signal amplitude and duration; non-uniform Fock distribution in initial coherent states causing over- or under-rotation; cavity and qubit dissipation; cavity nonlinearities.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Results of Grover-enhanced sensing. a-c , Experimental cavity photon-number distributions versus input signal frequency, for one-, two-, and three-iteration Grover sequences, respectively. The optimal initial coherent-state sizes are $|\alpha|^{2}\approx 4$ , $15$ , and $22$ , respectively. Columns correspond to different probe frequencies, and the vertical axis within each column indicates the population distribution of cavity photon states after the Grover sequence. A strong correlation is observed between the input signal and the final cavity state. d , Extracted MI from experiment data (green dots), compared with simulation results (black cross), the classical sequential-search bound (orange), and the Grover protocol in this work (blue). For a given number of sensing iterations, the Grover-enhanced approach yields higher MI than the sequential scheme. e , Number of resolvable candidate frequencies at maximum MI versus sensing iterations, representing the sensing bandwidth. The Grover-enhanced approach outperforms the sequential scheme by resolving a larger set of frequencies.
fields.figure_gloss: Measured cavity photon-number populations versus candidate signal frequencies for 1, 2, and 3 Grover iterations, showing extracted mutual information and resolvable candidate frequencies compared to sequential search.

fields.result: Multistep repeat-until-success computation guided by intermediate ancillary POVM measurements reduces qubit count and unitary operations polynomially compared to deferred end-of-circuit measurements, achieving total success probability $P_{\text{succ}} > \frac{1}{2}(1 + 1/e)$.
fields.question: Can intermediate ancillary measurements be leveraged in a multistep state-evolution path to reduce quantum computing resources relative to deferred-measurement circuits?
fields.prior: Deferred measurement requires $m$ control qubits and scales runtime as $\prod_{k=1}^m 1/p_k$, leading to an exponential decrease in success probability over $m$ steps.
fields.limits: Requires state overlap $d_k = |\langle\varphi^{(k-1)}|\varphi^{(k)}\rangle|$ and spectral gap $\Delta$ to be polynomially large, with evolution parameter $t_0 = \pi / (2c d)$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Quantum circuit for the RUS-POVM computation process. The circuit in the dashed square can be run repeatedly.
fields.figure_gloss: Quantum circuit schematic for an $m$-step repeat-until-success POVM computation on $n$ working qubits with one ancillary qubit, showing the repeated unit loop.

fields.result: Analytic Rabi sequence approximates degree-$R$ continuous-variable polynomial phase gates $e^{iTp(\hat{X})}$ over Fock subspace $\mathcal{H}_n$ with total interaction time $T_{\mathrm{tot}} = O(\log^{(R-1)/2+o(1)}(1/\varepsilon))$, matching the proven lower bound $\Omega(\log^{(R-1)/2}(1/\varepsilon))$.
fields.question: Can continuous-variable non-Gaussian polynomial phase gates be synthesized via linear qubit-oscillator Rabi control with polylogarithmic total interaction time in the inverse target error $1/\varepsilon$?
fields.prior: Fourier-Trotter approaches require sequence length $O(1/\varepsilon)$ to achieve target error $\varepsilon$.
fields.limits: Applies to input states within fixed finite Fock subspace $\mathcal{H}_n = \operatorname{span}\{\lvert 0\rangle,\dots,\lvert n\rangle\}$; exact synthesis is impossible for finite same-quadrature Rabi sequences.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Finite-resource convergence for representative CV evolutions. The curves show the numerical implementation errors as functions of the total Rabi interaction time $T_{\mathrm{tot}}$ for the cubic phase gate $e^{i\hat{X}^{3}}$ , the rotation $e^{i(\hat{X}^{2}+\hat{P}^{2})}$ , and the double-well evolution $e^{i(\hat{X}^{4}-\hat{X}^{2})}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Approximation error as a function of total Rabi interaction time $T_{\mathrm{tot}}$ for representative continuous-variable phase evolutions.

fields.result: Constructed an end-to-end quantum algorithm for the von Neumann equation with polynomial complexity in dimension $d$ and resource bounds containing no negative powers of the semiclassical parameter $\varepsilon$. Evaluated physical observables uniformly across $\varepsilon \in [10^{-4}, 1]$ with observable error $E_{\rm obs} \le 6.8126 \times 10^{-7}$ under fixed grid parameters.
fields.question: How can quantum dynamics in the semiclassical regime $\varepsilon \ll 1$ be simulated on a quantum computer without spatial mesh and query constraints scaling inversely with $\varepsilon$?
fields.prior: Standard spatial spectral methods and wave-function representations require spatial mesh $h = O(\varepsilon)$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-d})$ spatial unknowns due to the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem; Gaussian wave-packet methods require $h = O(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ and cost $O(\varepsilon^{-d/2})$ per step.
fields.limits: Applies to smooth physical observables (pairing with $L^2_{x,y}$ windows) rather than full density matrix state reconstruction; requires uniform regularity of the density operator in Weyl variables.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Observable accuracy against an independent reference. (a) Joint refinement for $\varepsilon=1,10^{-1},10^{-4}$ . (b) A single choice $(M,K,Q)=(256,36,16)$ gives $E_{\rm obs}<10^{-5}$ for all nine tested values of $\varepsilon$ . The dashed line marks the prescribed tolerance.
fields.figure_gloss: Observable error $E_{\rm obs}$ as a function of grid refinement parameters and across nine values of $\varepsilon$ from $10^{-4}$ to $1$, demonstrating $\varepsilon$-uniform convergence below the $10^{-5}$ tolerance with fixed $(M,K,Q)=(256,36,16)$.

fields.result: Approximate compilation reduces the largest 40-qubit Krylov circuit depth from 2413 to 26 and two-qubit gates from 6840 to 74 with 0.941 fidelity, overcoming depolarizing noise stagnation to restore monotonic ground-state energy convergence in Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization.
fields.question: How does hardware noise affect sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization support recovery, and can approximate circuit compilation mitigate the resulting exponential depth penalty?
fields.prior: Uncompressed Qiskit circuits stagnate at an energy error $\Delta E \approx 9 \times 10^{-2}\,t$ due to noise accumulation across increasing Krylov depth.
fields.limits: One-dimensional single-impurity Anderson model with bounded entanglement allowing single-block Trotter compression, evaluated on 20 sites (40 qubits) with 1000 shots per state.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 2: Energy error $\Delta E$ (top) in units of the hopping parameter $t$ and dimension of the classical subspace (bottom) versus Krylov dimension $d$ , for uncompressed (Qiskit) and compressed (Haiqu) circuits, each shown with and without configuration recovery. Samples are taken on ibm_fez with $1000$ shots per Krylov state. The original Qiskit circuits stagnate near $\Delta E\approx 9\times 10^{-2}$ at every depth, dominated by noise, while the number of bitstrings included in the classical subspace keeps growing with $d$ , a direct signature of the invalid samples of Eq. ( 10 ). Approximate compilation restores monotonic convergence toward the reference ground-state energy. Reference ground-state energy is obtained by DMRG.
fields.figure_gloss: Energy error $\Delta E$ (top) and classical subspace dimension (bottom) plotted against Krylov dimension $d$. Uncompressed circuits stagnate near $\Delta E \approx 9 \times 10^{-2}\,t$, while compressed circuits achieve monotonic convergence with smaller classical subspaces.

fields.result: Unified compilation pipeline produces hardware-tailored FTQC resource estimates across three connectivity classes, showing that small-molecule chemistry (trimethylenemethane) requires $\sim 10^4$ physical qubits with runtimes of $10^2\text{ ms}$ (photonic, superconducting) to $10^5\text{ ms}$ (neutral atoms).
fields.question: How can quantum circuits and fault-tolerant architectures be compiled to enable accurate, platform-aware end-to-end resource estimation across distinct physical hardware modalities?
fields.limits: Trotterized phase estimation and simulation; surface-code Clifford + $T$ gate model; physical error rates $p = 10^{-3}$ and $p = 10^{-4}$.

fields.result: Diagonalizing ladder-string-pair (Lasp) operators directly avoids Pauli expansion for electronic Hamiltonian simulation, reducing CX-gate count from 36 to 12 in a 4-index triad and from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ across $O(n)$ ordered triads without introducing Trotter error at the triad level.
fields.question: How can electronic Hamiltonian simulation circuits be constructed and optimized directly from fermionic ladder operators without Pauli expansion?
fields.prior: Standard simulation expands fermionic ladder products into Pauli strings, producing 16 Pauli strings per two-body Lasp operator and $O(n^2)$ CX scaling.
fields.limits: Theoretical circuit construction and gate-count optimization. Systematic optimization for global triad ordering and composition across all index groups left for future work.

fields.result: Emulation of Raman-spectroscopy dynamical structure factor protocol on neutral-atom quantum processors successfully reconstructs magnon excitation dispersions for 1D and 2D transverse-field Ising models with $N$ up to 36 atoms, remaining robust under realistic laser noise and positional disorder.
fields.question: Can programmable neutral-atom quantum processors accurately measure dynamical structure factors in 1D dimerized and 2D non-integrable transverse-field Ising models under realistic experimental noise?
fields.limits: Numerical emulation rather than physical hardware. Assumes paramagnetic regime $h_{x}/J \gg 1$; classical validation accuracy degrades near quantum phase transition ($J/h_{x} = 0.4$). Noise averaging performed over 50 trajectories before Fourier transformation.

fields.result: Optical pulses to trion states restore resonant tunneling in asymmetric double quantum dots via Coulomb compensation, enabling ultrafast orthogonal single-qubit rotations despite suppressed single-electron tunneling.
fields.question: Can optical excitation to trion states enable fast single-qubit operations in semiconductor double quantum dots with suppressed baseline tunneling?
fields.limits: Theoretical model in two dimensions; relies on specific Coulomb compensation of structural asymmetry.

fields.result: Parametric spin control achieves a $\sim 155$ ps Pauli-$X$ gate with average gate fidelity $\ge 99.9\%$ under uncooled GaAs/InAs nuclear-spin noise and trion lifetime $\tau \ge 1.25$ ns using $\sim 44$ GHz acoustic driving.
fields.question: How to achieve fast, universal single-electron spin control in a quantum dot using an acoustic field without being constrained by bare Zeeman resonance and limited rotation axes?
fields.prior: Acousto-optical spin control required resonance with bare Zeeman splitting, was $\sim 290\times$ slower for noise-mitigating gates, and restricted rotation axes (Ref. 31); all-optical Faraday control was $\sim 14\times$ slower.
fields.limits: Numerical simulations; requires $\sim 43.88$ GHz acoustic driving with $2$ meV modulation amplitude ($\,\sim 2\text{--}3\times 10^{-4}$ strain) and trion lifetime $\tau \ge 1.25$ ns for fidelity $\ge 99.9\%$.

fields.result: Parametric gates formulated in the instantaneous eigenbasis describe exchange and nonadiabatic $ZZ$ couplings via the non-Abelian Berry connection, matching exact numerical simulations in large-amplitude regimes where idle-frame models fail.
fields.question: How can strongly driven parametric two-qubit gates using tunable couplers be accurately and compactly modeled beyond conventional idle-frame approximations?
fields.limits: Excitation-number-conserving approximation for leading-order analytical estimates; applied to double-transmon, capacitively shunted double-transmon, and single-transmon couplers with a single flux loop.

fields.result: Two-step analogue protocol prepares the singlet Bell state $|\Psi_{-}\rangle$ using transverse-field Ising controls alone, reaching infidelity of $2\times 10^{-4}$ at $J=1\text{ GHz}$ within $\sim 100\text{ ns}$ to $200\text{ ns}$.
fields.question: Can high-fidelity Bell states be prepared purely via analogue Hamiltonian control in transverse-field Ising architectures?
fields.prior: Gate-based digital Bell-state preparation in superconducting processors takes $\sim 80\text{--}130\text{ ns}$ with infidelity $\sim 10^{-3}$.
fields.limits: Numerical simulations in the computational subspace; open-system environmental decoherence omitted; assumes perfect initial state $|--\rangle$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Achieved infidelity versus the total time, considering the energy to be in GHz units. Circles correspond to the simulated data, with larger sizes indicating larger $J$ values and their colour referring to their $\varepsilon$ value. The crosses and associated error bars indicate the mean and standard deviation over all $J$ values for a given $\varepsilon$ . These are intended as a guide for the eye to highlight the tendency of the data.

fields.result: Dynamical Casimir effect-induced qubit synchronization persists under weak cQED dissipation rates, with pure dephasing acting as the dominant limiting mechanism. High Pearson correlation in strong dissipation reflects classical relaxation to a common state, not quantum synchronization.
fields.question: How robust is dynamical Casimir effect-induced synchronization between superconducting qubits against realistic environmental dissipation and decoherence?
fields.limits: Theoretical and numerical open-quantum-system simulations within the rotating-wave, Born, Markov, and secular approximations under single-mode cavity and two-level transmon approximations.
tools: Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonian with parametric DCE driving
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5 : Pearson correlation coefficient as a function of time for the four dynamical regimes considered. The blue curve corresponds to the unitary evolution, while the red, green, and black curves represent the weak-, intermediate-, and strong-dissipation regimes, respectively. The vertical dashed lines indicate the corresponding decoherence times whenever they lie within the simulated time window. The parameters are $\kappa=\gamma=0.0002g$ and $\Gamma=0.004g$ for the weak regime, $\kappa=\gamma=0.0005g$ and $\Gamma=0.01g$ for the intermediate regime, and $\kappa=\gamma=0.01g$ and $\Gamma=0.1g$ for the strong regime.
fields.figure_gloss: Pearson correlation coefficient plotted against time for unitary, weak-, intermediate-, and strong-dissipation regimes. Weak dissipation preserves unitary synchronization behavior, while strong dissipation exhibits high Pearson correlation driven by classical relaxation.

fields.result: Brickwork dual-unitary circuits improve quantum reservoir memory and nonlinear capacity at short-to-moderate delay, while increasing the readout measurement variance to mitigate finite-shot exponential concentration.
fields.question: How does dual-unitarity in brickwork quantum circuits affect reservoir computing performance, memory, nonlinearity, and resilience to exponential concentration?
fields.limits: Numerical simulations on 1D spin chains of sizes up to $L=7$ qubits. Constant prefactor protection rather than altered exponential scaling of finite-shot noise.

( 28 )], parity check [(c), (d) – Eq. ( 29 )], sine-square [(e), (f) – Eq. ( 31 )], MGTS [(g), (h) – Eq. ( 32 )] and NARMA( $\tau+3$ ) [(i), (j) – Eq. ( 30 )] tasks. fields.result: Solid-state quantum platforms share a common structure-coherence bottleneck driven by light elements and defects in disordered or buried interfaces, with no platform yet quantitatively connecting a specific atomic structure directly to measured coherence.
fields.question: What shared material constraints limit performance across solid-state quantum platforms and how can characterization methodologies address them?
fields.limits: Focuses on solid-state platforms (superconducting qubits, color centers, quantum photonics, 2D heterostructures); proxy metrics remain unvalidated across multi-facility fabrication.

fields.result: Single-zone transversal-gate layout and loss-aware compilation cut accumulated atom loss per syndrome-extraction round by $1.25\times$ on average (up to $2.15\times$) and CX routing time by up to $8.5\times$, reducing logical error rates by up to $212.4\times$ on 100-qubit circuits.
fields.question: How can physical layout, compilation, and decoding be co-designed to mitigate atom loss across fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum computing architectures?
fields.prior: ZAC zoned rearrangement compiler on separate storage/entangling architectures had $2.9\times$ longer average CX routing times ($8.4\times$ longer on 32-qubit Ising) and higher logical error rates (e.g. $1.39\times 10^{-6}$ vs $6.56\times 10^{-9}$ on 100-qubit Heisenberg).
fields.limits: Circuit-level numerical simulations under rotated surface codes. Relies on continuous mid-circuit atom reloading rates of $2.24\times 10^4$ to $1.53\times 10^7\text{ atoms/s}$, which exceeds current extraction demonstrations by orders of magnitude.

fields.figure_gloss: CX-routing time in milliseconds (log scale) across benchmark circuits comparing the zoned baseline against the loss-aware layout with 4 AODs. Shorter times reflect higher gate parallelism and fewer trap handoffs.

fields.result: Demonstrated two-photon interference with raw visibility of 82% between remote $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ color centers in separate cryostats over a 26-day campaign. Achieved spectral narrowing below 60 MHz and overlap across 19 randomly selected centers in industrial-grade SiC p-i-n diodes requiring bias readjustment only every 8.4 hours.
fields.question: Can silicon vacancy centers in industrial-grade silicon carbide devices provide stable, high-visibility two-photon interference across remote nodes over long timescales?
fields.limits: Measured between two cryostats separated by 2 meters. Electrical tuning requires bias readjustment every 8.4 hours.

p-i-n diodes with electrical voltage biasing
two separate cryostat setups spaced by 2 m

fields.result: Compiled quantum-classical workloads across heterogeneous targets directly from Python, reaching median steady-state round-trip latencies over RoCE v2 of 2.305 μs from an FPGA controller to an AMD CPU and 4.5 μs to an AMD MI210 GPU.
fields.question: Can high-level Python quantum programming frameworks be compiled directly onto heterogeneous distributed hardware to achieve microsecond-scale co-processing latencies for real-time quantum error correction?
fields.limits: Round 0 exhibits higher latency (4.640 μs on CPU, 9.270 μs on GPU) due to one-time endpoint initialization. Evaluated on AMD hardware over local RoCE v2 connections.

fields.result: Entangled non-Clifford magic states $|CS\rangle=CS|++\rangle$ are cultivated directly with no accepted closed-boundary logical-failure mechanisms through fault order two and an operation-count reduction of 34.8% at $p=5\times 10^{-4}$ and 37.3% at $p=10^{-3}$ via optimized $d=5\rightarrow 13$ surface-code expansion.

fields.prior: Indirect synthesis of $|CS\rangle$ from three logical $|T\rangle$ states via a Clifford+$T$ circuit.
fields.limits: Evaluated under a uniform active-location stochastic-Pauli noise model omitting idle memory errors, leakage, coherent errors, and routing. Evaluated for $p=10^{-4}$ to $10^{-3}$; active locations count operations with early-abort accounting rather than spacetime volume.

fields.result: Gated belief propagation pre-decoding reduces Tesseract $\text{A}^{*}$ node expansions by $\approx 15\times$ at physical error rate $p = 0.05$ (peak reduction 14.79 at $p_{\mathrm{gated}} = 0.1$, $\tau = 0.0025$) for the $[[126, 12, d < 11]]$ code, and by $8.8\times$ for the $[[72, 12, 6]]$ bivariate bicycle code, while matching standalone Tesseract logical error rates.
fields.question: Can pre-processing syndromes with belief propagation accelerate $\text{A}^{*}$-based Tesseract search without degrading logical error rates in QLDPC codes?
fields.prior: Stand-alone Tesseract $\text{A}^{*}$ search decoder and un-gated BP-Tesseract hybrid.

fields.result: Constructing magic-state cultivation records as binary linear codes over Clifford parities saturates the Plotkin bound, resolving distance-four $|CS\rangle$ in 6 logical measurements and $|CCZ\rangle$ in 7 measurements, while reducing active locations in compiled Steane $|CS\rangle$ cultivation by 26.6%.
fields.question: How to minimize the classical measurement record length and logical redundancy required to cultivate multiqubit non-Clifford resource states without sacrificing fault tolerance?
fields.prior: Independent repetition required 8 logical measurements for distance-four $|CS\rangle$ and 12 logical measurements for distance-four $|CCZ\rangle$.
fields.limits: Applies strictly to record-only classical errors; does not eliminate data-coupled fault mechanisms occurring inside measurement gadgets. Validated with 5000 shots per point without full-factory downstream decoder modeling.

fields.result: Depth-independent upper bound on local depolarizing noise for fermionic quantum computation is $p=(8-2\sqrt{6})/5 \approx 62\%$ (0.6202). Above this depolarizing rate, all 2-qubit parity-preserving non-Gaussian gates map into convex Gaussian channels.
fields.question: What is the upper bound on local depolarizing noise after which fault-tolerant fermionic quantum computing with matchgates and non-Gaussian gates becomes impossible?
fields.prior: Local depolarizing noise limit was $\approx 45\%$ for Clifford + T circuits (Bravyi, Browne, Calpin, Campbell, Gosset, Howard 2016).
fields.limits: Restricted to 2-qubit parity-preserving gates followed by local depolarizing noise, assuming noise-free matchgates and Gaussian input states.

fields.result: Unifies quantum linear algebra via a standardized five-primitive pipeline (block-encoding, qubitization, QSP, QSVT, and GQSP) and provides a decision workflow matching operator structure to polynomial synthesis.
fields.question: How can the parallel frameworks of QSVT and GQSP be unified into a systematic algorithm design workflow for matrix transformations?
fields.limits: GQSP extension to the singular value domain for arbitrary matrices remains open; synthesis relies on efficient block-encoding availability and complementary polynomial finding.

fields.result: Iterative refinement using fixed-precision QLSA and tomography yields classical solutions to $Ax=b$ with error $\|x-A^{-1}b\|\le\epsilon$ in $\mathcal{O}(\log(\|b\|\kappa_A/\epsilon))$ iterations, reducing precision dependence from polynomial to polylogarithmic.
fields.question: How can one extract high-precision classical solutions from quantum linear system algorithms combined with tomography without suffering polynomial overhead in the target accuracy?
fields.prior: Combining QLSA with quantum state tomography had polynomial dependence on the target inverse precision $1/\epsilon$ to reconstruct classical vectors.
fields.limits: Fixed per-iteration quantum precision $\xi$ must be strictly smaller than $1/\kappa_A$; requires classical matrix-vector residual computation at each step.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Cumulative circuit depth required to reach the residual threshold $\|Ax-b\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon$ , with and without iterative refinement. Solid curves with filled markers are measured transpiled depths: HHL + IR at the target $\varepsilon=10^{-6}$ , and direct HHL at the relaxed threshold $\varepsilon=10^{-2}$ , for which the required QPE register sizes are directly compilable. The dashed curve with hollow markers is the extrapolated direct-HHL depth at $\varepsilon=10^{-6}$ , obtained from a fitted depth model; the shaded band is the fit’s 95% prediction interval. Boxed labels indicate the required QPE register size $q$ on each plateau.
fields.figure_gloss: Condition number $\kappa_A$ versus cumulative transpiled circuit depth to achieve target residual norm $\varepsilon$. Iterative refinement maintains near-constant cumulative depth around $10^4$ at $\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$, avoiding the $10^{10}\text{--}10^{11}$ depth required by direct HHL.

fields.result: Decomposing quantum dynamics onto a Dynamic Observable Subspace (DOS) gives polynomial-time classical simulation of observable expectation values for circuits with polynomial-dimension dynamic Lie algebras, scaling to hundreds of qubits.
fields.question: How can quantum circuit expectation values and variational dynamics be classically simulated in polynomial time for large qubit counts without barren plateaus?
fields.limits: Polynomial efficiency requires a polynomial-sized DLA or a small induced DOS orbit. Restricted circuits may lack the expressivity to fully span arbitrary Hamiltonian target spaces.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : Liouville von Neumann Dynamics in the Heisenberg Picture. In the skew Heisenberg picture, an observable $iO$ evolves by a Hamiltonian $H(t)=\sum_{k}H_{k}(t)$ in reverse time from $T$ to $0$ to an operator state $iO(0)$ contained inside $\text{orb}_{\mathfrak{g}}^{iO}$ . Then the measurement of $iO$ is associated with $\text{Tr}\left(iO(0)\,\text{proj}_{\mathfrak{g}}^{iO}(i\rho(0))\right)$ in the Heisenberg picture (or $\text{Tr}\left(iO\,\text{proj}_{\mathfrak{g}}^{iO}(i\rho(T))\right)$ in the Schrödinger picture).
fields.figure_gloss: Reverse-time Heisenberg evolution of an observable $iO$ within its dynamic Lie orbit $\text{orb}_{\mathfrak{g}}^{iO}$, enabling expectation value simulation via projection of the initial state.

fields.result: A continuous-time quantum walk driven by a generalized Laplacian $L_\alpha = L + \alpha D$ searches irregular complete bipartite graphs with runtime $t_* = (\pi/2)\sqrt{N_1 B F_- / [k_1(B F_- - 2N_1 N_2)]}$, reaching optimal search time as $|\alpha| \to \infty$.
fields.question: Can a generalized Laplacian quantum walk solve computational search problems faster than standard Laplacian or adjacency matrix walks?
fields.prior: Generalized Laplacian search offered no speedup over adjacency walks on weighted barbell graphs.
fields.limits: Asymptotic regime for large vertex counts $N_1, N_2 \gg 1$; holds for irregular complete bipartite graphs ($N_1 \neq N_2$).
fields.figure_gloss: Success probability plotted against time for searching complete bipartite graphs. Runtime decreases monotonically as $\alpha$ moves toward $-\infty$ when $N_1 > N_2$ or toward $+\infty$ when $N_1 < N_2$.

fields.result: Averaging over a family of approximations via quantum randomized compiling reduces systematic QMC error from $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})$ at negligible extra cost. In path integral Monte Carlo, QDrift replaces Trotter error $\mathcal{O}(L^{3}\beta^{3}/r^{2})$ with $\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{2}\beta^{2}/r)$, eliminating explicit scaling with term count $L$.
fields.question: Can randomized compiling techniques from quantum computing be used to reduce systematic approximation errors and computational costs in classical Quantum Monte Carlo simulations?
fields.prior: Standard QMC uses a single fixed approximation with systematic error $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$ and Trotter error $\mathcal{O}(L^{3}\beta^{3}/r^{2})$.
fields.limits: Suppresses systematic error only; does not reduce statistical sampling variance or resolve the QMC sign problem.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Overview of the randomly compiled QMC (RC-QMC) framework. Standard QMC algorithms estimate an observable $\langle\hat{O}\rangle$ by averaging an estimator function $F(\hat{O},X)$ over a random variable $X$ sampled from a fixed approximate distribution $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$ (see Eq. ( 4 )), incurring systematic error $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$ . RC-QMC instead averages over a collection of approximate distributions $\{\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{j}\}$ weighted by probabilities $p_{j}$ (see Eq. ( 17 )), which suppresses the systematic error to $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})$ at essentially the same computational cost. This improvement is demonstrated in two settings: Randomly Compiled Path Integral Monte Carlo for thermal state estimation, where QDrift replaces the standard Trotter decomposition and eliminates the explicit dependence on the number of Hamiltonian terms, and Randomly Compiled Quantum Trajectories Method for open system dynamics, where randomly corrected Trotterization doubles the effective Trotter order.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic comparing standard QMC (single fixed distribution, $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$ systematic error) against randomly compiled QMC (distribution averaging, $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^2)$ systematic error) across path integral Monte Carlo and quantum trajectory methods.

fields.result: Splitting the Dirac Cellular Automaton evolution into $M$ fractional sub-steps in momentum space breaks the artificial phase-matching symmetry that cancels Zitterbewegung on finite lattices ($c\delta t = \delta x / M$), recovering continuous-time velocity oscillations and entanglement dynamics without increasing spatial register size.
fields.question: How can finite-grid Dirac Cellular Automata simulate continuous-time Dirac dynamics and interference phenomena like Zitterbewegung without requiring an inflated spatial qubit register?
fields.limits: Circuit depth scales with temporal refinement factor $M$, causing accumulated gate error decay at $t > 4$; dynamic QFT circuits are constrained by mid-circuit measurement errors and relaxation times.

(b) and (c) Experimental spacetime probability diagrams, $P(x,t)$ of the initial state $|\Psi(0)\rangle_{c}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0\rangle_{c}+|1\rangle_{c})\otimes|x=0\rangle$ for (b) a massless particle and (c) a massive particle with $m=\pi/4$ . The insets display the corresponding ideal spacetime diagrams. (d) Fidelity of the experimental probability distributions relative to the ideal distributions over time step $t$ for both the massless and massive cases.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots internal Pauli expectation values, entanglement entropy, and spacetime probability distributions $P(x,t)$ across time steps $t$ on ibm_aachen for massless and massive ($m=\pi/4$, $m=\pi/2$) Dirac particles under $M=2$ SDCA.

fields.result: Theoretical design of a quantum random access memory architecture using Rydberg-EIT cross-phase modulation to execute quantum random walks in an $n$-level binary tree, reducing operational query complexity to $\mathcal{O}(n)$.
fields.question: Can a scalable, non-cryogenic photonic quantum RAM be implemented without active geometric phase gates or coherence over exponential qutrit arrays?
fields.prior: Conventional bucket-brigade qRAM required maintaining coherence across $n \times 2^{n}$ active qutrit switches with $\mathcal{O}(n^{-2})$ error tolerances (Giovannetti 2008).
fields.limits: Theoretical proposal; assumes optical depth $\kappa_l L \sim 600$, atom number $N=10^4$, control Rabi frequency $\Omega = 10^6\text{ rad/s}$, and pulse bandwidth $T^{-1} \sim 10^4\text{ s}^{-1}$ below the EIT bandwidth.

The color map shows the phase-to-bandwidth ratio $\mathcal{R}=2\phi_{ll}n_{l}/\delta\omega_{l}$ across optical depth $\kappa_{l}L$ and conditional phase shift $\Phi_{\text{total}}$ .

fields.result: Simulations of a three-qubit CCZ gate with a single Gaussian pulse across the finite-to-strong Rydberg blockade transition achieve a maximum gate fidelity of $99.92\%$, with the symmetric bare $8\times 8$ manifold reduced to an exact $4\times 4$ model.

fields.result: qRAM architecture achieves $\mathcal{O}(n\log(n+m))$ temporal complexity using $\mathcal{O}(n+m)$ phase-encoded photonic walkers in a Rydberg EIT waveguide tree, yielding cumulative routing transmission probability $P_{\text{transmission}}\approx 99.993\%$ at tree depth $n=20$.
fields.question: How to implement a scalable, fault-tolerant qRAM without exponential gate overheads or error-prone active qutrit switches?
fields.prior: Fanout qRAM required exponential gates along $2^n$ paths; Giovannetti bucket-brigade qRAM required $n=\log(N)$ steps across active qutrits with error rates below $\mathcal{O}(n^{-2})$.
fields.limits: Theoretical model and numerical scaling; assumes cold atoms where Doppler broadening is smaller than the spin-relaxation rate, weak probe regime, strict EIT resonance, and ignores independent waveguide transmission losses.

fields.result: Realised linear-optical logical Bell-state measurement using a two-qubit repetition code, reaching a mean success probability of $(70.8\pm 0.4)\%$ and an average measurement discrimination fidelity of $(91.7\pm 0.5)\%$.
fields.question: Can quantum error-correcting codes be used to experimentally demonstrate a logical Bell-state measurement with a success probability exceeding the linear-optical limit without ancillary photons?
fields.prior: Standard static linear-optical Bell-state measurements on dual-rail qubits without ancillary photons are fundamentally limited to a maximum success probability of $50\%$.
fields.limits: Post-selected on four-fold coincidences with background subtraction; repetition code only detects single bit flips rather than providing full error correction.

fields.result: Lifted surgery executes fast, parallel, and addressable logical Pauli measurements on Abelian group algebra QLDPC codes in a single syndrome extraction round. For a $[[90, 8, 10]]$ radial code, it matches the logical performance of standard code surgery while using 10 times fewer syndrome measurement rounds.
fields.question: How can fast, low-time-overhead code surgery be constructed for general Abelian group algebra QLDPC codes without large spatial overheads?
fields.prior: Standard code surgery incurs repeated syndrome extraction rounds scaling with distance $d$, while existing fast surgery approaches require large auxiliary qubit overheads or specialize only to hypergraph product codes.
fields.limits: Restricted to CSS-type (purely $Z$- or purely $X$-type) logical Pauli measurements; benchmarked via numerical circuit-level depolarizing noise simulations.
