fields.result: Every translation-invariant topological Pauli stabilizer code is locally decodable under phenomenological noise with a non-zero threshold, and a 2D fault-tolerant quantum computer can operate using strictly local operations and constant quantum and classical resource density.
fields.question: Can scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation based on topological codes in fewer than four dimensions be implemented using strictly local operations, bounded communication speeds, and constant resource density?
fields.prior: All prior local decoders for two-dimensional topological codes required per-site classical resources scaling at least polylogarithmically with system size, and prior fault-tolerant architectures in $<4$ spatial dimensions required non-local classical computation or communication.
fields.limits: Classical computation and communication components are assumed to be noiseless; phenomenological noise assumes $p$-bounded Pauli and bit-flip errors on data qubits and syndrome measurements.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : A two-dimensional fault-tolerant quantum computer that uses only geometrically local quantum and classical operations, bounded-speed classical communication and computation, and a constant density of quantum and classical resources. Logical operations are performed on a line of surface-code patches decoded by a network of constant-size, noiseless classical processors (local decoders). Each patch is folded along one of its diagonals: stripes indicate spatially overlapping $X$ - and $Z$ -type stabilizers; qubits overlap in pairs, except along the fold. Logical $H$ gates are implemented fold-transversally, and logical CNOT gates between neighboring patches are implemented via lattice surgery. State injection, stabilizer-state preparation, and transversal readout are used to complete this gate set to a universal set of fault-tolerant primitives. The local decoders run continuously during all of these primitives. The patches lie along the boundary of a noiseless, local, two-dimensional classical computer whose only functions are to control which primitive each patch executes at each step of the quantum program and to receive decoded logical measurement outcomes. This classical computer is never used for decoding.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of the 2D local fault-tolerant quantum architecture, showing a 1D array of folded surface-code patches decoded on-chip by constant-density classical cellular automata alongside a local 2D classical program-control computer.

fields.result: Unified algorithm-to-execution framework reduces fault-tolerant space-time volume up to $241.5\times$ via non-Clifford supply co-design and cuts routed latency across twenty benchmark circuits.
fields.question: How can circuit scheduling, spatial patch layout, and non-Clifford resource supply be coordinated to minimize physical execution overhead in surface-code quantum computing?
fields.limits: Modeled on surface-code simulations with fixed physical error rate $p_{\mathrm{phys}}=10^{-3}$ or $10^{-4}$ and $500~\mathrm{ns}$ stabilizer rounds; excludes repetitions for algorithmic success probability.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Three sources of physical-resource variation across twenty benchmark circuits. Panels (a) and (b) use the compact-block reporting baseline of the ordinary end-to-end resource estimator; panel (c) uses a matched comparison with a standardized fast-block layout to isolate spatial-organization effects. (a) Fraction of the total modeled physical-qubit footprint assigned to data blocks, $T$ -state factories, and direct- $R_{z}$ rotation patches. Each stacked bar is normalized to the circuit’s total footprint, so the panel shows which resource component occupies the processor. Data blocks are the largest component for 17 of the 20 circuits, whereas $T$ -state factories dominate the other three; no circuit is direct-rotation dominated. (b) Space–time-volume advantage of the optimized hybrid rotation policy over an all-synthesis policy in which every nonzero residual rotation is synthesized into Clifford+ $T$ . The plotted reduction factor is $G_{\rm hyb}=V_{\mathrm{all\text{-}synthesis}}/V_{\mathrm{optimized\ hybrid}}$ ; $G_{\rm hyb}=1$ means no modeled benefit. Thirteen circuits show a reduction of at least $10\times$ , the median reduction is $23.8\times$ , and the maximum is $241.5\times$ for QAOA amplitude amplification. These are model-based space–time reductions under the stated direct-rotation calibration, not experimental speedups. (c) Physical-qubit and routed-runtime ratios of each circuit-specific optimized layout relative to its matched standardized fast-block layout, $Q_{O}/Q_{F}$ and $t_{O}/t_{F}$ . The code distance, non-Clifford strategy, factory fleet, and physical assumptions are held fixed within each pair, so this panel isolates the effect of circuit-specific spatial organization and routing. The dashed equal-volume boundary is $t_{O}/t_{F}=(Q_{O}/Q_{F})^{-1}$ ; points below it have lower space–time volume. All 20 circuit-specific layouts reduce the routed-runtime estimate, and 13 of 20 also reduce space–time volume, showing that layout optimization is effective for a substantial subset of circuits but is workload-dependent rather than universal.
fields.figure_gloss: Space-time volume and latency variations across twenty benchmark circuits comparing standard baseline layouts and synthesis against circuit-specific layouts and optimized non-Clifford allocations.

fields.result: Two zero-overhead walking honeycomb Floquet code circuits remove leakage periodically while maintaining code distance to Pauli errors. They correct as many leakage errors as Pauli errors for two noise models and outperform the same-distance walking surface code in the finite-error-rate waterfall regime.
fields.question: Can leakage reduction units be integrated into honeycomb Floquet code syndrome extraction circuits with zero gate and depth overhead while preserving code distance?
fields.limits: Simulated on toric honeycomb lattices with periodic boundary conditions using minimum-weight perfect matching decoders, uniform leakage probability $p$, and idealized Clifford/leakage channels.
tools: swirling and sliding honeycomb Floquet code circuits
fields.figure_caption: Figure 11: Numerical comparison of the swirling and sliding hFCs with the walking surface code under (i) depolarizing leakage, (ii) tailored leakage, (iii) skip-gate leakage, and (iv) skip-gate leakage with $10\%$ leakage transport. Top panels in (a) show the LER per $d$ rounds of error correction ( $3d$ QEC rounds simulated), where one QEC round corresponds to three check subrounds for the hFC. The bottom panels in (b) show the scaling exponents $\alpha$ of LERs fitted to $\sim p^{\alpha}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate versus physical error rate across code distances for swirling and sliding honeycomb Floquet codes compared against the walking surface code under four leakage noise models.

fields.result: Zeng–Chen–Chuang generalised semi-Clifford conjecture is false: an explicit five-qubit gate in $\mathcal{C}_{5}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{4}$ is not generalised semi-Clifford, and its inverse lies outside the entire Clifford hierarchy.
fields.question: Are all quantum gates in the Clifford hierarchy generalised semi-Clifford gates of the form $C_1 \Pi D C_2$?
fields.prior: Held for all third-level gates $\mathcal{C}_3$ for arbitrarily many qubits (Beigi–Shor 2008).
fields.limits: Counterexample constructed at five qubits ($n=5$) and level $k=5$; extends to all $n\geq 5$ and $k\geq 5$ via identity tensors.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: The five-qubit counterexample as a circuit: the first two gates implement the controlled-Clifford gate $\operatorname{ctrl}_{\mathtt{d}}(A)$ ; the last three implement the controlled-Clifford gate $\operatorname{ctrl}_{\mathtt{c}}(B)$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Five-qubit quantum circuit counterexample composed of two-control multiplexed Clifford operations: $\operatorname{ctrl}_{\mathtt{d}}(A)$ followed by $\operatorname{ctrl}_{\mathtt{c}}(B)$.

fields.result: Polynomial-time classical simulations of quantum dynamics are often outpaced by direct quantum hardware execution due to high one-time quantum sampling and shadow post-processing overheads when preparing unknown input states.
fields.question: Whether classically simulable quantum evolutions are in practice more resource-efficient to simulate classically or to execute directly on quantum hardware.
fields.limits: Independent unentangled input copies only (no multi-copy quantum memory); unitaries and observables restricted to efficient classical representations.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Estimated wall-clock time for QS and CS on IonQ Forte, Google Sycamore, and IBM Heron. Here, the runtime corresponds to the total runtime $t_{\rm sim}^{(X)}$ given by Eq. ( 104 ), which sums both the runtime on the quantum and classical hardware. Rows correspond to the three quantum hardware platforms, while all classical operations are assumed to run on the same classical hardware. The horizontal axis denotes the total number of circuit instances $T$ . Columns correspond to ADAPT-VQE, $S_{n}$ -equivariant circuits, and Matchgate circuits with $\kappa=4$ and $6$ , while rows correspond to the three hardware models. Solid lines denote CS and dotted lines QS. Marker shapes indicate the system sizes $n=20,40,80$ . The estimates use the hardware specifications in Table 2 and assume $t_{\rm C}=0.25$ ns per elementary classical operation. For superconducting devices, we include the routing overhead used in the numerical estimate arising from the fixed qubit connectivity. Two-qubit gates acting on disjoint qubits are assumed to be parallelized. Results exceeding the available device size, namely $n>36$ for IonQ Forte and $n>53$ for Google Sycamore, extrapolate the reported hardware specifications and should therefore be interpreted only as scaling estimates.
fields.figure_gloss: Estimated total wall-clock time versus qubit count $n$ for direct quantum simulation and classical simulation across IonQ Forte, Google Sycamore, and IBM Heron architectures.

fields.result: Classical algorithm samples from the optimized random feature distribution within total variation distance $d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon}, \mathcal{D}') \leq \delta$ in runtime $O(D \operatorname{polylog}(G) + \mathbf{q}(\bm{Q}^{(\tau)}) + \mathbf{sq}(\sqrt{\hat{\bm{q}}^{(\rho)}})) \times \widetilde{O}((Q^{(\tau)}_{\max}/\epsilon)^{18}/\delta^{6})$, dequantizing the QSVT-based sampler.
fields.question: Can quantum machine learning algorithms for matrix functions of diagonally weighted matrices be classically dequantized when sampling access is available only to the diagonal factor rather than the composite matrix?
fields.prior: Quantum sampler ran in time $O(D\log(G)\log\log(G) + \mathbf{q}(\bm{Q}^{(\tau)}) + \mathbf{sq}(\sqrt{\hat{\bm{q}}^{(\rho)}})) \times \widetilde{O}((Q^{(\tau)}_{\max}/\epsilon) \operatorname{polylog}(1/\delta))$, while standard classical matrix inversion required time exponential in $D$ ($G^D \times G^D$ matrix).
fields.limits: Runtime scales polynomially as $1/\delta^6$ rather than quantum polylogarithmic dependence $\operatorname{polylog}(1/\delta)$; assumes $\mathrm{SQ}(\bm{D})$ and $\mathrm{Q}(\bm{A})$ oracle access.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Diagonal truncation and small-block computation. Samples from $\mathrm{SQ}(\bm{D})$ identify the heavy coordinates and define the truncated matrix $\widetilde{\bm{D}}$ . The matrix $\widetilde{\bm{D}}\bm{A}\widetilde{\bm{D}}$ is supported on the corresponding principal block, where the matrix function is computed exactly and efficiently.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of the dequantization method: sampling from $\mathrm{SQ}(\bm{D})$ isolates heavy diagonal indices to truncate $\bm{D}$ to $\widetilde{\bm{D}}$, reducing $\gamma\bm{I} + \widetilde{\bm{D}}\bm{A}\widetilde{\bm{D}}$ to a small principal block $\widetilde{\bm{M}}_S$ computed classically.

fields.result: Distributed variational quantum computing protocol deterministically tunes shared Bell-pair entanglement via LOCC with unit success probability ($p_{\mathrm{M}}=1$) and concurrence $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{M}}(\theta)=\cos\theta$, keeping state infidelity below 0.05 across full range.
fields.question: How can entanglement between distributed quantum processing units be tuned continuously and deterministically without the probabilistic losses of filtering or the high Bell-pair consumption of gate teleportation?
fields.limits: Demonstrated on bipartite single-qubit photonic processors; feed-forward conditional operations performed offline rather than in real time; pure-state majorization requires initial entanglement to be equal to or greater than target.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Experimental results of entanglement tuning. (a) Experimentally reconstructed density matrix of a partially entangled state prepared by applying the deterministic transformation in Eq. ( 6 ) to a Bell state, with $\theta=5\pi/18$ . (b) Concurrence and state infidelity of the output states as a function of $\theta$ . Red dots represent experimental data, and the black curve indicates the theoretical prediction. Error bars denote statistical uncertainties estimated via Monte Carlo sampling based on Poissonian photon count distributions.
fields.figure_gloss: Concurrence (top) and state infidelity (bottom) plotted against the tuning angle $\theta$, demonstrating deterministic modulation of entanglement from 1 down to 0 while keeping state infidelity below 0.05.

fields.result: Worst-case block-encoding $T$-count scales as $\Theta(n^2\sqrt{\log(n^4/\varepsilon)})$ for general second-quantized fermionic Hamiltonians and $\Theta(n+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ for bond-dependent Kitaev honeycomb spin Hamiltonians.
fields.question: What is the asymptotically optimal worst-case $T$-count required to construct an $\varepsilon$-approximate block encoding of structured fermionic and spin Hamiltonians?
fields.prior: For fermionic Hamiltonians, upper bound was $O(n^2\sqrt{\log(n^4/\varepsilon)})$ (Liu 2024), but matching lower bounds and spin-Hamiltonian optimal scalings were unknown.
fields.limits: Unitary Clifford$+T$ model without mid-circuit measurements or classical feed-forward. Bounds are worst-case over the full coefficient family and do not exploit specific molecular structure.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : T-gate counts for different chemistry Hamiltonian in second quantization with STO-3G basis, comparing out lower bound (black line) with prior constructions in Ref. [ 3 ] and Qualtran [ 18 ] . The constant factor $\sqrt{48}/24\approx 0.288$ is included for our lower bound. $\epsilon=10^{-5}$ is chosen for all cases.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots $T$-gate count versus number of spin orbitals $n$ for molecular electronic Hamiltonians in STO-3G basis, comparing the theoretical lower bound against existing block-encoding implementations.

fields.result: Extending quantum neural networks to linear combinations of completely positive trace-preserving maps via sampling and classical post-processing mitigates hardware noise and recovers ground-state energy curves under depolarizing noise.
fields.question: Can quantum neural networks enlarge their optimization space beyond completely positive trace-preserving maps using randomized sampling and classical post-processing to boost expressivity and noise robustness?
fields.prior: Standard QNNs and VQEs are restricted to a single parametric completely positive map ($\|\bm{c}\|_{1}=1$), yielding inaccurate energies under circuit noise.
fields.limits: Demonstrated in numerical simulations under depolarizing noise ($p=0.01$ single-qubit, $p=0.02$ two-qubit), depth $d=5$, and Chebyshev truncation $K=100$.
fields.figure_caption: Fig 7: Ground state energy of the molecule $\rm HeH^{+}$ estimated via the VVQE algorithm. The dashed line shows the exact values of the ground state energy as a function of the nuclear separation. The orange stars and red triangles show the energy values found by our VVQE algorithm for different values of the sampling budgets, set to $\gamma=1.5$ and $\gamma=2.5$ , respectively. The light blue squares show the energies computed with the conventional VQE, which is equivalent to a VVQE with unit budget $\gamma=1$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Calculated ground state energy of $\rm HeH^{+}$ plotted against nuclear separation. Increasing the sampling budget from standard VQE ($\gamma=1$) to VVQE with $\gamma=1.5$ and $\gamma=2.5$ pulls noisy estimates back to the exact error-free curve.

fields.result: Extracts full $2^N$ eigenenergies of an $N$-site transverse-field Ising model and the $N$ single-particle energies of its mapped Kitaev chain via stroboscopic DQC1 readout on a single control spin.
fields.question: How can the full spectrum and topological crossover of a simulated Kitaev chain be extracted in quantum-dot spin qubit arrays lacking multi-qubit simultaneous readout?
fields.limits: Requires simulation time $T_{\mathrm{tot}} > 2\pi / \delta\epsilon_{\min}$ and gate infidelity $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{gate}} < \min[1 / (N(J+h)T_{\mathrm{tot}}), \delta\epsilon_{\min}^2 / (N h^2)]$; demonstrated numerically for $N=6$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Simulations for $N=6$ : (a) Expectation value of $\sigma_{x}$ at stroboscopic times $t=nT$ for $h=0.25J$ and $h=1.25J$ , averaged over $10^{3}$ noise realizations. The simulations were performed with $J=2\pi\times 50$ kHz, $T_{2}^{*}=30$ $\mu$ s, and $T=500$ ns, corresponding to a total simulation time of $T_{\mathrm{tot}}=250$ $\mu$ s. (b) Single-particle spectrum of the Kitaev chain as a function of $h/J$ , illustrating the splitting of the nearly degenerate ground state as the strength $h$ of the transverse field (equivalently, chemical potential) is increased. The values of $h/J$ used in (c) and (d) are indicated by vertical dashed red and blue lines, respectively. (c) Spectrum $|S(\omega)|$ of the postprocessed qubit measurement outcomes for $h/J=0.25$ , corresponding to the topological regime of the Kitaev chain, as a function of both $\omega/J$ (bottom axis) and $\omega T$ (top axis). The spectrum was calculated using a fast Fourier transform of the simulated coherence data and has been normalized so that $|S(\omega=0)|=1$ for $S(t)=1$ . (d) Spectrum $|S(\omega)|$ for $h/J=1.25$ , corresponding to the trivial regime.
fields.figure_gloss: Stroboscopic control-qubit expectation value vs time, showing resolution of single-particle Kitaev spectrum across trivial and topological regimes under $1/f$ noise.

fields.result: Tying physical-noise strength to Trotter step size as $\lambda(s)=c(sT)^{p+1}$ aligns physical and algorithmic errors at order $s^p$, letting a single 1D Richardson extrapolation replace 2D grid extrapolation with provable commutator-scaling resource overhead.
fields.question: Can joint extrapolation along a single coupled path simultaneously eliminate algorithmic Trotter bias and hardware noise while preserving provable commutator scaling?
fields.prior: Sequential/2D extrapolation requiring an $m \times m'$ grid of circuit evaluations with independent Trotter and zero-noise fits.
fields.limits: Requires noise strengths above the intrinsic device-noise floor; assumes local Hamiltonians with local Lindbladian noise.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : Coupled extrapolation path as a one-dimensional replacement for a two-dimensional Richardson grid. The horizontal coordinate $s$ is the Trotter step size, the vertical coordinate $\lambda$ is a tunable physical-noise strength, and the black star marks the ideal target limit $(s,\lambda)=(0,0)$ . (a) A conventional two-axis construction samples an $m\times m^{\prime}$ rectangular grid, where $m$ and $m^{\prime}$ denote the Richardson node counts along the step-size and noise-strength axes: one first extrapolates each fixed- $s$ column to zero noise, shown by the cyan diamonds, and then extrapolates those zero-noise estimates toward $s=0$ . (b) The coupled construction instead samples only $m$ paired Richardson nodes on a single path. For the schematic first-order case shown here, the per-layer noise strength is chosen as $\lambda(s)=c(sT)^{2}$ , where $T$ is the total simulated time and $c$ sets the noise scale. This matches the noise correction to the order- $(sT)^{2}$ Trotter error within each step, so both corrections enter at order $s$ over the full evolution at fixed $T$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Comparison of error-mitigation paths on the step size $s$ vs noise strength $\lambda$ plane: 2D rectangular Richardson grid needing independent zero-noise and Trotter extrapolations versus coupled 1D path $\lambda(s)=c(sT)^{p+1}$ reaching $(0,0)$ in a single fit.

fields.result: Stationary current across a tight-binding chain coupled to boundary Markovian reservoirs is derived analytically for arbitrary on-site dephasing $\kappa$. At $\kappa = 0$, inter-site currents follow an asymmetric Laplace distribution with covariance $\mathrm{cov}(\hat{\mathcal{I}}_{\ell}, \hat{\mathcal{I}}_{\ell+1}) = I_{\mathrm{st}}^2 / 2$ and zero covariance for separation $|\ell - \ell'| \geq 2$.
fields.question: What are the exact stationary current, site populations, and current fluctuation distributions in a boundary-driven tight-binding chain with dephasing?
fields.limits: Non-interacting particles (bosons or fermions). Full many-body characteristic function and current distributions derived specifically for bosons in the absence of dephasing ($\kappa = 0$).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Distribution for the dataset generated from the stochastic differential equations ( 36 ) – bins, and the analytic distributions Eqs. 31 , 32 and 33 – red solid lines. The parameters are $\bar{n}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\rm L}}=100$ , $\bar{n}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\rm R}}=1$ , $\gamma_{\scriptscriptstyle{\rm L}}=\gamma_{\scriptscriptstyle{\rm R}}=0.5$ , $L=4$ and $J=1$ . The number of samples is 8800.
fields.figure_gloss: Probability distribution of bond and boundary currents plotted against analytical predictions (red curves) from stochastic simulations (bins) for $\kappa=0$.

fields.result: Misleading convergence in self-consistent boson-exchange schemes (TRILEX, SBE, MBE) is caused solely by algorithmic iteration instability—where Jacobian eigenvalues exceed unity—rather than fundamental multivaluedness of the Luttinger–Ward functional. Inverting the unstable Jacobian eigendirections stabilizes convergence to exact physical solutions across strong-coupling regimes and through vertex divergences.
fields.question: What causes self-consistent diagrammatic boson-exchange algorithms to converge to unphysical fixed points at intermediate-to-strong electronic coupling, and how can they be stabilized?
fields.limits: Demonstrated on exactly solvable local models (Hubbard atom and zero-point model) without spatial momentum dependence.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Threshold mixing parameter $p(c=1)$ , Eq. ( 20 ), which still stabilizes the physical fixed point of the respective diagrammatic schemes (a) TRILEX, (b) SBE, (c) MBE. The red dashed lines mark where the first crossing $\mathrm{Re}\,j_{\alpha}=1$ occurs, i.e., in the regions above/within the red lines, the conventional damped iteration, Eq. ( 15 ), does not converge to the physical solution. The orange and green dashed lines mark the first 2PI divergence and the SBE divergence. The inset in panel (c) magnifies the region around the first vertex divergence in MBE.
fields.figure_gloss: Phase space of coupling $\beta U$ versus chemical potential shift $\beta\delta\mu$. Shaded regions mark where standard iteration fails ($|j_\alpha| > 1$), defining the threshold mixing parameter $p(c=1)$ required for stability across TRILEX, SBE, and MBE.

fields.result: Superconductor–insulator–superconductor–insulator–superconductor (SISIS) quantum circuit refrigerator selectively activates two-photon absorption near $eV/h \simeq 82.8\text{ GHz}$, cooling dephasing-induced leakage states back into Kerr parametric oscillator qubit subspace while avoiding single-photon parity-flipping errors.
fields.question: Can a quantum circuit refrigerator suppress pure-dephasing leakage in Kerr-cat qubits without driving parity-changing single-photon phase-flip errors?
fields.prior: SINIS-based QCR suppresses dephasing leakage via single-photon absorption but broad normal-metal density of states accelerates intra-qubit phase-flip errors.
fields.limits: Theoretical and numerical simulation; assumes second-order perturbative Born–Markov coupling, zero magnetic field, and specific Dynes subgap density of states parameter $\gamma_\text{D}$.
tools: quasiparticle tunneling rate via Fermi's golden rule
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Time evolution of state populations under pure dephasing, internal loss, and QCR. (A) Population of excited (leakage) states as a function of time for SISIS (thick solid line), SINIS (thin solid line), and QCR off (dotted line). (B) Population of $|\phi_{0}\rangle$ . A shorter time window is shown to highlight the effect of QCR-induced phase-flip processes. (C) Population of $|\phi_{\alpha}\rangle$ . The initial state is $|\phi_{0}\rangle$ in (A) and (B), and $|\phi_{\alpha}\rangle$ in (C). The values of the internal loss rate $\kappa$ and pure dephasing rate $\gamma_{p}$ are $\kappa/2\pi=1.6$ kHz and $\gamma_{p}/2\pi=0.8$ kHz, respectively, and are comparable to the ones measured for flux-tunable superconducting qubits [ 53 , 54 ] . The tunnel resistance is $R_{T}=500$ k $\Omega$ for SISIS and $R_{T}=50$ k $\Omega$ for SINIS. The bias voltage is chosen such that two-photon absorption is dominant for SISIS ( $eV/h=82.8$ GHz) and single-photon absorption is dominant for SINIS ( $eV/h=40$ GHz). The coupling parameters are $\rho_{c}=0.01$ for SISIS and $\rho_{c}=5\times 10^{-5}$ for SINIS. All remaining parameters for SISIS are as in Fig. 3 ; the SINIS parameters are identical to those used in Ref. [ 34 ] .
fields.figure_gloss: Excited leakage state populations (A) and qubit state population (B) over time under dephasing and loss. SISIS QCR suppresses leakage nearly as effectively as SINIS while maintaining much higher logical state population against phase flips.

fields.result: Implemented cryo-CMOS current-steering DAC in planar 90 nm CMOS process providing digitally tunable pulse amplitude, rise/fall slopes, and trigger-controlled pulse width for superconducting qubit control and readout.
fields.question: Can a digitally tunable CMOS current-based DAC operate reliably at cryogenic temperatures to control flux and readout in superconducting circuits?
fields.limits: Demonstrated for specific superconducting circuit driving requirements at cryogenic temperatures.

fields.result: Atomic spontaneous emission at rate $\gamma$ stabilizes a metastable superradiant phase via a coherent phase-space bridge, whereas pure dephasing at rate $\delta$ actively destroys this coherence and suppresses superradiant order.
fields.question: How do atomic spontaneous emission and pure dephasing compete with cavity loss to modify nonequilibrium criticality and metastable dynamics in the anisotropic open Rabi model?
fields.limits: Semiclassical limit $\eta = \Omega/\omega \to \infty$; numerical calculations truncated at bosonic cutoff $N_{\rm cutoff} \le 400$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Wigner functions of the cavity field in the NP ( $\tilde{\lambda}_{x}=\tilde{\lambda}_{y}=0.5$ ), SP ( $\tilde{\lambda}_{x}=1.5,\tilde{\lambda}_{y}=0.5$ ), and BP ( $\tilde{\lambda}_{x}=2.3,\tilde{\lambda}_{y}=1.1$ ). Rows from top to bottom represent NP, SP, and BP; columns from left to right represent $\kappa$ only, $\kappa+\gamma$ , $\kappa+\delta$ , and $\kappa+\gamma+\delta$ . Parameters: $\kappa/\omega=\gamma/\omega=\delta/\omega=0.5$ , $N_{\rm cutoff}=400$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Wigner quasiprobability distributions $W(\alpha)$ of the steady-state cavity field across normal, superradiant, and bistable phases under combinations of cavity loss $\kappa$, spontaneous emission $\gamma$, and pure dephasing $\delta$.

fields.result: Real-time distributed error detection and feedforward correction demonstrated across two trapped-ion quantum processors separated by $\sim 2\text{ m}$. Stabilises logical qubit in a $[[2,1,1]]$ repetition code and actively corrects arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state.
fields.question: Can stabiliser measurements and quantum error detection/correction be performed across spatially separated quantum processors using photonic interconnects?
fields.limits: Interleaved recooling reduces entanglement generation rate from $\sim 100\text{ s}^{-1}$ to $\sim 10\text{ s}^{-1}$. Calibration drifts and gate phase offsets not fully captured in error budget.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 1: Remote stabiliser measurements. a , Illustrative example of remote stabiliser measurements in a modular quantum architecture. i , Tanner graph of the $[[18,4,4]]$ bivariate bicycle code Bravyi et al. [2024] , Wang et al. [2026] , comprising 18 data qubits divided into left and right sets, together with $X$ - and $Z$ -check nodes. Each stabiliser acts on six data qubits, but the code requires interactions between qubits that cannot all be made local in a two-dimensional device layout. ii , The code can instead be distributed across three modules, each containing six data qubits, reducing both the number of qubits and the required local connectivity within each processor. iii , Inter-module stabiliser measurements are mediated by photonic interconnects. Entanglement between network qubits provides the shared resource required to perform these measurements across separate processors. b , Experimental implementation of a two-qubit remote stabiliser measurement. Two modules each hold a 88 Sr + ion providing a network qubit, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{N}{}}$ , and a 43 Ca + ion providing a data qubit, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{D}{}}$ , and auxiliary qubit, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{X}{}}$ . A Bell pair shared between the network qubits provides a distributed ancilla for measuring remote data-qubit stabilisers. Each module applies a local CNOT gate between the network and data qubits, mediated temporarily by the auxiliary qubit, mapping the joint data-qubit parity onto the network qubits. Their mid-circuit measurement outcomes are exchanged in real time via a classical (TTL) link. c , Characterisation of the two-qubit remote stabiliser measurement. The data qubits are prepared in the four $X$ -basis product states before an $X_{1}X_{2}$ stabiliser measurement. The probability of measuring odd parity on the network-qubit Bell pair is plotted as a function of the phase, $\phi$ , of the final analysis pulse applied to both network qubits before measurement. The $+1$ ( $\ket{++},\ket{--}$ ) and $-1$ ( $\ket{+-},\ket{-+}$ ) stabiliser eigenspaces oscillate $\pi$ radians out of phase, demonstrating syndrome discrimination. Error bars are the half-widths of $68\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}$ binomial confidence intervals, and solid lines are sinusoidal fits to the data.
fields.figure_gloss: Remote stabiliser measurement scheme and network qubit parity readout. Network qubit parity plotted against analysis pulse phase demonstrates syndrome discrimination between $+1$ and $-1$ eigenspaces of data-qubit pairs.

fields.result: Adiabatic edge-to-edge quantum state transfer of localized winding states across a 1D quasiperiodic optical lattice achieves fidelities up to 99.6% under locally adiabatic protocols.
fields.question: How can quantum state transfer protocols based on quasiperiodic edge winding states be efficiently implemented in realistic continuum ultracold atomic systems?
fields.limits: Noninteracting bosons ($g=0$), single-particle regime, finite-size rational approximants ($N_w = 13, 21$), simulation rather than experiment.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Performance diagram for the state-transfer fidelity. Final-state fidelity $\mathcal{F}$ as a function of the dimensionless transfer time $TJ_{\mathrm{bulk}}/\hbar$ and detuning strength $\rho$ for (a) the tangent protocol ( $N=0$ ) and (b) the Roland-Cerf protocol ( $N=1$ ). Each panel was obtained with 2160 MCTDH-X simulations over a $72\times 30$ grid in $(\rho,T)$ space. The color scale is logarithmic, and fidelities below $\mathcal{F}=0.75$ are omitted to emphasize the high-fidelity region. The dashed red line indicates the adiabatic boundary from Eq. ( 21 ). In the right panel, we additionally show the times $T_{n}$ from Eq. ( 29 ) for which the two-level assumptions predict unit fidelity.
fields.figure_gloss: Transfer fidelity $\mathcal{F}$ plotted against dimensionless transfer duration $TJ_{\mathrm{bulk}}/\hbar$ and detuning strength $\rho$ for the tangent protocol ($N=0$) and the Roland-Cerf protocol ($N=1$), showing coherent fidelity oscillations and improved high-$\rho$ robustness for $N=1$.

fields.result: Postselected infidelity scales as $210.2p^3 + O(p^4)$ under uniform circuit-level depolarizing noise, bounded at $2.2\times10^{-7}$ at $p=10^{-3}$ (99.9% joint confidence, 86.9% acceptance) using 19 qubits and 82 CNOT gates.
fields.question: Can co-designing the stabilizer-generator basis with flag circuits reduce the qubit and circuit overhead of fault-tolerant magic-state preparation?
fields.prior: 100 CNOTs, 31 measurements, and leading correction error $25.5p^2$ in the two-block benchmark of Daguerre and Kim (2025).
fields.limits: Applies strictly to destructive postselected error-detection diagnostic; minimum-weight error correction has leading infidelity $183.81p^2$. Omits memory errors, routing, idle time, crosstalk, and coherent leakage.
tools: quantum Reed-Muller to Steane code gauge fixing

fields.result: Parallel sparse blossom decodes an $O(d)$-round syndrome extraction window on a distance-$d$ rotated surface code in average parallel runtime bounded by $\exp[O((\log\log d)^{2})]$, yielding $o(1)$ average parallel runtime per round.
fields.question: Can minimum-weight perfect matching decoding via sparse blossom be parallelized with an exact correctness guarantee and a runtime per round that scales as $o(1)$?
fields.prior: Decoding time per round scaled as $O(d^{2.34})$ in sequential sparse blossom, requiring $O(d^{3.34})$ total latency for a $d$-round window (Higgott and Gidney 2023).
fields.limits: Circuit-level local stochastic error model below a finite threshold $p_{\mathrm{th}}$, with finite-size numerical comparisons assuming negligible parallelization overhead.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4 : Event counts per shot per syndrome-extraction round for global sparse blossom and parallel sparse blossom in rotated surface-code memory experiments as a function of the code distance $d$ . We consider code distances $d\in\{9,13,\ldots,49\}$ . The upper three panels correspond to physical error rates (a) $p=10^{-3}$ , (b) $p=10^{-4}$ , and (c) $p=10^{-5}$ under the uniform noise model. The lower three panels correspond to physical error rates (d) $p=10^{-3}$ , (e) $p=10^{-4}$ , and (f) $p=10^{-5}$ under the physically motivated noise model. The blue lines denote the event counts of global sparse blossom. The orange lines denote the event counts of parallel sparse blossom using the fixed parameter schedules. The dotted lines are guides proportional to $d^{2}$ . Error bars indicate standard errors of the mean. Under both noise models, the parallel event counts per shot per syndrome-extraction round decrease at larger code distances for $p=10^{-5}$ , indicating that a larger code distance increases the total amount of work but does not necessarily increase the critical-path length. For $p=10^{-4}$ , the $d$ dependence of the parallel event count is weaker under the physically motivated noise model than under the uniform noise model, indicating that the effective noise strength relevant to the decoder depends on the details of the noise model even at the same nominal physical error rate $p$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Event counts per shot per syndrome extraction round plotted against code distance $d\in\{9,13,\ldots,49\}$, demonstrating that parallel sparse-blossom runtime per round decreases with increasing $d$ at low physical error rates.

fields.result: Code-adapted basis-population dynamics under circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise are mapped to an exact $(2^{n}+1)$-dimensional Markov kernel, reducing Steane code dynamics from 129 to 11 states via orbit lumping.
fields.question: At what granularity can the multi-cycle dynamics and post-selection of quantum error detection protocols under noise be modeled exactly and tractably?
fields.limits: Restricted to circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise and data-preserving Clifford syndrome-extraction circuits; transition matrix scales as $2^n + 1$ before symmetry lumping.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Transition-matrix validation. Lines join exact accepted-block matrix predictions at integer QED cycles; markers show $10^{6}$ -shot Stim estimates (pointwise $95\%$ Wilson confidence intervals) for the $[[4,2,2]]$ (blue) and $[[5,1,3]]$ (orange) codes at $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$ and $\eta=0$ . Panel (a): acceptance probability $p_{\mathrm{acc}}(t)$ . Panel (b): accepted-state correctness $\mathrm{ASC}(t)$ . Matrix predictions use Pauli fault averaging and the reduction $\mathcal{R}$ of Section 4.4 , independently of the simulator. Agreement over $20$ cycles supports the implementation of the population-level construction under the specified circuit and readout noise.
fields.figure_gloss: Accepted logical population and rejection probabilities as a function of integer QED cycle count for the $[[4,2,2]]$ and $[[5,1,3]]$ codes at physical error rate $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$, comparing exact transition-matrix curves with $10^6$-shot Stim Monte Carlo data.

fields.result: DFE overlap $Y\equiv\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\widetilde{\rho})$ and purity $\mathscr{P}\equiv\operatorname{Tr}(\widetilde{\rho}^2)$ of PEC-mitigated state $\widetilde{\rho}$ serve as hardware witnesses and directional diagnostics: consistent underestimation yields $Y \le 1$ and $\mathscr{P} \le 1$, while consistent overestimation yields $Y \ge 1$ and $\mathscr{P} \ge 1$.
fields.question: How to test whether the noise parameters used in Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) are accurate directly on hardware, and diagnose whether they are overestimated or underestimated?
fields.limits: Requires positive Pauli fidelities ($>1/2$ identity coefficient) and absence of hybrid miscalibration; overestimation directionality for $Y$ in arbitrary circuits holds perturbatively under a nondegeneracy condition, while purity condition $\mathscr{P}$ holds non-perturbatively.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Exact DFE overlap between the ideal state and the effective mitigated state for the global depolarizing model as a function of the deviated error parameter $\widetilde{p}_{e}$ . We set the true error parameter to $p_{e}=0.02$ and plot the DFE overlap for $N=50$ qubits and $s=50$ , $100$ , and $150$ gates.
fields.figure_gloss: DFE overlap $\operatorname{Tr}(\widetilde{\rho}\rho)$ plotted against assumed depolarizing parameter $\widetilde{p}_e$ for $N=50$ qubits and $s=50, 100, 150$ gates. The curve crosses 1 exactly at the true parameter $p_e=0.02$, being $<1$ for underestimated $\widetilde{p}_e$ and $>1$ for overestimated $\widetilde{p}_e$.

fields.result: Defines QUOPS to benchmark quantum capability by circuit size and execution rate. Translating utility challenge problems (factoring RSA-2048, FeMoco) shows computational capability must grow by 5 orders of magnitude over current physical processors (Quantinuum Helios-1 $Q=1504$, H2-1 $Q=1320$).
fields.question: How can quantum computational power be directly benchmarked and compared across disparate physical and logical architectures relative to utility-scale challenge problems?
fields.prior: Quantum volume and physical gate error rates; quantum volume scaling requires exponential classical verification and does not map directly to fault-tolerant utility resource requirements.
fields.limits: Historical score inferences rely on global depolarizing noise, two-qubit gates as the sole error source, and simplified compilation models accurate to within roughly a factor of two.
tools: IBM ibm_boston and Google Willow superconducting processors
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Measured capabilities of three state-of-the-art quantum computers. ( a – d ) Experimentally measured QUOPS capability regions for ( a ) Google’s Willow (105 transmon qubits), ( b ) IBM’s ibm_boston (156 transmon qubits), ( c ) Quantinuum’s H2 - 1 (56 ion qubits), and ( d ) Quantinuum’s Helios - 1 (98 ion qubits). Blue regions indicate successful execution of circuits directly on physical qubits, using the standard success threshold of $1/\sqrt{e}$ . Pink indicates leakage-postselected performance, and orange indicates error-mitigated capability regions using a $1\%$ success threshold, corresponding to sampling overhead of $10^{4}$ . Pale hatching indicates interpolated or extrapolated capability. The green region in ( d ) shows the capability of a fault-tolerant architecture using logical qubits encoded in the Steane $\llbracket 7,1,3\rrbracket$ code, chosen for simplicity rather than optimal QUOPS performance. ( e ) Historical QUOPS scores inferred from quantum volume data for IBM and Quantinuum systems, together with direct QUOPS measurements on Helios - 1 , H2 - 1 , and ibm_boston and the $\llbracket 7,1,3\rrbracket$ fault tolerant processor implemented on Helios - 1 . Dashed lines show exponential fits. ( f ) QUOPS rate versus QUOPS score for the experimentally measured architectures, projected surface-code architectures, and the smallest known requirements for solving RSA-2048 and FeMoco in 5 days. Error mitigation increases QUOPS scores at reduced throughput (orange markers); curves show the continuum of speed–size tradeoffs, achieved by varying the success threshold between $1/\sqrt{e}$ and $1\%$ . Dashed lines correspond to a constant number of maximally-sized circuit executions per second.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots QUOPS capability regions (circuit size vs width), historical capability score scaling vs time with exponential trend lines showing 1.4-year (Quantinuum) and 2.1-year (IBM) doubling times, and QUOPS execution rate vs score for physical, logical, and projected architectures against utility milestones.

fields.result: FastSched uses reinforcement learning and importance sampling to synthesize syndrome extraction schedules, reducing logical error rate by 25.9% versus AlphaSyndrome and 71.7% versus PropHunt on average, reaching a 97.8% reduction for distance-15 surface codes.
fields.question: How can automatic schedule synthesis find quantum error correction syndrome extraction schedules with low logical error rates without sacrificing scalability to large code distances?
fields.prior: AlphaSyndrome (MCTS) and PropHunt (MaxSAT) synthesized schedules matching or improving hand-designed baselines, but suffered from poor scaling at large distance or degraded logical error rates.
fields.limits: Evaluated under simulated noise models (e.g. Brisbane noise), one noisy extraction round, ideal boundaries, and specific decoders (PyMatching, BP-OSD). Search ceilings capped at 10 to 30 minutes.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3. Surface-code LER versus distance under Brisbane noise (lower is better). Lines join point estimates; Figure 11 adds confidence bounds. The dashed PropHunt curve shows starting circuits because its searches returned no optimized schedules. Three curves show measured logical error rates at rotated surface-code distances three, five, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, and fifteen. The horizontal axis is code distance. The vertical axis is LER on a logarithmic scale. Blue circles mark FastSched, rust squares mark AlphaSyndrome, and a purple dashed line with open triangles marks PropHunt initialization-only circuits. Names appear beside the curve endpoints in larger type. FastSched is labeled FastSched (This work). All results come from our matched Brisbane study with one noisy extraction round, ideal boundaries, and PyMatching. LER is the sum of X-memory and Z-memory failure rates. Lines join point estimates. Evaluation reports confidence bounds. The curves have no numerical point annotations.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate on a logarithmic vertical axis versus rotated surface-code distance from 3 to 15 on the horizontal axis. FastSched maintains lower logical error rates than AlphaSyndrome and PropHunt across all evaluated code distances.

fields.result: Every detector in a composed stabilizer circuit splits across serial boundaries via virtual syndromes; composing gadget Extended Detector Error Models (EDEMs) under $Q_{t}A_{t-1} + P_{t}C_{t-1} = 0$ reproduces the monolithic detector error model as a block lower bidiagonal matrix $d_{t} = D_{t}f_{t} + (Q_{t}B_{t-1} + P_{t}E_{t-1})f_{t-1}$.
fields.question: How can detector error models be constructed incrementally and modularly from reusable logical gadgets without reanalyzing the full physical circuit?
fields.prior: Stim and stimflow compose chunk relations to reconstruct the monolithic circuit, then derive the DEM globally.
fields.limits: Stabilizer circuits with stochastic Pauli noise. Connected ports must share matching stabilizer codes and code presentations.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 12 : One step of sequential sliding-window decoding on the block-banded channel-check matrix $A_{\mathsf{D}}$ of a chain of gadget calls $g_{1}\to\cdots\to g_{10}$ (top strip). Column blocks are the fault partitions $\mathsf{F}_{t}$ and row blocks the detector partitions $\mathsf{D}_{t}$ . Causality empties the upper triangle. The figure assumes detector span $w=1$ , so nonzero blocks lie on the diagonal and the first subdiagonal; Sec. 5.2 and App. C provide locality conditions for the two-block band for repeated stabilizer, subsystem, and Floquet syndrome extraction, and Sec. 7.3 discusses gadgets that widen it. At step $j$ the inference window $W_{j}=\{g_{4},\dots,g_{8}\}$ (black outline) supplies the visible detectors and the fault variables included in the inference problem. Its commit window $C_{j}=\{g_{4},g_{5}\}$ (green) is separated from the buffer (purple) by the commit boundary (bold dashed line), which cuts the wire between $g_{5}$ and $g_{6}$ in the interior of $W_{j}$ ; the interface data $b$ and $\Delta v$ on that wire are handed to step $j+1$ . The committed correction reaches later detectors only through the orange block $(\mathsf{D}_{6},\mathsf{F}_{5})$ , which Proposition 7.1 folds into the frontier. Calls $g_{1}$ to $g_{3}$ (grey) were committed at earlier steps and discarded; their block $(\mathsf{D}_{4},\mathsf{F}_{3})$ was folded at step $j-1$ and fixes the input frontier of $W_{j}$ . The trailing boundary of $W_{j}$ plays no role in composition, and calls $g_{9}$ and $g_{10}$ (dashed) are not yet issued.
fields.figure_gloss: Sequential sliding-window decoding across a chain of gadget calls. Matrix columns represent fault partitions $\mathsf{F}_{t}$ and rows represent detector partitions $\mathsf{D}_{t}$, forming a block-banded structure where committed corrections fold across window boundaries.

fields.result: Purely dissipative Lindbladian solves $Ax=b$ via residual-reset jumps with trace-distance mixing time $\Theta(\kappa^2 \log(1/\varepsilon))$ and digital quantum query complexity $O\!\left(\kappa^2 \log(1/\varepsilon) \frac{\log(\kappa/\varepsilon)}{\log\log(\kappa/\varepsilon)}\right)$.
fields.question: Is it possible to solve linear systems from dissipation?
fields.prior: was $O(\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon))$ query complexity in coherent algorithms (Costa et al. 2022, Chakraborty et al. 2023)
fields.limits: Requires $0 < \varepsilon < 1/4$, $\kappa \geq 1$, and unitary access to block encoding $U_A$ and state preparation $U_b$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Population flow for the purely dissipative residual-reset solver.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of population flow in the dissipative solver showing jump-induced reset to state $|r\rangle$ and decay towards the target stationary state.

fields.result: Parallel circuit execution on 156-qubit ibm_boston processor reduces billed QPU execution time by $3.5\times$--$5.5\times$ while retaining $83$--$92\%$ of sequential fidelity.
fields.question: How can idle qubits on large quantum processors be utilized to execute multiple independent circuits simultaneously and reduce execution time?
fields.prior: Qiskit ParallelExperiment provided multi-circuit execution mechanics but required manual partition selection without error awareness.
fields.limits: Dependent on availability of low-error disjoint device partitions and prone to transpiler escape constraints; multi-GPU classical scaling evaluated up to 28 qubits and 16 GPUs.
tools: CUDA-Q and MPI on NERSC Perlmutter
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 6 : Fidelity and Billed Execution-Time Comparison for Standard QED-C Benchmarks on IBM Boston. Parallel and sequential execution results for the Bernstein–Vazirani (BV), transverse-field Ising model (TFIM), and Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) benchmarks. The top row reports the Hellinger fidelity as a function of qubit width, with error bars indicating the standard deviation across repeated runs; the secondary axis shows the corresponding transpiled circuit depth. Parallel execution generally exhibits lower fidelity than sequential execution because partitioning constrains qubit placement and routing within each partition, introducing additional routing overhead. As circuit depth increases, particularly for TFIM and QFT, the fidelity of both execution strategies decreases, with the parallel implementation experiencing a larger degradation. The bottom row reports the billed execution time together with the percentage reduction achieved through parallel execution. Executing independent circuits simultaneously on disjoint qubit partitions consistently reduces billed execution time, although the achievable reduction decreases for larger circuits as the number of available partitions becomes more limited.
fields.figure_gloss: Hellinger fidelity and billed QPU execution time on ibm_boston plotted against circuit qubit width. Parallel execution achieves $3.5\times$--$5.5\times$ runtime reductions while closely matching sequential fidelity across benchmarks.

fields.result: Covariance-orthogonal projection $\pi_{m}^{\sigma_{0}}$ compresses Heisenberg observables onto at-most-$m$-body subspaces while preserving expectation values $\langle{\bf O}\rangle_{\sigma_{0}}$ and spatial support for product states $\sigma_{0}$.
fields.question: How can Heisenberg-picture Pauli propagation be truncated reliably and stably during coherent many-body dynamics?
fields.prior: Conventional Hilbert--Schmidt weight-based truncation and state-informed methods like xSPD discard components above weight $m$, losing target expectation value preservation and suffering from instability.
fields.limits: Product reference states $\sigma_{0}$; requires exponential tail concentration $\Theta_{r}^{(g)}(s) \leq C_{g}e^{2{\cal M}_{1}(s)}e^{-2\kappa_{g}r}$ for certified sufficiency; rank-deficient states can suffer compatibility failures in covariance quotient geometry.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Accuracy and computational cost for the $3\times 3\times 2$ TFIM benchmark. (a) Instantaneous absolute error $\Delta Z_{0}(t)=|\langle Z_{0}(t)\rangle_{\rm approx}-\langle Z_{0}(t)\rangle_{\rm exact}|$ for covariance and HS adaptive PP at $m=1,2,3$ , together with representative TN results at $\chi=8,32,128$ . (b) Maximum instantaneous error $\Delta_{\max}=\max_{tJ\in[0,1.215]}\Delta Z_{0}(t)$ versus measured end-to-end wall time, including the full TN hierarchy $\chi=8,16,32,64,128$ . The $\chi=16,64$ trajectories are omitted from panel (a) for clarity.
fields.figure_gloss: Instantaneous absolute error $\Delta Z_{0}(t)$ and computational resource cost versus time for covariance PP, Hilbert--Schmidt PP across $m=1,2,3$, and tensor-network benchmarks on a $3\times 3\times 2$ transverse-field Ising lattice.

fields.result: The maximum effective sub-resonant drive amplitude before the onset of chaos scales as $\eta_{\max} \propto \gamma^{0.61}$, where $\gamma = \omega_q / \alpha$. For four-wave iSWAP/beamsplitter gates, the interaction rate figure of merit scales weakly as $\alpha \eta_{\max}^2 \propto \alpha^{-0.22} \omega_q^{1.22}$, establishing an upper limit of approximately $\omega_q / 20$.
fields.question: How does the sub-resonant drive strength threshold for chaos in transmon qubits depend on transmon parameters and drive frequency?
fields.limits: Isolated transmons driven sub-resonantly; assumes transmon single-mode approximation.
tools: 14 transmon devices ($E_J/E_C$ varying over two orders of magnitude)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Relationship between chaos threshold $\eta_{\max}$ and $\gamma$ . a , Threshold drive strength $\eta_{\max}$ as a function of $\gamma$ at drive frequency $\Omega_{\textrm{d}}=0.35$ . Error-bars shows the peak to peak variation observed about the mean over 10 values of $n_{\textrm{g}}$ . Both Floquet and semi-classical simulations show quantitative match with experiments. $n_{\textrm{zpf}}=\sqrt{\gamma}/4$ is plotted as a black dashed line for reference. b , Linear fit applied to log-plot for both measured and simulated $\eta_{\max}$ to obtain the power scaling. c , Heatmap of MBC threshold, $\eta_{\max}/\gamma^{0.61}$ vs $\Omega_{\textrm{d}}$ , for all simulated transmons after dividing out the power-scaling with $\gamma$ obtained from b . 63 transmons with $\gamma$ evenly spaced between $11$ and $132$ were simulated. The density is normalized such that its sum along any vertical linecut is $1$ . The thresholds for all transmons collapse to one curve that shows the drive frequency dependent factor in $\eta_{\max}$ , which varies by a factor of two over the entire frequency range. d , Same rescaling applied to the experimentally measured threshold for 14 transmons (scatter points) overlaid on the rescaled BC threshold. The black line is the mean over all simulated transmons whereas the boundary of the gray shaded region shows the max deviation from this mean. While the MBC threshold gives a clear picture of the threshold for transition to the chaotic regime, the experimental data is compared to the BC threshold because it includes the effect of individual resonances as described in Sec. II .
fields.figure_gloss: Chaos threshold drive strength $\eta_{\max}$ plotted against the ratio $\gamma = \omega_q / \alpha$, showing the universal $\eta_{\max} \propto \gamma^{0.61}$ scaling across experiment and simulation.

fields.result: Superconducting unconventional magnet junctions realize transverse spin and charge diode effects with perfect rectification efficiencies ($ho_y = \pm 1$ and $\eta_y = \pm 1$) at zero net magnetization.
fields.question: Can transverse superconducting diode effects emerge in unconventional magnet hybrids without net magnetization?
fields.limits: Zero temperature calculations, tight-binding discretization with proximity-induced s-wave superconductivity.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: (a) Sketch of a four-terminal setup consisting of three normal-metal leads ( $N_{j}$ ) and one superconducting AM lead, where a bias voltage $V_{0}$ is applied to the injector lead $N_{0}$ . The red and blue arrows indicate spin-up (spin-down) transport channels. (b) Charge diode quality factor $\eta_{y}$ versus $eV_{0}$ and $\theta_{J}$ . fields.result: Pauli blocking of inelastic recoil channels by identical fermions in a trap enables directed spontaneous emission and strong light-matter coupling with single-atom cooperativity $\mathcal{C} \ge 1$ in free space.
fields.question: Can an antenna formed by the center-of-mass wavefunction of a single atom exhibit large cooperativity $\mathcal{C} \ge 1$ in free space?
fields.prior: A single point atom driven by a focused Gaussian mode with waist $w_0 = \lambda$ had cooperativity bounded by $\mathcal{C}_{\text{point}} \le 3/2\pi^2$.
fields.limits: Single-excitation subspace; requires tight fermionic trap loading, $\Omega^{\text{R}}_2 \gg \Omega^{\text{R}}_1, \Gamma_{s_1 e}$, and $\Gamma_{s_2 g} \gtrsim |\mathbf{\Omega}_{s_2}|, |\mathbf{\Omega}_e|, \hbar k_{12}^2/2m$.
tools: Pauli blocking in a Fermi sea
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Arbitrary emission via an external drive: (a) Four internal states $e,s_{1},s_{2},g$ , coupled by two external driving fields $\Omega_{1}^{\text{R}},\mathbf{k}_{1}$ and $\Omega_{2}^{\text{R}},\mathbf{k}_{2}$ (i), which induce a wavepacket antenna (red) to emit to the right (blue) when arranged as shown with $\mathbf{k}_{12}$ along $+z$ . (ii). (b) Effect of $\mathbf{k}_{12}$ on spontaneously emitted photons $\ket{s_{2}}\rightarrow\ket{g,\mathbf{0}}$ . Radar plot (i) shows the unidirectional emission increasing to the right as $\mathbf{k}_{12}$ increases, with inset showing log scale. The effect of $\mathbf{k}_{12}$ is to shift the allowed momentum to the right in $k$ -space (ii). When $\mathbf{k}_{12}$ is zero, photons are emitted on the dotted white circle; the transition probabilities $|A_{\mathbf{00}}(\mathbf{k})|^{2}$ are symmetric. The drive $\mathbf{k}_{12}$ shifts the allowed emission wavevectors to the right, so the transition probability $|A_{\mathbf{00}}(\mathbf{k})|^{2}$ projected onto the solid white circle is asymmetric. fields.result: Two-photon dissipative confinement autonomously restores dephasing-induced leakage back to the logical cat-state subspace with restoration rate $\Gamma_{\rm R,1}\approx 4\kappa_{2}|\alpha|^{2}$, yielding final population $P_{-}(t_{f})\approx 99.64\%$ at $t_{f}=0.5/\kappa_{a}$ under pure dephasing $\kappa_{a}^{\phi}=\kappa_{a}$.
fields.question: How to design fast, high-fidelity state transfer protocols for dissipative cat-state qubits that are robust against systematic drive errors and suppress dephasing-induced leakage?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation only. Requires drive amplitude $\varepsilon_{d}(t)\ll 2\kappa_{2}|\alpha|^{2}$ and operation within the bounded time window $\frac{1}{2\kappa_{2}|\alpha|^{3}}\ll t_{f}\ll\frac{1}{\kappa_{a}|\alpha|^{2}}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: With pure dephasing, the population of $|\mathcal{C}_{-}\rangle$ at the final time $P_{-}(t_{f})$ is denoted by the red solid curve. The light-blue solid curve denotes the average of the population of leakage. The evolution time $t_{f}\in(0,1/\kappa_{a}]$ and other parameters are the same as those in Fig. 2 .
fields.figure_gloss: Final target population $P_{-}(t_{f})$ (red curve) and time-averaged subspace leakage $P_{\rm Leak}^{(\rm Avg)}$ (light-blue curve) plotted against total evolution time $t_{f}\in(0,1/\kappa_{a}]$ in the presence of pure dephasing.

fields.result: Telecom-heralded single photons stored across 10 spatial cells and 6 temporal modes (60 spatio-temporal modes total) in a $\mathrm{Pr}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ array yield a 60-fold enhancement in detected correlated photon rate over a 39.1 km metropolitan fiber link.
fields.question: Can spatial and temporal multiplexing be combined in a solid-state quantum memory array to distribute light-matter quantum correlations over deployed metropolitan fiber?
fields.limits: Round-trip communication time is 393 $\mu\mathrm{s}$; communication trials fill up to 15% of this window. Cross-correlations limited by control-pulse fluorescence noise and neighbor crosstalk between cells separated by 200 $\mu\mathrm{m}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Enhancement in distribution rates of quantum correlation. Heralding and coincidence rates as a function of the filled communication time $F$ and spatio-temporal modes $N$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Heralding and coincidence rates as functions of the filled round-trip communication time and number of spatio-temporal modes, showing linear rate scaling up to 60 modes.

fields.result: At the working point $f_\star=\sqrt{\bar n+1}$ with zero detuning and zero Kerr, the collapsed mean-rung excited population of the anti-Jaynes--Cummings (AJC) vertex is exactly $1/4$ (compared to $1/2$ for the Jaynes--Cummings vertex), and the continuum revival-time ratio $t_R^{\rm AJC}/t_R^{\rm JC}$ equals $\sqrt{2}$.
fields.question: How can the residual sum-frequency detuning of an isolated anti-Jaynes--Cummings vertex be used for reference-normalized differential sensing against the Jaynes--Cummings vertex?
fields.limits: Requires zero Kerr coupling $\chi=0$, resonance $\xi=0$, and static transverse rate $g_0\ll g_1$; isolated-vertex dynamics ignores parent Rabi-model virtual transitions when $\lambda/\omega$ is non-negligible.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Collapsed mean-rung excited population Eq. ( 14 ) versus $f$ at $\bar{n}=16$ , $\chi=0$ , $\xi=0$ . AJC (solid) drops through $1/4$ at $f_{\star}=\sqrt{17}=4.123$ ; JC (dashed) is flat at $1/2$ . The dotted horizontal line is $1/4$ ; the vertical dashed line is $f_{\star}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Collapsed mean-rung excited population plotted against $f=\omega/\lambda$ at $\bar n=16$. The AJC population curve crosses exactly $1/4$ at $f_\star=\sqrt{17}\approx 4.123$, while the JC population is constant at $1/2$ across all $f$.

fields.result: Cluster-As-You-Go (CAYG) grows and resolves syndrome clusters incrementally during stabilizer measurements, cutting post-measurement growth steps and outperforming batch Union-Find logical error rates when idling noise during decoding exceeds physical noise.
fields.question: Can quantum error correction decoding begin during syndrome extraction to reduce post-measurement latency and overall logical error rates under idling decoherence?
fields.prior: Standard Union-Find waits for all $d$ syndrome extraction rounds, yielding higher accuracy but larger post-measurement latency and faster threshold degradation under idling noise.
fields.limits: Phenomenological noise model with equal-strength idling decoherence, rotated surface codes only; hardware-level timing and circuit-level noise not evaluated.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8 : Logical error probability $p_{L}$ as a function of the physical error rate $p$ , for UF (blue) and CAYG( $l=2$ ) (orange), at distances $d=7,9,11$ , shown for four idling-noise strengths $1/N\in{0,0.010,0.016,0.023}$ (left to right). Error bars show 95% Wilson confidence intervals computed using $N_{p}$ , the number of independent decoded syndrome histories. Vertical dashed lines mark the estimated threshold $p_{th}$ for each decoder, taken as the lowest- $p$ crossing (via linear interpolation between the two nearest sampled points) of the $p_{L}(p)$ curves for neighboring distances. As $1/N$ increases, both thresholds shift to lower $p$ , but $p_{th}^{\mathrm{UF}}$ drops substantially faster than $p_{th}^{\mathrm{CAYG}}$ , due to its longer post-processing time prone to idling errors. Further, for increasing, finite idling noise the logical error rate approaches a constant for when decreasing the error rate $p$ . This is visible in terms of the bending of the logical error rate curves for increasing $1/N$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error probability $p_L$ plotted against physical error rate $p$ across code distances $d=7,9,11$ for four increasing idling-noise strengths $1/N$, showing CAYG maintaining a higher effective threshold than standard Union-Find as idling noise increases.

fields.result: Probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC) on a five-qubit permutation-invariant code achieves fidelity loss that scales quadratically with generalized amplitude-damping strength $\gamma$, $O(\gamma^2)$, under post-selected recovery.
fields.question: Can probabilistic and approximate quantum error correction frameworks be combined to suppress first-order generalized amplitude-damping errors in short codes?
fields.prior: Deterministic quantum codes (such as the $[5,1,3]$ stabilizer code) cannot eliminate first-order generalized amplitude-damping errors and incur fidelity loss scaling linearly with $\gamma$.
fields.limits: Requires post-selection over successful recovery outcomes, reducing total success probability below 1.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5 : Performance comparison of the $[5,1]$ PI code and the numerically optimized code. (a) Entanglement fidelity vs. $\gamma$ . (b) Recovery probability vs. $\gamma$ . The numerical code outperforms the PI code at $p=0.05$ . This improvement comes at the cost of a lower probability of success (increased overhead).

fields.result: Code space of any non-trivial $[[n, k, d_{\mathrm{F}}]]$ fermionic code with $d_{\mathrm{F}} \geq 3$ contains zero pure fermionic Gaussian states. Exact unitary codeword preparation via $q$-mode non-Gaussian gates requires at least $g \geq \lfloor (d_{\mathrm{F}}-3)/(q-2) \rfloor + \lceil k/q \rceil$ non-Gaussian gates.
fields.question: Can fermionic quantum error correction and error detection be implemented using only free-fermion (Gaussian) operations?
fields.limits: Pure fermionic Gaussian states; bounded-weight non-Gaussian unitary circuits acting on $n$ modes; exact and fidelity-bounded codeword preparation.

fields.result: Unitary sequential circuits with non-Clifford gates prepare 3D symmetry-broken order and 4D $(3,1)$ toric code topological order stably against Pauli noise, with the 4D toric code syndrome cluster size vanishing asymptotically below critical single-qubit error probability $p^c_{\hat{X}} \approx 0.013$.
fields.question: Can unitary sequential quantum circuits prepare long-range ordered states stably against circuit-level Pauli noise without propagating local errors into nonlocal order-destroying defects?
fields.prior: Standard sequential circuits for 1D GHZ states and 2D toric code wavefunctions are unstable to Pauli noise at any non-zero error rate due to gate-propagated errors.
fields.limits: Requires spatial dimension $D \ge 3$ for purely unitary stabilization (or $D \ge 2$ with active measurement and classical feedback); stabilizer syndromes must form closed manifolds of dimension $d \ge 2$.
tools: majority-vote and Toom's rule gate updates
fields.figure_caption: Figure S3: Normalized average maximum syndrome cluster diameter $\langle\max_{c\in S}d_{\mathrm{max}}(c)\rangle/L$ as a function of error probability $p_{\hat{X}}$ . Below the threshold $p^{c}_{\hat{X}}\approx 0.013$ , the relative cluster size decreases towards zero with increasing $L$ , demonstrating that errors remain confined to small, isolated patches. Above $p^{c}_{\hat{X}}$ , the curves cross and saturate at $1$ , indicating a transition to a regime dominated by a system-spanning cluster.
fields.figure_gloss: Normalized average maximum syndrome cluster diameter plotted against Pauli error probability $p_{\hat{X}}$ across multiple linear system sizes $L$. Below $p^c_{\hat{X}} \approx 0.013$, relative cluster size scales to zero as $L$ increases, confirming error confinement.

fields.result: Optimal SAT compilation improves globally controlled WISE logical clock speed from 1.94 Hz to 4.28 Hz for a distance-7 surface code, but remains roughly $3\times$ slower than local QCCD control at 12.8 Hz.
fields.question: Is the performance gap between globally multiplexed trapped-ion control and standard QCCD an intrinsic architectural bottleneck or an artifact of suboptimal compilation and hardware choices?
fields.prior: Heuristic compilation on WISE achieved 1.94 Hz clock speed and $3.3\times 10^{-6}$ logical error rate (Jones and Murali 2026), compared to 12.8 Hz on QCCD.
fields.limits: Evaluated on logical memory benchmarking rather than full computation; assumes optimistic physical noise reductions and ignores boundary-qubit routing from lattice surgery.
tools: physics-grounded ion noise and heating model
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6 . QEC tier-trajectories at fixed hardware settings $(k^{*},M^{*},n_{t}^{*})=(2,16,0.0)$ . Each connected trajectory corresponds to one $(\text{code},d)$ pair and links technology tiers in order Pessimistic $\rightarrow$ Current $\rightarrow$ Optimistic (square, diamond, circle markers). The horizontal axis is logical error rate (LER, log scale, inverted so rightward is better), and the vertical axis is logical clock speed (Hz, log scale, upward is better). fields.result: Patch rotations cause 55.3% to 77.6% of execution time in transversal neutral-atom FTQC. The D3-ROT architecture eliminates this bottleneck, yielding an average $2.27\times$ speedup (up to $2.57\times$) at 22.4% average footprint overhead.
fields.question: How can full-stack co-optimization across compiler, control hardware, and qubit plane reduce logical operation latency in transversal neutral-atom FTQC architectures?
fields.prior: Patch rotations executed via space-efficient reflection on baseline transversal surface-code architectures.
fields.limits: Evaluated via classical CPU simulation across 8 FTQC benchmark circuits (QPE and FTCircuitBench) using rotated transversal surface codes.
tools: SLM laser toggling with AOD atom holding
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 15: Average per-layer latency (bar), LER (line), and spatial footprint (indicated in labels) across various rotation implementations (averaged across FTQC workloads in Table II ).
fields.figure_gloss: Per-layer latency breakdown (bars, left axis) and logical error rate (line, right axis) across six routing and patch-rotation architectures, showing D3-ROT minimizing latency without sacrificing error rates.

fields.result: CUDA-Q Logical provides an MLIR-based, retargetable compiler pipeline that lowers logical quantum programs through five explicit semantic profiles (P0 to P4), directly deriving resource estimates, detector error models, and physical execution schedules from compiler artifacts while preserving provenance.
fields.question: How can fault-tolerant quantum compilation unify target-independent logical intent, heterogeneous QEC encodings, physical scheduling, and real-time control to provide verifiable, reproducible resource estimates and cross-architecture comparisons?
fields.limits: Deterministic and single-shot behavior only; rejects retry averaging, stochastic queues, dynamic routing, packetization, and runtime boundary-changing surgery in compact models.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1. CUDA-Q Logical progressively refines one logical program from target-independent intent to real-time control. Each profile adds a new class of target commitment, while research components attach at typed boundaries and analyses observe the same evolving build. Compilation may stop at any verified profile accepted by the selected target. A horizontal pipeline from a logical kernel through the P0 logical intent, P1 logical architecture, P2 QEC binding, P3 physical materialization, and P4 real-time control levels, with research components attached at the boundaries between levels and analyses reading the build.
fields.figure_gloss: Progression of compiler lowering across five semantic profiles from P0 logical intent down to P4 real-time control, illustrating typed boundaries for research components and analysis passes.

fields.result: For an 18-qubit QFT circuit on a 2-QPU network, replacing all-to-all with nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity increases EPR-pair consumption by more than an order of magnitude. Under stochastic link generation, shortest-duration and critical-path arbitration policies reduce completion time by $17.7\pm 1.3\%$ and $17.9\pm 1.5\%$ relative to FIFO.
fields.question: How can hardware network topology and link contention be incorporated into an open-source software stack for partitioning, compiling, and scheduling distributed quantum circuits?
fields.prior: Prior distributed compilers (such as Pytket-DQC) lack timestamped operation scheduling and rely on idealized, optimistic all-to-all connectivity assumptions.
fields.limits: NISQ-era compilation only; does not model decoherence, noise, link fidelity degradation, entanglement distillation, or quantum error correction.
tools: Hypergraph and Dynamic Interaction circuit partitioners
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 10: Cost of intra-QPU connectivity, for an 18-qubit QFT circuit (top) and a 64-qubit Adder circuit (bottom). The cost, in EPR pairs, of changing the intra-QPU connectivity assumption from all-to-all to nearest-neighbor, for each circuit executed on a 2-QPU network. For each partitioning strategy, the paired bars give the EPR cost under all-to-all (left) and nearest-neighbor (right) intra-QPU connectivity. The dashed lines on the QFT panel mark the static optimum for each network, obtained by compiling every one of the $\binom{18}{9}$ balanced qubit assignments and taking the lowest cost; static here means the assignment is fixed for the whole circuit, so no qubit is moved between QPUs. The dynamic interaction partitioner is not bound by these lines, and on the nearest-neighbor network it falls below the static optimum by leveraging state teleportation.
fields.figure_gloss: EPR-pair consumption (y-axis) for 18-qubit QFT and 64-qubit Adder circuits on a 2-QPU network under all-to-all versus nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity (x-axis) across three partitioning strategies.

fields.result: DNA retrieval accuracy reaches $>0.98$ with $M_0=2048$ samples per oracle across $Q=8$ applications out of $16\,288$ corpus windows, scaling in relative error as $E_F^{(Q)}\propto Q^2/M$. Transpiled circuits remain deep, exceeding $4.17\times 10^5$ depth even after phase fusion.
fields.question: What are the practical system and compilation requirements for implementing Quantum Oracle Sketching (QOS) on current batched quantum hardware?
fields.limits: Offline simulation only; transpiled circuits require hundreds of thousands of CX gates, exceeding current NISQ coherence times.

(a) Mean relative error $E_{F}^{(Q)}$ of the fingerprint matrix. (b) Mean top-one family-retrieval accuracy. Error bars in (a) and (b) show one sample standard deviation over 32 trials. (c) Mean pairwise absolute fingerprint error for $Q=4$ and $M=8192$ .

fields.result: OpenQARP executes operator algebra one to two orders of magnitude faster than OpenFermion and matches mature compilers on two-qubit gate count while keeping strict unified conventions.
fields.question: How to build an open-source quantum computing framework that eliminates silent convention errors across the research workflow while maintaining high simulator and operator performance?
fields.prior: OpenFermion, Qiskit/Aer, PennyLane/Lightning, Qulacs, qsim, and pytket required cross-framework plumbing with differing qubit orderings and phase conventions.
fields.limits: Benchmarks measured on a single Apple-silicon host using scalar C++ block kernels without SIMD or AVX vectorization; no pulse-level control, autodiff, or direct hardware execution engine.
tools: C++20 compiled core with Python interface
gate fusion and flip-mask Pauli contraction

fields.result: Sample complexity dependence on gate-wise stabilizer extent drops from quadratic to linear in the low-variance regime via empirical variance-based confidence bounds instead of Hoeffding's inequality, maintaining prior space complexity.
fields.question: Can classical expectation value estimation for non-Clifford quantum circuits be accelerated by combining sum-over-Clifford and quasi-probability methods with adaptive stopping criteria?
fields.prior: Standard quasi-probability and sum-over-Clifford stabilizer simulators relied on Hoeffding's inequality, yielding quadratic sample-complexity overhead in the gate-wise stabilizer extent.
fields.limits: Sample complexity advantage holds in the low-variance regime. Validated on random circuits, T-doped Clifford circuits, QAOA, and quantum kernel models.

fields.result: Unitary oracle separates pseudorandom function-like state generators (PRFSGs) from pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs). Adaptively secure, quantum-accessible PRFSGs do not imply non-adaptively secure, forward-only PRUs, even for non-unitary implementations with polynomial ancilla space.
fields.question: Can pseudorandom function-like state generators be used to construct pseudorandom unitaries when unrestricted ancillary qubits are permitted?
fields.prior: Partial oracle separations existed only for candidate PRU constructions with severely bounded ancilla space.
fields.limits: Black-box separation relative to a unitary oracle combined with $\mathsf{QPSPACE}$.

fields.result: Operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE) updates parameterized circuits by matching Ehrenfest equations on polynomial-sized operator sets without quantum geometric tensor calculation. Reaches ground-state energy error $\sim 3\times 10^{-3}$ when generating QSCI subspaces on a 20-qubit simulator and executes on up to 24 superconducting qubits.
fields.question: How can variational real-time dynamics be formulated to avoid measuring the quantum geometric tensor while reducing quantum circuit and measurement costs?
fields.limits: Demonstrated for systems up to 24 qubits, tested with $N_s=22$ SPSA samples per gradient step, requires selected reduced operator manifolds.
tools: Low-depth unitary coupled cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz

Energy error $|E-E_{\rm FCI}|$ versus cutoff fraction of the subspace size $R$ , colored by the number of evolution iterations. (Left) State evolved by exact matrix exponentiation $e^{-i\hat{H}t}$ , sampled and passed to QSCI at each of $10$ – $150$ iterations. (Right) State evolved by OVQRTE with SPSA gradient estimation at $N_{s}=22$ samples per step, sampled and passed to QSCI at each of $5$ – $50$ iterations.

fields.result: Disentangled QAOA projected to product states (bond dimension $\chi=1$) achieves cut ratios above 0.95 relative to best-known values on GSet MaxCut instances up to 20000 variables without per-instance tuning.
fields.question: How much of the optimization power of expanding-depth QAOA survives when circuit entanglement is completely removed?
fields.limits: Restricted to the fixed-parameter expanding-depth QAOA regime; not a general claim for all variational quantum optimization or other parameter schedules.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: MPS bond-dimension dynamics for the fixed-parameter QAOA evolution. (a) Bond dimension $\chi$ after each QAOA layer for a random QUBO instance with $n=20$ , shown as a function of the normalized layer index $\ell/p$ for depths $p=5$ and $p=100$ . The quantity $\chi_{\max}$ denotes the maximum bond dimension reached during the circuit. For the shallow circuit, the bond dimension grows throughout the evolution, whereas for the larger depth it first increases and then decreases toward the end of the circuit. (b) Mean maximum bond dimension $\chi_{\max}$ as a function of QAOA depth $p$ for various problem sizes $n$ , averaged over $20$ random QUBO instances for each $n$ . fields.result: Pedagogical review and lecture notes covering open quantum systems, microscopic derivations of GKSL master equations, Liouvillian spectral properties, and foundational quantum thermodynamics.
fields.question: How do environmental interactions generate decoherence, dissipation, and thermodynamic behavior in reduced quantum systems?
fields.limits: Primarily treats weak-coupling Markovian regimes via Born-Markov and secular approximations; omits non-Markovian dynamics, strong-coupling thermodynamics, and collision models.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Representation of a general qubit state $\rho$ on the Bloch sphere.
