fields.result: Exact quantum circuits for three-spin Heisenberg-$DM$ triangles require at most 8 CNOT gates for pure $DM$ interactions, 10 CNOT gates for uniform exchange and $DM$ couplings, and 14 CNOT gates for unequal couplings satisfying $J^2 = D_{12}D_{23} + D_{23}D_{31} + D_{31}D_{12}$.
fields.question: How can coupled time evolution on a three-spin Heisenberg triangle with Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interactions be compiled into exact, time-independent-depth quantum circuits across the full Hilbert space?
fields.limits: Unequal DM with exchange requires $J^2 = D_{12}D_{23} + D_{23}D_{31} + D_{31}D_{12}$. Valid on spin-1/2 systems without noise or decoherence.

The central rotations describe evolution in the transformed basis; the CNOT pair in (b) implements $R_{ZZ}^{(12)}(\varphi)$ .

fields.result: Shot-based VQE with parameterized circuits detects the toric code magnetic-field transition via energy derivatives and conditional global entanglement $\Delta G$, yielding $h_{c}\approx 0.395$ on a $2\times 2$ lattice. Under depolarizing and readout noise, $h_{c}$ decreases linearly with noise scaling factor $s$, extrapolating to zero at $s\approx 16.2$.
fields.question: Can parameterized variational circuits on small periodic lattices reliably detect the toric-code topological phase transition and its entanglement signatures under finite-shot sampling and hardware noise?
fields.limits: Simulations restricted to $2\times 2$ (8-qubit) and $3\times 3$ (18-qubit) lattices; shot budgets limited to 1024 and 64 shots respectively; linear noise scaling holds only for low-noise regime ($s\le 2.5$).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 14 : Critical magnetic field $h_{c}$ versus noise strength factor $s$ for $2\times 2$ (8-qubit) and $3\times 3$ (18-qubit) lattices, obtained using 1024 and 64 measurement shots, respectively. Solid lines indicate linear fits within the reliable noise regime, while dashed lines show the extrapolation. Error bars denote statistical uncertainty.
fields.figure_gloss: Critical magnetic field $h_{c}$ as a function of noise scaling factor $s$ for $2\times 2$ (1024 shots) and $3\times 3$ (64 shots) lattices. Solid lines show linear fits in the weak-noise regime demonstrating linear suppression of $h_{c}$ before high noise obscures the transition.

fields.result: Merged-element transmon built entirely from a $\mathrm{NbSe}_2$-$\mathrm{hBN}$-$\mathrm{NbSe}_2$ van der Waals heterostructure achieves $T_{1,\mathrm{avg}} = 55~\mu\mathrm{s}$, $T_{2\mathrm{E},\mathrm{avg}} = 21~\mu\mathrm{s}$, and $T_{2\mathrm{R},\mathrm{avg}} = 1.9~\mu\mathrm{s}$.
fields.question: Can an all-van-der-Waals Josephson heterostructure yield a superconducting transmon with coherence times competitive with conventional $\mathrm{Al}$-$\mathrm{AlO}_x$-$\mathrm{Al}$ circuits in a compact lumped footprint?
fields.limits: Ratio $E_{\mathrm{J}}/E_{\mathrm{C}} \approx 33$, making Ramsey coherence sensitive to quasiparticle-induced charge-parity switching and offset-charge drift.

fields.result: Parametric two-qubit gates enabled by consecutive Landau-Zener transitions achieve population swap fidelity $F\approx 0.98$ on transmons with drive frequency tunable over a continuous window from 10 MHz to 100 MHz.
fields.question: Can quantum interference between consecutive Landau-Zener crossings of a tunable coupler enable fast parametric two-qubit gates at arbitrary drive frequencies?
fields.limits: Swap fidelity $F\approx 0.98$ is limited by decoherence ($T_{2}^{\text{echo}}=2.2$ $\upmu$s). Simplified model truncates Hilbert space to three-qubit computational subspace.

fields.result: Purcell-limited relaxation time $T_{1,\mathrm{P}}$ exceeds 1 ms over a 1.2 GHz bandwidth (4.7–5.9 GHz) with 500 ns readout and 100 ns reset at 99.6% efficiency. fields.question: Can donor-bound exciton transitions be detected opto-electrically in silicon-on-insulator substrates?

fields.result: Nonadiabatic holonomic quantum computation generalizes to a $d$-pod system of $d$ ground states coupled to a single excited state, realizing universal single- and two-qudit gates in the Grassmannian $\mathcal{G}(d+1;d)$. For qutrits ($d=3$), $\mathbb{X}_{3}$, $\mathbb{Z}_{3}$, and $\mathbb{T}_{3}$ require two pulses, the entangling controlled-$\mathbb{Z}_{3}$ gate requires two pulses, and the Hadamard gate $\mathbb{H}_{3}$ requires at most three pulses.
fields.question: How can nonadiabatic holonomic quantum computation be systematically generalized from three-level $\Lambda$ qubit systems to qudit configurations using only a single auxiliary excited state?
fields.prior: Prior nonadiabatic holonomic qudit schemes required multiple auxiliary excited states or dark-path configurations.
fields.limits: Rotating wave approximation with resonant monochromatic fields, equal temporal envelopes $\Omega(t)$ across couplings, and time-independent coupling parameters during each pulse.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Setup for a qudit system implemented using the $d$ -pod configuration. Left panel: Each computational basis state $|1\rangle,\dots,|d\rangle$ is coupled to an excited state $|e\rangle$ . Right panel: The same system expressed in the dark-bright Morris-Shore [ 66 ] basis $\{|b\rangle,|\mathcal{D}_{1}\rangle,\ldots,|\mathcal{D}_{d-1}\rangle\}$ . Note that only the bright state $|b\rangle$ is coupled to $|e\rangle$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Level schematic of the $d$-pod qudit system showing $d$ computational ground states coupled to an excited state $|e\rangle$ (left) and the equivalent Morris-Shore basis where only the single bright state $|b\rangle$ couples to $|e\rangle$ (right).

fields.result: Implemented a programmable 2+1D free massive Dirac Hamiltonian in multimode circuit QED. Observed rotational Zitterbewegung whose oscillation frequency increases while amplitude decreases with higher effective mass $\Delta\Omega$.
fields.question: Can a fully programmable two-dimensional massive Dirac Hamiltonian, with dynamical quantum operators for both momentum components, be simulated in circuit QED?
fields.prior: 1D Dirac dynamics and 2D massless Weyl dynamics were demonstrated in trapped ions, while photonic lattices and fixed-coupling superconducting circuits lacked independent dynamical quantum momentum degrees of freedom.
fields.limits: Fidelity bounded by transmon charging energy $E_c/h = 230\text{ MHz}$ limiting drive power, spin-locking decoherence ($T_{2\rho} = 17\ \mu\text{s}$), non-RWA terms, and $\pm 5\text{ kHz}$ Rabi calibration uncertainty.
tools: multimode 3D flute cavity (TE101 and TE102 modes)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4 : Experimental data and numerical simulations of two-dimensional Zitterbewegung for two effective particle masses. Black dashed lines show the ideal Dirac dynamics, while navy solid lines show simulations including experimental conditions, with navy squares indicating time points sampled every $0.5~\mu\mathrm{s}$ . Red circles show the experimental data sampled at the same time intervals up to $10~\mu\mathrm{s}$ . (a) Dynamics for $\Delta\Omega/2\pi=0.10~\mathrm{MHz}$ , shown as the two orthogonal position components versus evolution time and their projection onto the two-dimensional position plane. (b) Two-dimensional trajectory for $\Delta\Omega/2\pi=0.15~\mathrm{MHz}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Trajectories and time traces of the simulated 2D position quadratures $\langle \hat{X}_1 \rangle$ and $\langle \hat{X}_2 \rangle$. Measured data match open-system simulations showing mass-dependent rotational Zitterbewegung loops.

fields.result: Presents a full-stack taxonomy organizing fault-tolerant quantum computing compilation into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC optimization, physical-level hardware realization across superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms, and classical real-time decoder runtime integration.
fields.question: How should quantum compilers be architected across the entire hardware and software stack to bridge logical fault-tolerant operations, physical syndrome extraction, and real-time classical decoding?
fields.limits: Literature survey covering peer-reviewed papers and substantive preprints available through June 2026.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2. Overall picture of the QEC-protected quantum computing stack: logical-level compilation transpiles and lowers a logical circuit into fault-tolerant primitives and an optimized instruction stream; physical-level optimization compiles it to native operations across superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms; and the decoder stack processes the resulting syndrome stream to feed corrections back via the Pauli frame.
fields.figure_gloss: Full-stack abstraction of QEC-protected quantum computation, illustrating the compilation flow from logical circuit synthesis to physical hardware mapping and the classical decoding feedback loop.

fields.result: Mean back-decay count $\langle N\rangle$ during excitation pulses sets tight upper and lower bounds on Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility $V_{\mathrm{HOM}}$ for Raman single photons; for long-distance ($>10$ km) dual-rail entanglement swapping over standard fiber, $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^+$ Raman schemes achieve the highest coincidence rates.
fields.question: How do spontaneous back-decays during few-nanosecond Raman excitation pulses degrade photon indistinguishability, and how can excitation parameters be optimized across different trapped-ion species?
fields.limits: Numerical simulations of effective three-level $\Lambda$ systems; trapped-ion species comparison relies on published single-photon conversion efficiencies and fiber attenuation rates.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: Coincidence probability in dependence of SMF-28e+ fiber length for different ion species and single Raman photon generation schemes based on reported conversion efficiencies and fiber losses according to [ 17 , 67 ] . The photon generation schemes corresponding to the numbers 1–9 in the legend are listed in Table 1 . Two arrows connect to the expected cavity-enhanced coincidence probability for the first scheme, with two assumed values of the Purcell enhancement, $F_{\mathrm{P}}\approx 1$ and $F_{\mathrm{P}}\approx 2.86$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Dual-rail entanglement-swapping coincidence probability versus SMF-28e+ fiber length across nine Raman photon schemes in $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^+$, $^{88}\mathrm{Sr}^+$, $^{138}\mathrm{Ba}^+$, and $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}^+$, with and without Purcell enhancement.

fields.result: Protocol generates microwave-optical heralded Bell pairs without an optical pump, reaching heralding rates up to 3.71 kHz with 0.97 fidelity in a ${}^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$ ensemble.
fields.question: Can microwave-optical Bell pairs be generated for teleportation-based transduction without relying on an optical pump?
fields.limits: Theoretical and numerical simulation; assumes zero optical pump during generation, trapping fields switched off in ensembles, and transmon relaxation time $T_{1,t}=300$ µs.
tools: single spins, atomic ensembles, and spin-phonon systems
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Figures of merit for our MO-NODE across different platforms and transmon lifetimes $T_{1,t}$ with fixed $\epsilon=0.01$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Heralding rate and Bell-state fidelity plotted against transmon relaxation time $T_{1,t}$ across color centers, atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated platforms.

fields.result: Evaluates 2D materials and van der Waals interfaces to mitigate fabrication-induced chemical residues, structural disorder, and interface non-uniformity in scalable solid-state quantum chips using CMOS-compatible processes.
fields.question: Whether CMOS channel fabrication processes for 2D materials can be transferred to solid-state quantum hardware to improve coherence and scalability.
fields.limits: Perspective and literature assessment; focus on solid-state qubit platforms compatible with standard semiconductor fabrication.

fields.result: Local quantum error correction recovery rules compile into fixed, open-loop microwave pulses on leaf auxiliary transmons via condition-dependent spectral shifts, executing a four-qubit repetition code cycle in 560 ns within a 1 ̀s repetition period.
fields.question: Can joint syndrome measurement, decoding, and conditional feedback be compiled into a fixed open-loop control waveform via the conditional energy spectrum of an interacting transmon network?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation assuming ideal, instantaneous auxiliary reset and calibrated branch phases; noise during drives is approximated by interleaved channel factors.
tools: Spectrally selective longitudinal and two-photon transverse drives
Transmon circuit full-Hamiltonian numerics (4 levels per mode)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Repeated-cycle protection under two noise models. a, Under dressed Pauli- $X$ noise, recovery slows the decay of logical coherence $C_{Y}$ relative to both a physical qubit and the unrecovered encoded state. b, Under independent amplitude damping, recovery slows the decay of logical-one population $P_{1_{L}}$ relative to a physical excited state. Both panels use the same recovery cycle but different initial states and observables.
fields.figure_gloss: Decay of logical coherence $C_Y$ under dressed Pauli-$X$ noise ($̃_X = (30 \mu\mathrm{s})^{-1}$) and logical-one population $P_{1_L}$ under amplitude damping ($T_1 = 30 \mu\mathrm{s}$) versus time over repeated 1 ̀s cycles. The compiled open-loop recovery slows decay compared to uncorrected encoded states and single physical qubits.

fields.result: Probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) applied over a round of continuous-variable GKP error correction yields quasiprobability sampling overheads $C_{\mathrm{em}}$ for single- and two-qubit logical Clifford gates as a function of finite squeezing parameter $\Delta_{\mathrm{dB}}$, evaluated for square and hexagonal GKP codes under Steane and teleportation syndrome extraction.
fields.question: How can probabilistic error cancellation be applied together with continuous-variable GKP error-correcting cycles to mitigate residual logical noise from finite squeezing?
fields.limits: Noise modeled as isotropic Gaussian random displacement; single round of QEC; finite squeezing treated with twirled/well-characterized approximations without experimental noise learning.
fields.figure_gloss: Circuit equivalence maps converting hexagonal GKP syndrome extraction circuits into equivalent square GKP code gates and states for teleportation-based and Steane-type continuous-variable error correction protocols.

fields.result: Constructed flagged syndrome extraction for non-CSS $[\[8,3,3]\]$ code achieving memory pseudo-threshold near $1.5\times 10^{-3}$, but block-level logical Trotter circuits exhibit circuit distance $1$ via ancilla phase-fault propagation into undetected logical-$Z$ errors.
fields.question: Can block-level logical Trotter circuits on non-CSS stabilizer codes maintain fault-tolerant circuit distance without transversal gate sets?
fields.limits: Depolarizing and asymmetric Pauli circuit noise models, diagnostic protected limit assumes ideal phase gate and flag couplings, single-shot cleanup boundaries.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Logical- $X$ and logical- $Z$ failure rates for the encoded Trotter evolution in Eq. ( 29 ), followed by one round of Chao–Reichardt flagged error correction [ 16 ] and a final ideal weight-one cleanup. The final logical measurements use the ideally propagated observables rather than the corresponding bare input observables. Neither logical-error curve exhibits a pseudo-threshold relative to the unencoded reference $P_{L}=p$ over the sampled parameter range. Each point is estimated from $N=200,000$ Monte Carlo shots.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical-$X$ and logical-$Z$ failure rates versus physical error probability $p$ for encoded Trotter evolution under circuit-level noise, showing logical-$Z$ degradation from ancilla fault propagation while logical-$X$ remains protected.

fields.result: Hyperbolic color codes in dimension $D=2m\ge 4$ achieve parameters $[[n, \Theta(n), \Omega(n^{(m-1)/(m(2m+1))})]]$, providing constant rate with polynomial distance. In general dimensions $D\ge 4$, logical count scales as $\Omega(n^{\delta(i,D)-\epsilon})$ with polynomial distance for all types $2\le i\le D-2$.
fields.question: Can hyperbolic color codes achieve both a constant encoding rate and a code distance scaling polynomially with the number of physical qubits?
fields.prior: Hyperbolic color codes had distance scaling at most logarithmically $O(\log n)$ in two dimensions (Guth & Lubotzky 2014) or constant distance $d=4$ (Lavasani & Barkeshli 2024); hyperbolic toric codes achieved constant rate and polynomial distance in four dimensions (Guth & Lubotzky 2014).
fields.limits: Applies to closed arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds in dimension $D\ge 4$. No polynomial-time decoder combining a finite threshold with polynomial decoding radius is provided.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Overview of the construction and main results of this work. (a) Starting from an arbitrary triangulation of a closed hyperbolic manifold, we obtain a colex by barycentric subdivision, which ensures the required vertex colorability for defining a color code (Sec. III ). (b) To derive a lower bound on the distance of the resulting hyperbolic color code, we transform the color code into a collection of associated toric codes using restriction maps and show that the color-code distance is bounded from below by the distances of these toric codes (Sec. IV ). (c) We explicitly determine the scaling of the number of logical qubits $k$ and the code distance $d$ with the number of physical qubits $n$ , where $D$ denotes the dimension of the underlying hyperbolic space and $i$ the type index of the color code. The Betti-number bounds determine the scaling of $k$ , while the systolic bounds, together with the result in (b), yield a polynomial lower bound on $d$ . The exponents $\delta(i,D)$ and $\gamma(i,D)$ in these polynomial lower bounds depend only on the code type $i$ and the dimension $D$ (Sec. V ).
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic workflow showing barycentric subdivision of triangulated hyperbolic manifolds into colexes, mapping to toric codes via restriction maps to lower-bound distance, and resulting scaling bounds for logical qubits $k$ and distance $d$.

fields.result: Simulates noisy preparation of logical magic states via an equivalent Clifford circuit in polynomial time and space, with no dependence on stabilizer or Pauli rank. Validated on magic state cultivation up to fault distance $f=7$.
fields.question: Can noisy preparation circuits for third-level Clifford-hierarchy logical magic states under circuit-level Pauli errors be simulated exactly in classical polynomial time?
fields.prior: Existing rank-decomposition algorithms scale exponentially with target-state stabilizer or Pauli rank, and Clifford proxies (such as $S|+\rangle$ instead of $T|+\rangle$) yield unverified approximations.
fields.limits: Restricted to circuit-level Pauli noise models and states satisfying the algebraic Clifford-stabilizer commutation criteria. Statistical uncertainty remains for extremely low logical error rates ($f=7$) due to Monte Carlo sampling costs.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Comparison of the logical error rate and acceptance rate for the $f=3$ fold-transversal magic state cultivation obtained using state-vector and the proposed Clifford-stabilizer simulations. The number of Monte Carlo samples is $10^{8}$ . (a) Logical error rate. (b) Acceptance rate. The insets show the corresponding differences of the values from the two simulation methods as functions of the number of Monte Carlo samples at the physical error rate $p=10^{-3}$ . The differences are computed as state-vector simulation minus Clifford-stabilizer simulation.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate and acceptance rate versus physical error rate $p$ for $f=3$ magic state cultivation. Clifford-stabilizer simulation matches exact state-vector simulation across all values of $p$.

fields.result: Defines a taxonomy of 7 structural primitives for quantum programs and presents an open benchmark suite in the `jeff` exchange format to compile structured programs without unrolling.
fields.question: How can quantum compilation representations and tools be adapted to support and optimize dynamic and structured algorithms without unrolling them into flat straight-line circuits?
fields.prior: Compiling flat unrolled circuits scales polynomially or exponentially with problem size; some classical and emerging quantum IRs show constant compilation scaling.
fields.limits: Support across current software tools is fragmented; dynamically-bounded loops fail at parsing in Qiskit and depend on backend profiles in QIR.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 1: Preserving program structure can enable constant compilation times, even when the problem instance size increases. On the other hand, unrolling loops generally leads to polynomial or even exponentially-increasing program size. Programs used for this comparison were generated using mqt-cc [ 25 ] . See section IV for details on benchmark programs.
fields.figure_gloss: Compilation time and program size as a function of problem instance size, contrasting unrolled circuits with structure-preserving representations.

fields.result: Recursive code doubling with mid-circuit qubit recycling yields single-output state distillation protocols at any Clifford level $r$ and distance $d$ requiring a constant number of active logical qubits independent of $d$, producing a new $111 \to 1$ distance-7 $|T\rangle$ protocol.
fields.question: Can distillation protocols for diagonal magic states at arbitrary Clifford levels and arbitrary error distances be constructed with a constant number of logical qubits via qubit recycling?
fields.limits: Restricted to diagonal states under $Z$-type rotation errors assuming free lower-level Clifford operations; two-output extension achieves only bounded support scaling $s^\star(P^{(r,d,2)}) \le d^{r-1}$ rather than constant support.

fields.result: Equalizing cumulative state-derived hardness rather than physical time improves low-energy sampling probabilities by 22% to over 100,000% under matched circuit depths and measurement budgets across systems up to 156 qubits.
fields.question: How should finite quantum computational resources be allocated along the trajectory of a quantum algorithm without altering physical hardware or requiring full spectral gap reconstruction?
fields.prior: Linear-ramp QAOA schedules allocate computational layers uniformly along physical time.
fields.limits: Surrogate classical training relies on MCMC mixing and representation accuracy without guaranteed spectral-gap recovery; tested on fixed one-dimensional paths for sparse QUBO instances via offline schedule freezing rather than dynamic online feedback.
tools: QAOA circuits on IBM quantum processors
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: State-Proxy Equalization and Adaptive Algorithmic Control (A2C). a , A quantum state $|\psi(s)\rangle$ evolves along a normalized trajectory $s\in[0,1]$ , where the computational hardness $r(s)$ varies according to the local quantum dynamics. The trajectory is partitioned into $p$ computational intervals $\{[s_{\ell-1},s_{\ell}]\}_{\ell=1}^{p}$ . b , Variational formulation of the optimal computational allocation. Theorem 1 shows that the optimal computational coordinate is obtained by cumulative state-proxy equalization, leading to equal accumulated hardness in every computational interval. c , Geometric interpretation of the State-Proxy Equalization principle. Instead of equalizing physical time, the optimal schedule equalizes cumulative computational hardness, $\int_{s_{\ell-1}}^{s_{\ell}}r(s)\,\mathrm{d}s=\frac{1}{p}\int_{0}^{1}r(s)\,\mathrm{d}s,\qquad\ell=1,\ldots,p.$ d , Continuous adaptive warp. The cumulative hardness defines a monotone computational coordinate $u(s)$ and its inverse warp $s=w(u)$ , which concentrates computational effort in dynamically difficult regions while preserving the total computational budget. e , Illustration of discretized evolution. Compared with the uniform linear-ramp schedule (LR-QAOA), A2C reallocates the same number of circuit layers towards regions of higher computational hardness without increasing circuit depth. f , Empirical improvement in sampling probability. Under identical computational budgets, adaptive scheduling consistently increases the probability of sampling exact and near-optimal solutions for representative quantum optimization problems with $N=5$ (depth $p=8,12$ ) and $N=50,156$ ( $p=12,18,20$ ) qubits.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic and empirical summary of Adaptive Algorithmic Control, showing how the cumulative computational hardness reallocates fixed circuit layers along the normalized trajectory to boost ground- and low-energy sampling probabilities across varying qubit counts.

fields.result: Constant-error circuit complexity $\mathcal{C}_{1/2}(U_T)$ for all-to-all 2-local random unitary circuits grows as $\Omega(T/\log T)$ for all $2 \leq T \leq 4^n$.
fields.question: Does a typical random sequence of local quantum gates admit a substantially shorter implementation for constant approximation error throughout pre-saturation times?
fields.prior: Was $\Omega(T / (n \log T))$ derived via spectral gap methods (Brandão-Harrow 2026).
fields.limits: Applies to all-to-all 2-local Haar-random unitaries; relies on operator-norm and Hilbert-Schmidt distance approximations without explicit $n$-dependence in lower bound.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Schematic decomposition of the circuit into $R$ blocks, each consisting of a mixing segment of length $m$ followed by an active segment of length $d$ . Thus, the total number of gates is $T=(m+d)R$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of circuit partitioning into $R$ blocks of length $m+d$ (mixing segment $m$ and active segment $d$) used to control gate variations.

fields.result: Total Boolean functions exhibit quantum versus randomized communication complexity separations of $\mathrm{Q}^2(f)=\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ versus $\mathrm{R}(f)=\widetilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$ with 2 quantum messages, and $\mathrm{Q}^{2\lceil k/2\rceil+1}(f)=\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ versus $\mathrm{R}(f)=\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{1-1/k})$ for any integer $k \ge 2$.
fields.question: How large can the exponential separation between quantum and randomized communication complexity be for total Boolean functions?
fields.prior: was $\mathrm{R}(f)=\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{1/6})$ for two-message quantum protocols (Gavinsky 2026)
fields.limits: Worst-case bounded error at most $1/3$; quantum protocols assume no prior entanglement; asymptotic in input length $n$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Proof of Theorem 4.1 , following [ 3 , Figure 1] . Red marks Lemma 9 , which replaces Claim 22; all other claims are from [ 3 ] .

fields.result: Hadamard matrix transformations partition into 6 to 97 isomorphism classes distinguished by degree polynomials, with simple cycle counts exhibiting discrete plateau ceilings at 84, 412, and 2365 cycles.
fields.question: How do graph-theoretic topological invariants scale across input-state superpositions for real versus complex Hadamard operators?
fields.limits: Analysis restricted to matrix orders up to 16 (4 qubits) and largely order 8 due to combinatorial scaling; evaluated across a dataset of 15 matrices.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: Simple cycle counts across sorted isomorphism classes for representative Hadamard matrices ( $M001$ – $M004$ , $M008$ – $M010$ , and $MS002$ ).
fields.figure_gloss: Simple cycle counts plotted across sorted isomorphism classes for eight Hadamard matrices, demonstrating convergence to quantized maximums at 84, 412, and 2365 simple cycles.

fields.result: Truncated hybrid tensor networks compress cross-partition Schmidt bonds to dimension $\chi$, achieving readout sampling overhead $O(\chi^{2B}/\varepsilon^{2})$ across $B$ cuts instead of circuit knitting's exponential growth in remote gate counts.
fields.question: How can distributed quantum simulation under Trotter evolution avoid the exponential gate-sampling overhead across subsystem cuts when cross-cut correlations are bounded?
fields.prior: Circuit knitting scaled with single-cut factor $(1+2|\sin\theta_{ij}|)^{2}$, yielding sampling cost exponential in total remote gate count.
fields.limits: Validated by classical numerical simulation. Requires estimating Gram matrix and applying Case 2/3 contractions. Shot overhead remains exponential in cut count $B$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Orthogonalization and connector truncation at a partition cut. (a) Hybrid sites are orthonormalized along the cut index through the Gram matrix and mapping tensor $\mathcal{R}$ . (b) The classical connecting tensor $\bm{\lambda}_{\perp}$ undergoes singular value decomposition. Its nonzero singular values equal the Schmidt coefficients of the bipartite state across the cut. Truncation keeps the largest $\chi$ singular values and the matching blocks of $U$ and $V$ . After contracting them into the sites, the cut index of $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}$ (and likewise of $\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}$ ) is reduced from dimension $d$ to $\chi$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Gram orthogonalization via mapping tensor $\mathcal{R}$ on cut indices, followed by singular-value decomposition of connector $\bm{\lambda}_{\perp}$ to retain the top $\chi$ Schmidt modes.

fields.result: Real-space renormalization yields a closed-form analytical expression for stabilizer Rényi entropies (quantum magic) in the low-energy, large-distance regime of a class of spin Hamiltonians.
fields.question: How do stabilizer Rényi entropies evolve under coarse-graining across different quantum phases in spin chains?
fields.limits: Valid specifically in the low-energy, large-distance regime.

fields.result: Simulated liquid-state proton NMR spectrum of 1,2-di-tert-butyl-diphosphane on trapped-ion hardware across 70 Trotter steps and circuit depth 1442, reproducing methyl peak at 1.35 ppm and the weak double peak at 4.1 ppm.
fields.question: Can digital quantum hardware accurately reproduce the nontrivial NMR spectral features of classically challenging multi-spin molecules?
fields.prior: Failed to reproduce the distinctive 3.9–4.3 ppm double-peak structure on 22-qubit IBM superconducting and IonQ trapped-ion hardware (prior hardware demonstration).
fields.limits: Simulated effective 21-spin model rather than full 22-spin Hamiltonian, removing two outer proton peaks. Maximum evolution time limited to 29.4 ms (spectral resolution ~0.07 ppm), preventing resolution of ~0.01 ppm fine splittings.
tools: Quantinuum System Model H2-1 trapped-ion quantum computer
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : Comparison of diphosphane NMR spectra obtained from simulations on the Quantinuum H2-1 trapped-ion quantum computer and from classical reference calculations. The H2-1 results are based on the projected Hamiltonian used in the hardware implementation, whereas the classical reference spectrum was calculated using the full 22-spin diphosphane Hamiltonian. Panels (a) and (b) show the classical spectrum with small line broadening, resolving the fine spectral structure, while panels (c) and (d) use larger line broadening to match the resolution of the quantum-hardware simulation [ 2 , 6 , 30 ] . The H2-1 hardware spectrum has been plotted with a pointwise bootstrap uncertainty band of width $\pm 2\sigma$ to illustrate the sensitivity of the spectrum to finite-shot sampling noise.
fields.figure_gloss: Simulated proton NMR spectrum (intensity versus chemical shift in ppm) comparing Quantinuum H2-1 hardware execution against full classical reference and time-truncated classical reference spectra.

fields.result: Coherent phase reference transferred from a Josephson voltage standard via superconducting order parameter increases ICTA averaged gain by 14 dB to ~27 dB and achieves degenerate phase-sensitive amplification.
fields.question: How can a stable phase reference be provided to dc-biased Josephson photonics devices to suppress voltage-noise-induced linewidth broadening and enable phase-coherent parametric operation?
fields.prior: Unstabilized ICTA had maximum gain of 13 dB, ~1.5 photon input-referred noise, and lacked degenerate phase-sensitive features due to phase diffusion across >2π within ~30 ns.
fields.limits: Millikelvin operation with low RF power (-65 dBm to -40 dBm). Resonator linewidth Γ/2π ≈ 1.2 GHz. Squeezing deforms into an S-shape at 31 dB gain due to amplifier saturation.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 2: Comparison of ICTA without and with JVS stabilization. All data were acquired at a constant ICTA critical current $I_{c}\approx$80\text{\,}\mathrm{nA}$$ . (a) Two-dimensional gain map of the unstabilized ICTA (JVS RF tone off) as a function of signal frequency ( $f_{\text{S}}$ ) and voltage bias expressed as Josephson frequency ( $f_{\text{dc}}$ ); gain is maximal near the $LC$ resonance ( $f_{0}=$6\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$$ ). (b) Corresponding two-dimensional gain map with the JVS activated (JVS RF tone $f_{\text{JVS}}=$12\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$$ , $P_{\text{JVS}}=$-65\text{\,}\mathrm{d}\mathrm{B}\mathrm{m}$$ ), locking the actual Josephson frequency at $12\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$ over a $\pm$50\text{\,}\mathrm{MHz}$$ bias range. (c) Cut of panel (a) at $f_{\text{dc}}=$12\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$$ showing gain of up to $13\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}$ with a bandwidth of $\sim$80\text{\,}\mathrm{MHz}$$ (red curve) and an input-referred noise of $\sim 1.5$ photons (purple curve), no particular feature is observed at degeneracy $f_{\text{S}}=f_{\text{dc}}/2$ . (d) Cut of panel (b) at $f_{\text{dc}}=f_{\text{JVS}}=$12\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$$ showing average gain of up to $\sim$27\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}$$ (orange curve). Non-averaged traces (gray and blue) show strong phase dependance of gain. The non-averaged input-referred noise (purple curve) is close to the quantum limit of 1 photon near degeneracy and $0.5$ photons at the degeneracy, corresponding to the black gain curve in panel (d).
fields.figure_gloss: Gain and noise versus frequency for unstabilized and JVS-stabilized ICTA. Activating the JVS at 12 GHz locks the Josephson frequency over a ±50 MHz bias range, boosts peak gain from 13 dB to 27 dB, and reaches input noise of 0.5 photons at degeneracy.

fields.result: Unprotected CZ gate for capacitively coupled soft $0$-$\pi$ qubits achieves simulated fidelity of approximately $99.9\%$ at gate time of approximately $160\text{ ns}$.
fields.question: Can an unprotected two-qubit gate with high fidelity and short duration be designed for experimentally realizable soft $0$-$\pi$ superconducting qubits?
fields.limits: Simulated in zero-disorder limit with identical circuit components; uses phenomenological noise model with reduced $60$-level Hilbert subspace.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 9: CZ gate performance. (a) Gate error ( $1-F$ ) versus gate time $t_{g}$ , using optimized pulse parameters for each $t_{g}$ . Solid lines show errors for unitary (closed-system) evolution, while dashed lines include decoherence with $T_{1}=T_{\phi}=T\in\{3,30,170\}\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ . The star marks the operating point illustrated in fig. 8 . We use a reduced model with 60 states to simulate this gate. See section E.2 for additional modeling details. (b) Coherent gate error as a function of the drive-detuning deviation $\Delta\delta_{1}=\delta_{1}-\delta_{1,\mathrm{opt}}$ at $t_{g}=182$ ns, with the drive amplitude fixed at its optimized value. (c) Coherent gate error as a function of the relative drive-amplitude deviation $\Delta A_{1}/A_{\mathrm{opt}}=(A_{1}-A_{1,\mathrm{opt}})/A_{1,\mathrm{opt}}$ at $t_{g}=182$ ns, with the detuning fixed at its optimized value. Full pulse parameters for both highlighted pulses are given in table 4 .
fields.figure_gloss: Gate error ($1-F$) versus gate time $t_g$ for the CZ gate under closed-system unitary evolution and open-system noise models with coherence times $T_1=T_\phi=T\in\{3, 30, 170\}\,\mu\text{s}$.

fields.result: Proximity-induced superconducting gap reaches up to 80 $\mathrm{\mu eV}$ in bilayer graphene contacted by $\mathrm{NbSe}_2$ and follows a dwell-time-limited ballistic decay $\Delta^*(x) = \pi\hbar v / (4x)$ with $v \approx 5.2 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{m/s}$, remaining detectable over distances exceeding 1 $\mu$m.
fields.question: How does the proximity-induced superconducting gap decay spatially in a gate-defined bilayer graphene channel coupled to a layered superconductor?
fields.limits: Base temperature $\approx 80\,\mathrm{mK}$; out-of-plane critical magnetic field $B_c \approx 8\,\mathrm{mT}$; effective velocity $v$ extracted near the flattened band edge with order-unity uncertainty.
tools: bilayer graphene encapsulated in hexagonal boron nitride
electrostatic split- and finger-gate quantum dot definition
Coulomb blockade and finite-bias tunneling spectroscopy
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: (a) Differential conductance as function of source-drain voltage $V_{\mathrm{sd}}$ and finger gate voltage $\Delta V_{\mathrm{G{\it i}}}$ ( $i=1-4$ ) with respect to the center of the Coulomb diamond for the four different finger gates $1-4$ , respectively (see labels 1 to 4 in the sub-panels and inset in panel (b)). (b) Proximity-induced gap $\Delta^{*}$ as function of $x$ , the distance from the edge of the NbSe 2 flake, extracted (i) from the Coulomb diamond measurements (dashed lines in panel (a)) and (ii) from tunneling spectroscopy measurements. fields.result: Surveys discrete- and continuous-variable optical quantum computing architectures, measurement-based cluster-state models, and non-universal algorithms (boson sampling, VQEs, QML).
fields.question: How do optical encoding schemes and computing architectures compare across universal and non-universal quantum platforms?
fields.limits: Photonic scaling is constrained by weak single-photon nonlinearities, probabilistic gate generation, and optical propagation losses.

fields.result: Multipoint coupling of giant atom provides additional destructive interference paths, enabling simultaneous unconventional photon blockade in two and three coupled cavities with driven first cavity. Point-atom configuration cannot produce simultaneous unconventional photon blockade.
fields.question: Can multipoint coupling of a giant atom enable simultaneous unconventional photon blockade across multiple coupled cavities?
fields.limits: Weak driving regime ($F \ll \kappa$), equal cavity and atomic dissipations $\kappa_1=\kappa_2=\kappa_3=\gamma \equiv \kappa$, theoretical model without experimental verification.

fields.result: Dispersive Rydberg atom chains act as coherent quantum buses to mediate effective quasi-all-to-all interactions between data units via virtual excitations, analytically derived using Green's-function continued fractions.
fields.question: Can a Rydberg atom array provide a stationary quantum bus to mediate coherent nonlocal connectivity between distant data units?
fields.limits: Off-resonant dispersive regime with $J_\mu \ll \min_k |E_k|$; validated with Gaussian positional uncertainty $\sigma = 0.02~\mu\text{m}$ and Rydberg lifetimes up to $T = 77~\text{K}$.

fields.result: Two-level giant atom coupled to two waveguides via two points with tunable phase differences $\theta_a,\theta_b$ acts as a programmable 50:50 beam splitter, yielding a Hong–Ou–Mandel dip and continuous tuning between two-photon bunching and antibunching.
fields.question: Can a giant atom with tunable coupling phases serve as a programmable Hong–Ou–Mandel interferometer and enable coupling-phase quantum parameter estimation?
fields.limits: Theoretical model assuming identical coupled cavities, two-level approximation for the giant atom, rotating-wave approximation, and lossless wave-packet propagation.

fields.result: Two-qubit and multi-qubit controlled-phase gates $C(\varphi)$ can be implemented in optically trapped polar molecules via an ancilla-assisted dark-state mechanism driven solely by two smooth adiabatic microwave $\pi$ pulses on the ancilla.
fields.question: How can high-fidelity entangling quantum gates be realized in optically trapped polar molecules without suffering from motional decoherence or Rydberg-state decay?
fields.limits: Theoretical and numerical simulation; assumes zero rotational Zeeman effect or weak rotational Zeeman effect relative to nuclear spin Zeeman effect (evaluated for $^{23}\text{Na}^{133}\text{Cs}$ at $B=2\text{ G}$); requires specific tweezer alignment to suppress inter-data molecule DDI.

The peak value of $\Omega_{\mu}$ in Eq. ( 24 ) is $J_{\text{at}}/(4\hbar)$ , where the DDI between the a and t molecules is $J_{\text{at}}/h=1$ kHz. fields.result: In transversely driven Fermi gas inside an optical cavity, bare attraction triggers direct transition into an intertwined charge-density-wave plus pair-density-wave superradiant phase, whereas repulsive interaction separates density-wave ordering from finite-momentum pairing until higher pump power.
fields.question: How preexisting superfluidity and photon-pair coupling govern the sequence and nature of self-organized spatial and pairing orders in a degenerate Fermi gas?
fields.limits: Zero temperature ($T=0$), effective 1D geometry along cavity axis, dispersive regime (large single-atom and molecular detunings $\Delta_e, \Delta_B$), mean-field cavity treatment.

fields.result: For $d=5$ regular surface-code fold-transversal cultivation, $|Tangle$ logical error rates match $|Sangle$ Clifford proxy error rates across the tested noise range. A rotated surface-code scheme achieves $\sim 1.3\times$ lower expected space-time cost while reaching $10^{-9}$ logical error rate.
fields.question: What is the exact non-Clifford performance and logical error rate of fold-transversal magic state cultivation schemes on surface codes?
fields.prior: Color-code cultivation (Gidney et al.) showed a $7\times$ to $30\times$ higher logical error rate for $|T\rangle$ state cultivation compared to the $|S\rangle$ Clifford proxy.
fields.limits: Depolarising SD6 circuit noise model, post-selection on all syndrome detectors and final noiseless decoding, classical simulation on commodity CPU.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Performance of cultivation schemes under uniform depolarising noise for $\ket{S}$ and $\ket{T}$ , at output code distance $d=3$ and $5$ . Reg 3/5 are based on Sahay et al. [ 41 ] circuits, which make use of the regular surface code fold-transversal S gate. Rot 3/5 and Rot 3×4 are circuits proposed in this work, based on the partially fault-tolerant fold-transversal S gate of the rotated surface code. The $\ket{S}$ results are obtained with Stim, the $\ket{T}$ results with CAMPS simulations. These results are obtained with the addition of the final noiseless syndrome extraction in the post-selection. Except for the $\ket{S}$ results, the three points from each curve are obtained with the same samples through subset sampling and are thus not statistically independent. Error bars span the values whose likelihood is within a factor of 100 of the maximum ( $\sim 3\sigma$ ) in likelihood relative to the maximum-likelihood estimate, see Appendix D .

fields.result: Exact logical error rates for magic state cultivation computed without Monte Carlo sampling; $P_{\mathrm{L}}^{(5)}(p=10^{-3}) = 3.32842537\dots \times 10^{-9}$ with series expansion $P_{\mathrm{L}}^{(5)}(x) = \frac{574}{375}x^3 + \frac{972959741}{810000}x^4 + O(x^5)$ for $x=p/(1-p)$.
fields.question: What are the exact post-selected logical error rates and acceptance probabilities of magic state cultivation circuits across all fault orders using actual $T$ gates instead of sampling with $S$-gate proxies?
fields.limits: Standard uniform circuit-level depolarising noise at parameter $p$. Excludes escape, grafting, and decoding stages; logical readout is assumed noiseless.
tools: Chinese remainder theorem over modular primes

fields.result: Flagged double-check circuits eliminate malignant hook errors in magic state cultivation, suppressing pre-escape logical error rate from $\mathcal{O}(p^3)$ to $\mathcal{O}(p^5)$ and achieving a 4.9$\times$ error rate improvement at $p = 10^{-3}$ for a 1.36$\times$ attempt overhead.
fields.question: Why does $T$-state cultivation suffer higher logical error rates and lower fault distances than $S$-state cultivation under circuit-level noise, and how can the full fault distance be restored?
fields.prior: Unflagged distance-3 (distance-5) $T$-state cultivation degraded to fault distance 2 (fault distance 3), while $S$-state cultivation retained full fault distance 3 (fault distance 5).
fields.limits: Evaluated under standard circuit-level depolarising noise at error rate $p = 10^{-3}$; applies to fixed logical-qubit count with physical qubit count $n$.
tools: analytic propagation of Pauli hook errors into coherent Clifford errors

fields.result: Linear quantum graph framework automates design of heralded linear optical circuits for multipartite entangled states, producing an $N=4$ cluster state circuit with 26 beam splitters (10 initial photons).
fields.question: How can heralded linear optical circuits for arbitrary multipartite entangled quantum states be designed systematically rather than via state-specific manual trial and error?
fields.prior: Generating an $N=4$ cluster state required 45 beam splitters with 9 photons at a success probability of $2.05\times 10^{-3}$ (Banchi et al. 2024 / Ref. [16]).
fields.limits: Unweighted initial graph search; ideal photon-number-resolving detectors; computational scaling grows exponentially with ancilla mode count $M$.
tools: reduced density matrix spectral signature matching

fields.result: Proves equivalence between quantum decomposable randomized encodings (QDRE) and quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM). Every $n$-to-$m$-qubit channel has an $m$-qubit quantum communication QPSM with exponential entanglement, while with $\le c n$ pre-shared entanglement, communication is bounded by $\Omega(n)$.
fields.question: Is the linear dependence of quantum randomized encoding size on circuit size inherent, or can it be characterized more tightly via pre-shared entanglement and communication complexity?
fields.prior: Prior QDRE constructions scaled encoding size linearly with circuit size $|Q|$.
fields.limits: Small quantum communication protocols for general channels require pre-shared entanglement exponential in $n$. Bounded linear entanglement yields an unavoidable worst-case $\Omega(n)$ communication/encoding lower bound.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Pauli-Port Complementarity Protocol. The protocol is non-interactive. Teleportation arrows denote local teleportation measurements using pre-shared entanglement, not communication between Alice and Bob.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of the Pauli-Port Complementarity protocol showing non-interactive local teleportation using pre-shared entanglement before quantum and classical messages are forwarded to the referee.

fields.result: Approximates Lindbladian evolution to diamond-norm error $\varepsilon$ using $O\!\left(\tau+\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log(e+\log(1/\varepsilon)/\tau)}\right)$ oracle queries for $\tau=(\alpha_H+\alpha_B^2)t$, matching the Hamiltonian simulation lower bound.
fields.question: What is the optimal query complexity of simulating Lindbladian dynamics as a function of evolution time and target precision?
fields.prior: Was $O(\tau\log(\tau/\varepsilon)/\log\log(\tau/\varepsilon))$ queries for general Lindbladians (Li and Wang 2023).
fields.limits: Requires block encoding of Hamiltonian and projected unitary encoding of stacked jump operators. Time-dependent case requires Lipschitz continuity and coherent time-indexed oracle access.

fields.result: Passive syndrome-history distributions are exactly symmetric under coherent-rotation sign reversal $R_X(-	heta) = R_X(	heta)^\dagger$, but signed terminal logical calibration resolves the ambiguity to certify QEC recovery updates. An evaluator using confidence sets and drift bounds blocks 100% of tested harmful AI advice proposals under valid drift premises while accepting 60 of 96 beneficial updates with a channel-specific derivative bound.
fields.question: Can an attacker turn influence over an AI adviser into a harmful quantum error-correction recovery update?
fields.limits: Simulated evaluation assuming trusted records, evaluator, clock, and bounded noise drift rate $v$; violating the drift premise permits harmful updates.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: The same passive record can conceal opposite recovery consequences. The passive-history theorem extends the sign blindness to every history length. (b) Terminal logical measurements distinguish the signs: each circle or square is one of two independently simulated 8192-memory acquisitions at each angle, with a 99% binomial interval. (c–e) Independent estimates of excess recovery infidelity for every Qwen proposal under honest advice, misleading advice, and a sign flip that violates the drift bound. The same 12 calibration workloads are used in all three panels. Filled circles mark full-safeguard acceptance; open circles show the independently estimated consequence of applying a rejected proposal. Rejection retains the incumbent, giving zero deployed excess risk. Colors identify benefit or harm established beyond $\pm 0.001$ . Supplemental Fig. S23 includes both controllers and every rule.

fields.result: Presents Qurrium, a Qiskit-based Python library implementing classical shadow and Haar-measure randomized measurement protocols to estimate purity, second-order Rényi entropy, Pauli expectation values, and asymmetric unbiased state overlap $\hat{f}_{2}(\rho,\rho^{\prime})$.
fields.question: How can randomized measurement protocols like classical shadows be implemented in a native Python/Qiskit workflow for both end-to-end execution and standalone hardware data analysis?
fields.limits: Demonstrated on a two-qubit superconducting processor and noiseless 6-to-8 qubit circuit simulations; currently lacks integrated real-time end-to-end hardware execution.

fields.result: Translating quantum rotation encoding and circuit interactions into classical trigonometric embeddings and gated mixing yields 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with 45.7M parameters and 11.5 GFLOPs. On a 1-epoch benchmark, QiT runs 882–997× faster than a 4-qubit PennyLane simulator while running 1.58–1.76× slower than standard classical ViT.
fields.question: Can quantum-motivated structural motifs like periodic angle encodings and multiplicative interactions be realized as scalable, fully classical Transformer operations for visual recognition without quantum hardware?
fields.prior: 4-qubit simulated quantum Transformer in PennyLane, which is 882–997× slower on wall-clock time in 1-epoch testing.
fields.limits: All point estimates without repeated seeds or uncertainty intervals. No controlled component ablations against parameter-matched classical ViTs. Emulates functional motifs without physical entanglement or quantum speedup.

fields.result: Four matrix product state (MPS) extensions of TEBD integrate the 1D Lindblad equation: vectorized TEBD, positive-operator-preserving purification TEBD, quantum trajectories, and quantum state diffusion.
fields.question: How do standard MPS-based time-evolution algorithms compare in accuracy, positivity preservation, and computational cost when solving Lindbladian dynamics of 1D open quantum systems?
fields.limits: One-dimensional quantum lattice systems. Evaluated on an exactly solvable free fermion chain benchmark.

fields.result: Evaluates the complete Hadamard-reduced sixth-order time-convolutionless master-equation generator time series in $O(N_t\log^2 N_t)$ operations and $O(N_t)$ storage at fixed system dimension.
fields.question: How can the two remaining ordered integrals in the sixth-order time-convolutionless master-equation generator be evaluated faster than direct quadrature?
fields.prior: Direct quadrature of the Hadamard-reduced TCL6 generator requires $O(N_t^3)$ operations at fixed system dimension.
fields.limits: Stationary centered Gaussian bath, finite-dimensional system, single Hermitian coupling operator, and dynamics within the perturbative TCL validity regime.

fields.result: Formulation of lattice detector operators via continuity current $j_{j}^{E}$ reproduces continuum energy-flow observables $\mathcal{E}(\hat{n})$ and matches $2$d Ising CFT predictions at criticality.
fields.question: Can asymptotic energy-flow detector observables be formulated and computed quantitatively on finite lattice spin systems?
fields.limits: Exploratory calculations on 1D spin chains ($N=24, 48$ sites); results retain finite-bandwidth and packet-preparation systematic dependence.

fields.result: Evaluates high-order graph lattice sums for long-range interacting quantum models deterministically, reducing compute times from tens of thousands of core-hours down to 10 minutes on a single core for a 10th-order series (7,136 graphs, up to 30-dimensional sums) on a 4,096-point 3D momentum grid.
fields.question: How can the high-dimensional oscillatory graph lattice sums in linked-cluster perturbation theory of long-range interacting quantum lattice models be computed without stochastic Monte Carlo methods?

fields.result: Reformulates non-relativistic quantum electrodynamics as a density-functional theory over combined internal and external Maxwell sources, yielding a Moreau--Yosida regularized universal functional that removes the ultraviolet cutoff non-perturbatively via a Kohn--Sham construction.
fields.question: How can equilibrium non-relativistic quantum electrodynamics be formulated non-perturbatively as an exact, mathematically regularized density-functional theory without unphysical representability issues and with the ultraviolet cutoff removed?
fields.limits: Equilibrium ground states in Coulomb gauge. Requires confining potentials (e.g. harmonic) or periodic boundaries to break translational invariance.

fields.result: Coaxial cable mediating multi-mode $ZZ$ interaction achieves remote adiabatic controlled-Z gate with optimized infidelity of $4.71\times 10^{-7}$ and 376.7 ns duration for 30-cm cable length without tunable couplers.
fields.question: Can an adiabatic CZ gate be realized across a remote multi-mode coaxial cable coupling architecture with low leakage and high-fidelity conditional phase accumulation?

fields.result: Perpendicular electric field $E_{\perp}$ tunes exciton-dispersion anisotropy to produce linear transverse exciton transport in monolayer and twisted bilayer TiSiCO, with bilayer transverse conductivities reaching several $1/h$ at $100\,\mathrm{K}$.
fields.question: Can perpendicular electric fields in valley-layer-coupled 2D materials control exciton dispersion anisotropy to generate and tune linear transverse exciton transport?
fields.limits: Zero-Berry-curvature limit; neglects side-jump and skew-scattering high-temperature disorder processes.

fields.result: Measured total thermodynamic entropy of a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule across the transition from isolated dots to a merged single dot via single-charge-sensor spectroscopy, resolving thermal suppression of antibonding and triplet states as interdot tunneling increases.

fields.question: How can neutral-atom arrays be efficiently and directionally coupled to on-chip waveguide networks as scalable, indistinguishable single-photon sources?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation assuming $C_6 = 8\text{ GHz}/\mu\text{m}^6$, sub-wavelength spacing $a < 0.5\lambda_0$, instantaneous lossless mapping from Rydberg state $|r\rangle$ to $|s\rangle$, and neglecting thermal motion or laser field distortion.

fields.result: Bidirectional middle-out CNOT cascade prepares surface-code logical states in depth $(d{+}3)/2$ with fault distance $d$ in the protected error direction, requiring $\approx\frac{3}{4}(d{+}3)$ collective AOD shuttles and $\approx\frac{1}{4}(d{+}3)$ row pickups.
fields.question: How can unitary stabilizer-expanding surface-code state preparation be adapted to minimize depth and shuttling constraints on neutral-atom processors?
fields.prior: Unitary single-pivot preparation was $3(d{-}1)$ CZ layers and $4(d{-}1)$ shuttles; unidirectional cascade was $d$ CZ layers and $\approx\frac{3}{2}d$ shuttles.
fields.limits: Fault-tolerant only in protected direction (conjugate direction allows weight-2 errors requiring an intermediate QEC round). Circuit-level numerical simulation up to $10^{7}$ shots under calibrated device noise, not physical hardware measurement.

fields.result: Neutral atom arrays scale past $10^{3}$ physical qubits and provide $>99.5\%$ two-qubit gate fidelities, enabling continuous-time Hamiltonian simulation, QUBO/MWIS graph optimisation, and transversal logical operations for quantum chemistry and materials science.
fields.question: How do neutral atom quantum computing platforms address simulation and optimisation challenges in materials science and quantum chemistry across analogue and digital paradigms?
fields.limits: Materials and chemistry applications require utility-scale hardware ($10^{5}$ physical qubits, $>10^{6}$ T-gates), far exceeding current device sizes. Single-species mid-circuit readout causes light scattering and crosstalk.

fields.result: For stabilizer codes encoding $k\geq 3$ logical qubits, largest logical group achievable via automorphisms is generated by all addressable $S$ and $\mathrm{CX}$ gates, requiring $n=\Theta(2^k)$ physical qubits ($n=2^k-1$ exactly). By contrast, all addressable diagonal Clifford gates require only $n=k(k+1)/2 = \Theta(k^2)$ physical qubits via physical single-qubit Cliffords alone.
fields.question: What is the maximum logical gate group achievable by automorphism gates on stabilizer codes, and what is the minimum physical-qubit cost needed to realize it?
fields.limits: Restricted to stabilizer codes (with refinements for CSS and self-dual CSS codes); physical operations limited to single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations (extended to single-qubit diagonal gates for higher hierarchy levels).
tools: symplectic group and Clifford group classification

For scale, markers indicate $k=9$ on each curve when the corresponding point lies within the displayed range.
fields.figure_gloss: Gate group size as a function of the number of logical qubits $k$ across different gate implementations. Solid curves show automorphism, transversal, and permutation gate limits, while dotted lines show diagonal gate groups up to level $t$ of the Clifford hierarchy.

fields.result: Created QECirc (qecirc.com), an open, verified library providing standardized Stim and OpenQASM implementations for quantum error correction circuits spanning encoders, state preparation, and logical gates.
fields.question: How can quantum error correction circuits scattered across papers and ad-hoc repositories be standardized, verified, and made interoperable?
fields.prior: Error Correction Zoo catalogs QEC code properties, but lacks concrete, format-agnostic implementation circuits.
fields.limits: Syndrome-extraction schedules and larger qLDPC code families such as bivariate-bicycle codes remain planned work.

fields.result: Defines scalable logical qubits and establishes a unified framework evaluating them across four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance.
fields.question: How to define, benchmark, and compare progress in fault-tolerant logical qubits for utility-scale quantum computing.
fields.limits: Conceptual/benchmarking framework; assumes fault-tolerant operations, real-time decoding, and scaling to hundreds or thousands of logical qubits.

fields.result: Proves general stabilizer qLDPC codes with distance $d_n = \Omega(\log n)$ have nonzero code capacity thresholds under local coherent noise, with logical diamond-distance error decaying as $\sup_U \varepsilon_n^{\star}(U,\eta) \le C\sqrt{n}e^{-cd_n}$ for optimal recovery and $\sup_U \varepsilon_n^{\rm MW}(U,\eta) \le \frac{2n}{\chi_{\rm MW}(1-\rho_{\rm MW})}\rho_{\rm MW}^{d_n}$ under minimum-weight decoding.
fields.question: Do general quantum LDPC codes admit rigorous nonzero error correction thresholds under coherent and general local noise?
fields.prior: Rigorous fault tolerance under coherent noise had been established for constant-rate qLDPC codes with linear distance $d = \Theta(n)$ (Fawzi et al. 2024), but not for sublinear distance codes such as topological or quantum expander codes.
fields.limits: Applies to code capacity model: noiseless syndrome measurements and recovery circuits following depth-$D$, bounded-support ($r$) local coherent or local CPTP noise.
tools: diamond norm bounds on complementary channels
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Schematic illustration of cluster resummation. (a) A configuration in Eq. ( 7 ) that contains two large components and several small components. Each large component provides a factor $t$ . (b) Differentiating with respect to $t$ is equivalent to marking each large component $C$ of $B$ in turn and removing its associated factor of $t$ . (c) The terms are grouped by the marked component $C$ , and $F_{C}$ is factored out. Summing the remaining terms, with their associated powers of $t$ , over all configurations $B\setminus C\subseteq W\setminus N_{W}[C]$ gives $\mathcal{T}_{W\setminus N_{W}[C]}(t)$ , yielding Eq. ( 8 ).
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of the cluster resummation technique, showing how differentiating with respect to the interpolation parameter $t$ marks a single connected large component while resumming all disconnected error configurations.

fields.result: Hybrid quantum repeater chains combining fast, multiplexable type-1 memories with long-coherence type-2 memories achieve higher end-to-end entanglement distribution rates than pure architectures of either platform alone, even when inter-platform gate errors are non-zero.
fields.question: How should heterogeneous quantum memory platforms and quantum error-correction capabilities be allocated along a repeater chain to maximize entanglement distribution rates under realistic hardware constraints?
fields.limits: Circuit-level noise model simulations; fixed inter-node spacing of $l_{0}=20\text{ km}$; independent logical error channels after physical combinatorial counting.
tools: Fault-tolerant stabilizer measurement via GHZ ancillae
Three-qubit repetition, Steane [[7,1,3]], and Shor [[9,1,3]] codes
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: (top) Entanglement distribution rate $R_{\infty}$ and (bottom) end-to-end fidelity as a function of total chain length $L=l_{0}(N_{2}-1)$ at fixed inter-node spacing $l_{0}=20$ km. $N_{2}$ is the total number of nodes. gate error rate for type-2 memories is fixed to $\varepsilon_{g}^{(2)}=10^{-4}$ and $p_{\ell}=0.01$ . fields.result: Constructed blind quantum computation (Blind PBC) requiring a quantum server of only $t$ qubits for an $n$-qubit circuit with $t$ non-Clifford $T$ gates, achieving perfect information-theoretic input secrecy with four-way random state preparation and a single $t$-qubit quantum communication step.
fields.question: How can blind quantum computation be performed while minimizing the required quantum processor size on the server?
fields.prior: Server size was $n+t$ qubits for single-instance communication or $n+1$ qubits with $t$ sequential communication rounds in quantum computing on encrypted data (QCED).
fields.limits: Hides computational basis input $\textbf{x}$ (or orthonormal stabilizer bases) but reveals circuit structure $C$. Qubit virtualization incurs classical sampling cost exponential in simulated virtual qubit count $k$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: (a) Pauli-based computation (PBC) and (b) Blind PBC, for a circuit $C$ with $t$ $T$ gates. Information flows from left to right; single (resp. double) lines denote quantum (resp. classical) information. Each protocol has three stages. (i) Preparation of an initial state. In Blind PBC, the client chooses secret random bits $c_{i},d_{i}\in\{0,1\}$ and applies rotations. (ii) Measurement of $t^{\prime}\leq t$ Pauli observables $Q_{j}$ , with outcomes $b_{j}\in\{0,1\}$ , selected adaptively by the classical PBC.Sel algorithm. In Blind PBC, the client runs PBC.Sel on a circuit $C^{*}_{\textbf{x}}$ derived from $C$ and her secret classical input x . (iii) Output of a sample from the desired distribution, determined by PBC.Sel . In Blind PBC, the client corrects PBC.Sel classically before returning the output.
fields.figure_gloss: Comparison of standard Pauli-based computation (a) with Blind PBC (b), illustrating state preparation with client random phase rotations $S^{c_i}Z^{d_i}$, adaptive Pauli observable measurement via client-side circuit modification $\mathsf{PBC.Sel}(C^*_{\textbf{x}})$, and output sample decoding.

fields.result: Realizes bounded finite impulse response (FIR) filtering on a quantum computer via a unitary state-space lattice decomposition without mid-circuit measurements or gain loss, demonstrated on $N=32$ samples with filter order $M=12$.
fields.question: How can discrete-time sample-based linear signal processing and FIR filters be implemented in a composable unitary quantum circuit without losing signal gain?
fields.prior: In prior quantum FIR filters (Majumdar et al. 2021), input samples were consumed without reuse, preventing composability without intermediate classical conversion.
fields.limits: Simulated on ideal quantum simulator with 1024-shot sampling; requires known power complementary transfer function and large circuit depths (59,292 elementary gates for $N=32, M=12$) requiring fault-tolerant hardware.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Two input signals (red) shown at the top, the impulse $x_{0}(n)$ and the randomly generated sequence $x_{1}(n)$ , are filtered with a lowpass FIR filter ( $M=12$ ) to produce the bottom outputs (blue), $y_{0}(n)$ and $y_{1}(n)$ , respectively. The input signals are encoded in the superposition $\ket{0}\ket{A_{x_{0}}}+\ket{1}\ket{A_{x_{1}}}$ and are filtered simultaneously. Data is extracted from the simulator QSV before (red) and after filtering (blue). The dotted lines show 1024-shot measurement results.
fields.figure_gloss: Sample index $n$ versus normalized amplitude for two parallel input signals (impulse $x_0(n)$ and fractal sequence $x_1(n)$, red) and their resulting lowpass filtered outputs ($y_0(n)$ and $y_1(n)$, blue), comparing exact statevector amplitudes with 1024-shot Hadamard test estimates.

fields.question: How can discrete-time quantum walks combined with amplitude amplification benchmark quantum computers on graph search problems?

fields.result: Finding a path from entrance to exit in a welded tree of height $n$ requires at least $\Omega(2^{n/24})$ quantum queries (or $\Omega(N^{1/24})$) to succeed with constant probability.
fields.question: Does there exist an efficient quantum algorithm that outputs a path between the entrance and exit vertices of a welded tree?
fields.prior: Childs, Coudron, and Gilani (CCG23) proved pathfinding hardness restricted to rooted and genuine quantum algorithms, but general quantum algorithms remained open.
fields.limits: Welded tree graphs of height $n$ ($N = 2^{n}$ leaves) with $q \le \sqrt{N}/100$ queries and a single-cycle weld distribution with fixed edge colorings.

fields.result: The number of quantum measurement shots required to reconstruct NMR spectra at fixed accuracy scales sub-exponentially with spin-chain length $L$, showing a pronounced flattening for 1D and 2D molecular geometries with distance-decaying couplings up to $L=50$.
fields.question: How does the number of projective measurement shots required to compute NMR spectra to a given accuracy scale with the number of nuclear spins?
fields.limits: Low-field NMR setting only. All gate noise, decoherence, and Trotterization errors neglected (pure shot-noise limit). Full Heisenberg dynamics verified only up to $L=12$ and on four real molecules.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Scaling of the infidelity for Heisenberg Hamiltonians. (a) Infidelity $\mathcal{I}(R,L)$ as a function of system size $L$ for the one-dimensional geometry with broadening parameter $\eta=3\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $R=1024$ shots. The infidelity increases only weakly with system size and does not exhibit a pronounced growth over the considered range of $L$ , suggesting that the favorable shot noise behavior observed for the Ising model is not qualitatively changed by the more general Heisenberg interaction, although the data should be understood as an illustrative small-system check rather than a scaling analysis. (b) Infidelity $\mathcal{I}(R,L)$ for four example molecules with Heisenberg couplings, evaluated from noisy spectra obtained with $R=500$ shots and compared to exact reference spectra with a field strength of $20\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and a broadening parameter of $\eta=1\,\mathrm{Hz}$ . The infidelity does not show a steeply increasing trend with $L$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Spectral infidelity versus system size $L$ (at $R=1024$ shots) for 1D chains and four real molecules under full Heisenberg interactions, demonstrating weak growth with $L$.

fields.result: Unitary propagators for real-time molecular and condensed-phase dynamics are synthesized via Solovay-Kitaev braiding of Fibonacci and Ising anyons, achieving an accuracy target of $10^{-8}$ across two-level, spin-boson, and molecular reaction systems.
fields.question: Can real-time quantum dynamics in molecular and condensed-phase systems be represented and executed using non-Abelian anyon braiding on topological quantum hardware?
fields.limits: Classical digital simulation of anyon braiding circuits rather than execution on topological quantum hardware; requires probabilistic imaginary time evolution for thermal states.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Braiding sequences generated for a two-level system using the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm are employed to simulate the time propagation of the system. In panel (A), the exact propagation of population dynamics, obtained by directly exponentiating the Hamiltonian, is depicted with solid lines, while the result obtained from Fibonacci anyon braiding is shown with scattered dots. The first 10 elements of the Fibonacci braiding sequence are displayed above panel (B). Panel (B) also shows the matrix elements for the braiding operations and the individual braiding diagrams for 4 gates; $\sigma_{1}$ , $\sigma_{2}$ , and their inverses. Panel (C) presents the population dynamics of a similar Hamiltonian, where we utilized Ising anyon braiding. The first few braiding sequences and the matrix elements of the braiding elements are shown in panel (D). The set of gates for Ising anyons possess a non-topological gate, specifically a rotation gate ( $T$ in the figure), which is represented by a dashed circle in the braiding diagram to stress that the rotation is not a topological gate. $\Delta t=0.1\hbar$ is used in both cases, the braiding word above approximates the unitary propagator $e^{-i\Delta tH/\hbar}$ with infidelity $10^{-7}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Population dynamics versus time for a two-level system under exact unitary evolution compared to Fibonacci and Ising anyon braiding sequences generated by the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm with $10^{-7}$ infidelity.

fields.result: Efficient classical sampling and decoding success estimation for fault-tolerant third-order circuits (CSS operations plus diagonal gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy like $T$, $\mathrm{CS}$, $\mathrm{CCZ}$) with non-Clifford simulation overhead independent of logical qubit count.

fields.limits: Logical failure rate estimate is an overestimate. Efficient sampling requires combined $X$-like errors to satisfy a contractibility condition (Condition C); checking this condition exactly is exponentially hard in circuit volume without topological or geometric structure.

fields.result: 300mm wafer-scale QSOI platform achieves $69\%$ yield for first-electron charge detection across 546 plunger-gate stability diagrams, with first-electron position dispersion of $21\text{ mV} \pm 35\text{ mV}$ over 377 quantum dots.

fields.result: Review synthesizes quantum algorithms for nonperturbative quantum field theory dynamics alongside quantum sensing platforms (cavities, circuits, magnetometry, and pair-breaking superconducting detectors with thresholds around 0.1 meV) for dark matter and gravitational wave searches.
fields.question: How can quantum simulation and quantum sensing technologies be applied to resolve nonperturbative dynamics and detect subtle beyond-the-Standard-Model physics?
fields.limits: Digital quantum field theory algorithms are limited by digitization of higher-dimensional non-Abelian gauge theories, state preparation, and continuum extrapolation; sensor sensitivity is limited by low-energy excess events, excess quasiparticles, and two-level system noise.

fields.result: Memory-assisted single-atom interconnect achieves linear scaling with photon delivery probability $\tilde{p}$ , reducing the attempt rate required for a $10^{4}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ entanglement rate from $190\,\mathrm{MHz}$ (type-II fusion) to $3.2\,\mathrm{MHz}$ at $\tilde{p}=1\%$ .

fields.limits: Infidelity budgets $\delta=1\%\text{--}5\%$ limit waiting window length due to unheralded photon-atom scattering and atom dephasing $\bar{T}_2^*$; excludes input state preparation errors, motional ground-state cooling downtime, and atom reloading.

fields.result: Fock-state-enhanced quantum heterodyne protocol decouples sensitivity from dephasing-limited interrogation time $\tau$, sustaining $T^{-3/2}$ scaling across seven orders of magnitude in measurement time. The $\ket{n=3}$ Fock state achieves 7.1(1.0) dB gain over $n=0$, reaching $0.5\text{ }\mu\text{Hz}$ frequency precision on an 86 MHz carrier ($6\times 10^{-15}$ fractional precision).
fields.question: Can quantum metrological advantage in frequency sensing persist to long measurement times without being eliminated by accelerated decoherence of nonclassical states?
fields.prior: Pulsed dynamical-decoupling Qdyne implementations in solid-state spin defects were restricted to tens of MHz.
fields.limits: Operating bandwidth limited by Nyquist rate $1/(2 T_s)$; single trapped ion mode in cryogenic environment; ultimate precision bounded by reference clock stability.
tools: trapped $^{40}\text{Ca}^+$ ion in cryogenic linear Paul trap
motional Raman transitions for Hamiltonian frequency mixing
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Quantum-enhanced Qdyne extends metrological gain to arbitrarily long measurement times. Colors denote measurements on the $n=0$ (blue circles), $n=1$ (yellow diamonds), $n=2$ (orange squares), and $n=3$ (purple triangles) Fock states. (a) The overlap response ( eq. 5 ) sharpens with $n$ and becomes non-injective as Wigner negativity allows overlap to vanish before states fully separate [ 45 ] . Solid curves are fits to eq. 5 with additional factors to account for protocol infidelities ( Supplementary Note C ). Insets show the product $W_{\ket{n}}W_{\hat{D}(\alpha)\ket{n}}$ at $\alpha=0.44$ , which is integrated to yield the overlap; 90% contours of the $\ket{n=0}$ Wigner function (solid, black) are shown for scale. Points represent 5000 averages; $1\sigma$ error bars are smaller than markers. (b) Fisher information extracted from data (points) and fits (solid curves) in (a). Departures from the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) $\mathfrak{F}_{n}=4(2n+1)$ grow with $n$ as SPAM errors compound over the more complex preparation sequences required for higher $n$ ( Supplementary Note B ); the SQL (black line, dashed) represents $\mathfrak{F}_{n=0}$ . (c) Microhertz frequency precision with Fock states. Precisions $\sigma_{\delta}/(2\pi)$ are extracted as $1\sigma$ uncertainties on fitted Lorentzian linecenters from DFTs on contiguous data subsets $[0,T]$ . All $n>0$ states improve on $n=0$ for $\sigma_{\delta}$ across the full range, reaching a minimum $\sigma_{\delta}/(2\pi)=$0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro Hz}$$ with no indication of saturation. Linear fits to log-transformed data (solid lines) agree with the expected $T^{-3/2}$ scaling. Fast oscillations are spectral leakage tied to shared DFT bin times. Inset: DFT spectra show increasing peak amplitude with $n$ from suppression of quantum noise; solid curves are Lorentzian fits. Parameters are listed in Table S3 .

fields.limits: Numerical simulations; tested on 12-vertex 3-regular graphs and 14-vertex Erdős–Rényi graphs ($p=0.3$) for the MaxCut problem; capped hybrid switching between second- and first-order update rules.

fields.result: Cavity-assisted quantum memory using pre-created long-lived macroscopic spin coherence synthesizes and stores arbitrary frequency-bin photonic qubits using only RF rotations via spectrally nonlocal impedance matching.
