fields.prior: Extends the single-spin-coherence PLMC protocol (Moiseev 2024), which required optical controls and stored only single-frequency photonic states.
fields.limits: Spectral width of input pulse must be much smaller than inhomogeneous absorption linewidth and cavity linewidth ($\delta\omega_s \ll \Delta_{in}, \kappa_{2,3}$); requires strongly correlated inhomogeneous optical broadening and negligible ground-state spin dephasing during the protocol.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: a) Atomic energy levels of the REIs and timing sequence of control two $\pi$ -laser pulses and three RF pulses with pulse areas $\theta_{1}$ , $\theta_{2}$ , $\theta_{3}$ ; arrival times of the incoming signal pulse $\hat{a}_{s}$ and the emitted frequency-bin echo $\hat{a}_{echoes}$ . b) Simplified experimental schematic: a REIs-doped crystal is placed inside a dual-mode optical resonator; REIs are excited by two $\pi$ -laser pulses and a signal pulse $\hat{a}_{s}$ coupled through the cavity; the emitted frequency-bin echo $\hat{a}_{echoes}$ follows; coherent spin rotation is induced by an inductively coupled RF pulses.
fields.figure_gloss: Panel (a) shows the 5-level rare-earth ion level scheme and the optical/RF pulse timing sequence. Panel (b) shows the crystal inside a dual-mode optical resonator controlled by an RF coil.

fields.result: Lifetimes of low angular momentum Rydberg P states in singly charged alkaline-earth metal ions are enhanced by factors $> 8$ relative to Hydrogenic scaling predictions, approaching neutral alkali-metal atom lifetimes. In $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^{+}$, P-state lifetimes are up to $\sim 20$ times higher than S states with the same principal quantum number.
fields.question: Do Rydberg states in singly charged alkaline-earth metal ions strictly follow the Hydrogenic scaling law that predicts a 16-fold lifetime reduction compared to neutral alkali-metal atoms?
fields.prior: Hydrogenic scaling $\tau(Z_{\mathrm{eff}}) \propto Z_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-4}$ predicted ionic Rydberg state lifetimes are reduced by a factor of 16 relative to neutral atoms.
fields.limits: Calculations assume single active valence electron in parametric model potentials within the dipole approximation, tested for $n = 20$ to $80$ at $T = 0\,\mathrm{K}$ and $T = 300\,\mathrm{K}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Rydberg-state lifetimes. (a) Numerically computed lifetimes of Rydberg S (dots) and P (squares) states of $\mathrm{{}^{85}Rb}$ . Blue and red data show the radiative ( $T=0\,\mathrm{K}$ ) lifetimes ( 3 ), $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}$ , and the room-temperature ( $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$ ) lifetimes ( 4 ), $\tau_{\mathrm{bbr}}$ , respectively. The data points are connected to guide the eye. (b) Analogous plot to panel (a) but for $\mathrm{{}^{88}Sr^{+}}$ . (c) Comparison of lifetimes. The panel shows the ratio $\tau(\mathrm{{}^{85}Rb})/\penalty\tau(\mathrm{{}^{88}Sr^{+}})$ between the lifetimes $\tau(\mathrm{{}^{85}Rb})$ and $\tau(\mathrm{{}^{88}Sr^{+}})$ of Rydberg states in $\mathrm{{}^{85}Rb}$ and $\mathrm{{}^{88}Sr^{+}}$ . The Hydrogenic scaling law ( 1 ) predicts the constant ratio of 16, indicated by the black horizontal line. The lifetimes shown in panels (a) and (b) are tabulated in the Supplemental Material [ 16 ] and can be compared to numerical calculations of Rydberg-state lifetimes for neutral Group-I and singly charged Group-II elements conducted in Refs. [ 50 , 25 , 10 , 9 , 23 , 24 ] . Benchmarks of the numerically computed lifetimes for $\mathrm{{}^{85}Rb}$ against experimental data can be found in the End Matter.
fields.figure_gloss: Computed Rydberg S and P state lifetimes of $^{85}\mathrm{Rb}$ and $^{88}\mathrm{Sr}^{+}$ alongside their ratio versus principal quantum number $n$ at $T=0\,\mathrm{K}$ and $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$, showing deviation of P states from the predicted Hydrogenic scaling ratio of 16.

fields.result: Combining Wannier-Stark localization with local dissipative hopping induces a quantum Mpemba effect where localized single-particle lifetimes scale super-exponentially as $\tau_{j}\approx\frac{1}{\gamma}[(j-2)!]^{2}(\Delta/J)^{2(j-2)}$ for $\gamma\ll\Delta$.
fields.question: How can an energy landscape with local dissipation be designed in a quantum system to produce an anomalous relaxation hierarchy analogous to the classical Mpemba effect?
fields.limits: Strong-localization regime $J/\Delta \lesssim 1$, local Markovian jump dissipation restricted to an isolated boundary site.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: (a) Schematic of single-particle setup, illustrating rates $\gamma$ , $J$ and energy gaps $\Delta$ , $\varepsilon$ . (b) Time evolution of the energy for initial states localized on different sites. High energy states close to site 2 relax faster than low energy states that are localized farther to the right. The $\tau_{j}$ are relaxation times obtained from Eqs. ( 2 ), ( 3 ) via Padé interpolation. (c) Curves show average position for a few quantum-jump trajectories of the unraveled Lindblad equation, starting from site 3. Background shows heatmap of site occupancies, $n_{j}$ , from the full Lindblad evolution. (d) Perturbative estimates from Eq.’s ( 2 , 3 ) compared to numerical results obtained from Lindbladian spectrum. For panels (b,c,d) we used $L=7$ sites, $\varepsilon/\Delta=1.0$ , $J/\Delta=0.15$ . For (b,c), $\gamma/\Delta=1.0$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Energy versus time for states initialized at different lattice sites $j$, showing faster relaxation for higher-energy states near the dissipative site, alongside quantum jump trajectories and perturbation-theory timescale predictions.

fields.result: Extracting clock error from collective nuclear coherence through resonator field enables clock cycle reset on fast decoherence timescale ($1/\gamma_z$) rather than long radiative lifetime ($1/\gamma$). Instability is minimized when collective cooperativity $C_N = 1$ in the low-saturation limit and $C_{N,\rm opt} = 1 + 4\Omega^2/(6\gamma\gamma_\perp)$ under saturation.
fields.question: How can collective cavity quantum electrodynamics overcome the mismatch between short nuclear coherence time and long radiative lifetime in solid-state $^{229}\text{Th}$ clocks?
fields.prior: TU Wien nuclear clock absorption spectroscopy achieved $\sigma_y(\tau=1\text{ s}) = 3\times 10^{-12}$ using $N\sim 10^{16}$ nuclei; proposed cavity scheme matches instability with $N\sim 10^{11}$ nuclei.
fields.limits: Mean-field theory in the bad-cavity regime ($\kappa_2 \gg 4G^2N/\kappa_2$). Assumes homogeneous coupling via phase matching and CaF$_2$ host parameters with $\gamma = 1.59\times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: From transient to steady-state frequency standards . (a) Transient frequency standard interrogation scheme and corresponding optimized frequency instability as a function of $\rho_{\rm Th}$ and $P_{1}$ . (b) Output photon flux dynamics $\Phi_{2}^{\rm out}$ and nuclear excitation $\sigma_{ee}$ for three pump powers, featuring the transient pulse-like behavior and the relaxation towards the steady state. (c) General frequency instability as a function of pump power $P_{1}$ , thorium density $\rho_{\rm Th}$ , at each point separately numerically optimized with respect to $\delta$ . All plots are at fixed $Q_{1}=5\times 10^{6},Q_{2}=Q_{1}/8$ . The red region on the colormap shows the bistability range predicted by mean-field analysis.
fields.figure_gloss: Fractional frequency instability $\sigma_y\sqrt{\tau}$ as a function of pump power $P_1$ and thorium density $\rho_{\rm Th}$, showing the analytical optimal power curve (dashed green), optimal collective cooperativity (dashed orange), and the mean-field bistability boundary (red).

fields.result: Two-photon driving strongly enhances the drive input energy current and signal-to-noise ratio via multiphoton resonances $\omega_d^{(m)} \simeq \omega_0 + (2m-1)U$, substantially modifying non-Gaussian higher-order current cumulants compared to single-photon driving.
fields.question: How two-photon driving reorganizes nonlinear dressed-state transitions to control nonequilibrium average energy current and higher-order current fluctuations in open quantum optical systems.
fields.limits: Weak-driving regime, low-energy three-state approximation, Ohmic spectral density.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Effect of two-photon loss on nonequilibrium transport in the driven nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings model. (a) Drive input energy current $\log_{10}(J_{\rm{P}})$ , (b) second-order current fluctuations $\log_{10}(J^{(2)}_{l})$ , and (c) signal-to-noise ratio $\mathcal{S}_{l}$ as functions of driving frequency $\omega_{d}$ . The red dashed line represents single-photon dissipation alone, and the blue solid line represents coexisting single- and two-photon dissipation channels. The parameters are $N_{\rm{ph}}=30$ , photon frequency $\omega_{0}=1$ , qubit splitting $\varepsilon=\omega_{0}$ , $\eta=0.01\omega_{0}$ , $U=0.25\omega_{0}$ , coupling strength $\lambda=0.02\omega_{0}$ , $\alpha_{l}=\alpha_{r}=0.001$ for both single- and two-photon dissipation, $\omega_{c}=10\omega_{0}$ , $k_{\rm{B}}T_{l}=1.2\omega_{0}$ , and $k_{\rm{B}}T_{r}=0.6\omega_{0}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Drive input energy current $\log_{10}(J_{\rm{P}})$, second-order fluctuations $\log_{10}(J^{(2)}_l)$, and signal-to-noise ratio $\mathcal{S}_l$ versus drive frequency $\omega_d$, showing enhancement when two-photon loss is added to single-photon dissipation.

fields.result: A 4-mode hybrid cavity magnomechanical system operated in the linearized Gaussian regime enables quantum reservoir computing and delayed signal reconstruction using quadrature fluctuation covariance features. For finite measurement budgets ($N_m = 10^{10}$ shots), intermediate encoding strength $\epsilon_\Delta$ minimizes reconstruction error.
fields.question: Can a hybrid cavity magnomechanical platform act as a continuous-variable Gaussian quantum reservoir computer when driven through an auxiliary-cavity detuning port?
fields.limits: Linearized Gaussian regime at $T = 50\text{ mK}$; offline state tomography without continuous-measurement back-action; numerical simulation.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Effect of finite measurement statistics on the delayed signal probing performance. Panels (a)-(c) show the NMSE as a function of the delay $\tau$ for three input-encoding strengths, $\epsilon_{\Delta}/2\pi=0.1$ , $0.5$ , and $1$ MHz, respectively. Panel (d) shows the NMSE as a function of $\epsilon_{\Delta}$ at fixed delay $\tau=3$ . Results are shown for $N_{m}=10^{4}$ , $10^{6}$ , $10^{8}$ , and $10^{10}$ measurements and compared with the ideal $N_{m}\rightarrow\infty$ limit.
fields.figure_gloss: Delayed signal reconstruction NMSE plotted against delay $\tau$ and encoding strength $\epsilon_\Delta / 2\pi$ across finite measurement counts $N_m = 10^4$ to $10^{10}$ versus ideal limit $N_m \to \infty$, revealing a statistical trade-off minimum in reconstruction error.

fields.result: Twin-beam communication alphabet extended from 2 to 4 states (2 bits per use) using superimposed thermal noise, with record-and-resend attacks detected at $90\%$ probability for attacked fractions $f \approx 0.10$ to $0.40$ across block sizes $N = 8\times 10^4$ down to $5\times 10^3$.
fields.question: Can a twin-beam quantum communication protocol be extended from binary to four-state encoding while retaining eavesdropping detection via the noise reduction factor?
fields.prior: Binary hybrid encoding scheme by Razzoli et al. [4] delivering 1 bit per symbol using mean photon number with noise reduction factor $R$ as a security witness.
fields.limits: Channel detection efficiency $\eta = 9.0 \pm 3\%$; state discrimination on $R$ limited by calibration mismatch and test statistics fluctuations; communication evaluated on bootstrapped blocks from stored datasets rather than live independent transmissions.
tools: rotating ground-glass diffuser for thermal noise generation
single-arm Fano factor $(\langle m\rangle, F)$ threshold decoding and ML classifiers
fields.figure_caption: Figure 17: Probability of detecting the record-and-resend attack as a function of the attacked fraction $f$ . Left: average over the four states at the three block sizes; the dashed lines are the Gaussian prediction described in the text, with no adjusted parameters. Right: per-state detection probability at $N=$2\text{\times}{10}^{4}$$ . The dotted horizontal line marks the nominal $5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}$ false-alarm level; at $f=0$ the curves start above it, mostly because of the calibration mismatch of the references (largest for state 00).
fields.figure_gloss: Detection probability of record-and-resend attack versus attacked fraction $f$ across block sizes $N = 5\times 10^3$, $2\times 10^4$, and $8\times 10^4$, compared to a $5\%$ false-alarm baseline.

fields.result: Realized complete set of modular fault-tolerant logical operations for the non-CSS $[[5,1,3]]$ code on a 16-qubit trapped-ion processor, including state teleportation, QEC with real-time feedback, and magic-state injection yielding $85\pm 8\,\%$ average gate fidelity for a logical $T$ gate.
fields.question: Can universal modular fault-tolerant quantum operations, including inter-register state teleportation and non-Clifford gate injection, be realized experimentally on a compact non-CSS quantum error-correcting code?
fields.prior: Logical teleportation and lattice-surgery primitives had previously been demonstrated only on topological Calderbank–Shor–Steane (CSS) codes (such as surface and color codes).
fields.limits: State preparation uses postselection on syndrome verification flags; SPAM-error removal method requires trace-preserving noise channels and is restricted to operations without error-detection postselection.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Fault-tolerant magic state preparation and injection. (a) The schematic shows the FT preparation of a magic state $|H_{\mathrm{XZ}}\rangle_{\mathrm{L}}$ in the blue box and the corresponding Bloch-sphere representation on the left. The $T^{\mathrm{XZ}}_{\mathrm{L}}$ gate is applied to an arbitrary input state $|\psi\rangle_{\mathrm{L}}$ by magic state injection. The equivalent rotation on the Bloch sphere is shown on the right. (b) Experimental (dark) and numerically simulated (light) logical state infidelity of a fault-tolerantly prepared magic state $|H_{\mathrm{XZ}}\rangle_{\mathrm{L}}=\cos{(\pi/8)}|0\rangle_{\mathrm{L}}+\sin{(\pi/8)|1\rangle}_{\mathrm{L}}$ is presented. (c) A logical pieceably FT C $Y_{\mathrm{L}}$ gate is characterized by the state infidelities of the entangled state for logical input states $|+,0\rangle_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $|+i,0\rangle_{\mathrm{L}}$ . In both figures, the uncertainty is given by $1\sigma$ Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals. (d) The logical C $Y_{\mathrm{L}}$ gate is used to implement the logical $T^{\mathrm{XZ}}_{\mathrm{L}}$ gate. We perform logical state tomography for the prepared state $T^{\mathrm{XZ}}_{\mathrm{L}}\ket{+}_{\mathrm{L}}$ determining the density matrix on the left and reaching a state fidelity of $96^{+3}_{-16}\,\%$ . The black dashed boxes correspond to the fault-free ideal outcomes. On the right, the noise process matrix of the $T^{\mathrm{XZ}}_{\mathrm{L}}$ gate determined in Sec IV is shown and a process fidelity of $85\pm 8\,\%$ is calculated. Since the values of the matrices are complex numbers, the absolute value determines the size of the square and the color represents the phase.
fields.figure_gloss: Magic-state preparation circuit and quantum process tomography of the non-Clifford logical $T$ gate injection, showing reconstructed logical Pauli transfer matrix elements and process fidelity.

fields.result: Jointly compiles Clifford routing via maximum-flow and runtime magic state cultivation in a 3D topological pipe diagram, cutting spacetime volume by $2.3\times$ (geometric mean) and running $10.8\times$ faster than TopoLS under free magic states, and cutting volume by $2.3\times$ at code distance $d=13$ relative to PureMagic.
fields.question: How can topological lattice surgery compilation simultaneously embed full circuit layers of Clifford operations and account for stochastic, in-place magic state cultivation in a single 3D representation?
fields.prior: TopoLS routes Clifford gates sequentially or via MCTS order search while omitting magic state preparation footprints; PureMagic schedules cultivation on a 2D layout with per-instruction path search.
fields.limits: Evaluated on rotated surface codes with distances $d=11, 13, 15$; volume advantage drops to $1.6\times$ at $d=15$ where expected cultivation time rises to 5.5 logical cycles.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 9. Comparison between PureMagic and FlowRouter execution times per logical cycle.
fields.figure_gloss: Execution latency per logical cycle compared between PureMagic and FlowRouter across circuit benchmarks, showing runtime dispatch speed relative to surface code cycle times.

fields.result: Constructed quantum hash function mapping $n$-bit inputs to $k = \lceil n/2 \rceil + O(\log^2 n)$ single-qubit BB84 states, achieving collision threshold $F(\psi_C) \leq 1/(2n)$ from shortened binary BCH codes.
fields.question: Can quantum hashing be implemented on existing commercial QKD hardware using standard BB84 states?
fields.limits: Requires $n = 32$ or $n \geq 44$ to guarantee output qubit compression $k < n$.

fields.result: Linear algebraic algorithm with complexity $O(|K|^3)$ computes a reduced repair group $J \subseteq K$ of codeword qudits and a set of observables $O$ of strictly minimal size $|O| = \dim \pi_I(C^{\perp s})$ to locally recover erasures at positions $I \subsetneq K$.
fields.question: How can one simultaneously reduce both the number of measured observables and the number of measured codeword qudits in local recovery for general entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes?
fields.prior: Simultaneous reduction was limited to unassisted quantum stabilizer codes from Hermitian dual-containing linear codes (Matsumoto 2024), without methods for general entanglement-assisted codes or general CSS codes.
fields.limits: Computed set of observables is provably minimal, but reduced repair group $J$ is not guaranteed to achieve globally minimal size.

fields.result: NP-hard to approximate quantum code distance and graph-state distance within additive error $c N$ for constant $c>0$, via deterministic reductions.
fields.question: Does quantum-code distance or graph-state distance admit a linear additive hardness gap under deterministic reductions?
fields.prior: Additive hardness gap was $N^{1/2}$ for quantum code distance (Kapshikar and Kundu 2023; Grigorescu et al. 2024) and $N^{1/3}$ for graph-state distance (Grigorescu et al. 2024).
fields.limits: CSS codes with identical $X$- and $Z$-check spaces, constant rate, and constant relative distance. Does not establish hardness for quantum LDPC codes.

fields.result: Hybrid qudit-qubit integer programming reduces fault-tolerant resource requirements by $\sim 180\times$ for qutrits ($d=3$) and $\sim 2220\times$ for ququints ($d=5$) compared to qubit-only implementation.
fields.question: What is the quantitative resource advantage of a hybrid qudit-qubit quantum algorithm over qubit-only encoding, and is it classically simulable based on its entanglement structure?
fields.limits: Simplified fault-tolerant resource counting model, numerical evaluations limited to $d \le 5$ and small system sizes, classical hardness inferred via scaling bounds rather than rigorous simulation runtime proofs.
tools: von Neumann entropy and Schmidt rank tracking
Matrix Product State classical simulation bounds
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3 : Growth of the reduced-state entropy $S(A)$ with subsystem size $\langle\log_{2}(\dim A)\rangle$ , averaged over all subsystems of a given size formed from qudits and qubits, for $d=2$ [(a)], $d=3$ [(b)], and $d=4$ [(c)]. Solid curves are Stage-I states and dashed curves are Stage-II states. The growth curves are calculated while solving the example problem given by Eq. ( 1 ).
fields.figure_gloss: Reduced-state entropy $S(A)$ plotted against subsystem dimension $\langle \log_{2}(\dim A) \rangle$ across algorithm stages for dimensions $d=2, 3, 4$, showing volume-law-like scaling up to the Page saturation limit.

fields.result: Formulates Controlled-Bloch-Sphere Universality (CBSU) for $(N+1)$-dimensional $SU(2)$ BEC qubit systems across Fock-basis and coherent-state representations. Proves an analogue of Gottesman-Knill theorem for BEC circuits composed of Stokes-Hermite Clifford gates and Fock basis measurements.
fields.question: How can universal quantum computation and the Gottesman-Knill theorem be formulated for Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) qubit systems spanning $(N+1)$-dimensional $SU(2)$ representations?
fields.limits: Excludes distorted Bloch spheres caused by errors. Assumes Fock states can be fully manipulated as qudits without specifying experimental physical implementations.

fields.result: Proves the query complexity lower bound $\Omega(\kappa\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ for quantum linear system solvers in the sparse-access model, capturing condition number $\kappa$, sparsity $s$, and precision $\varepsilon$ simultaneously.
fields.question: What is the joint query complexity lower bound for quantum linear system solvers as a function of condition number, sparsity, and precision in the sparse-access model?
fields.prior: Was $\Omega(\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon))$ across $\kappa,\varepsilon$ (Harrow & Kothari / somma et al.) and $\Omega(\kappa\sqrt{s})$ for constant $\varepsilon$ (Mori et al. 2026).
fields.limits: Holds in the standard sparse-matrix oracle access model for real, symmetric, but indefinite input matrices; requires $\kappa\geq 31$ and $s\geq 5$.

fields.result: Discretized Euclidean $O(4)$ ladder Bethe-Salpeter equation mapped to $n$ qubits yields maximum von Neumann entanglement entropy $S_{\rm vN}^{\rm max} \in [0.544, 0.568]$ bits across $N=16$ to $128$ ($n=4$ to $7$), proving the system is classically tractable with bond dimension $\chi=2$ achieving $\ge 99\%$ MPS fidelity.
fields.question: Can the homogeneous Bethe-Salpeter equation for relativistic two-body bound states be formulated and solved efficiently using gate-based VQE with tensor-network ansätze?
fields.limits: Scalar ladder approximation in Euclidean space with $O(4)$ single S-wave channel; numerical simulations up to $n=7$ qubits ($N=128$) without physical quantum processor noise.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: Entanglement analysis for $N=16$ , $32$ , $64$ . (Left) $S_{\rm vN}^{\rm max}$ is flat in $N$ , far below the area-law maximum. (Center) Schmidt weights $s_{k}^{2}$ decay steeply, almost identically for all sizes. (Right) Cumulative MPS fidelity: $\chi=2$ achieves $\geq 99\%$ at all $N$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Plots maximum von Neumann entanglement entropy $S_{\rm vN}^{\rm max}$ against $N$, Schmidt weight decay, and cumulative fidelity vs bond dimension $\chi$, demonstrating that $\chi=2$ provides $\ge 99\%$ state fidelity across all tested discretization sizes.

fields.result: Zero-knowledge proofs of quantumness prevent classical verifiers from extracting computational advantage or problem solutions from quantum provers by adding an extractable non-interactive zero-knowledge argument to the verifier's challenge.
fields.question: How can a quantum prover demonstrate quantum capability to a classical verifier without allowing a malicious verifier to solve hard problem instances?
fields.limits: Relies on the post-quantum hardness of the learning with errors problem and standard common reference string setup for NIZK.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Illustration of our new zero-knowledge property for proofs of quantumness.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic comparing real interaction between a quantum prover and classical verifier with a probabilistic polynomial-time classical simulator interacting with the same verifier.

fields.result: Targeted variational updates extend median time within target-error tolerance by factors of $1.06$ to $4.22$ across six-qubit spin, Fermi-Hubbard, and LiH benchmarks compared with standard McLachlan evolution at matched shot budgets.
fields.question: Can updating variational circuit parameters to reproduce equations of motion of selected observables improve the simulation time of specific expectation values under finite measurement budgets without ancillary qubits?
fields.prior: McLachlan variational quantum simulation (VQS) optimized for full-state dynamics using Hadamard tests.
fields.limits: Numerical simulations restricted to six-qubit systems with shot sampling noise ($S = 10^6$ to $10^9$) but without device/gate noise.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Observable dynamics under finite measurement statistics. Median reachable time $T_{\varepsilon}$ versus shots per velocity evaluation for (a) mixed-field Ising, (b) XXZ, (c) disordered Heisenberg, (d) XY, (e) Fermi–Hubbard, and (f) LiH. The tolerance is $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$ in (a)–(e) and $\varepsilon=10^{-4}$ in (f). Blue and dark red denote observable-targeted and McLachlan evolution, respectively. Both methods use six qubits and two circuit layers. Error bars show the interquartile range over 100 independent measurement realizations. The open marker for targeted LiH evolution at $S=10^{9}$ indicates a lower bound: 85 of 100 trajectories remain within the tolerance through $T_{\max}=3$ , so the median and both quartiles lie beyond the observation window. Time is measured in inverse lattice energy units in (a)–(e) and atomic units $\hbar/E_{\mathrm{h}}$ in (f), where $E_{\mathrm{h}}$ is the Hartree energy. The target expectation is evaluated exactly along each sampled trajectory.
fields.figure_gloss: Median reachable time $T_{\varepsilon}$ within error tolerance plotted against measurement budget $S$ per velocity evaluation across six Hamiltonian models.

fields.result: Incoherent quantum channel tomography to diamond-norm error $\epsilon$ requires $\Omega(d_1 d_2 r^2/\epsilon^2)$ queries and can be achieved with $O(d_1 d_2 r^2 \log(2d_1)/\epsilon^2)$ queries for general channels, or $\Theta(d_1 d_2 r^2/\epsilon^2)$ when non-zero Choi eigenvalues are $\Omega(d_1/r)$.
fields.question: What is the query complexity of quantum channel tomography under the diamond norm in the incoherent model?
fields.prior: Known only for $r=1$ and $r=d_1 d_2$; coherent tomography takes $\Theta(d_1 d_2 r/\epsilon^2)$ for dilation rate $\tau = r d_2 / d_1 \ge 1+\Omega(1)$ and $\Theta(d_1 d_2 r/\epsilon)$ for $\tau=1$.
fields.limits: Holds for incoherent protocols (no quantum memory across queries, measurements after each query); success probability at least $2/3$; $d_2 \ge 2$ and $d_1 \le r d_2$.

fields.result: QSVT-based quantum Jacobi algorithm solves linear systems using polynomial transformation of a block-encoded operator with constant ancilla overhead and circuit depth scaling linearly with iteration count $k$.
fields.question: Can the classical Jacobi iterative method be implemented on gate-based quantum computers with constant ancilla overhead instead of linear ancilla growth?
fields.prior: Product-of-block-encodings LCU Jacobi method (Williams et al. 2024) required ancilla qubit count scaling linearly with iteration number $k$.
fields.limits: Iteration matrix $M=D^{-1}R$ must be Hermitian (or normal) to yield matrix polynomials via QSVT; requires efficient state preparation and block encodings.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : Circuit representation of the QSVT-enhanced Jacobi algorithm, where three QSVT subroutines are combined via LCU. The ancilla qubits $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ encode the LCU coefficients, $a_{s}$ denotes the signal qubit on which the phase rotations of the QSVT sequence are performed, and $a_{\text{be}}$ represents the ancilla register used for the block encoding of $M$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Quantum circuit schematic combining three QSVT subroutines via LCU using signal qubit $a_s$, select ancillae $a_1, a_2$, and block-encoding ancilla $a_M$.

fields.result: Majorana BBGKY closure at the two-particle level with projective positivity purification simulates non-number-conserving and spin dynamics in $O(N^{6})$ time, capturing strong-coupling Hubbard transport and early Kitaev flux motion missed by Hartree-Fock.
fields.question: Can a two-particle reduced-density-matrix method formulated in Majorana fermions simulate non-equilibrium dynamics in systems lacking fermion-number conservation?
fields.prior: Hartree-Fock (one-particle reduced density matrix) misses strong-coupling dynamics and gauge-correlated flux motion entirely.
fields.limits: Scaling $O(N^{6})$. Positivity projection introduces non-unitary effective irreversibility that causes artificial thermalization at late times; post-projection gauge reconstruction degrades when magnetic fields act on multiple sites.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Time evolution of the expectation value of the occupation number $\braket{\hat{n}_{1,\uparrow}}$ for the four-site Hubbard model following a quantum quench. Three algorithms are compared: exact diagonalization, TP 1/10 , and HF. Here TP 1/10 denotes that one projection is performed every ten time steps. Panel (a) shows the weak-interaction case $U=0.3J_{h}$ . Panel (b) shows the strong-interaction case $U=5J_{h}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Evolution of $\braket{\hat{n}_{1,\uparrow}}$ versus time after a quench in a 4-site Hubbard model. Hartree-Fock fails to capture strong-coupling dynamics, while the two-particle method matches exact diagonalization at early times before projection damping sets in.

fields.result: Introduced clifford_qc, an open-source Python research toolkit integrating sparse Clifford/Pauli operator algebra, subspace/variational eigensolvers, and shared measurement caching with provenance-tracking and explicit device cost models.
fields.question: How can quantum simulation workflows integrate operator algebra, subspace methods, and measurement resource allocation within a consistent, reproducible framework?
fields.limits: All benchmarks restricted to small active spaces ($8$ to $12$ qubits); device cards and routing costs are illustrative surrogates rather than hardware measurements; sparse multivector support can grow exponentially.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Compiled settings (left axis, blue) and maximum logical entangling depth per setting (right axis, red) along the block-size axis, for the two committed banks. Annotations give the added entangling cost over the avoided preparation cost against $k=1$ ; the verdict in each title is that ratio against unity. The protocol is identical on both panels, and the trade changes sign between them.
fields.figure_gloss: Number of compiled measurement settings (left axis, blue) and maximum logical entangling depth per setting (right axis, red) as a function of commuting block size $k$ for two 8-qubit active-space banks. It demonstrates how larger commuting blocks reduce readout settings but increase entangling circuit overhead.

fields.result: Phase-modulated concatenated continuous driving (CCD) stabilizes Rabi oscillations and extends oscillation decay time for silicon hole spin qubits while maintaining coherent gate control.
fields.question: Can low-frequency charge and hyperfine noise in silicon hole spin qubits be suppressed during coherent driving via microwave phase modulation?
fields.limits: Subject to low-frequency noise from intrinsic spin-orbit coupling and residual nuclear spins in the silicon substrate.
tools: silicon quantum dot hole spin qubit

fields.result: Superconductor-altermagnet-superconductor junctions engineered into the $2\phi$-junction regime provide intrinsic charge-noise protection via qubit wavefunction parity while retaining large anharmonicity from coherent double-Cooper-pair tunneling.
fields.question: Can altermagnetic Josephson junctions realize programmable non-sinusoidal current-phase relations that combine high coherence with strong anharmonicity in superconducting qubits?
fields.prior: Unconventional $d$-wave superconducting qubits such as flowermon and $d$-mon enhance anharmonicity via higher CPR harmonics, but operate in the $\phi$-junction regime and suffer from quasiparticle and charge noise.
fields.limits: Short-junction limit ($L \ll \xi_{0}$); symmetric junction design for the flux-tunable SQUID; single- and double-Cooper-pair harmonics retained.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: (a) Qubit transition frequency, (b) anharmonicity, (c) transverse charge-noise coupling strength $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{DC}}^{Q}$ , and (d) longitudinal flux-noise coupling strength $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{DP}}^{\mathrm{Flux}}$ as functions of the external flux $\phi_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and the ratio $\eta$ . The fixed parameters are $E_{J}/E_{C}=50$ and $N_{g}=0$ .

fields.result: Avoided-crossing, energy participation ratio (EPR), induced electromotive force (EMF), and impedance-matrix methods extract transmon-to-package bare mode couplings with relative deviation under 5%.
fields.question: How can weak electromagnetic couplings between localized transmon qubits and distributed package modes be accurately and efficiently extracted in multi-scale superconducting processor simulations?
fields.limits: Numerical full-wave simulations; transmons modeled as linear LC resonators under the rotating-wave approximation; assumes weak coupling to bare modes.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: Comparison of coupling extraction methods. The couplings between the qubits and the fundamental package mode extracted via EPR, avoided-crossing, induced-EMF, and impedance-matrix methods are shown for the 25 qubits, with the numbering indicated in the inset. Because of the coupling symmetry (see the inset and Fig. 6 ), data is presented only for one quadrant of the $10\times 10$ qubit array. The four methods yield couplings with a maximum relative difference of only 4.8% across the entire qubit array.
fields.figure_gloss: Coupling strength $g/2 ar{\pi}$ between individual transmons and the fundamental package mode across 25 array positions, comparing avoided crossing, EPR, induced EMF, and impedance matrix techniques.

fields.result: Cascading a 736-element SNAIL-based TWPA and a 1632-element TWPA achieves nearly 30 dB total gain over ~1 GHz bandwidth, with added noise near $(1/2)\hbar\omega$ and a 1 dB compression point of -101 dBm.
fields.question: Can low added noise and high gain be achieved simultaneously by cascading two TWPAs, with the first optimized for minimum added noise and the second for high gain?
fields.prior: was around 20 dB gain in single TWPAs with comparable noise and compression
fields.limits: Requires interstage bandpass filtering to prevent wideband amplified quantum noise and idler tones from saturating the second amplifier stage; gain ripples persist from imperfect interstage impedance matching.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: a) Gain and compression comparison: Gain of S-TWPA $G^{\textrm{S}}$ (blue trace), L-TWPA $G^{\textrm{L}}$ (orange trace) measured individually, simultaneously $G^{\textrm{B}}$ (green trace) and also plotted as linear combination of both individual measurements $G^{\textrm{C}}=G^{\textrm{S}}+G^{\textrm{L}}$ (purple trace) as a function of signal frequency $f_{s}$ around the half frequency of the S-TWPA’s pump at $f^{\rm S}_{p}=11$ GHz. b) Gain saturation in the cascade: Averaged S-TWPA gain $\langle G^{S}\rangle$ (over $f=5.25-5.65$ GHz) and difference between linear combination and simultaneous operation $\langle\Delta_{G}\rangle=\langle{}G^{\textrm{C}}-G^{\textrm{B}}\rangle$ as a function of pump power of the S-TWPA, with L-TWPA at a fixed setpoint. c) Gain compression and $\Delta{}$ SNR: Measured gain $G^{\textrm{B}}$ (green, left axis) and corresponding improvement in signal-to-noise ratio, $\Delta\textrm{SNR}^{\textrm{B}}$ (red, right axis) as function of the probe power at frequency $f_{\textrm{probe}}=5.503~\textrm{GHz}$ . d) System noise temperature from $\Delta{}\textrm{SNR}$ : Measured total system noise temperature at frequency $f_{\textrm{probe}}=5.503~\textrm{GHz}$ with both TWPAs on as function of probe power (green line), compared to minimum achievable noise $\hbar\omega_{s}+T_{\textrm{HEMT}}/G^{\textrm{B}}$ (dashed line).
fields.figure_gloss: Gain versus frequency for individual and simultaneous TWPA operation, gain saturation versus pump power, and gain compression alongside signal-to-noise ratio improvement as a function of probe power at 5.503 GHz.

fields.result: Proximitized Cooper pairs from periodic superconducting leads produce a real-space Talbot carpet repeating at $Z_T = \lambda_p / (1 - \sqrt{1 - \lambda_p^2 / d^2})$, steerable via inter-lead phase differences $\Delta\phi$ to extract Fermi wavelengths with sub-9% fitting error.
fields.question: Can macroscopic quantum near-field diffraction occur for proximitized Cooper pairs in a ballistic 2DEG, and can active phase control map its Fermi surface?
fields.limits: Ballistic 2DEG regime; requires sub-wavelength lithographic pitch ($d \sim 200$ nm) and planar junction lengths $L \lesssim 1\;\mu$m due to $r^{-2}$ power-law decay of induced order parameter.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: The superconducting Talbot effect. (a) Schematic of superconductivity induced in a 2DEG by a source array. (b) Measurement scheme illustrating the two groups of collector array, where Group A aligns while Group B misaligns with the source. (c,d) Real-space intensity of induced superconductivity for a single helical (c) and spin-degenerate (d) Fermi surfaces. Solid (dashed) lines mark integer (half integer) multiples of the Talbot distance. (e,f) Total critical current $I_{c}$ between the source and each collector group versus the pair wavelength for a single helical (e) and spin-degenerate (f) Fermi surfaces.
fields.figure_gloss: Real-space induced superconducting order parameter showing Talbot self-imaging at integer $Z_T$ and inverted patterns at half-integer $Z_T$ for helical and spin-degenerate 2DEGs, with corresponding critical-current oscillations versus pair wavelength $\lambda_p$.

fields.result: Kondo effect observed in hexalayer rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices. With increasing magnetic field, longitudinal magnetoresistance transitions from increasing to decreasing across critical field $B_c$, while Hall resistance $R_{xy}$ reverses sign near $B_c$; longitudinal resistance $R_{xx}$ increases logarithmically as temperature decreases before transitioning to a $T^2$ heavy-fermion liquid behavior.
fields.question: Can the Kondo effect be realized and tuned via topological flat bands in rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices?
fields.limits: Observed in hexalayer rhombohedral graphene moiré structures under low temperatures and external magnetic and displacement fields.
tools: electrostatic gating (carrier density $n$ and displacement field $D$ tuning)

fields.result: Demonstrated an in-orbit programmable quantum photonic processor operating on a nanosatellite, generating and manipulating two-photon states in a six-mode universal integrated circuit and observing two-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference.
fields.question: Can quantum interference conditions (spectral degeneracy, phase stability, and optical alignment) be established and maintained on a programmable photonic circuit in space?
fields.limits: Payload constrained to 10 W average power, 9.8 kg mass, and 15 x 15 x 45.3 cm volume; low-noise coincidence measurements restricted to ~30 min per 92 min orbit during Earth shadow due to sunlight leakage and radiation-induced detector noise.
tools: Custom FPGA System on a Module (SoM)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Hong-Ou-Mandel interference in space. ( a ) Two-photon interference scan with respect to the crystal temperature, including data from three different operation days. The uPIC is set such that two input photons (corresponding to the state $|010010\rangle$ ) are sent to MZI6, whose internal phase is set to $\varphi=\pi/2$ and whose outputs are then routed to detector pairs CC 05 (green) or CC 15 (light blue, violet). Individual data points of normalized coincidence counts for consecutive days in orbit (i.O.) are marked in the background while the inverse-variance weighted average of these points (dark blue) highlights the overall trend. Error bars indicate one standard deviation, obtained by Gaussian uncertainty propagation, and there is an explicit dip in coincidences around a crystal temperature of $\sim 32.5\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , which also corresponds to the value measured on Earth (red-shaded area). The peak in coincidences just before the dip is discussed in the Supplemental Material [ 28 ] (Sec. S9 N). ( b ) The registered average coincidence rate of distinguishable photons when the internal phase of MZI6 is set to $\varphi=\pi/2$ (light blue), is half with respect to the setting of $\varphi=\pi$ (violet), as can be seen exemplarily for detector pair CC 15 . This feature served as a reference measurement for the HOM scan. It was consistently observed when routing photons from MZI6 across all detector pairs (inset) and shows good agreement with theoretical predictions (grey) [ 2 ] . ( c ) Close-up of the HOM dip around the expected degeneracy temperature (red-shaded area) highlights the explicit drop of coincidence counts for the individual operation days (light blue, green) and the corresponding weighted average (dark blue).
fields.figure_gloss: Normalized two-photon coincidence counts plotted against the ppKTP crystal temperature, showing the characteristic Hong-Ou-Mandel interference dip observed during orbital operation across multiple days.

fields.result: Strong atom-cavity coupling on the telecom ${}^{3}\mathrm{P}_{0}\leftrightarrow{}^{3}\mathrm{D}_{1}$ transition of ${}^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ at 1389 nm reaches single-atom internal cooperativity $C_{\mathrm{in}}=5.6(1.0)$ with single-atom coupling strength $g/2\pi=1.86(17)$ MHz. Collective coupling scales as $\sqrt{N}$ up to $N=5$ atoms across a $\sim 200~\mu\mathrm{m}$ length.
fields.question: Can neutral atoms in a reconfigurable tweezer array achieve the single-atom strong-coupling cavity-QED regime directly on a telecom-band transition using a nanofiber cavity?
fields.prior: Strong coupling in nanofiber cavities was previously demonstrated only with single trapped alkali atoms at non-telecom wavelengths (e.g. Kato 2015, Goban 2012), while prior telecom atom-cavity interfaces lacked single-atom strong coupling.
fields.limits: Operated with single-sided cavity geometry at $1~\mu\mathrm{m}$ standoff from the nanofiber axis; internal loss rate $\kappa_{\mathrm{in}}/2\pi=1.28(6)$ MHz; entanglement rate projection of 40 kHz neglects detector and transmission losses.
tools: 550-nm-diameter nanofiber cavity with fiber Bragg gratings
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Telecom-band nanofiber cavity with an array of 171 Yb atoms in optical tweezers. a , Overview of the platform. The nanofiber cavity is formed by a pair of fiber Bragg gratings (FBG1, FBG2) inscribed in the standard-fiber sections on either side of the nanofiber region, directly connected to the detection system. 171 Yb atoms are loaded into a 759-nm optical tweezer array and transported to $1\,\upmu$ m from nanofiber axis, where the atoms are strongly coupled to the evanescent cavity mode. b , Single-shot raw image of a five-site tweezer array, measured with standard 556-nm fluorescence imaging for ground-state atoms. Individual sites remain clearly resolved under illumination by two retroreflected excitation beams propagating in the $y$ – $z$ plane, with atoms placed at $1\,\upmu\mathrm{m}$ from the nanofiber axis; the black dashed line denotes the nanofiber axis at $x=0$ . For illustrative purpose, this image was taken without light-assisted collision, while for all other data presented in this paper we perform it to ensure single occupancies. c , Scanning electron micrograph of a fabricated nanofiber, with a nominal diameter of 550 nm. d , Calculated 759-nm tweezer potential in the transverse plane of the nanofiber; the dashed line marks the contour of atom-cavity coupling strength, $g_{\mathrm{0}}/2\pi=$ 2.95 MHz, calculated from the $\mathrm{HE}_{11}$ mode for the 550-nm-diameter nanofiber at the position of the trap center (white cross). Dash-dotted and dotted lines are the contours for $1.7g_{\mathrm{0}}$ and $0.3g_{\mathrm{0}}$ , respectively. e , Cavity-reflection spectra with (purple) and without single atom (gray) loaded to a single-site tweezer next to the nanofiber, where the reported photon-detector (PD) counts are scaled to correct for the frequency-dependent input power (Methods). Solid lines are fits to the input-output model, yielding $g/2\pi=1.86(17)$ MHz. The lower panel shows the residuals of the fit to the single-atom ( $N=1$ ) spectrum, with no evident systematic structure. f , Relevant 171 Yb levels. Atoms initialized in ${}^{1}\mathrm{S}_{0}$ are optically pumped (OP) to ${}^{3}\mathrm{P}_{0}$ using 556- and 1539-nm light and coupled to the cavity whose resonance is tuned to the ${}^{3}\mathrm{P}_{0}\leftrightarrow{}^{3}\mathrm{D}_{1}$ transition at $1389\,$ nm.
fields.figure_gloss: Cavity reflection as a function of detuning from the cavity resonance, showing the empty cavity dip (gray) versus vacuum Rabi splitting (purple) induced by a single trapped ${}^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ atom positioned $1~\mu\mathrm{m}$ from the nanofiber axis.

fields.result: Heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery with an enlarged ancilla ($d_{A}=2d+1$) spanning the inter-QPU boundary achieves logical readout error rates nearly independent of link noise, cutting $5-11-5$ physical qubit sites by 28.4% compared to uniform distance-9 (373 vs 521 qubits).
fields.question: How effectively can additional fault-tolerant error protection be concentrated at a noisy quantum processor interface while preserving the code distance of local data patches?
fields.prior: Uniform distance-3 and distance-5 implementations, which exhibit steep increases in logical error rates as link noise grows; at $p_{\mathrm{link}}=10^{-2}$, heterogeneous $3-7-3$ reduces decoding failure by factors of $\approx 13$ and $\approx 19$ relative to uniform distance-3.
fields.limits: Evaluated under circuit-level stochastic depolarizing noise with fixed local noise $p_{\mathrm{local}}=10^{-4}$; excludes idle noise, link-generation latency/failures, leakage, and correlated link faults. Requires more total inter-QPU gate applications despite fewer physical sites.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 13: Control- $X$ decoding failure probability per CNOT for mixed $5-11-5$ (blue circles) and uniform distance-5, -7, and -9 circuits (cyan squares, orange diamonds, and red triangles), with local noise parameter $10^{-4}$ . The inset resolves the mixed and distance-9 results. Each point uses 45 million shots; error bars show 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals.
fields.figure_gloss: Control-$X$ decoding failure probability per CNOT plotted against physical link error probability $p_{\mathrm{link}}$ from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$. Heterogeneous $5-11-5$ stays nearly flat and matches uniform distance-9 at high link noise while outperforming uniform distance-5 and -7.

fields.result: DMRG-based tensor network simulation natively evaluates dynamic circuits via single-path stochastic sampling and multi-path branch ensemble tracking on MPS and TTN structures, achieving scalable branch propagation with bounded peak memory on 27-qubit random circuits.
fields.question: How can tensor-network DMRG algorithms be extended to classically simulate dynamic quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward without exponential path overhead?
fields.limits: Evaluated up to 27 qubits and depth 8; fixed bond dimensions $\chi \in \{8, 16, 32\}$; multi-path branch count capped at $M=8$.
fields.figure_gloss: Runtime (left) and peak memory usage (right) versus qubit count for dynamic GHZ state preparation comparing unpruned multi-path simulation against single-path sampling with 16, 64, and 256 runs.

fields.result: Seam construction for distributed lattice surgery maintains minimum CNOT depth of 4, achieves fault distance $d-1$, and delivers lower, more stable logical error rates than alternating or interleaving schedules under link noise swept from $10p$ to $100p$ (with bulk noise $p = 10^{-4}$).
fields.question: How can distributed lattice surgery merge rotated surface-code patches with arbitrary boundaries across noisy inter-module links while avoiding distance-reducing hook errors and minimizing CNOT depth?
fields.prior: Prior Bell-measurement lattice surgery achieved a fault distance of $3d/4$ under noisy bulk conditions (and standard interleaving schedules required larger qubit overheads and higher CNOT depth).
fields.limits: Evaluated via circuit-level numerical simulations under uniform depolarizing noise with fixed bulk error rate $p = 10^{-4}$. Requires native three-qubit CXX gates at module seams.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3 : Merged surface-code layout for a logical Pauli- $XX$ measurement. Red (blue) plaquettes denote X (Z) type stabilizers. Each ancilla at the seam is split into two two-body checks. This allows us to join patches of differing boundary structure across a module boundary.
fields.figure_gloss: Merged rotated surface-code layout for logical Pauli-$XX$ measurement, showing weight-4 stabilizers at module seams split into paired weight-2 checks mediated across the boundary.

fields.result: Quantum error correction matrices are morphisms of group representations; Schur's lemma forces error matrix blocks to vanish when the symmetric power of the error representation shares no irreducible component with the codespace representation, reducing Knill-Laflamme conditions to character decomposition checks.
fields.question: How can finite-group representation theory be used to systematically construct multimode covariant bosonic codes and determine their error-correction capabilities?
fields.limits: Analyzes finite subgroups of $SU(2)$ under the amplitude damping channel; predicts error correctability in principle without specifying recovery protocols.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Error-correction performance of the two-mode quaternion ( $Q_{8}$ ) code with logical representation $\lambda\cong\rho_{2}\oplus\rho_{4}$ , evaluated against the amplitude damping channel for $\gamma=0.095$ . a) Near-optimal infidelity, $1-\tilde{F}$ , Eq. 15 as a function of the initial coherent state $\ket{\sqrt{r}\alpha,\sqrt{1-r}e^{i\theta}\alpha}$ where $r$ is the energy ratio between the first mode and the total energy and $\theta$ is the relative phase between modes. The near-optimal fidelity is plotted for the optimal initial state energy and results in $1-\tilde{F}\approx 0.023$ . b) Uncorrectable part of the QEC matrix plotted for the optimal initial parameters $r=0.5$ , $\theta=0$ and $|\alpha|^{2}\approx 0.528$ . Rows and columns are indexed by the two-mode loss label $\hat{E}_{k_{1}}^{\dagger}\otimes\hat{E}_{k_{2}}^{\dagger}$ and $\hat{E}_{l_{1}}\otimes\hat{E}_{l_{2}}$ and grouped (solid lines) by total error order $|l|=l_{1}+l_{2}$ . c) Minimum near-optimal infidelity optimized over $r$ and $\theta$ as a function of total energy $|\alpha|^{2}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Plots near-optimal infidelity $1-\tilde{F}$ against initial coherent state parameters under the amplitude damping channel with photon loss probability $\gamma = 0.095$ for the two-mode quaternion code.

fields.result: Alternating mixed Hadamard deformations within each concatenation level (`Alternate_Mixed_within_Level`) yields near-identical $X$ and $Z$ logical error rates while minimizing total logical error rate across one to four concatenation levels. Undeformed concatenation exhibits up to a $60\times$ higher $Z$ error rate than $X$ error rate at concatenation level $l=4$.
fields.question: How can Clifford deformations balance the asymmetric $X$ and $Z$ syndrome checks and logical error rates in concatenated $[[4,1,2]]$ Iceberg codes?
fields.prior: Undeformed concatenated $[[4,1,2]]$ Iceberg code produced skewed $X$ and $Z$ error rates due to having asymmetric check counts ($2\times X$ and $1\times Z$).
fields.limits: Code capacity phenomenological depolarizing noise (unbiased and $8\times$ biased), single-qubit Hadamard deformations only, simulated up to four concatenation levels with $500,000$ Monte Carlo shots.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 3 : LER under unbiased noise across one to four levels of concatenation.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate versus physical error rate under unbiased noise across concatenation levels $l=1$ to $4$, comparing total, $X$, and $Z$ LER and the $Z/X$ error ratio across six deformation strategies.

fields.result: Asymptotically good $[ ld{N}, ld{\Theta(N)}, ld{\Theta(N)}]$ qLDPC and qLTC codes with soundness $\Theta(1)$ support nontrivial transversal logical $\mathrm{C}^{r-1}Z$ non-Clifford gates for any integer $r\ge 2$.
fields.question: Can asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes and quantum locally testable codes directly support transversal non-Clifford logical gates simultaneously with linear distance and constant soundness?
fields.prior: Nontrivial transversal logical multi-controlled-$Z$ gates were achieved on almost-good qLDPC codes and qLTCs with polylogarithmic losses in distance and soundness (Li-Li-Liu 2026).
fields.limits: Characteristic 2 base fields; odd-sheeted covering towers; asymptotic $N\to\infty$ regime.
tools: cup product pairing with sheaf coefficients

fields.result: Mamba-based neural decoder matches Transformer accuracy on surface codes while dropping inference-cost scaling from quartic to quadratic in code distance. Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration reduces validation residuals and update variance in neural quantum states.
fields.question: How do learned representations, statistical regularization, and hardware constraints optimize quantum machine learning and classical neural methods for quantum error correction and simulation?
fields.prior: Transformer neural decoders scaled quartically with surface code distance; fixed-shift stochastic reconfiguration suffered from sample-noise trade-offs.
fields.limits: NMR demonstrations limited to small-scale DQC1; multi-shift SR adds computational cost; Mamba decoder evaluated under specific decoder-induced noise models.

fields.result: Strong $\varepsilon$-approximate relative error matchgate $k$-designs can be generated in depth $\mathcal{O}(k^2 {\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})\log n\log(n/\varepsilon))$ on a graph $\mathsf{G}$ with routing number ${\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})$, and exact strong matchgate $3$-designs in depth $\mathcal{O}({\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})\log n)$ without ancillae.
fields.question: Can non-local qubit connectivity enable the formation of matchgate designs in sublinear circuit depth, circumventing the linear-depth barrier present in one-dimensional architectures?
fields.prior: 1D nearest-neighbour circuits require $\Omega(n)$ depth to form approximate 2-designs over matchgates.
fields.limits: Applies to ancilla-free circuits; depth requires connectivity graphs $\mathsf{G}$ with low routing number (${\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})=2$ for all-to-all connectivity).
tools: random walks on the matchgate group
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1. Our construction proceeds in three steps: (1) Randomly sample $m\in\mathcal{O}(k^{2}n\log(n/\varepsilon))$ pairs $1\leqslant a_{i}<b_{i}\leqslant 2n$ , and $m$ angles $\vartheta_{i}$ ; apply the corresponding Majorana rotations $\{R_{a_{i},b_{i}}(\vartheta_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m}$ . (2) Check if those rotations can be parallelised into $\mathcal{O}(k^{2}\log(n/\varepsilon))$ layers of commuting gates; if not, go back to step one. (3) Compile each parallel layer of Majorana rotations into two qubit gates of depth $\mathcal{O}({\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})\log n)$ via a fermionic router. Concatenate two such independently accepted circuits; the total depth is then given by (# Layers) $\times\,\mathcal{O}({\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})\log n)=\mathcal{O}(k^{2}{\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})\log(n/\varepsilon)\log n)$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of the design construction showing generation via random 2-Majorana rotations, compression into parallel non-overlapping commuting layers, and compilation through a fermionic routing permutation.

fields.result: Explicit quantum locally testable CSS codes over binary alphabet with constant rate, quantum distance, soundness, and locality, conditional on Reed-Solomon product expansion conjecture.
fields.question: Can structured local codes with compatible symmetries overcome the polylogarithmic distance and soundness bottleneck in high-dimensional expander quantum locally testable code constructions?
fields.prior: Almost-good qLTCs with constant rate and locality but inverse-polylogarithmic relative distance and soundness (Dinur, Lin, and Vidick 2023).
fields.limits: Conditioned on validity of product expansion conjecture (Conjecture 5.6) for Reed-Solomon codes; asymptotic code family over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: The local view of vertex $v$ is a tensor code up to rescaling and permutations.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of local view at vertex $v$ showing how edge symmetries and coordinate changes map local views into tensor codes via rescaling and permutations.

fields.result: Any classical machine solving the structureless Yamakawa–Zhandry search problem with constant success probability must generate entropy $S[\rho] \ge \Theta(\lambda 2^{\lambda^c})$, requiring exponential Landauer heat dissipation and energy consumption $W \ge k_B T S[\rho]$, whereas the quantum solver needs only polynomial energy.
fields.question: Does the exponential quantum advantage for unstructured search persist for macroscopic physical resources like energy consumption?
fields.prior: Exponential quantum energy advantage was proven only for Simon's problem with a highly structured oracle (Meier & Yamasaki 2024), leaving unstructured search open.
fields.limits: Asymptotic security parameter $\lambda$, random oracle model, constant success probability $\Delta > 0$, cyclic computation reset to standard initial state.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Classical energy-consumption lower bound for a representative parameter choice at $T=300\,{\rm K}$ . The dots show $k_{B}TS$ using the explicit entropy bound from the Supplemental Material. The comparison lines indicate the annual energy consumption of CERN [ 16 ] and the annual luminosity of the observable universe [ 47 ] .
fields.figure_gloss: Classical energy-consumption lower bound $k_B T S$ at $T = 300\text{ K}$ versus security parameter $\lambda$, compared against macroscopic benchmarks like CERN annual energy consumption.

fields.result: Simulates generic lattice Lindbladian observables with gate count $\mathcal{O}((Nt)^{3/2 - 1/(4d+2)}\,\mathrm{polylog}(Nt/\varepsilon))$ per sample (in 1D, $\mathcal{O}((Nt)^{4/3}\,\mathrm{polylog}(Nt/\varepsilon))$) at sampling complexity $\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2})$. Achieves $\mathcal{O}(Nt\,\mathrm{polylog}(Nt/\varepsilon))$ for sparsely dissipative lattice dynamics.
fields.question: Can quantum simulation algorithms for generic lattice Lindbladians achieve gate counts approaching the fundamental lower bound $\Omega(Nt)$ while retaining polylogarithmic error scaling?
fields.prior: Best previous gate count for generic lattice Lindbladian observables with polylogarithmic error scaling was $\mathcal{O}((Nt)^{3/2}\,\mathrm{polylog}(Nt/\varepsilon))$ via extrapolation of second-order product formulas.
fields.limits: Finite-range interactions and dissipation on $d$-dimensional lattices with $d \in \mathcal{O}(1)$. Generic algorithm estimates observables via sampling rather than outputting coherent quantum states.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: (a) The patching strategy for generic local Lindbladians, giving $\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{Patch}}(\tau)$ by Eq. ( 97 ). We optimize the block size $R_{\mathrm{p}}$ to minimize the gate count while we set $R\in\Theta(\log(Nt/\varepsilon))$ . (b) The merging strategy based on Eqs. ( 103 ) and ( 104 ). The internal layers are merged and regarded as a set of disjoint green blocks with the size $\order{R}$ . (c) The outline of Algorithm 2 . We repeat the operation with the time $\tau=t/r_{t}$ . The orange blocks with the size $\order{R_\mr{p}}$ are reproduced by the LCU based approach for Lindbladian dynamics, while we use quasi-probabilistic sampling for the merged green blocks. The repetition number $r_{t}$ is determined so that the sampling overhead can be suppressed.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of patching and merging strategies for generic local Lindbladians: decomposition into blocks of size $R_{\mathrm{p}}$ with boundary regions of size $R$, followed by merging to absorb backward time evolution.

fields.result: Diagrammatic many-body perturbation theory is solved directly on real-frequency axis using systematically improvable complex pole and moment expansions. Controlled ESPRIT-based recompression truncates pole count, avoiding pole proliferation in self-consistent $GW$ and second-order Born (GF2) calculations.
fields.question: Can real-frequency finite-temperature diagrammatics be evaluated self-consistently without grid discretization or numerical analytic continuation while controlling pole proliferation?
fields.limits: Equilibrium Keldysh framework, weak-coupling conserving approximations without vertex corrections.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 10: Pole count of $\Sigma^{R}$ , $W^{R}$ , and $A$ after the re-compression step within the GW approximation, for the half-filled Bethe lattice at $\beta t=10$ and $U/t=2$ , (a) as a function of the specified compression tolerance $\varepsilon$ at convergence and (b) as a function of iteration for $\varepsilon=10^{-8}$ . (c) Enlarged view of $\mathrm{Im}\,\Sigma^{R}(\omega)/U^{2}$ from Fig. 6 (c) at convergence for tolerances $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$ to $10^{-12}$ . Inset: deviation from the $\varepsilon=10^{-12}$ result as a function of $\varepsilon$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Pole counts for retarded self-energy, screened interaction, and spectral function versus compression tolerance $\varepsilon$ (left) and iteration step (right) for GW on a half-filled Bethe lattice ($U/t=2$, $\beta t=10$). Recompression bounds the number of poles across self-consistency iterations.

fields.result: Rabi and Ramsey coherence times do not improve universally when scaling from four-dot to six-dot artificial Kitaev chain qubits under realistic disorder. Six-dot qubits suffer from increased leakage during Ramsey rotations due to larger detuning needed to overcome suppression of energy splitting.
fields.question: How do Rabi and Ramsey coherence times scale when expanding quantum-dot-based Majorana qubits from four dots to six dots?
fields.limits: Theoretical simulations with modeled quasi-static disorder under three parameter regimes (small gap, large gap, experimental parameters); non-adiabatic transitions out of Majorana subspace included.

fields.result: Electron-phonon coupling $g$ increases the effective interaction-to-hopping ratio $u^{\text{eff}}/t^{\text{eff}}$, enhancing bias-driven spin currents and transport spin polarization in asymmetric quantum ring junctions despite suppressing charge transport current.
fields.question: How do electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions affect bias-driven circular charge and spin currents in an open quantum ring nanojunction?
fields.limits: Tight-binding 1D ring, zero temperature, dispersionless out-of-plane optical Einstein phonons, acoustic phonon modes neglected.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 9: (Color online). Spin polarization (SP) coefficient as a function of bias voltage $V$ for four different sets of $u$ and $g$ , as described in the figure using four distinct colors.
fields.figure_gloss: Spin polarization coefficient plotted against bias voltage $V$ across different electron-electron interaction strengths $u$ and electron-phonon coupling strengths $g$. Increasing $g$ enhances spin polarization at low bias, which collapses toward zero at higher voltages where transport windows overlap.

fields.result: Cold-atom optical quantum memory achieves simultaneous temporal waveform adaptation across durations from $20\text{ ns}$ to $30\text{ \mu s}$ and average storage-and-retrieval efficiency $\eta=90.4(1.6)\%$ with conditional overlap $\mathcal{I}_{c}=97.9(2)\%$.
fields.question: Can an optical quantum memory provide deterministic temporal pulse reshaping without sacrificing high storage-and-retrieval efficiency?
fields.limits: Coherent pulses with mean photon number $\approx 1$; memory lifetime limited by thermal atomic motion and residual eddy-current magnetic field gradients ($10\text{ ms}$ MOT preparation duty cycle).
tools: optimal control theory for control field waveforms
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Bandwidth adaptation of single-photon Gaussian pulses. a-b, Examples of pulse stretching and compression. When the read pulse has lower power and longer duration than the write pulse, the signal pulse bandwidth is reduced and the pulse is temporally stretched. Conversely, when the read pulse has higher power and shorter duration than the write pulse, the bandwidth increases and the pulse is compressed. c, By simultaneously varying the power and duration of the read pulse while keeping their product constant, the same input pulse can be either compressed or stretched in time, providing over three decades of tunable output bandwidths. d, Bandwidth of the output pulse $\Delta f_{\mathrm{out}}$ as a function of the power of the read pulse $P_{c}$ (along with the appropriate duration) for different input bandwidths. e, The efficiency of the memory is largely independent of the input and output bandwidths over the large explored range, with a slight reduction for the lowest input bandwidth (circles) due to noise in the phase lock between the signal and control lasers. The control power is calibrated such that $P_{c}=1$ corresponds to $81(1)\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{W}$ and a Rabi frequency $\Omega/2\pi=$90(1)\text{\,}\mathrm{M}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$$ (Appendix). Data were collected with coherent pulses with an average photon number of $\approx 1$ . The error bars are obtained from the Poissonian error of the photon counting probabilities as well as power fluctuations during data acquisition.
fields.figure_gloss: Output pulse bandwidth $\Delta f_{\mathrm{out}}$ and memory efficiency $\eta$ plotted against read control pulse power $P_{c}$ for four different input pulse bandwidths. Demonstrates over three decades of continuously tunable bandwidth compression and stretching while maintaining near-constant high storage efficiency.

fields.result: Cavity Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency generates optical hybrid entangled states reaching size $|\alpha|^2 = 2.4$, with measured generation loss $L_g = 20\%$.
fields.question: Can quantum nonlinear optical systems based on cavity Rydberg EIT produce hybrid entangled Schrödinger cat states with larger coherent state amplitudes?
fields.prior: was $|\alpha|^2 = 1.4$ using a single atom in a cavity (Hacker et al. 2019) and $|\alpha|^2 = 0.8$ using traditional nonlinear media
fields.limits: Generation loss of $L_g = 20\%$, atom loss from recoil heating at higher target photon numbers, and self-blockade of target pulses.

All Wigner functions have negative regions (green), thus featuring a nonclassical property. The loss-corrected cat size increases from left ( $\alpha_{g}^{2}=0.18$ ) to right ( $\alpha_{g}^{2}=2.4$ ).
fields.figure_gloss: Reconstructed Wigner functions $W(x,p)$ of odd coherent state superpositions for six state sizes from $\alpha_g^2 = 0.18$ to $\alpha_g^2 = 2.4$, displaying negative regions that confirm nonclassical interference.

fields.result: Realized Hole Anti-hole Grating Echo Memory (HAGEM) in chemically engineered molecular $\mathrm{Eu^{3+}(TMHD)_{3}(phen)}$, demonstrating 14.9% quantum optical storage efficiency over a 200 MHz bandwidth.
fields.question: How can broadband quantum optical storage be achieved in non-Kramers rare-earth ions with more than two hyperfine levels?
fields.prior: Memory bandwidth in solid-state $\mathrm{Eu^{3+}}$ was restricted by narrow hyperfine splittings to a few MHz up to tens of MHz.
fields.limits: Input pulse mean photon number must remain well below 1 to avoid saturation of the 45 ns dead time single-photon detector; tested at 200 MHz bandwidth.

(c) 200 MHz optical density spectrum of powder and crystal after spectral pumping sequence. (d) SPD (single photon detection) measurements of quantum storage for powder. fields.result: Derives analytical filter functions and error formulas for Mølmer-Sørensen gate fidelity under fast laser phase noise (at trap frequencies) and slow noise (order of $1/\tau$), giving a simplified error estimate $\epsilon_{\mathrm{slow}}\sim\Delta\omega\tau$.
fields.question: How do fast and slow laser phase noise components quantitatively impact the fidelity of Mølmer-Sørensen gates across common beam geometries?
fields.prior: was numerical simulations without analytical expressions for fast noise (Nakav 2023) and filter functions restricted to optical path fluctuations (Kang 2023)
fields.limits: Assumes common laser source, white-noise approximation above cutoff frequencies of 10–100 Hz, equal intensities of bichromatic components, and finite measurement duration $T_0$.

For other details of the calculation see main text

fields.result: Engineering a bright-dark coupling $\Delta$ creates equally spaced dressed-dark states, yielding at least a 20-fold increase in steady-state energy storage over the Rabi-split blockade channel and near-quadratic power scaling $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{s}} \propto N^2$ in the bad-cavity limit.
fields.question: How can energy blockade and dynamical bistability in driven quantum batteries with level splitting be circumvented to enhance energy storage and charging power?
fields.prior: Conventional Rabi-split design blocked continuous excitation and suffered from bistability, giving at least 20 times lower energy storage and scaling at most as $\sim N^{3/2}$ without bad-cavity collective dissipation.
fields.limits: Requires resonant condition $\omega_c = \omega_0$, bad-cavity regime $\kappa \gg \gamma$, and operation within the superradiant window $1/\mathcal{C}_0 \ll N \ll N_{\mathrm{max}} = \kappa^2/g^2$.
tools: Adiabatic elimination in the bad-cavity limit

fields.result: Dissipative photon-magnon coupling in a planar inverted octa-ring resonator and YIG thin film produces Purcell factors $F_P$ between 4.11 and 5.27 for coupling strengths $g/2\pi$ from 40.7 to 46.1 MHz, entering the Purcell regime under $({\kappa}_m - {\kappa}_c)/2 \geq g > {\kappa}_c$.
fields.question: How do magnetic damping and saturation magnetization govern non-Hermitian spectral evolution and Purcell-enhanced cavity photon decay in dissipatively coupled planar photon-magnon systems?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation and theoretical modeling without experimental data; magnetocrystalline anisotropy neglected; static field along the in-plane x-axis.

fields.result: Realized standalone bosonic QEC in planar architecture using heavy fluxonium ($T_1^q = 451 	ext{ 	extmu s}$) and Archimedean spiral resonator, extending logical GKP state lifetime by factor of $1.59 \pm 0.05$.
fields.question: Can a long-lived fluxonium control qubit and an on-chip planar resonator implement standalone bosonic quantum error correction?
fields.prior: Bosonic QEC relied on 3D cavities controlled by fixed-frequency transmons with logical lifetimes limited by transmon $T_1^q \approx 200 \text{ 	extmu s}$.
fields.limits: Demonstrated at half-flux sweet spot; storage-fluxonium dispersive coupling $\chi/2\pi \approx 23\text{ kHz}$.

fields.result: Hybrid-integrated 780 nm microcomb engine achieves 100-kHz-level frequency drift over 2,000 s via $^{85}$Rb modulation-transfer spectroscopy lock, provides 102 mW injection-amplified single-tooth output, and coherently controls $^{87}$Rb BEC quantum states.
fields.question: Can a fully chip-integrated laser microcomb deliver sufficient coherence, stability, and optical power to drive coherent quantum manipulation of an ultracold gas?
fields.prior: Unstabilized self-injection-locked pump drifted by >200 MHz over 2,000 s.
fields.limits: Demonstrated for a single $^{87}$Rb BEC system; hold time limited by a 53.2 ms slow atom-number decay and spontaneous photon-recoil heating (0.556 μK/s minimum equivalent rate).

The CW pump is stabilized to an atomic transition $\lvert g\rangle\rightarrow\lvert e\rangle$ via a modulation-transfer spectroscopy (MTS) lock. A far-detuned comb line is filtered and amplified via injection locking (IL & ampl.) into a secondary laser diode, creating a high-power, narrow-linewidth CW laser for downstream cold-atom manipulation. b, Configuration for cold-atom manipulation. Counter-propagating beams (CW1) from the high-power diode form an optical lattice (left inset). A frequency-shifted secondary beam (CW2) from the same diode intersects CW1 to drive two-photon Raman coupling between the magnetic spin-up ( $\lvert\uparrow\rangle$ ) and spin-down ( $\lvert\downarrow\rangle$ ) states (right inset), where $\Delta$ represents the laser detuning from the atomic transition. c, Wafer-scale fabrication of Si 3 N 4 microresonators on a 150-mm substrate. Insets display an individual chip (top) and a single microresonator (bottom). d, Photograph of the packaged microcomb module. e, Photograph of the packaged CW-laser module. Inset shows the enclosed FP laser diode. f, Size, weight, and complexity comparison of our packaged modules against a standard commercial Ti:sapphire laser commonly used in cold-atom experiments.
