fields.result: Realized eight-photon half-excitation Dicke state with fidelity $0.922(11)$, enabling open-destination teleportation to seven remote agents with fidelities $0.926(7)-0.941(6)$ and $1\!\rightarrow\!7$ telecloning with average fidelity $0.713(3)$.
fields.question: Can a quantum network continue to outperform classical strategies when photon detection imperfections and missing assisting-agent information occur at different stages of operation?
fields.prior: Six-photon Dicke state generation previously demonstrated.
fields.limits: Postselected eightfold coincidences from four-pair SPDC emission recorded at $3.5\times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$; threshold detectors cannot resolve multi-photon path occupancies.
tools: Type-II spontaneous parametric down-conversion in ppKTP
Projector decomposition into 29 collective polarization settings
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Teleportation and Telecloning Fidelities. a , Open-destination teleportation fidelity for each of the seven possible receivers, evaluated over the uniformly sampled input ensemble $\mathcal{E}=\{\ket{H},\ket{V},\ket{D},\ket{A},\ket{R},\ket{L}\}$ . All receiver choices remain well above the classical limit of 2/3 (black dashed line). b , Average $1\!\rightarrow\!7$ quantum telecloning at each of the seven remote agents. The red dashed line marks the optimal universal cloning fidelity of 5/7. Error bars denote one standard deviation from counting statistics.

fields.result: Dynamic control of the frequency detuning $2\	ext{delta}$ between two superconducting qubits spaced by $\	ext{lambda}/2$ realizes an effective $\	ext{Lambda}$-type quantum memory without microwave control drives, achieving near-unity fidelities $F_\text{q} \approx F_\text{c} \approx \eta \approx 1$ for pulse bandwidth $\gamma_\text{ph} = 2\Gamma$.
fields.question: Can an effective $\Lambda$-type quantum memory be implemented in superconducting circuits without applying an external strong coherent microwave drive?
fields.limits: Theoretical simulation; assumes Markovian regime $\Gamma\tau, \Omega_\text{p}\tau \ll 1$, qubit detuning $\delta \ll \omega_0$, weak probe $\Omega_\text{p} \ll \Gamma$, and pure dephasing $\Gamma_\phi/2\pi = 5\text{ kHz}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Quantum-light storage and retrieval. (a) Photon flux and detuning control for the storage and retrieval of a single-photon state. (b) Photon flux (top) and normalized squared field amplitudes (bottom) for the photonic superposition state. Panels (a) and (b) are obtained in the absence of dephasing. (c) Quantum-memory performance as a function of $t_{\rm r}$ under dephasing $\Gamma_{\upphi}/2\pi=5\ {\rm kHz}$ for $\gamma_{\rm ph}=0.2\Gamma$ , and (d) for $\gamma_{\rm ph}=2\Gamma$ . Black dashed lines show theoretical predictions based on exponential decay at rate $\Gamma_{\upphi}$ .

fields.result: Explicit binary CSS codes achieve constant rate $K_i = \Theta(N_i)$ and linear distance $D_i = \Theta(N_i)$ while supporting fully addressable transversal logical $T$ gates via physical powers of $T$ without Clifford corrections.
fields.question: Can an explicit family of asymptotically good binary quantum codes admit fully addressable transversal $T$ gates?
fields.prior: Transversal $T$ achieved growing distance $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log N})}$ at constant rate (Wills 2026) or linear distance with vanishing rate (Hastings and Haah 2018), but not both simultaneously with addressability.
fields.limits: Asymptotic regime in code block length $N_i \to \infty$. Binary CSS code construction without stabilizer generator weight bounds.
tools: Binary embedding with fivefold overlap identities
Affine space minimum Hamming weight formulation

fields.result: Under a schedule-resolved circuit noise model, analog-informed BP–OSD decoding of GKP-concatenated qLDPC codes yields crossing estimates of $\sigma_{\mathrm{th}}\simeq 0.212$ (10.46 dB squeezing) for bivariate bicycle (BB) codes and $0.142$ (13.94 dB squeezing) for tricycle codes.
fields.question: How do structured quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) outer codes perform when concatenated with Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) modes under circuit-level noise and analog-informed decoding?
fields.prior: A passive-linear-optical measurement-based GKP architecture with BB outer codes achieved a threshold of $\sigma_{\mathrm{gkp}}\simeq 0.209$ (10.6 dB) using foliated graph states and correlation-aware decoding.
fields.limits: Finite-size crossing estimates evaluated on selected finite-length code instances ($N \le 144$ for BB, $N \le 108$ for tricycle), not universal asymptotic code family thresholds.
tools: Bivariate bicycle (BB) and tricycle qLDPC codes
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Word logical error rates under the full propagated circuit model for (a) GKP–BB and (b) GKP–tricycle concatenation. The finite-size crossing estimates are $(0.212,0.198)$ for analog and hard BB decoding and $(0.142,0.130)$ for analog and hard tricycle decoding, respectively.
fields.figure_gloss: Word logical error rate versus displacement noise width $\sigma$ for BB and tricycle codes under the full propagated circuit model, showing analog-informed BP-OSD crossings at $\sigma_{\mathrm{th}} \simeq 0.212$ and $0.142$, respectively.

fields.result: Simulation-secure one-time memory (OTM) using BB84 states achieves simulation advantage $\le(n+3)(3/4)^n$ against quantum adversaries restricted to at most $q\le 2^{\ell/2-1}-1$ classical random-oracle queries.
fields.question: Can an efficient one-time memory protocol be constructed under assumptions robust to early fault-tolerant quantum computers instead of shallow NISQ circuits?
fields.limits: Adversary can perform arbitrary quantum computation and long-term quantum storage but cannot query the random oracle coherently on superpositions.

fields.result: Reduces compiled circuit depth by $2.57\times$ over Qiskit and $10.35\times$ over t|ket⟩ for 2-local Hamiltonian simulation on quantum chiplets, while cutting compilation time $19.54\times$ compared to 2QAN.
fields.question: How can 2-local qubit Hamiltonian simulation circuits be compiled to minimize cross-chiplet communication depth and operation count on multi-chiplet quantum architectures?
fields.prior: Domain-specific compiler 2QAN timed out on most large benchmarks due to $O(m^2 n)$ routing and $O(m^4)$ scheduling, and chiplet compiler MECH produced $1.69\times$ higher circuit depth.
fields.limits: Simulated hardware models; ancilla qubit allocation on chiplets is not automated; cross-chiplet and measurement error rates fixed at $p_{\text{cross}}/p_{\text{on}}=7.4$ and $p_{\text{meas}}/p_{\text{on}}=0.7$.
fields.figure_caption: (a) Depth (normalized by Qiskit).
fields.figure_gloss: Normalized circuit depth relative to Qiskit across benchmarks as multi-chip module size scales from 3 to 16 chiplets, demonstrating increasing depth reduction advantages.

fields.result: Correlated error conjecture posits that for any entangled physical qubits, the effective noise channel necessarily retains a joint fully depolarizing component of rate comparable to elementary two-qubit entangling gates, even when entanglement is created indirectly.
fields.question: What structural constraints on correlated noise in entangled physical qubits could inherently obstruct quantum fault tolerance?
fields.prior: Standard stochastic fault-tolerance models predict the largest joint fully depolarizing component for indirect entanglement (e.g. via an intermediate mediator qubit) has weight $t^2$ rather than $t$.
fields.limits: Open theoretical conjecture; assumes noise correlates directly with physical entanglement rather than obeying standard weak-decay or independent error assumptions.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Given a proposed architecture for a quantum computer, it is possible that for some hypothetical states that cannot be achieved, the proposed properties of noise are “unphysical.” The place to examine the conjectures is for attainable states.
fields.figure_gloss: Conceptual schematic distinguishing physically attainable states in a proposed quantum architecture from unphysical hypothetical states where conjectured noise properties are tested.

fields.result: Any single-qubit unitary can be synthesized to precision $\varepsilon$ in constant depth using $O(\log^{1+\delta}(1/\varepsilon))$ clean ancillae, single-qubit gates $\{H, T\}$, and generalized Toffoli gates without Fan-Out. In the bounded-width gate model, synthesis achieves optimal depth $\Theta(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$.
fields.question: Can quantum computation be restricted to a fixed gate set without increasing circuit depth?
fields.prior: Kim-Laakkonen online synthesis achieved constant $T$-depth using an $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$-qubit catalyst, but without an end-to-end constant-depth unitary catalyst preparation.
fields.limits: Asymptotic in precision $\varepsilon$; bounded-width compilation achieves $\Theta(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$ depth instead of constant depth.

fields.result: Wrapping high-level routines across 5 quantum frameworks into Apache NiFi processors using OpenQASM 2.0 exchange enabled $N\times M$ multi-version execution, uncovering 3 real hardware and cloud-adapter defects.
fields.question: What quantum programs can be expressed at the visual component level without manual circuit coding, and what does running all framework-engine combinations reveal?
fields.limits: Evaluated on small Grover and adder circuits; 4-qubit Grover outputs approached random chance (probabilities of 0.01–0.19) due to hardware noise; shared Qiskit transpiler across builders.
tools: IBM, IQM, and Quantum Inspire backends
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 3: The version matrix as it runs on quantum computers: one case, three Grover builders, three devices, and the nine resulting paths meeting at one oracle.
fields.figure_gloss: The $N\times M$ multi-version execution topology, mapping one test case across 3 framework builders to 3 quantum devices for 9 parallel execution paths that converge at an oracle.

fields.result: Query complexity of quantum linear systems problem is $\Theta(\kappa\sqrt{d}\log(1/\epsilon))$. Any $N\times N$ unitary can be implemented to error $\epsilon$ using $O(\sqrt{N}\log(1/\epsilon))$ queries to matrix entries.
fields.question: What is the optimal query complexity of the quantum linear systems problem in condition number $\kappa$, sparsity $d$, and precision $\epsilon$?
fields.prior: Best previous upper bounds were $O(\kappa d\log(1/\epsilon))$ (Costa et al. 2022) and $\kappa\sqrt{d}(\kappa d/\epsilon)^{o(1)}$ (Low 2024); prior lower bounds were $\Omega(\kappa\log(1/\epsilon))$ (Costa et al. 2022) and $\Omega(\kappa\sqrt{d})$ (Mori et al. 2024). Black-box unitary implementation was $O(N^{2/3}(\log\log N)^{4/3})$ (Berry & Childs 2012) and $O(N^{1/2+o(1)})$ (Low 2024).
fields.limits: Asymptotic regime for large $\kappa$, $d$, and $1/\epsilon$. Standard sparse-matrix location and value oracle model.
tools: split linear system exact block encoding

fields.result: Two quantum eigenvalue transformation algorithms for $n$-tuples of commuting matrices implement holomorphic functions via multivariable contour integrals or smooth functions via Fourier transforms; matrix polynomial query complexity depends on global bounds rather than monomial degree or term counts.
fields.question: How can general matrix-valued eigenvalue transformations be efficiently implemented on a quantum computer for multivariable tuples of commuting matrices?
fields.prior: Direct monomial multiplication and LCU scaled exponentially with polynomial degree $d$ as $\mathcal{O}(d \alpha_1^d / \|A_1^d |\psi\rangle\|)$ for block-encoding factor $\alpha_1 > 1$, while multivariable QSP extensions lacked general completeness.
fields.limits: Applies strictly to pairwise commuting matrices; requires block-encodings for each input matrix; Fourier transform approach requires smooth cutoffs and Hermitian inputs.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : Compression gadget for coherently implementing the ordered product $A_{L}\cdots A_{1}$ . The open controls indicate conditioning on the block-encoding ancilla register being in $|0^{a}\rangle$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Quantum circuit schematic for the compression gadget used to implement the ordered product $A_L \dots A_1$ while reducing ancilla overhead to logarithmic scaling in $L$.

fields.result: Trotterisation accuracy thresholds survive under Markovian dissipation, persisting into steady-state observable limits; genuine dissipative quantum chaos emerges beyond the same step-size threshold $\tau$ when dissipation $f_\gamma$ balances underlying unitary chaos.
fields.question: Does the Trotterisation threshold and the onset of quantum chaos persist in digital quantum simulation when environmental noise, decoherence, and dissipation are present?
fields.limits: Weak-coupling Markovian regime (Lindblad master equation). Eigenvector Ginibre RMT matching requires filtering complex-conjugate eigenmatrices and restricting to bulk eigenvalues.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Characterising quantum chaos in open-system DQS. The first, second, and third columns correspond to the kicked top (with $j=10$ ), Heisenberg (chain of $N=5$ qubits), and Rabi (with cavity truncation dimension $\text{dim}_{c}=4$ ) models, respectively. The x-axes and y-axes of all panels correspond to the Trotter step size $\tau$ and dissipation strength scaling factor $f_{\gamma}$ , respectively. (a-c) Contribution $d_{1}/D$ of the dominant Kraus operator $K_{1}$ to the evolution. (d-f) Deviation from the unitarity of the dominant Kraus operator $K_{1}$ quantified using the Frobenius norm as $\|K_{1}^{\dagger}K_{1}-I\|/D$ . (g-i) Goodness-of-fit $X^{2}_{\mathrm{RMT}}$ of the eigenvector statistics of the dominant Kraus operator $K_{1}$ to RMT predictions. Goodness-of-fit $X^{2}_{\mathrm{RMT}}$ of the (j-l) left and (m-o) right eigenvector statistics of the Floquet superoperator to Ginibre RMT predictions. The light-coloured part of the colour bars corresponds to the 99% confidence regions of the $X^{2}_{\mathrm{RMT}}$ test to determine whether the eigenvector statistics are consistent with RMT predictions. The dashed lines show the boundaries of the dissipative quantum chaotic regions in the eigenvector statistics of the Floquet superoperator found heuristically from the individual eigenvector statistics of the Floquet superoperator in Fig. 6 .
fields.figure_gloss: Heatmaps of the Kraus weight $d_1/D$, non-unitarity norm, and $X^2_{\mathrm{RMT}}$ goodness-of-fit against RMT for dominant Kraus and Floquet superoperator eigenvectors as a function of Trotter step size $\tau$ (x-axis) and dissipation scaling factor $f_\gamma$ (y-axis). Highlighted regions show 99% confidence agreement with RMT beyond the Trotterisation threshold.

fields.result: Introduces reactivity $R(w)$, a complexity metric based on the total contribution of Pauli paths of weight $w$ to an entire quantum experiment. Experiments with low reactivity $w_*$ admit classical simulation in $2^{\mathcal{O}(w_*)}$ time (global) or $N^{\mathcal{O}(w_*)}$ time (Pauli-random circuits).
fields.question: Which quantum circuits and dynamics can be efficiently simulated classically using local-information algorithms, and can their complexity be probed directly in experiments?
fields.prior: was $n^{\mathcal{O}(1/\gamma)}$ for noisy circuits with rate $\gamma$ (Aharonov 2023) and $n^{\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon)}$ for random Clifford circuits (Haferkamp 2023)
fields.limits: Adversarial experiments can spoof high reactivity while remaining simple by other means; rigorous time-slice theorem applies specifically to Pauli-random circuits.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: (a) Any quantum experiment, $\tr(O\,\mathcal{C}(\psi))$ , can be expanded as a sum over Pauli paths (illustrated as space-time patterns of Pauli operators). (b) Pauli path spectroscopy probes this decomposition by measuring the response of the experiment to controlled local perturbations. This allows one to extract the reactivity function , $R(w)$ , which quantifies the total contribution to $\tr(O\,\mathcal{C}(\psi))$ from Pauli paths of weight $w$ . Contributions from small $w$ (green) are easy to classically simulate, while contributions from high $w$ (red) are hard to simulate for classical algorithms based on local information.
fields.figure_gloss: Decomposition of an expectation value $\operatorname{tr}(O\,\mathcal{C}(\psi))$ into space-time Pauli paths (a) and extraction of the reactivity $R(w)$ across Pauli path weights $w$ via response to local perturbations (b).

fields.result: Infinite-temperature dynamical correlation deviations $\Delta C(t)$ under finite-window truncation grow as $t^{m_A+m_B}$, doubling the short-time order of observable deviations $t^{m_A}$ and yielding a computable, rigorous error bound $\mathcal{B}_C(t)$.
fields.question: How can finite-region local dynamics provide rigorous and tight error bounds for infinite-temperature correlation functions in non-integrable many-body systems?
fields.limits: Infinite temperature limit; requires traceless Pauli boundary couplings $\text{tr}_{\text{out}}V=0$; error bounds grow rapidly once operator support reaches window boundaries.
tools: equations of motion for observable deviations

( 18 )) for a chain of $n=51$ spins with bond dimension $\chi$ , using TeNPy fourth order TEBD with time-step $dt=0.02$ . fields.result: State-vector-emulated dual-basis quantum SCF matches classical Kohn–Sham DFT within 0.02 mHa for an $\text{H}_8$ chain using $32\,768$ plane waves and PWOO bases up to cc-pVTZ; dual-basis contraction shifts PWOO energies by at most $5.7\,\mu\text{Ha}$.
fields.question: Can first-quantization, all-electron, full-potential Kohn–Sham DFT be solved self-consistently on quantum hardware across systematically enlarged orthonormal bases?
fields.prior: Senjean, Yalouz, and Saubanère (2022) demonstrated simulated molecular KS-DFT for $\text{H}_8$ using subspace-search VQE in a Löwdin-orthonormalized STO-3G atomic-orbital basis.
fields.limits: All full-loop SCF calculations are emulated via state vectors or shot-noise models; physical hardware tests on IonQ Forte-1 evaluate single-step state readout rather than an active SCF loop.
tools: Dual-basis quantum eigensolver (Rotosolve coordinate descent + Rayleigh–Ritz updates)
Penalty deflation and modified Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization

fields.result: Perfect Born sampling on purified thermal tensor networks enables simultaneous importance sampling and direct non-Abelian symmetry acceleration, simulating square-lattice Hubbard cylinders up to width $W=10$ and triangular-lattice Hubbard states down to $T/t = 1/64$.
fields.question: How can stochastic sampling of thermal tensor networks incorporate both importance sampling efficiency and Abelian/non-Abelian symmetry acceleration?
fields.limits: Born sample states must be generated at an intermediate temperature $T_0$ before stochastic cooling, and 2D PEPS contraction relies on approximate boundary-MPS truncation.

fields.result: Optimizing in-plane magnetic-field orientation minimizes longitudinal spin-electric susceptibility, increasing $T_{2}^{\rm Echo}$ 5-fold and reaching a maximum single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.82 % via gate set tomography.
fields.question: How does the longitudinal spin-electric susceptibility correlate with qubit coherence and single-qubit control fidelities across different in-plane magnetic-field orientations in planar germanium hole spin qubits?
fields.limits: Single-hole spin qubit in a dilution refrigerator at base temperature 15 mK; in-plane magnetic field fixed at $B_{0} = 900$ mT swept over $\pm 50^{\circ}$; limited to 1-qubit gate operations.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: (a–b) Control infidelities of the gate set ${I/2,X/2,Y/2}$ as functions of the in-plane magnetic-field angle $\theta_{\rm xy}$ . The infidelities of the $X/2$ and $Y/2$ gates exhibit non-monotonic angular dependence, first increasing and then decreasing with $\theta_{\rm xy}$ . The maximum gate error occur at magnetic-field orientations corresponding to the shortest $T_{2}^{\rm Echo}$ . For qubit Q1 (Q2), the control infidelity at the optimal operating point is reduced by approximately one order of magnitude (a factor of five) compared to the worst case. The insets show the $I$ gate infidelity. The horizontal axis is $\theta_{\rm{xy}}$ , and the vertical axis is the gate infidelity, as in the main panel. Although the $I$ gate infidelity is determined by both $T_{2}^{*}$ and $f_{\rm Rabi}$ , the nearly constant $T_{2}^{*}$ across the measured range of $\theta_{\rm{xy}}$ indicates that the observed angular dependence is governed predominantly by $f_{\rm Rabi}$ . For Q1, the $I$ -gate infidelities exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on $\theta_{\rm xy}$ , consistent with the behavior of $f_{\rm Rabi}$ in Appendix C . For Q2, the infidelities initially decreases and then saturates, following the trend of $f_{\rm Rabi}$ in Appendix C . This saturation indicates that further enhancement of $f_{\rm Rabi}$ yields diminishing returns for gate fidelity, and that additional improvements require optimization of other qubit coherence properties, such as $T_{2}^{*}$ and $T_{2}^{\rm Rabi}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Gate infidelities for $X/2$, $Y/2$, and $I$ gates as a function of the in-plane magnetic field angle $\theta_{\rm xy}$. Infidelities drop by nearly an order of magnitude at the optimal field orientation where longitudinal spin-electric susceptibility is minimized.

fields.result: Non-adiabatic geometric quantum gates on a germanium hole spin qubit reach maximum gate-set-tomography fidelities of 99.98% for $I$, 99.80% for $X/2$, and 99.97% for $Y/2$, maintaining $>99\%$ fidelities across a wide range of Rabi frequencies.
fields.question: Can non-adiabatic geometric quantum computation overcome off-resonance noise and achieve single-qubit gate fidelities exceeding fault-tolerant thresholds in germanium hole spin qubits?
fields.prior: Dynamical gates on the same device achieved maximum GST fidelities of 97.48% for $I$, 99.81% for $X/2$, and 99.88% for $Y/2$, where consecutive $I$ gates were severely limited by off-resonance noise.
fields.limits: Single-qubit operations only; geometric gates require approximately four times longer duration than dynamical gates.
tools: planar strained germanium double quantum dots
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Noise-resilient feature of single-qubit geometric gates. The upper panels of a-c show that control fidelities of the $I$ , $X$ /2 and $Y$ /2 gates, realized by both geometric and dynamical approaches, as a function of $\Delta f$ . The light grey lines represent 99 $\%$ control fidelity threshold. Notably, even with detuning $\Delta f$ by ±2.5 MHz (±1.2 MHz), the control fidelities of geometric $X$ /2 and $Y$ /2 ( $I$ ) gates can still reach 99 $\%$ . The differences in the control fidelities between the two approaches are displayed in the lower panels. The black dashed arrows serve as visual guides to emphasize that as $\Delta f$ increases, the control fidelities of the dynamical gates decrease faster than those of the geometric gate. Error bars represent the 95 $\%$ confidence level. The experimental results are consistent with the numerical simulations (blue and red dashed lines).
fields.figure_gloss: Gate fidelities for geometric and dynamical $I$, $X/2$, and $Y/2$ gates as a function of microwave detuning $\Delta f$. Geometric gates retain $>99\%$ fidelity up to detunings of $\pm 2.5\text{ MHz}$ for $X/2$ and $Y/2$ ($\,\pm 1.2\text{ MHz}$ for $I$), decaying significantly slower than dynamical gates.

fields.result: Grover amplitude amplification in a single transmon qubit dispersively coupled to a cavity reduces signal required for binary frequency classification by $>10\times$ at detection bandwidths $>10$ MHz.
fields.question: Can Grover's search algorithm be implemented on near-term quantum hardware to enhance the detection of unknown frequency signals over large bandwidths?
fields.prior: Coherent-probe baseline without Grover amplification required $>10\times$ more sensed signal resource for high accuracy and large bandwidth.
fields.limits: Demonstrated for binary classification of pulsed signals with known arrival intervals; coherent probe initialization introduces non-uniformity across bandwidth.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3 : Demonstration of a Grover-based enhancement in quantum sensing. a Scatter plot of total signal sensed, defined as $n_{\mathrm{shots}}(2N+1)$ , required to reach $75\%$ classification accuracy as a function of the target bandwidth $\Delta f$ for a signal-pulse duration of $0.25/\chi$ . Classification accuracies and bandwidths were calculated for a range of initial displacements using methods detailed in Appendix C . A protocol with $N$ Grover iterations has a sensing cost of $2N+1$ signal-interaction per shot. Colors denote the number of Grover iterations $N$ , with $N=0$ giving the coherent-probe baseline. Points show the mean over 100 trials, and error bars show the standard deviation across these trials. In each trial, 1,000 points are randomly drawn from a dataset of 10,000 points, with 800 used for training and 200 for validation. Dashed curves are fits to the shot-estimate model described in the Appendix E . The green shaded region marks the bandwidth range over which Grover-based sensing requires less total signal sensed than the coherent-state baseline. Gray vertical bands indicate the three representative bandwidths shown in panels (i) – (iii) . Grover-based sensing achieves a given sensing bandwidth at a smaller coherent-state amplitude $\alpha$ , extending the bandwidth accessible before possible breakdown of the dispersive approximation. The upper-right inset shows the bandwidth at which the fitted shot requirement diverges as the contrast between in-band and out-of-band signals vanishes. Unlike the response bandwidth in Fig. 2 c, this quantity characterizes the bandwidth limit imposed by the resources required for classification. Its increase with the number of Grover iterations shows that amplitude amplification extends the range over which classification can be performed with finite resources. b Grover enhancement, defined as the ratio of the total signal sensed by the coherent-probe baseline to that required by the Grover protocol, as a function of sensing bandwidth for signal-pulse durations $L=1/4\chi$ and $1/2\chi$ . Results are shown for target classification accuracies of $75\%$ (top) and $90\%$ (bottom). The horizontal dashed line marks unity, above which the Grover protocol provides a resource advantage, highlighted in green.
fields.figure_gloss: Total signal sensed ($n_{\mathrm{shots}}(2N+1)$) versus target bandwidth $\Delta f$. Shows Grover iterations exceeding non-Grover baseline performance for bandwidths above 10 MHz.

fields.result: Silicon vacancies ($V_{\mathrm{Si}}$) at 3C/4H-SiC heterophase interfaces exhibit zero-phonon optical transitions with zero-phonon linewidth narrowed to 4.71 meV at room temperature.
fields.question: Can heterophase crystal interfaces engineer defect-phonon interactions to enhance zero-phonon lines in wide-bandgap solid-state emitters?
fields.prior: Single-phase 4H-SiC membranes exhibit broader phonon sidebands and weaker zero-phonon-line transitions due to intrinsic electron-phonon interactions.
fields.limits: Demonstrated at room temperature for $V_{\mathrm{Si}}$ in 3C/4H heterophase SiC membranes.

fields.result: In a three-QPC open-dot interferometer, the anyonic exchange phase $\theta=\pi\nu$ can be extracted from Aharonov-Bohm phase shifts via co-tunneling, yielding relative errors from $-0.29\%$ to $+0.41\%$ at $T=10\text{ mK}$ and $2.97\%$ to $5.25\%$ at $T=20\text{ mK}$ for $\nu=1/3$ by linear extrapolation.
fields.question: Can the bare anyonic exchange phase $\theta$ be extracted directly from Aharonov-Bohm interference oscillations in an interferometer where an open quantum dot edge segment mediates resonant co-tunneling?
fields.prior: Cross-geometry interferometers require four tunneling amplitudes to produce Aharonov-Bohm interference, whereas this three-QPC design yields interference at third order in tunneling amplitudes.
fields.limits: Valid for Laughlin states $\nu=1/m$ with single chiral edge modes and minimal quasiparticle charges $e^*=\nu e$. Neglects hole-conjugate and multi-mode edges.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Estimation of the exchange phase from simultaneous measurements of the currents in drains D3 and D2 for $V_{1}=-V_{2}\equiv V/2$ and $V_{3}=0$ at temperature $T=$10\text{\,}\mathrm{mK}$$ (upper and center panels) and $T=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{mK}$$ (lower panel). The upper panel shows the phase shift to the Aharonov–Bohm phase of the current on edges 2 ( $\delta_{2}$ , red) and 3 ( $\delta_{3}$ , blue) for QPC distance $a=$1\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$$ . The center and lower panels depict the estimated exchange phase from the difference of these phases and an additional $\pi$ shift for various values of $a$ . Because both currents are measured at the same voltages, common electrostatic phase shifts cancel, while finite-temperature and time-of-flight corrections produce a voltage dependence rather than stable plateaus. Linear fits to the region $V\in[$60\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro V}$,$80\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro V}$]$ are shown as dashed lines. From the $V=0$ intercepts of these fits, the exchange phase can be obtained with relative errors well below $10\%$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Phase shift difference $\delta_2 - \delta_3 + \pi$ as a function of voltage bias $V$ for different quantum point contact separations $a$ at $T=10\text{ mK}$ and $T=20\text{ mK}$. Zero-bias extrapolations from the linear regime recover the exchange phase $\pi/3$ with errors under $10\%$.

fields.result: Mitigation methods based on circuit reactivity functions eliminate zero-noise extrapolation bias errors up to 30% and lower the sampling overhead by up to $10^3$ compared to probabilistic error cancellation at $\sim 10^{-2}$ root-mean-square error.
fields.question: Can quantum error mitigation methods be given systematic tuning parameters and guided by a compact physical representation of circuit information dynamics?
fields.prior: Conventional zero-noise extrapolation has no systematic convergence parameter and suffers biases up to 30%, while probabilistic error cancellation incurs exponential sampling overhead.
fields.limits: Demonstrated numerically on three circuit families (nuclear spin OTOCs, Stark MBL in XY model, and 2D TFIM) under single-qubit depolarizing noise.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 9: Error mitigation results for the 2D TFIM. a , b : Comparison of the accuracies when increasing the number of shots for the different error mitigation methods, analogous to Fig. 7 , for the $\gamma$ -cumulant method (blue), the $\gamma$ -multi-exponential method (red), and the $k$ -TEC method using either the analytic filter function (dash-dotted green) or numerically-optimized filter functions (dashed green). For either filter function, the threshold weight is chosen via the adaptive algorithm described in the main text. For comparison, the PEC scaling (dash-dotted black) and the theoretically optimal result is shown (dashed black).
fields.figure_gloss: Root-mean-square error versus total shot count for 2D TFIM order parameter estimation. The plot shows convergence of tunable error cancellation and Pauli-path extrapolation methods toward the exact zero-noise value with lower sample overhead than probabilistic error cancellation.

fields.result: Cavity dressing creates a crossover boundary scaling as $G_{\rm c}\propto\sqrt{\Omega}$ in a single-electron double quantum dot, where increasing Rashba coupling from $\alpha/J=1$ to $\alpha/J=2$ increases maximum ergotropy from $\mathcal{E}_{\max}/J\simeq 2.84$ to $\mathcal{E}_{\max}/J\simeq 4.48$.
fields.question: How do cavity-photon couplings and Rashba spin-orbit interaction jointly control quantum correlations, stored energy, and ergotropy in a semiconductor double quantum dot?
fields.prior: Prior work investigated Rashba coupling alone without cavity-photon interactions [Ferreira et al., Phys. Rev. A 107, 052408 (2023)].
fields.limits: Numerical truncation of cavity photon number to $N=5$; closed unitary charging without explicit environment dissipation or cavity photon decay.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: Maximum ergotropy $\mathcal{E}_{\max}/J$ achieved within the $(g_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{opt}}/g_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{max}};G/J;tJ)$ grid for (a) $\alpha/J=1$ and (b) $\alpha/J=2$ . We have assumed $k_{\text{B}}T/J=0.01$ , $B/J=2$ , $\Omega/J=5$ and $N=5$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Normalized optimal charge-photon coupling $g_{\rm c}^{\rm opt}/g_{\rm c}^{\max}$ (vertical axis) and maximum ergotropy $\mathcal{E}_{\max}/J$ (color scale) as functions of spin-photon coupling $G/J$ and charging time $tJ$ for $\alpha/J=1$ and $\alpha/J=2$.

fields.result: Repeated QND-based measurement-induced cat amplification prepares large-amplitude cat states without post-selection on specific photon numbers; success probability reaches $80.64\%$ after 6 rounds for GKP-breeding resources yielding at least 10 dB effective squeezing, scaling with target fidelity $\mathcal{F} \approx 1 - 0.03/n_{\text{tot}}$ for $n_{\text{tot}} \ge 3$.
fields.question: How can optical large-amplitude squeezed cat states suitable for Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill breeding protocols be generated with near-deterministic efficiency?
fields.prior: Single-round 6 dB squeezer cat preparation achieves a success probability of $0.16\%$ for $n_{\text{tot}} \ge 8$.
fields.limits: Requires photon-number resolving detection and inline optical squeezing; susceptible to optical loss per squeezer and detector inefficiency.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Preparation of large-amplitude cat states compatible with GKP breeding schemes. (a) Cat generation based on a measurement-induced cat amplifier. In the first round, vacuum signal and ancilla modes are mixed via a QND interaction, after which the signal mode has its $q$ -quadrature anti-squeezed. A measurement of $n$ photons in the ancillary mode heralds an approximate cat state $\ket{\mathcal{C}(\sqrt{n},n)}$ at the output. The interaction can be repeated, using a new vacuum ancilla, to amplify the signal cat. After $N$ rounds with $n_{\text{tot}}$ total detected photons, the final state approximates $\ket{\mathcal{C}(\sqrt{n_\text{tot}},n_\text{tot})}$ , independent of the photon-numbers detected in each round. (b) Wigner functions for an example 4-round amplification series. (c) Conditional squeezing and phase flip. Depending on $n_{\text{tot}}$ , squeezing with $r_{c}=\ln(n_\text{tot}/\pi)/2$ and displacement $\pi/(4\sqrt{n_{\text{tot}}})$ in $p$ (if necessary) are applied to the amplified cats in (a), making them useful resources for GKP breeding. (d) Wigner functions for cat states with $\tilde{\alpha}=\sqrt{\pi}$ , suitable for one stage of GKP breeding. Upper: given 6 dB squeezers in (a), a squeezed cat with at least 4 dB of squeezing can be prepared with probability $0.16\%$ in a single round ( $n_{\text{tot}}\geq 8$ ). Lower: the probability can be significantly improved with multiple amplification rounds; after 6 rounds a squeezed cat resource to prepare a GKP state with at least 10 dB symmetric effective squeezing can be prepared with probability $80.64\%$ . (e) GKP breeding consumes two squeezed cat states and reduces their $q$ -peak spacing by $\sqrt{2}$ , but maintains the peak width. Deterministic breeding is enabled by a feedforward displacement. (f) Wigner functions for approximate GKP states produced with two copies of the states in (d).
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of the iterative cat amplification protocol and Wigner distributions across successive rounds, demonstrating increasing cat amplitude and breeding into approximate GKP states.

fields.result: Trapped atomic cloud in cavity tuned to a parity-forbidden second-harmonic mode amplifies sub-shot-noise coherent displacement $|\alpha_p|^2=0.5$ by over two orders of magnitude into macroscopic emission while preserving input optical phase.
fields.question: Can avalanche amplification detect sub-shot-noise quantum light fluctuations without destroying phase information?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation of $N_e=60$ two-level atoms; classical driver flat-top envelope with peak Rabi frequency $0.1\omega_0$ and CEP-averaged; ignores thermal bath and inter-atomic collisions.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Time-dependent output field shapes plotted for varying perturbing field phase. The phases plotted are: $\pi/2$ (blue), $\pi$ (yellow), $3\pi/2$ (green), $2\pi$ (magenta). The thin lines indicate the initially introduced fluctuation.
fields.figure_gloss: Normalized output field $\langle \hat{F} \rangle / \sqrt{\langle \hat{F}^2 \rangle_{\text{vac}}}$ versus time for input perturbation phases $\pi/2$, $\pi$, $3\pi/2$, and $2\pi$. Macroscopic emission rises well above shot noise while preserving the input $\pi/2$ phase increments.

fields.result: Single-step $(n+m)$ multiqubit gates implemented on transmon networks via cross-resonance drives without tunable couplers. Three-qubit gates reach simulated fidelities $>99.9\%$ in $60\text{ ns}$.
fields.question: How can single-step multiqubit gates with $n$ control and $m$ target transmons be implemented with all-microwave control without tunable couplers?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation only. Dispersive regime with shared or near-degenerate target frequencies and suppressed parasitic terms such as $ZXX$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Optimization and Fidelity of Multiqubit Gates (a) Optimization of the CYY gate. $\omega_{t1}=5.21\text{ GHz, }\omega_{t2}=5.2\text{ GHz}$ , the control qubit frequency is $\omega_{c}$ =5.5 GHz, and the coupling strengths are $g_{1,2}=8\text{ MHz}$ . The anharmonicity is $\alpha_{c}=-300\text{ MHz, }\alpha_{t1}=-320\text{ MHz, }\alpha_{t2}=-350\text{ MHz}$ . Five microwave pulses at frequency $\omega_{t}=5.2\text{ GHz}$ are applied It displays the optimized pulse shapes with Q1 on control and Q2,Q3 on target 1, Q4,Q5 on target 2. And the fidelity after optimization is shown on the top. (b) results for real CXX gates with the same parameters. (c) results for CZX gates. (d) Optimization of the CXXXX gate. Parameters for this gate are $\omega_{ti(i=1,2...)}=5.2\text{ GHz}$ and $\alpha_{i}=-300\text{ MHz}$ , $\omega_{c}=5.3\text{ GHz}$ and $g_{1,2...}=8\text{ MHz}$ . Five pulses at frequency $\omega_{t}$ are applied on each qubit. Besides, we also optimize the model for CCXXX gate with a fidelity of 92.6%.
fields.figure_gloss: Gate infidelity versus optimization iteration and target Pauli operation fidelity across three-qubit gates and larger multi-target configurations, showing convergence below $10^{-3}$.

fields.result: Constructs algebraic surgery directly over group algebras of cyclic lifted-product codes, yielding constant shuttling depth $O(1)$ on 2D neutral-atom arrays. A syndrome cycle with 33 parallel logical measurements is roughly $2\times$ faster than single-observable graph-based surgery schedules.
fields.question: Can the parallelism and reconfigurable connectivity of neutral-atom processors implement high-rate quantum LDPC logical operations without prohibitive shuttling overhead?
fields.prior: Graph-based surgery auxiliary constructions require general ancilla matchings with $O(\log w)$ shuttling depth on atom arrays and roughly double the memory cycle time.
fields.limits: Restricted to parallel measurements satisfying cyclic-symmetry or cyclically invariant subspace constraints; evaluated via numerical shuttling-time models and phenomenological/circuit noise simulations without experimental execution.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Shuttling time and total space overhead. Top two rows: shuttling and gate times per $Z$ - and $X$ -check syndrome-extraction round, using one or two crossed AOD pairs per-code-per-basis. Memory uses only the data code. Instances I–III have lifts $l=9,15,33$ , data codes $[\![306,52,8]\!]$ , $[\![510,76,10]\!]$ , $[\![1122,148,\leq 20]\!]$ , and algebraic merged codes $[\![585,41,8]\!]$ , $[\![975,59,10]\!]$ , $[\![2442,113,\leq 20]\!]$ , respectively. We denote the graph-based methods of Refs. [ 49 , 26 ] by Graph-WY and Graph-IGND, respectively; their timings cover one observable on that fibre only. Bottom: total physical qubits for parallel measurement of all logical operators of a cyclic basis, with memory as the baseline. Counts include all data and check qubits of the merged codes. Space counts for graph-based methods include $l$ disjoint surgery auxiliary qubits and shared data.
fields.figure_gloss: Syndrome-extraction cycle times (broken into shuttling and gate times) and total qubit counts across lifted-product code instances ($l=9, 15, 33$), comparing memory, algebraic surgery, and graph-based surgery schedules.

fields.result: Discrete-time CSS quantum error correction preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling $\delta\omega \propto T^{-1}$ against perpendicular noise within an interrogation window scaling as $t_p \sim 1/\tau$, before crossing over to SQL-like scaling $\delta\omega \propto T^{-1/2}$. Single recovery applied solely at interrogation end yields zero metrological advantage.
fields.question: How does finite-frequency discrete error correction with Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes preserve parameter sensitivity and affect the Heisenberg-to-SQL crossover under perpendicular Markovian noise?
fields.limits: Instantaneous and ideal recovery operations; initial logical-plus state $\left|+_L\right\rangle^{\otimes k}$ without noise optimization; local $Z$ signal Hamiltonian and perpendicular Markovian $X$ noise.
tools: Discrete syndrome extraction and recovery map
Classical Fisher information of stabilizer projector
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Crossover from the Heisenberg-like to the SQL-like regime under discrete $X$ -error correction for the Steane code (left) and the Shor code (right), for different correction intervals $\tau$ . The interrogation time $t_{\mathrm{opt}}(T)$ is optimized for the fixed final budget $T$ . Colored dots show the numerical results, while solid curves show the fitted two-factor envelope. Beyond $t_{\mathrm{opt}}$ , the protocol is repeated at fixed interrogation time, producing the staircase behavior. Stars mark the numerically determined $t_{opt}(T)$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Frequency sensitivity versus total sensing time budget $T$ for Steane and Shor codes across correction intervals $\tau$. Sensitivity scales linearly ($T^{-1}$) up to optimal interrogation time $t_{\mathrm{opt}}$, then transitions to square-root scaling ($T^{-1/2}$).

fields.result: Proposed Mach-Zehnder matter-wave interferometer for a rare-earth-doped microparticle reaches up to $10^3$ photons per beam splitter with millisecond coherence time. Mass-scaling keeps external decoherence rates constant or decreasing in the long-wavelength limit $\lambda \gg \Delta x$.
fields.question: How can matter-wave interference be observed for a microparticle without requiring ground-state cooling, orientational control, or ultrahigh vacuum?
fields.prior: Gravitationally mediated entanglement requires mass $\sim 10^{12}$ amu, a factor of $10^7$ higher than existing matter-wave interferometry.
fields.limits: Cryogenic environment ($\,\approx 6$ K) and moderate vacuum ($10^{-6}$ Torr); microparticle material requires maximum phonon frequency $\lesssim 7$ THz.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Estimated decoherence rate of $2\hbar k$ interferometer (light blue) and $1000\hbar k$ interferometer (dark blue) due to background gas scattering as a function of microparticle mass, assuming $10^{-6}$ Torr pressure at $6$ K. Dashed red line: decoherence rate of $10^{3}$ s -1 , the maximum rate at which coherence can be observed after 1 ms.
fields.figure_gloss: Calculated background gas decoherence rate as a function of microparticle mass for $2\hbar k$ and $1000\hbar k$ momentum transfers at $10^{-6}$ Torr and 6 K.

fields.result: Single-interferometer quantum double lock-in detection extracts amplitude $A$, frequency $\omega$, and initial phase $\beta$ of an oscillating signal, achieving Heisenberg-limited precisions $\Delta A, \Delta\omega, \Delta\beta \propto 1/N$ with an $N$-particle GHZ probe and interaction-based readout.
fields.question: Can quantum double lock-in detection extract full amplitude, frequency, and phase information from an unknown oscillating signal using a single quantum interferometry while achieving Heisenberg-limited precision?
fields.prior: Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two separate quantum interferometers, each requiring state preparation and readout (was $\propto 1/\sqrt{N}$ scaling without entanglement).
fields.limits: Theoretical derivation assuming instantaneous $\pi$ pulses and noiseless state initialization. Gaussian detection noise $\sigma = 0.5\sqrt{N}$ degrades scaling to between SQL and Heisenberg limit.
tools: Fast Fourier transform (FFT) / Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) analysis
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Log-log scaling of measurement precisions (a) $\Delta{A}$ ,(b) $\Delta\omega$ , (c) $\Delta\beta$ with respect to the total particle number $N$ for our scheme. The triangles correspond to the SCS state, and the circles correspond to the GHZ state. Here $A=\pi/2$ , $\beta=\pi/6$ , and $\omega=10\pi$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Log-log scaling of measurement precisions $\Delta A$, $\Delta\omega$, and $\Delta\beta$ versus particle number $N$, showing $1/\sqrt{N}$ standard quantum limit for spin-coherent states and $1/N$ Heisenberg scaling for GHZ states.

fields.result: Square-root-measurement-inspired 16-QAM receiver achieves $1.75$ ebits per mode at $0.5$ dB end-to-end loss, $3.8$ dB below the two-way assisted single-half-link PLOB capacity. Variational 32-outcome POVM increases 4-QAM rate by $4.0\%$ over the square-root measurement to $1.1289$ ebits per mode.
fields.question: Can high-order coherent-state modulation distribute multiple ebits per optical mode between stationary atomic memories through a collective midpoint measurement?
fields.prior: was at most $0.46$ ebits per mode at $0.5$ dB end-to-end loss for single-photon baseline links
fields.limits: Pure-loss channels; advantage over single-photon protocols requires per-interface loss $\lesssim 0.2$ dB and systematic phase error $|\delta\phi|\lesssim 0.2\pi$; physical linear-optical implementation of the collective midpoint POVM remains open.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Overview and achievable rates. (a) Conventional pairwise midpoint entanglement generation targets one remote Bell pair per elementary attempt. (b) Proposed $M$ -QAM protocol: repeated cavity interactions map a $q=\log_{2}M$ qubit register onto an $M$ -point coherent-state alphabet in one optical mode at each end node, followed by a collective two-mode measurement at Charlie. Each half-link has transmissivity $\eta$ , so the end-to-end transmissivity is $T=\eta^{2}$ and the end-to-end loss is $L_{\rm ch}=-10\log_{10}T$ . (c) Achievable hashing-bound rate per network mode use after optimizing the QAM spacing $d$ . “PLOB” denotes $Q_{2}(\eta)=-\log_{2}(1-\eta)$ , the two-way-assisted pure-loss capacity of one half-link and hence the min-cut benchmark when Charlie may implement an arbitrary quantum instrument [ 53 , 54 ] . SR-SP and DR-SP are the single-rail and dual-rail single-photon baselines [ 19 , 15 ] ; CTW is the coherent two-way protocol of Ref. [ 15 ] and COW-USD is the coherent one-way protocol of Ref. [ 15 ] , experimentally implemented by Ref. [ 64 ] . All $M$ -QAM curves use the SRM-inspired achievable POVM of Eq. ( 10 ); HexGKP curves are finite-squeezing benchmarks from Ref. [ 20 ] . Interface imperfections are treated in Fig. 3 .
fields.figure_gloss: Entanglement distribution rate per mode versus end-to-end channel loss $L_{\rm ch}$ (dB) for various $M$-QAM orders compared to single-photon baselines and the PLOB capacity limit.

fields.result: Fault-tolerant injection and ejection between bare physical qubits and $[[n = \Theta(k), k, d = \operatorname{poly}(k)]]$ quantum error-correcting codes achieves $O(k)$ space and $O(1)$ quantum circuit depth under locally stochastic circuit noise.
fields.question: Can state injection and ejection between bare physical qubits and quantum error-correcting codes be performed fault-tolerantly with constant space and time overhead?
fields.limits: Requires polynomial-sized noiseless classical computation per timestep; errors on bare physical qubits are not fully independent across all sites.
tools: code concatenation with non-uniform block sizes
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Use of injection and ejection to switch from many blocks of a code $Q_{1}$ to blocks of a different code $Q_{1}^{\prime}$ . We assume that $Q_{2}$ supports fault-tolerant injection and ejection, along with $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{+}$ state preparation and transversal $\mathsf{CNOT}$ gates.
fields.figure_gloss: A protocol for switching between quantum code states $Q_1$ and $Q'_1$ by injecting physical qubits into an intermediate code $Q_2$, executing the encoding transformation fault-tolerantly, and ejecting.

fields.result: Formulated unified algebraic framework for Clifford spacetime fault tolerance using spacetime chain complexes constructed from tensor networks, capturing gauge/stabilizer structures, fault propagation, and logical operations.
fields.question: Can spacetime codes, gadget-level fault tolerance, and various noise models be unified into a single algebraic formalism?
fields.limits: Restricted to Clifford spacetime circuits and Pauli fault models.

fields.result: Local operations with an $[[n,k,d]]$ stabilizer code distill $n$ copies of an $N$-qubit GHZ state into $k$ logical copies on a star network, improving output fidelity over a bare transmitted GHZ state for single-qubit depolarizing rates up to $13.8\%$ (5-qubit code) and $\ge 6\%$ ($[[144,12,12]]$ bivariate bicycle code).
fields.question: How can $n$ copies of an $N$-qubit multipartite entangled state be distilled into $k$ higher-fidelity logical copies across $N$ network nodes using only local operations and stabilizer codes?
fields.prior: Rengaswamy et al. (2021) linear-topology distillation for 3-qubit GHZ states requiring high-weight stabilizer measurements of an intermediate $[[2n,k]]$ code.
fields.limits: Independent single-qubit depolarizing noise channel, no measurement errors modeled, noiseless central state factory.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : A visual depiction of the $N$ -qubit GHZ distillation scheme on a star topology network for $N=3$ and $N=4$ . Dots represent physical qubits, while an $N$ -qubit GHZ state is drawn as a regular $N$ -sided polygon connecting $N$ dots, i.e. triangles in the $N=3$ figure and squares in the $N=4$ figure. Both figures depict an example beginning with three copies at the central hub (small red polygons). After the circuit is complete, each party has one qubit in a distributed GHZ state shared between all other parties (large green polygon). Time proceeds radially outward from the hub, and circuit operations inside a particular circle are performed on that party’s processor. Qubits experience a party-specific Pauli noise channel $\mathcal{E}$ en route from the Hub to the end party’s processor.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of the star network entanglement distillation scheme for $N=3$ and $N=4$ nodes, distributing $n$ raw copies of an $N$-qubit GHZ state to yield $k$ logical copies after local code generator measurements.

fields.result: Local equality between per-unit-cell noise entropy and syndrome entropy, $\widetilde{H}_{E}(p_{\star})=\lim_{i\to\infty}\frac{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}{n_{i+1}-n_{i}}\widetilde{H}_{S}(p_{\star})$, estimates error-correction thresholds across biased Pauli, erasure, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise without Monte Carlo simulations.
fields.question: Can quantum error correction thresholds be estimated directly and analytically across diverse codes and noise models without computationally intensive Monte Carlo decoding simulations?
fields.prior: was computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations across code sizes and decoders, zero-rate hashing bound (about 11% for depolarizing noise), or statistical-mechanical mappings
fields.limits: Requires syndrome bits to be approximately independent near threshold; neglects degeneracy entropy $H(E|L,S)$ (fails for codes with extensive gauge degeneracy such as Bacon-Shor); overly optimistic for soft measurement information.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: (a) Clifford-deformed surface codes [ 13 ] , including the XY and XZZX codes, are obtained from the surface code by applying $H$ and $HSH$ operators to some qubits (blue and red dots), modifying the original $X$ and $Z$ stabilizers (green and gray faces). (b) Threshold $p_{th}$ of the surface, XY and XZZX codes as a function of the noise bias $\eta$ . Solid lines capture the entropy threshold; dots correspond to approximate maximum likelihood decoding with a tensor network decoder [ 24 , 11 ] . (c) Logical error rate $p_{L}$ for all $3^{d^{2}}$ distance $d=3$ Clifford-deformed surface codes as a function of the conditional entropy $H(L|S)$ in the code capacity setting and Pauli biased noise with $p_{X}=p_{Y}=p_{Z}/2\eta$ , where $p_{X}+p_{Y}+p_{Z}=0.01$ and $\eta=500$ . Dashed lines capture the bounds in Eqs. ( 1 ) and ( 2 ). Note that Eq. ( 1 ) is Fano’s inequality [ 25 ] and Eq. ( 2 ) is the Hellman-Raviv bound [ 26 ] .
fields.figure_gloss: Threshold $p_{\text{th}}$ versus noise bias $\eta$ for surface, XY, and XZZX codes, comparing the local entropy threshold calculation (solid curves) against tensor-network maximum-likelihood decoding (dots). Also shows logical error rate $p_L$ correlated with conditional entropy $H(L|S)$ across all $3^{d^2}$ Clifford deformations at $d=3$.

fields.result: Explicit asymptotically good CSS codes ($k,d = \Omega(n)$) achieve fully addressable transversal $T$ gate along with transversal logical Paulis. Subsystem construction gives fully addressable transversal $T$, constant protected rate $K=\Theta(n)$, distance $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$, and sparse non-Pauli commuting checks.
fields.question: Can quantum error-correcting codes achieve constant rate, macroscopic distance, check sparsity, and logical addressability for transversal non-Clifford gates simultaneously?
fields.prior: Wills [5] constructed constant-rate codes with collective transversal $T$ but vanishing rate-distance scaling (subpolynomial distance) and no individual addressability.
fields.limits: Asymptotic regime. Sparse protected subsystem code uses non-Pauli commuting checks and leaves a Clifford action on gauge qubits. Pauli-LDPC transversal $T$ variant has $k=2$ (vanishing rate) and no logical addressability.

fields.result: Syndrome extraction across a hardware cut $L$ with data $U=Q\cap L$ requires at least $\chi_U/2$ crossing quantum operations and $\chi_U$ shared Bell pairs, where $\chi_U=\operatorname{rank}H_U+\operatorname{rank}H_{U^c}-\operatorname{rank}H$. For a fixed quantum Tanner code family, exact syndrome extraction on an $N$-qubit 2D grid achieves the optimal space--depth tradeoff $ND_{\min}^2=\Theta(n^2)$ over $n\leq N\leq cn^2$.
fields.question: How much depth does exact syndrome extraction of a stabilizer code require on hardware with a given connectivity graph?
fields.prior: Delfosse-Beverland-Tremblay (2021) lower-bounded depth by counting listed check crossings, yielding $\Omega(n/\sqrt{N})$, which is shown to fail for expanding presentations of annular surface codes that actually admit depth-13 extraction.
fields.limits: Exact noiseless syndrome extraction, bounded check weight and incidence, classical communication and computation are free, 2D grid hardware.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: The adaptive grid compiler. (a) Data sites are chosen in $4\times 4$ tiles and balanced over tile rows. A batch of terminal pairs uses disjoint endpoint rows, and pairs in different rows use distinct routing columns. (b) The tile has data at $(0,0)$ , terminal port $T=(0,1)$ , and directional ports $N=(0,2)$ , $E=(2,3)$ , $S=(3,2)$ , $W=(2,0)$ , with coordinates ordered as row and column. Its ancilla grid prepares each requested port pair locally, serializing up to two pair preparations in a shared tile while restoring all spectator states. (c) Bell measurements on disjoint facing ports fuse the locally prepared pairs into endpoint pairs, and classical parities determine their Pauli corrections. (d) Each corrected endpoint pair implements a remote CNOT, preserving the data sites. Bell-pair curves depict entanglement, not extra hardware edges. All quantum steps are counted, and classical feedforward is free. The mesh-permutation fallback covers grids too narrow for one tile per data qubit.
fields.figure_gloss: The grid architecture and $4\times 4$ tile layout used to compile syndrome extraction matchings into $O(n/\sqrt{N})$ depth via disjoint horizontal/vertical routing paths and local Bell state generation.

fields.result: Layer codes reach a circuit-level threshold of $p_{\mathrm{th}}=5.06(7)\times 10^{-3}$ in Z memory ($4.99(6)\times 10^{-3}$ in X) and sustain idle intervals $1.7$–$3.0$ times longer than rotated surface codes at equal distance.
fields.question: How do 3D layer codes perform as active quantum memories under noisy syndrome extraction circuits?
fields.prior: Rotated surface code threshold was $7.73(14)\times 10^{-3}$ in Z ($7.71(9)\times 10^{-3}$ in X); unrotated was $8.29(6)\times 10^{-3}$ in Z ($8.02(6)\times 10^{-3}$ in X) under the same decoder.
fields.limits: Circuit-level depolarizing noise model with per-tick idle. Tested on small CSS input codes ($[[4,2,2]]$, $[[6,4,2]]$, $[[7,1,3]]$, $[[9,1,3]]$). Requires non-planar cross-plane CNOTs.
tools: BP+LSD / BP+OSD decoders on raw DEM
YBW26 algebraic homology layer code construction
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Memory threshold of the $[[4,2,2]]$ family, $\chi=(d,d,d)$ , $d=4$ – $8$ ( $d_{X}=d_{Z}=d$ ): $d$ rounds of our SEC, circuit-level depolarizing noise with per-tick (depth-aware) idle, CSS-marginal detector convention, decoded with global BP+LSD on the raw DEM. Rates are normalized by the saturation value $1-2^{-k}$ throughout. (a),(c): logical error rate versus physical error rate $p$ across the crossing region for X and Z memory, respectively, one curve per distance $d$ ; error bars are Wilson 95% intervals, and the dotted vertical line marks the fitted $p_{\mathrm{th}}$ . (b),(d): the same data against the rescaled variable $(p-p_{\mathrm{th}})\,d^{1/\nu}$ with the joint quadratic fit (dashed), a local description of the crossing region that is not meaningful in the far tails, giving $p_{\mathrm{th}}=4.99(6)\times 10^{-3}$ (X memory) and $5.06(7)\times 10^{-3}$ (Z memory) with $\nu=0.86(8)$ and $0.87(9)$ respectively.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate per round versus physical error rate for layer codes of distance $d=4$ to $8$, showing the threshold crossing around $p \approx 5\times 10^{-3}$ for X- and Z-basis memories.

fields.result: Circuit depth for entry-wise Hadamard matrix polynomial transformations of degree $2^d-1$ reduced to $\mathcal{O}(n+d)$ via polynomial factorization into $m$ parallel factors, matching the query lower bound of $2^d-1$ single-oracle queries when $m=2^d-1$.
fields.question: Can the circuit depth for implementing a Hadamard matrix function on block-encoded data be reduced below linear in the polynomial degree?
fields.prior: Linear circuit depth in the polynomial degree with logarithmic auxiliary space (Kao et al. 2024 / Ref. [19]).
fields.limits: Entries of input matrix must lie on compact domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ with connected complement $\mathbb{C}\setminus\Omega$; relies on post-selection with success probability scaling inversely with the square of the normalization factor $\alpha$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5 : General trade-off circuit for implementing $P(A)=\bigcirc_{s=0}^{m-1}P^{(s)}(A)$ . Each $P^{(s)}(A)$ is implemented by a low-degree Hadamard-polynomial circuit. The parallel Hadamard product combines the results.
fields.figure_gloss: Circuit architecture decomposing a Hadamard matrix function into $m$ low-degree factors $P^{(s)}(A)$ combined via a parallel quantum Hadamard product.

fields.result: Transducer-based linear combination of unitaries implements block-encoding of $A/\alpha$ with rescaling $\alpha=\mathcal{O}(a)$ using $\mathcal{O}(C_{\max}\log(1/\epsilon) + (\lambda/a)\overline{C}(\log(1/\epsilon))^2)$ primitive queries. Converts transducer action to $\epsilon$-approximate block-encoding in $\mathcal{O}(K \log(1/\epsilon))$ queries via resolvent norm $K$.
fields.question: Can quantum coherence be preserved in linear combinations of unitaries while reducing query complexity from worst-case to weighted-average cost?
fields.prior: Standard LCU with amplitude amplification required $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(C_{\max}\lambda/a)$ queries (Gilyén et al. 2019).
fields.limits: Requires constituent unitaries to access a common family of primitive oracles coherently, and requires an a priori upper bound $a \ge \|A\|$.

fields.result: Observable estimation $\langle\psi|f(H)^\dagger O_j f(H)|\psi\rangle$ with QSVT achieves quantum circuit depth $O(r D_H)$ or $O(s D_H)$, where $r$ is the $H$-invariant Krylov dimension, $s \le r$ is the observable-visible Krylov dimension, and $D_H$ is the block-encoding depth of $H$.
fields.question: Can we use the QSVT framework to enable end-to-end quantum applications within the coherent circuit depth constraints of early fault-tolerant quantum computers?
fields.prior: Standard QSVT circuit depth scales linearly with polynomial degree $\deg(f)$ independent of state or observable structure.
fields.limits: Requires $H$-invariance or accurate low-dimensional truncation of the Krylov subspace $\mathscr{K}_r(H,|\psi\rangle)$, bounded polynomial norm ratios, and well-conditioned Gram/shadow matrices.

fields.result: Bosonic Energy-Preserving Quantum Computation (BEQC) model uses energy-conserving gates driven by coherent state ancillae, efficiently simulating polynomial-energy continuous-variable circuits while recovering $\mathsf{BQP}$ and enabling Solovay-Kitaev gate compilation.
fields.question: How can continuous-variable quantum computation be formulated to prevent unphysical energy blowups and restore universal compilation?
fields.prior: Standard Lloyd-Braunstein continuous-variable models allow doubly exponential energy growth in time $t$, diverging photon numbers, and lack general Solovay-Kitaev compilation guarantees.
fields.limits: Simulations of active non-energy-preserving operations require coherent ancilla amplitude $\alpha$ to scale with target precision $O(1/\varepsilon)$; computational equivalence to $\mathsf{BQP}$ holds specifically in the polynomial-energy regime.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Schematic depiction of BEQC. (a) A bosonic energy-preserving computation consists of a sequence of energy-preserving gates applied to an input vacuum state, together with a coherent state supplying the energy for the computation, while the outcome is obtained by measuring the photon number of one output mode. (b) Two universal sets of gates for BEQC, both of which obey an energy-preserving Solovay–Kitaev theorem ( Theorem 1.4 ).
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of the BEQC architecture: vacuum state inputs alongside a coherent-state energy reservoir undergo a sequence of energy-preserving unitaries before final photon-number measurement.

fields.result: Quantum algorithm computes exact maximum-weight perfect matching on general graphs with integer weights up to $W$ in $\widetilde{O}(n m^{2/3}\log W)$ time.
fields.question: Can quantum algorithms achieve an asymptotic speedup over the best classical combinatorial algorithm for maximum-weight perfect matching on general graphs?
fields.prior: Best classical combinatorial bound was $\widetilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}\log W)$ (Duan, Pettie, and Su 2018); this improves it in the dense regime $m\geq n^{3/2}$.
fields.limits: Asymptotic time bound in the dense regime $m\ge n^{3/2}$ under QRAM model with unit-time coherent reads.
tools: QRAM model with BBHT Grover search
Edmonds blossom contraction and laminar families
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : An example of an augmenting path in the contracted graph. The sequence of blossoms is $\langle B_{1},\cdots B_{r}\rangle$ . The endpoints of the edges $(u_{i},v_{i})$ are vertices in the original graph. The matched edge is bold.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of an alternating augmenting path across contracted blossom roots $\langle B_1, \dots, B_r \rangle$, showing original-graph endpoints $(u_i, v_i)$ and matched edges.

fields.result: Every bipartite Clifford unitary is implementable via exact deterministic LOCC at the optimal entanglement lower bound $\lceil\log_{2}\operatorname{OpSch}(U)\rceil$ Bell pairs using at most two auxiliary qubits per QPU. Non-Clifford unitaries with Clifford+$T$ decompositions require at most $2t$ additional Bell pairs, where $t$ is the $T$-count.
fields.question: Can the operator Schmidt rank lower bound on entanglement cost for distributed bipartite unitaries be achieved with constant auxiliary qubit overhead per QPU?
fields.prior: was $(2n_{A},2n_{B})$ auxiliary qubits for Choi-state teleportation attaining $\log_{2}\operatorname{OpSch}(U)$ Bell pairs (Eisert et al. 2000, Zhou et al. 2000)
fields.limits: Deterministic exact LOCC with perfect shared Bell pairs; bipartite setting with at most two QPUs.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Decomposition of the unitary $U$ in Fig. 5 into three elementary blocks obtained by applying Lemma 2 . Implementing $G_{3}$ , $G_{2}$ , and $G_{1}$ in this order consumes three ebits.
fields.figure_gloss: Decomposition of a 4-qubit Clifford unitary into three elementary blocks ($G_1, G_2, G_3$) executed sequentially to achieve optimal entanglement consumption.

fields.result: Proves fully general quantum query lower bound of $\Omega(n^{4/3}(\log\log n)/(S^{1/3}\log n))$ for sorting $n$ numbers from $[n^2]$ using at most $S$ qubits, and $\Omega(nm/S)$ queries for computing almost all hash functions from strongly universal families mapping $n$ bits to $m$ bits.
fields.question: Can unconditional time-space tradeoff lower bounds be proven for general (adaptive, non-output-oblivious) quantum sorting algorithms and universal hash families?
fields.prior: Only output-oblivious sorting bounds were known: $T = \Omega(n^{3/2}/\sqrt{S})$ (Klauck, Špalek, de Wolf 2003). For integer multiplication, prior quantum bound was $\Omega(n^2/(S\log n))$ (Beame, Kornerup, Whitmeyer 2024).
fields.limits: Asymptotic regime for large $n$. Inputs drawn uniformly from $[n^2]$ for sorting and $D^n$ for linear algebra problems. $S \le c g / 17$ for $(g, h, c)$-rigid matrix products.

fields.result: Two-message, publicly and classically verifiable quantum-advantage protocol constructed from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation (qiO) for ancilla-free unitaries assuming $\mathsf{BQP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{i.o.}\mathsf{BPP}$.
fields.question: Can the security of peaked-circuit quantum advantage and classical verification of $\mathsf{BQP}$ be based on cryptographic quantum indistinguishability obfuscation?
fields.limits: Requires quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for ancilla-free unitaries, $\mathsf{BQP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{i.o.}\mathsf{BPP}$, and post-quantum one-way functions for public verification of $\mathsf{BQP}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : Technical structure of the constructions. Solid arrows indicate implications.
fields.figure_gloss: Implication graph showing how quantum RIO, SCP, and qiO for ancilla-free and tidy circuits lead to private and public classical verification of $\mathsf{BQP}$ computations and verifiable quantum advantage.

fields.result: Dynamical diagnostics (magic, scrambling, anticoncentration, non-Gaussianity) decouple from classical simulation hardness in noisy quantum circuits. Local depolarising noise damps fourth-order Pauli moments asymptotically twice as fast as second-order moments, causing magic to vanish at depth $\Theta(N)$ while efficient classical sampling threshold remains $\Theta(1)$ under sparse noise.
fields.question: In noisy quantum circuits, do dynamical diagnostics such as magic, scrambling, and anticoncentration reliably track classical simulability?
fields.limits: Depolarising noise on brickwork Clifford+$T$ and Majorana dephasing on matchgate+SWAP circuits.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : Dynamical diagnostics and classical simulation boundaries do not coincide in noisy circuits. Each cell is coloured by the most efficient of the considered classical algorithms, the hatched region is covered by none of them, and the dotted line marks the uniform-sampling threshold. Dashed curves are the resource boundaries. (a) Brickwork Clifford $+T$ circuits with $N=6$ , $\nu=2$ and one noisy qubit; the resource is mixed-state magic, quantified by $\mathcal{W}>0$ in Eq. ( 2.5 ). For sufficiently strong noise, the witness is non-positive at every depth. (b) Matchgate $+$ SWAP circuits with $N=6$ and $n_{S}=1$ under Majorana dephasing; the resource is fermionic non-Gaussianity, Eq. ( 2.8 ). In both circuit families, the resource boundary cuts across the simulation landscape. The resource can thus remain detectable where efficient classical simulation is already possible, and disappear where no efficient simulation algorithm is known.
fields.figure_gloss: Circuit depth versus depolarising noise parameter (or dephasing parameter). Dashed curves mark dynamical resource boundaries; solid colors mark fastest classical simulation algorithms, showing the dynamical boundary crosscuts classical simulation efficiency regions in both directions.

fields.result: AKLT ground and scar states exhibit high non-stabilizerness via Stabilizer Rényi Entropy despite low entanglement. Quenches to the Heisenberg Hamiltonian melt string order faster as bimagnon excitation number increases.
fields.question: Are topological string-order features of AKLT scar states stable against symmetry-preserving quenches inside the Haldane phase when the supporting restricted Spectrum Generating Algebra is broken?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation of finite spin-1 chains up to $N=60$ sites, max bond dimension $\chi=512$, and evolution time $t\le 3 J^{-1}$; translational invariance is not preserved by the Clifford disentangling step.
tools: GCAMPS (qutrit Clifford augmented Matrix Product States)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: A plot of $O^{z}_{string}(N/2)$ in the long length limit as estimated from Figure 4 with the error bars showing one standard deviation in the fitted parameters. Note that the string order appears to decay to zero for higher-energy scar states after a short time, with the ground state and first scar state exhibiting comparatively slower decay over the same time interval.
fields.figure_gloss: Extrapolated thermodynamic-limit string order $O^z_{\text{string}}(N/2)$ as a function of time $t$ after quenching to the Heisenberg model. Ground state and $\ket{S_2}$ stabilize near $-0.23$ and $-0.21$, while higher scar states $\ket{S_4}$ and $\ket{S_6}$ rapidly decay to zero.

fields.result: Canonical reparametrisation of non-Abelian Kogut-Susskind lattice Hamiltonians into dual plaquette variables inevitably yields non-local operator strings whose interaction distance scales as $\Omega(\ell)$ with lattice extent $\ell$. Attempting to retain locality via auxiliary helper links and dynamic plaquette constraints fails because the constraints do not close into an algebra and overconstrain states to $\psi(\widetilde{U}_1, \widetilde{U}_2) = \mathrm{const}$.
fields.question: Can the Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian for non-Abelian lattice gauge theories be transformed into a dual formulation with a free magnetic term and strictly local interactions?
fields.prior: Dual plaquette formulations in $U(1)$ lattice gauge theory yield local next-neighbour interactions in the electric Hamiltonian with a free magnetic term.
fields.limits: Pure gauge $SU(N)$ theory on spatial lattices of dimension $d > 1$, preserving degrees of freedom and fundamental canonical commutators under static or dynamic constraints.
tools: maximal spanning tree on dual lattice
fields.figure_caption: (a) The choice of static constraint found in [ 6 ] .

fields.result: Synthesizes nonlinear, multimode bosonic phase gates via generalized Jacobi–Anger expansions inside quantum signal processing, yielding multimode benchmark circuits about one-third shorter than direct Fourier quantum signal processing.
fields.question: How can nonlinear and multimode bosonic phase gates for non-Born–Oppenheimer molecular quantum dynamics be synthesized near-optimally on oscillator-qubit devices without intermediate ancilla measurements or resets?
fields.prior: Direct oscillator-qubit generalized quantum signal processing (OQ-GQSP) and trigonometric-gate-implemented Fourier synthesis (TGIFS); TGIFS required $T_{\mathrm{CD}}/\tau_{\mathrm{unit}} = 476\,000$ (symmetric) vs $52\,000$ here on a $1$ ps $\mathrm{CO}_2$ vibrational benchmark.
fields.limits: Simulated rather than experimentally measured; short-window $\mathrm{CO}_2$ simulation slightly misses coherence error criterion ($0.050042$ vs $0.05$ threshold) under circuit QED noise at qubit and oscillator lifetimes near $2$ ms and $5$ ms; specific to declared nuclear-coordinate domains.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Recovered compiler costs. (a) Single-tone target with coordinate scale $L_{Q}=10$ and offset $\phi_{0}=0.025$ , common full-circle paired-unitary error tolerance $10^{-2}$ . The vertical axis is the CD time in units of one balanced query, $\tau_{\rm base}$ . Rings mark ties and the dashed guide marks the first strict saving on this grid. (b) Dense harmonics $1$ – $8$ [Eq. ( 49 )], eleven scales, common full-circle paired-unitary error tolerance $10^{-3}$ . Grouped GJA is compared with serial JA and first- and second-order product formulas (TGIFS). A harmonic- $m$ query costs $|m|\tau_{\rm base}$ . Each panel uses one common criterion across its families. Rotation and electronic-control durations are excluded. These reference costs are not calibrated device runtimes. Appendix D.3 gives the selection and independent checks.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots conditional-displacement time (in balanced query units $\tau_{\rm base}$) as a function of phase strength and precision, showing circuit cost scaling across different synthesis methods for single-tone and multimode targets.

fields.result: Quantum wall-clock runtime matches estimated classical HPC runtime (tens to hundreds of 36-core nodes) for nonequilibrium electronic dynamics of a 120-qubit [60]annulene ring model.
fields.question: Can quantum hardware reach wall-clock break-even against practical classical computing resources for chemical electronic dynamics on periodic macrocycles?
fields.limits: Restricted to 1D periodic Hamiltonians with short-range interactions; ignores small 3- and 4-center orbital overlap terms; assumes fixed electron-number parity sector for boundary Jordan–Wigner strings.
tools: Local Hilbert–Schmidt test (LHST) with channel–state duality
