fields.result: Assesses fully quantum (QLSA, QSVT, QLBM) and hybrid (QPINN, amplitude-encoded VQA, TP-VQA) partial differential equation solvers for computational fluid dynamics. Finds asymptotic speedup is constrained by condition numbers, state preparation, operator compilation, and classical measurement bottlenecks.
fields.question: Where can quantum computing algorithms offer genuine computational advantages over optimized classical solvers and tensor network methods in computational fluid dynamics?
fields.limits: End-to-end advantage requires efficient state preparation and observable extraction without full classical state reconstruction; current evaluations limited mainly to 1D and simplified benchmark equations.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 12: Tensor-programmable variational quantum algorithm of Siegl et al. Siegl et al. [2026a] . (a) TP-VQA workflow. The MPO representation of the discretized PDE operator $\hat{O}$ is compiled into the quantum circuit $\hat{U}_{\mathrm{MPO}}$ and applied to the variational state prepared by $\hat{U}(\bm{\theta}_{j})$ , where $\bm{\theta}_{j}$ denotes the variational parameters at step $j$ . The quantum register contains $n$ system qubits and $n_{\mathrm{aux}}$ auxiliary qubits initialized in $\ket{0}^{\otimes n_{\mathrm{aux}}}$ . Measurements of the auxiliary register provide $\alpha_{\mathrm{succ}}$ , which denotes the block-encoding postselection success probability corresponding to $p_{\mathrm{succ}}$ defined in Eq. 7 , while measurement of the global ancilla provides the expectation value $\langle\sigma_{z}\rangle_{\mathrm{anc}}$ . These quantities are used in the classical feedback loop to determine the rotation angle $\varphi$ and update the parameters to $\bm{\theta}_{j+1}$ . Here, $R_{Y}(-\varphi)$ denotes a rotation about the $y$ -axis, while CC and QC indicate the classical and quantum parts of the hybrid loop. (b,c) Representative solution fields $u(x,t)$ , plotted as functions of the spatial coordinate $x$ and the rescaled time $t/\Delta t$ , where $\Delta t$ denotes the time-step size used in the variational time evolution, for the linearized Euler equations with absorbing boundaries and the nonlinear Burgers’ equation, respectively.
fields.figure_gloss: Overview of the tensor-programmable variational quantum algorithm (TP-VQA) workflow, showing matrix product operator compilation of partial differential equation operators into quantum circuits alongside variational state optimization.

fields.result: Fixed-sequence microwave and baseband initialization prepares singlet-associated charge state with 99.4% median probability without electron reservoirs or measurement feedback. Sequence uses ~12 μs of microwave bursts and mixing dwells in Si/SiGe quantum dots.
fields.question: Can semiconductor spin-qubit pairs be initialized rapidly using only fixed microwave and baseband pulses, without local reservoir exchange or active measurement-based feedback?
fields.limits: Single-cycle transfer bounded by 0.5 dark-state limit; total time excludes fixed baseband transport overheads and readout verification.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Microwave-driven triplet transfer and repeated initialization. a , Simplified sequence for an initially polarized even state, illustrated for $\left|\downarrow\downarrow\right\rangle$ . b , Corresponding sequence for an initially odd state, illustrated for $\left|\uparrow\downarrow\right\rangle$ . c , Resonant triplet drive in the $(0,4)$ manifold. The chevron-like pattern reflects coherent transfer between polarized triplets and $\left|(0,4)T_{0}\right\rangle$ , with a maximum coherent transfer of 50% from one polarized triplet at common resonance because of a dark state. A weak additional resonance is attributed to a valley-related state. d , Rabi frequency of the triplet transition as a function of microwave drive amplitude, showing the expected linear EDSR scaling. e , Randomizing circuit based on $X/2$ rotations of Q 2 and Q 3 . f , Repetition of the initialization cycle. g , Singlet probability $P_{S}$ versus repetition number $n_{\mathrm{rep}}$ for a randomized input, reaching 99% after 11 repetitions. $P_{S}$ denotes the measured $(0,4)$ charge-outcome probability, assigned to the odd-parity outcome in Pauli-spin-blockade readout.
fields.figure_gloss: Measured initialization probability as a function of cycle repetitions for different initial spin states, showing convergence to >99% singlet state via repeated microwave-driven triplet transfer and mixing dwells.

fields.result: Two-magnon Raman scattering measures dynamical interlayer spin correlations $\langle(\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{A}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{B})(t)(\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{A}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{B})(0)\rangle$, observing two-magnon features at 46 meV and 82 meV in CrSBr that vanish above $T_{\mathrm{C}}\sim 150\text{ K}$ and collapse under out-of-plane field as $(1 - (B/B_{\mathrm{sat}})^2)^2$. Exciton-resonant excitation at 908 nm enhances two-magnon intensity roughly tenfold.
fields.question: Can interlayer spin–spin correlations in layered van der Waals antiferromagnets be directly probed by optical spectroscopy?
fields.limits: Measured on bulk CrSBr at $T=3.5\text{ K}$; two-magnon channel vanishes in field-induced ferromagnetic state above $B_{\mathrm{sat}}\approx 2.1\text{ T}$.

fields.result: Back-gated multilayer $\mathrm{WS}_2$ transistor operates down to $20~\mathrm{mK}$ with an on/off current ratio $>10^{5}$ and reproducible multi-stage turn-on shoulders described by parallel conduction branches.
fields.question: How do the electrical transport and turn-on characteristics of a back-gated multilayer $\mathrm{WS}_2$ field-effect transistor evolve at deep-cryogenic temperatures down to the millikelvin regime?
fields.prior: was on/off ratio $\approx 10^{4}$ at $77~\mathrm{K}$ for $\mathrm{WSe}_2$ devices (reference 16)
fields.limits: Single back-gated device on $\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiO}_2$ with $\mathrm{Ni}/\mathrm{Au}$ contacts; transport influenced by contact barriers, trap states, and electrostatic disorder.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Temperature-dependent transfer characteristics of the back-gated WS 2 transistor measured over the range $20~\mathrm{mK}\leq T\leq 25~\mathrm{K}$ at $V_{\mathrm{DS}}=0.5~\mathrm{V}$ . (a) Staggered three-dimensional plot of $I_{\mathrm{DS}}$ as a function of gate voltage, $V_{\mathrm{GS}}$ , and temperature, $T$ . FWD and BWD $V_{\mathrm{GS}}$ sweeps are shown as solid and dashed traces, respectively. (b) FWD-sweep transfer characteristics from panel (a) plotted on a logarithmic current axis, with colour denoting the experimental temperature. The inset shows the extracted effective on/off current ratio as a function of temperature. fields.result: Pairwise approximations capture nearly all junction energy variation, but median supercurrent errors range from 8.0 to 21.2 percent in disordered three- and four-terminal devices. Shifting a Fermi-level resonant mode with a gate suppresses pairwise current errors from tens of percent down to below 1 percent.
fields.question: How accurate is the pairwise network approximation of supercurrents in multiterminal planar Josephson junctions, and what physical mechanism controls its approximation error?
fields.limits: Equilibrium calculations omit voltage-biased multiplet transport; finite-gap validation is tested only on two clean devices, whereas ensembles rely on the energy-independent scattering approximation.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Pairwise accuracy of a multiterminal Josephson junction and its control by a gate. (a) Schematic of a planar three-terminal junction (not to scale). A normal InAs region of length $L$ and width $W$ is contacted by left, right and bottom superconducting leads, the bottom one of width $b$ , with phases $\theta_{L}=0$ , $\theta_{R}$ and $\theta_{B}$ , currents $I_{R}$ and $I_{B}$ , a perpendicular flux $\Phi$ and a gate. A normal-region mode is shared by the three contacts. The pairwise model beside it is built from two-terminal couplings. (b) Exact (black) and best pairwise (orange, dashed) energy and current $I_{R}$ along a phase cut through the point of largest current deviation ( $\theta_{L}=0$ , $\theta_{B}=3.34$ ), for a clean $160\times 120$ nm 2 three-terminal device with $40$ -nm contacts at zero flux. At resonance the pairwise terms capture 97.6 percent of the energy variation, yet the current error averaged over all phases is 30.4 percent. With the mode detuned by the gate, the two curves agree and the current error falls to 0.4 percent. (c) Pairwise current error versus the gate detuning $x=2\epsilon/\gamma$ of the mode, with $\epsilon$ its energy from the Fermi level and $\gamma$ its width, for this device (black) and seven further devices (grey). Orange dots mark the two settings shown in (b), at resonance ( $x=0$ ) and detuned ( $x=4$ ).
fields.figure_gloss: Plots show the exact versus pairwise junction energy and current $I_R$ alongside the root-mean-square pairwise current error as a function of the gate-induced normalized mode detuning $x=2̷/\gamma$. Detuning the shared resonant mode from the Fermi level reduces current errors from 30.4 percent down to 0.4 percent.

fields.result: Slow longitudinal field sweeps in dilute $\mathrm{LiY}_{1-x}\mathrm{Ho}_x\mathrm{F}_4$ ($x=0.003$) drive the system into three divergent effective temperatures, with cold lattice, warm electronic spins, and hot nuclear spins. Level crossings at $B_z \approx 0$ and $230\text{ G}$ facilitate fast dynamics driven by phonon-free nuclear spin diffusion.
fields.question: How do electron, nuclear spin, and lattice subsystems equilibrate with each other under swept magnetic fields at sub-Kelvin temperatures?
fields.limits: Dilute crystal ($x=0.003$), base temperatures down to 20 mK, longitudinal field sweeps up to $\pm 230\text{ G}$, subject to IR photon-induced heating and phonon bottleneck effects.
fields.figure_gloss: Faraday rotation and electronic magnetization versus magnetic field, showing hysteresis loops and relaxation dynamics at sub-Kelvin temperatures under varying sweep rates and transverse fields.

fields.result: Real-time simulation amplitudes classically reweight into thermal traces and correlators at target inverse temperature $\beta$, Euclidean time $\tau$, and chemical potential $\mu$. Truncating the redundant odd kernel component converts $1/t_{\rm cut}$ convergence to $O(\tau/[(E-c)t_{\rm cut}^2])$ and near-exponential $O(\log^{1/\alpha}(1/\epsilon_{\rm trunc}))$.
fields.question: Can imaginary-time evolution and thermal observables at finite $\theta$ and $\mu$ be extracted from real-time quantum simulations without thermal state preparation?
fields.prior: Guo, Shibu, Lin, and Zhao (2024) achieved $O(1/\epsilon_{\rm trunc})$ convergence via an exact real-time integral transform for pure-state matrix elements.
fields.limits: Depolarizing noise dampens real-time evolution, limiting accessible inverse temperature to $\beta=O(1/\lambda)$. Lower bound $c$ must fall within $O(1/\beta)$ of ground-state energy $E_{\min}$ to avoid an exponential variance penalty $e^{2\beta(F-c)}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Worst-case relative error of the reconstructed filter $e^{-E\tau}$ over the spectrum versus $t_{\rm cut}/\tau$ , for the kernels of Eq. ( 1 ) [ 18 ] , Eq. ( 4 ), and Eq. ( 5 ) [ 20 ] . Dotted lines and their adjacent labels show the predicted convergence laws.
fields.figure_gloss: Worst-case relative error of reconstructed $e^{-E\tau}$ against dimensionless cutoff $t_{\rm cut}/\tau$. Demonstrates $1/t_{\rm cut}$ algebraic scaling for the full kernel versus quadratic and near-exponential convergence for even and An-Childs-Lin kernels.

fields.result: Atom-mediated coupling induces limit cycles in undriven cavity modes and out-of-phase quantum synchronization when driven weakly, with Wehrl mutual information showing strict anti-correlation with field synchronization.
fields.question: Can atom-mediated coupling between two driven cavity modes induce a two-mode quantum limit cycle and generate phase-locked field dynamics?
fields.limits: Requires strong-coupling cavity QED regime with cavity decay rates $\kappa_{1}, \kappa_{2} \ll g_{1}, g_{2}, \Omega_{i}$, and large excited-state detuning $|\Delta_{d}| \gg g_{i}, \Omega, \Gamma_{d}$.
tools: SU(2) coherent states over Fock subspaces
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: $Q_{\rm field}$ (a) and Wigner distributions (c,d) for $\Omega_{1}=\Omega_{2}=0.005\Gamma_{d}$ , with all other parameters remaining fixed as in Fig. 2. Subplot (b) shows the corresponding $S_{\rm field}(\phi)$ . Subplots (c) and (d) display $W_{1}(x_{1},p_{1})$ and $W_{2}(x_{2},p_{2})$ , respectively. The phase localization in (a) along with the crescent-shaped $W_{1}(x_{1},p_{1})$ and $W_{2}(x_{2},p_{2})$ in (c) and (d), indicates that the cavity drives force the system to select a definite phase by distorting the phase-diffused limit cycle, leading to the emergence of an out-of-phase two-mode synchronized field state. Here $\langle\hat{a}_{1}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{1}\rangle=9.07$ , $\langle\hat{a}_{2}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{2}\rangle=8.97$ , $\langle\hat{a}_{1}\rangle=2.90-0.10i$ and $\langle\hat{a}_{2}\rangle=-2.93-0.14i$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Husimi-Q distribution $Q_{\rm field}(\theta,\phi)$, synchronization measure $S_{\rm field}(\phi)$, and single-mode Wigner distributions $W_{i}(x_{i},p_{i})$ for weak cavity drives $\Omega_{1}=\Omega_{2}=0.005\Gamma_{d}$, showing phase localization and out-of-phase synchronization across the two cavity modes.

fields.result: Hybrid fusion-network protocols for distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery achieve a $50\%$ interface-erasure threshold without local noise. Hybrid protocols with linear cluster states increase merge-observable interface distance from $d+1$ to $2d+1$ and restore perpendicular-observable interface distance from $\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor$ to $d$.
fields.question: How can photonic fusion networks and measurement-based protocols be integrated into distributed surface code lattice surgery to tolerate high photon loss and probabilistic operations at QPU interfaces?
fields.prior: Straight Bell-pair interface geometry had merge-observable interface distance $d+1$ and perpendicular-observable interface distance $\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor$.
fields.limits: Numerical simulations under phenomenological and circuit-level Pauli noise models. Interface distance advantages are masked at local noise rates of $10^{-3}$, becoming effective only at local noise of $10^{-4}$ and below.

fields.result: Unified differentiable simulation combines Fock-state quantum optics with structured-light propagation in JAX, allowing mode-dependent Gouy phases and lenses to directly alter Fock bases and quantum interference.
fields.question: How can photon-number quantum optics, open-system noise, and transverse spatial-mode propagation be unified into a single differentiable simulator for automated experimental design?
fields.prior: Existing tools separately model photonic quantum optics (MrMustard, Perceval) or wave optics (XLuminA, Chromatix) without combining Fock states and spatial propagation in a differentiable framework.
fields.limits: Classical pump approximation for squeezing; paraxial and Laguerre-Gauss beam assumptions without full non-paraxial vectorial propagation or open-system matter couplings.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: Radial-mode sorting with independent arm dephasing. The dephasing strength is $\gamma=1-\xi$ , where $\xi$ is the one defined in Eq. ( 18 ). (a) A single photon is heralded directly in a selected LG radial mode and sent through a three-lens interferometric sorter. (b) Output probabilities for $p=0$ and $p=1$ , conditioned on successful heralding. (c) Output counts for a heralded two-photon input containing one photon in each radial mode in the same path.
fields.figure_gloss: Heralded radial-mode sorting output probabilities versus dephasing strength $\gamma = 1 - \xi$. Single-photon input routing degrades to equal split ($1/2$), while two-photon inputs ($p=0, p=1$) approach $3/4$ anti-bunching due to common-path phase noise.

fields.result: Matrix product state encoding of non-local pseudopotentials yields a single Trotter step circuit depth of $O(\deg(V_{\mathrm{loc}}) n^{\deg(V_{\mathrm{loc}})} + 8Lnn_{\mathrm{atom}}\chi^2 + 2n^2)$. For $n = 7$ qubits, depth is 1,747 versus 23,775 for direct unitary decomposition.
fields.question: How to efficiently implement arbitrary non-local pseudopotentials within first-quantized quantum chemistry dynamics circuits?
fields.prior: Direct dense unitary decomposition scaled exponentially as $O(4^n)$, reaching circuit depth 23,775 at $n = 7$.
fields.limits: Demonstrated for a one-dimensional single-electron hydrogen ionization model in momentum representation. Assumes polynomial local potential $V_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and low bond dimension saturation for smooth projectors.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: Circuit depth of a single Trotter step for the one-dimensional hydrogen atom interacting with an ultrashort laser pulse, utilizing the MPS-encoded single-separable non-local potential with maximum bond dimensions $\chi=2,4,6,$ and $8$ for different numbers of qubits $n$ . For reference, the depth of the exact unitary decomposition without the MPS approximation is also shown (labeled as “Unitary decomposition”). Data for the exact unitary decomposition are only plotted up to $n\leq 7$ due to the exponential runtime of the synthesis algorithm. The dashed line represents the plot of $4^{n}$ and the dotted line represents the plot of $30n^{2}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Circuit depth of a single Trotter step plotted against qubit count $n$ for MPS bond dimensions $\chi = 2, 4, 6, 8$ compared to standard unitary decomposition.

fields.result: Compares omission fidelity bound $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ against hardware routing costs, cutting two-qubit gate count by up to 48.6% and increasing circuit fidelity by up to 47.7% on NISQ benchmarks.
fields.question: Can quantum circuit gate pruning be dynamically guided by routing distance and execution noise in both NISQ and fault-tolerant regimes?
fields.prior: was offline gate pruning considering only rotation angle $\theta$ without target hardware connectivity constraints
fields.limits: Evaluated via simulations on 4–14 qubit NISQ circuits and proxy two-CNOT lattice surgery paths rather than full end-to-end FTQC compilation; assumes fixed $1.25\times$ SWAP routing overhead multiplier for NISQ heuristics.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 3: Two-qubit gate count (top) and circuit fidelity (bottom) for the selected circuits containing between 4 and 14 qubits, when compiled with (hatched bars) and without (solid bars) the proposed pruning strategy. The percentage improvement in fidelity achieved by pruning is indicated above each bar.
fields.figure_gloss: Two-qubit CX gate counts (top) and final circuit state fidelities (bottom) plotted across 4- to 14-qubit benchmark algorithms for unpruned compilation versus the proposed routing-aware pruning.

fields.result: Connects nonlinear collective-spin twisting dynamics to solid-state platforms, surveying spin squeezing and quantum enhancements across NV ensembles (demonstrating $-0.50\pm 0.13$ dB squeezing or $6.7(6)\%$ amplification), donor spins in $^{28}\text{Si}$, and magnetic Kittel modes.
fields.question: How do microscopic interactions, disorder, and decoherence dictate the generation of quantum-enhanced metrological states via nonlinear collective-spin dynamics in solid-state platforms?
fields.limits: Spatial disorder and inhomogeneous couplings break collective permutation symmetry; technical noise, control errors, and decoherence cap effective nonlinear interaction time.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Wineland squeezing parameter $\xi^{2}$ as a function of the scaled evolution time $\chi t$ for OAT, TAT, and TNT dynamics.
fields.figure_gloss: Wineland squeezing parameter $\xi^2$ plotted against scaled evolution time $\chi t$, comparing noise reduction capabilities of one-axis twisting, two-axis twisting, and two-axis non-twisting dynamics.

fields.result: Direct measurement of basis-independent mean robustness of set coherence yields $\mathcal{R}_{1}(\vec{\varrho_{1}})=0.5$ for a two-state set and $\mathcal{R}_{1}(\vec{\varrho_{2}})=\frac{10\sqrt{2}}{27}\approx 0.524$ for a three-state set via interference visibility.
fields.question: Can basis-independent quantum coherence for an ensemble of quantum states be quantified directly in experiment?
fields.limits: Pure qubit states restricted to the X-Z plane of the Bloch sphere.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: The orange dots represent the average interference visibility $\overline{V}_{2}:=(V_{3}+V_{4}+V_{5})/3$ obtained from the measurements of states $|\phi_{3}\rangle$ ; $|\phi_{4}\rangle$ and $|\phi_{5}\rangle$ , the value range of $\alpha_{3}$ is from 2 ∘ to 92 ∘ with a step size of 2.5 ∘ . A total of 37 experimental data points were obtained. The blue line represents the theoretical curve obtained by averaging the theoretical values for states $|\phi_{3}\rangle$ ; $|\phi_{4}\rangle$ and $|\phi_{5}\rangle$ . The experimentally obtained minimum value is $\mathcal{R}^{exp}_{1}(\vec{\varrho_{2}})=0.519\pm 0.003$ , corresponding to $\alpha_{3}$ at $19.5^{\circ}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Average interference visibility $\overline{V}_{2}=(V_{3}+V_{4}+V_{5})/3$ as a function of half-wave plate rotation angle $\alpha_{3}$ for the 3-state set. Experimental data match the theoretical minimum $\mathcal{R}_{1}(\vec{\varrho_{2}})\approx 0.524$.

fields.result: Adiabatic state preparation reaches lower energies than Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT) on noisy hardware for tight-binding chains with $N\gtrapprox 20$ qubits at equal two-qubit gate counts. Noise heating per two-qubit gate scales as $\mathcal{O}(1)$ for FFT but remains constant $\mathcal{O}(1/N)$ for adiabatic evolution.
fields.question: How does circuit noise sensitivity compare between high-precision Fermionic Fourier Transforms and local Hamiltonian simulation or adiabatic evolution for state preparation and measurement?
fields.prior: FFT state preparation and momentum measurement (Ref [31]) exhibited high noise sensitivity due to global error propagation.
fields.limits: Antiperiodic boundary conditions, tight-binding free-fermion chains, non-post-selected initial state $|+...+\rangle$ introducing tiny energy shifts scaling as $1/N$, fixed number of measurement shots ($300$ to $375$).
tools: Quantinuum System Model H2-2 trapped-ion processor
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Left panel: Energy density as a function of system size, measured on Quantinuum H2-2 quantum computer (solid lines) and noiseless values (dashed lines), using a FFT (teal) and an adiabatic evolution (purple). We choose the number of steps in the adiabatic evolution so as to have approximately the same number of two-qubit gates as the FFT for every system size. Error bars indicate one standard deviation. Right panel: Energy increase per two-qubit gate due to noise, as a function of system size measured on Quantinuum H2-2 quantum computer, from the same data as left panel. The dotted lines show a linear fit of the data.
fields.figure_gloss: Measured energy density and energy increase per two-qubit gate versus system size $N$ for FFT and adiabatic evolution on Quantinuum H2-2. Shows adiabatic evolution achieving lower energies than FFT above $N\approx 20$ due to constant heating per gate compared to linear growth for FFT.

fields.result: GNN decoder taking only detection error models cuts logical failures by up to 25% versus correlated MWPM on rotated surface codes and up to 16% versus BP+OSD on $[[130,4,6]]$ qLDPC codes, maintaining constant latency across physical error rates.
fields.question: Can a code-agnostic neural decoder achieve high decoding accuracy across diverse stabilizer codes and noise models using only the detection error model as input?
fields.prior: was correlated MWPM for surface codes and BP+OSD for qLDPC codes
fields.limits: Numerical simulations; accuracy drops when generalizing to unseen codes with graphs larger than the largest training graph.
tools: Stim detection error model tripartite graph
fields.figure_caption: (a) Rotated surface code, phenomenological noise, $d\in\{3,5,7,9\}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate versus physical error rate $p$ for rotated surface codes ($d=3$ to $9$) and qLDPC LaCross codes under phenomenological and circuit-level noise, comparing the GNN decoder to correlated MWPM and BP+OSD baselines.

fields.result: Constructed trapdoored $n$-qubit Clifford operators sampled and implemented with $n^{1+\varepsilon}$ elementary gates (or $n\cdot\operatorname{poly}\log(n)$ under subexponential hardness) in polylogarithmic depth, computationally indistinguishable from uniform random Cliffords.
fields.question: Can the quadratic gate complexity and linear depth of sampling and implementing uniform random $n$-qubit Clifford operators be bypassed using pseudorandom trapdoored distributions?
fields.prior: Sampling and implementing uniformly random $n$-qubit Cliffords took $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ time with size $\Theta(n^2/\log n)$ circuits (Bravyi and Maslov 2021).
fields.limits: Relies on the computational hardness of the (dual) ring-LPN assumption; circuits require all-to-all connectivity for polylogarithmic depth and use $n^{1+\varepsilon}$ clean ancillary qubits.
tools: (dual) ring learning parity with noise (LPN) assumption

fields.result: GNN post-selection rejecting 10% of shots reduces per-cycle logical error rates by $3716.6^{+2158.6}_{-1365.4}\times$ for $[[72,12,6]]$ ($p=0.001$) and $738.2^{+171.1}_{-138.9}\times$ for $[[144,12,12]]$ ($p=0.003$) bivariate bicycle codes in a single forward pass without extra decoder runs.
fields.question: Can graph neural networks accurately predict quantum error correction decoder failure directly from syndromes and single-pass posteriors without running decoders multiple times?
fields.prior: For $[[72,12,6]]$ at $p=0.001$, $Q_{\text{LLR}}^{(2)}$ achieved $70.6^{+4.6}_{-4.3}\times$ suppression and 3R-LEC achieved $469.8\times$ at 2.66% rejection.
fields.limits: Evaluated on simulated rotated surface and bivariate bicycle quantum memories under uniform depolarising circuit-level noise; requires belief-propagation posteriors for qLDPC codes.
tools: Belief propagation with localized statistics decoding (BP-LSD)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Neural post-selection on the $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code under uniform depolarising circuit-level noise at a physical error rate $p=0.001$ , contrasted with popular benchmarks for quantum low-density parity-check code post-selection: $Q_{\text{LLR}}^{(2)}$ [ 37 ] and the three-round logical-error criterion (3R-LEC) [ 59 ] . LER per-cycle is defined as $1-(1-\text{LER})^{\frac{1}{T}}$ , for $T$ cycles.
fields.figure_gloss: Per-cycle logical error rate plotted against shot rejection percentage for the $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code at $p=0.001$, comparing neural post-selection against $Q_{\text{LLR}}^{(2)}$ and three-round logical-error criterion baselines.

fields.result: Depth-$d$, size-$s$ $\mathsf{QAC}$ circuits on $n$ qubits can be $\epsilon$-approximated by depth-$O(d)$, size-$O(s\log^2(s/\epsilon))$ circuits using only generalized Toffoli, Hadamard, and $S$ gates. Additionally, $\mathsf{TC}^0 \subseteq \mathsf{EQAC}^0 \circ \mathsf{NC}^0$, yielding $\mathsf{EQAC}^0 \not\subseteq \mathsf{AC}^0[p]$ for all primes $p$.
fields.question: Can $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits be made exact and restricted to a discrete gate set while retaining their computational power beyond $\mathsf{AC}^0[p]$?
fields.prior: Bounded-error $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ could simulate $\mathsf{TC}^0$ up to inverse-exponential error using non-standard single-qubit gates outside the Clifford hierarchy (Grier, Morris, Wu 2024).
fields.limits: Simulation of $\mathsf{TC}^0$ requires polynomially many copies of the classical input string; gate compilation is approximate within operator-norm distance $\epsilon$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: If $C$ computes $\mathsf{EX}_{n/2}^{\uparrow n^{k}}$ then we can construct a circuit $\tilde{C}$ which computes $\mathsf{EX}_{n/2}$ by simply copying the input and feeding it into $C$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Conversion schematic showing how an $\mathsf{AC}^0[p]$ circuit $C$ deciding lifted exact Hamming weight $\mathsf{EX}_{n/2}^{\uparrow n^k}$ is transformed into circuit $\tilde{C}$ computing unlifted $\mathsf{EX}_{n/2}$ by input duplication.

fields.result: Every best-found two-mode fixed-$n$ bosonic loss code for $4\leq n\leq 25$ corresponds to a finite subgroup $G\subset SU(2)$ representation, attaining the linear programming distance bound in 21 of 22 sectors, with binary-polyhedral codes reaching distance $d$ at $n_d = \lceil(3d^2+1)/4\rceil$ through $d=10$.
fields.question: What structure characterizes optimal fixed-total-photon-number two-mode bosonic codes for protecting quantum information against photon loss?
fields.prior: Dual-rail encodings and binomial/spin codes (Chuang et al. 1997, Albert et al. 2018, Aydin et al. 2024); prior lowest photon counts for distances $d=6,8,10$ were larger than $(n,d)=(28,6), (49,8), (76,10)$.
fields.limits: Pure photon-loss noise model on two bosonic modes restricted to the fixed-total-excitation subspace; code optimality certified up to $n=25$, sequence constructions tested through $d=10$.
tools: MacWilliams linear programs with Farkas certificates
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3 : Rank-two distance phase diagram. Each cell shows feasibility of the intrinsic $SU(2)$ MacWilliams linear-programming bound for total photon number $n$ and loss distance $d$ : blue cells are LP feasible, whereas hatched orange cells are excluded by exact Farkas certificates. The dark blue line marks the boundary between feasible and infeasible regions. LP feasibility is necessary, but not sufficient, for an actual code. Green markers show constructed codes at $d_{\mathrm{con}}$ and are labeled by their construction group; an outer green ring indicates $d_{\mathrm{con}}=d_{\mathrm{F}}$ , where $d_{\mathrm{F}}$ is the largest LP-feasible distance. At $n=18$ , the open orange circle marks the unattained LP bound. Constructed codes attain the LP upper bound in $21$ of the $22$ studied sectors $n=4,\ldots,25$ , with the sole gap at $n=18$ ( $d_{\mathrm{F}}=5$ , $d_{\mathrm{con}}=4$ ). The staircase follows LP-feasibility monotonicity. Distance $4$ is first permitted and attained at $n=13$ , and the $n=19$ $2T$ construction attains distance $5$ . The LP first permits distance $6$ at $n=26$ ; the exact $n=28$ $2O$ construction attains distance $6$ and saturates the bound.
fields.figure_gloss: Phase diagram of loss distance $d$ versus total photon number $n$. Feasible regions for the $SU(2)$ MacWilliams LP bound are shaded blue, while orange hatched regions are excluded by exact Farkas certificates.

fields.result: Parallel branch exploration using quaternary single-qubit flips achieves the block error rate of $T=1000$ learned sequential BP at an effective sequential decoding depth of $T_0+T_{\rm br}=200$ on the $[[288,12,18]]$ bivariate bicycle code.
fields.question: Can parallel bit-flipping branches reduce the decoding latency and escape local traps in reinforcement-learning-scheduled sequential belief propagation for quantum LDPC codes?
fields.prior: was RL-S requiring $T=1000$ iterations to achieve comparable block error rate
fields.limits: Depolarizing noise model only; fixed parameters $K=25$, $\beta=\eta=0.3$, $L_{\rm BF}=25$; hardware area scales with branch count $K$.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 2: Block error rate of our proposed RL-S-BF decoder for the $[[288,12,18]]$ BB code over the depolarizing channel. The proposed decoder is compared with BP, BPGD, and RL-S.
fields.figure_gloss: Block error rate versus physical error rate $p$ for the $[[288,12,18]]$ bivariate bicycle code, showing RL-S-BF with depth 200 matches $T=1000$ RL-S and improves over BP and BPGD by over one order of magnitude at $p=0.05$.

fields.result: Simulates $d$-sparse Hermitian Hamiltonian $H$ with maximum column Euclidean norm $\norm{H}_{1\to 2} \le \Lambda$ in $O(t\Lambda\sqrt{d} + \sqrt{d}\log(2/\varepsilon))$ sparse-oracle queries for $t\Lambda \ge 1/2$. Matches worst-case lower bound when $t\Lambda \ge \log(2/\varepsilon)$ and $d > 1$.
fields.question: Can the subpolynomial overhead in sparse Hamiltonian simulation scaled by the maximum column Euclidean norm be removed?
fields.prior: Was $O\left(\tau (\log(\tau/\varepsilon))^{O(\sqrt{\log d})}\right)$ queries with $\tau = t\Lambda\sqrt{d}$ (Low 2019).
fields.limits: Requires $t\Lambda \ge 1/2$ (or $t\Gamma \ge 1/2$ for spectral norm upper bound $\Gamma$), $d$-sparse Hermitian Hamiltonian, and standard sparse-oracle access model.

fields.result: One-pass quantum streaming solves $(\alpha, q, \ell)$-HOPI with $O(q\ell\log q)$ space and $\operatorname{poly}(q,\ell)$ time per entry for any approximation $\alpha < \alpha_\star = (2+\sqrt{3})/4 \approx 93.301\%$, while any classical $p$-pass algorithm achieving $\alpha > 75\%$ requires space $\Omega\bigl(\frac{q^{1+\ell\cdot\kappa(\alpha)}}{p}(\ell\log q)^{-C_\alpha\ell}\bigr)$.
fields.question: Does decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) yield unconditional quantum memory advantages in the data streaming setting?
fields.limits: Asymptotic in field size $q$; finite field of prime order $q \ge 3$; trade-off exponent applies for $\alpha > 3/4$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Streaming DQI for Hermite OPI.
fields.figure_gloss: Overview schematic showing how decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) processes input constraints sequentially in a single pass to output a low-degree polynomial satisfying optimal jet constraints.

fields.result: Optimal catalyst for quantum state conversion can always be chosen weakly covariant under the problem's symmetry group $\mathcal{G}$, reducing the canonical transducer unitary $S^{\circ}$ to an intertwiner block-diagonal in the isotypic decomposition. Yields exact optimal transduction complexities $W=\sqrt{(N-M)/(4M)}$ for unstructured search and $W=\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^{2}}/(2\varepsilon)$ for amplitude amplification.
fields.question: How can problem symmetries be exploited to systematically construct optimal quantum transducers and catalysts?
fields.limits: Optimality applies to query complexity and exact constants; time and space complexity of resulting unitaries are not bounded. Symmetrization over Lie groups requires infinite-dimensional catalysts isomorphic to $\ell^{2}(\mathbb{N})$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: An example of two algorithms solving two problems that are unitarily equivalent. The algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ solves the problem $\ket{\xi_{i}}\mapsto\ket{\tau_{i}}$ whereas the algorithm $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ solves the problem $\ket{\xi^{\prime}_{i}}\mapsto\ket{\tau^{\prime}_{i}}$ . This example shows that a single oracle call is needed with the application of two independent unitaries $U_{0}$ and $U_{1}$ .

fields.result: Adversary with $S$ qubits of non-uniform advice making $T$ oracle queries recovers random key $k$ from $n$-qubit binary phase state $|\psi_k\rangle$ with probability $O((T^2 + \sqrt{ST})/N)$ for $N=2^n$.
fields.question: What is the quantitative security of single-copy one-way and pseudorandom states against quantum preprocessing attacks in the quantum random oracle model?
fields.prior: Post-quantum one-way functions have inversion probability bound $O((T^2+ST)/N)$ (Liu 2023). Post-quantum PRG advantage was $O(T/\sqrt{N} + (ST/N)^{1/3})$ (Liu 2023), improved here to $O(T^2/N + \sqrt{ST/N})$.
fields.limits: Auxiliary-input quantum random oracle model (aux-input QROM). Key space size $K \leq N = 2^n$.
tools: operator norm bounding of random matrices

fields.result: Characterizes multivariate quantum signal processing (MQSP) via multiport IIR transfer functions. Achieves multi-oracle Hamiltonian simulation under $H=\sum_j H_j$ with query cost $\approx t\langle\vec{\lambda},\vec{C}\rangle_{1/2}+\mathcal{O}(\|\vec{C}\|_1\log(1/\epsilon))$ and optimal sparse simulation query cost $\Theta(\sqrt{d}\|H\|_{\rm 1\to2}t)$ with additive error dependence.
fields.question: Can quantum signal processing and quantum singular value transformation be generalized to implement multivariate matrix transformations of multiple noncommuting, nonnormal block-encoded operators?
fields.limits: Analytic bounds hold uniformly across oracle promises; requires block encodings of input matrices.

fields.result: Ground-state preparation requires only uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolutions $U_H = \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}H\tau}$ and $U_H^\dagger$ with query complexity $\widetilde{O}(\alpha_H / (\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$. This matches the lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors without requiring controlled Hamiltonian evolution.
fields.question: Can the near-optimal complexity of ground-state preparation be achieved using only uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolution instead of controlled Hamiltonian evolution?
fields.prior: Required $\widetilde{O}(\alpha_H / (\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$ queries to $\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$ or block encodings (Lin & Tong 2020; Dong et al. 2022).
fields.limits: Spectral norm bound $\|H\| \le \alpha_H$, known spectral gap lower bound $E_1 - E_0 \ge \gamma > 0$, overlap lower bound $\langle\phi_0|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\phi_0\rangle \ge \eta > 0$, and coherent query access to state preparation $U_\psi$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: The $t$ -th descent stage of CSD. The Length- $L$ FPAA sequence described in Section 7.2.1 coherently amplifies the witness subspace, after which the witness qubit is measured. If the measurement outcome is $q=1$ , an ordinary SWAP places the accepted candidate state in the anchor register; if the outcome is $q=0$ , no SWAP is applied. The candidate register and witness qubit are then discarded or reset, while the anchor register is retained for the next stage.
fields.figure_gloss: Quantum circuit schematic for the $t$-th stage of Coherent Spectral Descent (CSD), showing coherent witness subspace amplification followed by a witness measurement and anchor update.

fields.result: Ground energy of $n$-mode fermionic impurity models with constant impurity size $m$ is classically computable to error $\varepsilon$ in $\operatorname{poly}(n, 1/\varepsilon)$ time; Helmholtz free energy and thermofield double state take $\operatorname{poly}(n, \beta, 1/\varepsilon)$ time at inverse temperature $\beta$. Simulating time evolution $e^{-iHt}$ is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete.
fields.question: Can equilibrium properties of quantum impurity models be calculated in polynomial classical time, and can time-independent constant-size impurity models simulate universal quantum computation?
fields.prior: Classical ground energy algorithm runtime was $\operatorname{poly}(n)\exp[O(m\log^3(m/\varepsilon))]$ (Bravyi and Gosset 2017); universality was known only for time-dependent impurity models or impurity size scaling with $n$.
fields.limits: Impurity must have constant size $m = O(1)$; interaction norm satisfies $\|V\| \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ (or $\|V\| \leq 1$ for constructive thermofield double).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: The two stages of the construction. We first rewrite the quantum circuit as a sequence of interactions with the same constant-size system. We then realize this computation using the time evolution of a quantum impurity model.
fields.figure_gloss: Two-stage reduction showing a quantum circuit compiled into sequential interactions with a stationary register, then mapped into the time evolution of a constant-size impurity model coupled to a free fermion bath.

fields.result: A set of interactions $\mathcal{S}$ Floquet-simulates every target Hamiltonian in $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathcal{S})$ using physical interaction amplitudes with ratios bounded between 1 and 2, with frequencies bounded by $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ for $k$-local Hamiltonians whose intersection graph has chromatic number $\chi = \mathcal{O}(1)$.
fields.question: Which time-independent target Hamiltonians can be simulated by periodically driven Floquet Hamiltonians under bounded interaction strengths?
fields.prior: Time-independent analogue simulation required polynomially scaling multi-scale interaction strength ratios (Cubitt, Montanaro, Piddock 2018).
fields.limits: Frequency range scales exponentially with system size for general Hamiltonians lacking succinct descriptions; simulation runtime $N$ periods scales as $\operatorname{poly}(n)$.

fields.result: Hybrid quantum-classical NEO-VQE algorithm propagates Born-Oppenheimer dynamics including nuclear quantum effects, achieving under $5\,\%$ average vibrational frequency error on $\text{H}_2$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and $\text{H}_5\text{O}_2^+$ using 5 to 7 active orbitals (about 10 qubits).
fields.question: How can nuclear quantum effects be incorporated into ab initio molecular dynamics calculations using near-term quantum algorithms?
fields.limits: Simulated noiseless quantum circuits (classical emulation); only selected protons treated quantum-mechanically; canonical orbital basis rather than natural orbitals; hardware-efficient ansatzes fail on nonlinear couplings in the Zundel ion.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7: Comparison between the simulated NEO spectrum with $s$ - and $p_{z}$ -type nuclear orbitals, normal modes obtained via DFT(PBE0, def2-TZVP) and experimentally obtained predissociation spectra of Zundel ions tagged with Neon and Argon [ 17 , 34 ] .
fields.figure_gloss: Simulated NEO vibrational power spectrum (with $s$ and $p_z$ nuclear orbitals) of the Zundel ion versus DFT harmonic modes and experimental Ar/Ne-tagged predissociation spectra across $500\text{--}4000\text{ cm}^{-1}$.

fields.result: Nearest-neighbor quantum circuit simulates $n$-qubit, time-independent, finite-range lattice Hamiltonians for time $T\ge 1$ to error $\epsilon$ with circuit depth $O(T\log(nT/\epsilon))$ and gate count $O(nT\log(nT/\epsilon))$. Proves matching unconditional depth lower bound $\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)$ for uniform XXZ dynamics at fixed $T$ and $\epsilon$.
fields.question: Can geometrically local Hamiltonian dynamics be simulated on a lattice with circuit depth and gate count that depend only logarithmically on system size, time, and target accuracy?
fields.prior: Haah, Hastings, Kothari, and Low (2021) achieved circuit depth $O(T\operatorname{polylog}(nT/\epsilon))$ and gate count $O(nT\operatorname{polylog}(nT/\epsilon))$.
fields.limits: Fixed spatial dimension $D$, normalized local interaction strength $J\le 1$, fixed-range interactions, exact single-qubit gates and nearest-neighbor CNOTs with bounded ancilla density per site.
tools: concurrent control transport via snake routing
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Block encoding and distribution of its controls. (a) Gates act from left to right. PREPARE creates the labels and phase qubits; $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pre}}$ computes prefix values, $\mathcal{D}_{0}$ applies source phases, and $\mathcal{N}$ applies local phases and ordered data gates. Temporary distribution work is cleared before the prefix computation and preparation are reversed. The work wire includes both source and geometric ancillas. (b) A basis record is distributed to the shared words $\mathsf{R}_{g}$ , used without changing its control values, and returned for uncomputation. Solid and dashed arrows distinguish forward and return paths on separate qubits. The omitted tree levels and their local connections are specified in Appendix A ; Appendix B gives the one-dimensional schedule.
fields.figure_gloss: Circuit structure for block simulation showing label PREPARE, prefix arithmetic, phase distribution, and concurrent local data gate application across the logarithmic-diameter block.

fields.result: Ground-state energy and thermal partition function $Z = \operatorname{tr}(e^{-\beta H})$ of quantum impurity models are classically computable in $\mathrm{poly}(n, \delta^{-1})$ and $\mathrm{poly}(n, \beta, \delta^{-1})$ time respectively.
fields.question: Are quantum impurity models fundamentally classically tractable to simulate in static regimes, and can they provide superpolynomial quantum speedup?
fields.prior: Quasipolynomial-time classical algorithm for ground-state energy estimation (Bravyi & Gosset 2017).
fields.limits: Impurity size $m = \mathcal{O}(1)$ with arbitrary interaction; free noninteracting bath.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Illustration of the one-dimensional structure induced by a Krylov basis for the bath single-particle space. Each block represents a group of annihilation operators, and an edge indicates that the Hamiltonian contains coupling terms between the corresponding blocks. (a) Krylov basis. We choose a bath single-particle basis $\{g_{j}\}_{j}$ consistent with the Krylov shells $W_{0},W_{1},\ldots$ . When $H$ is expressed in terms of the annihilation operators $\{a(g_{j})\}_{j}$ , it has a one-dimensional block structure. Each block has at most $2m$ modes. The impurity couples only to the first block through the hybridization terms $\{O_{j}^{\dagger}a(\mu_{j})\}_{j}$ , and each subsequent block couples only to its neighboring blocks. (b) Bandwise Krylov basis. We first decompose the bath single-particle space into logarithmically spaced energy bands $[\omega_{\ell},2\omega_{\ell})$ and construct a Krylov basis separately within each band. The complexity of our classical simulation depends on $\kappa\coloneqq\sum_{\ell}\xi_{\ell}\omega_{\ell}^{-2}$ , where $\xi_{\ell}$ measures the squared hybridization strength in band $\ell$ . For the original impurity–bath partition, the hybridization vectors $\Pi_{\ell}\mu_{j}$ need not be small relative to $\omega_{\ell}$ . We therefore enlarge the impurity by including the first Krylov block from each band. The coupling between the enlarged impurity and the residual bath is an off-diagonal block of the bath matrix restricted to band $\ell$ and has norm at most $2\omega_{\ell}$ . Consequently, $\xi_{\ell}/\omega_{\ell}^{2}=O(m)$ for each band, and hence $\kappa$ is controlled. Note on renaming the operators. After choosing the bandwise Krylov basis, we relabel the enlarged-impurity modes as $\{b_{j}\}_{j}$ and the residual-bath modes as $\{a_{j}\}_{j}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: One-dimensional block-coupling structure generated by transforming the noninteracting bath single-particle space into a Krylov basis.

fields.result: Single Trotter step for atomic orbital Hamiltonians implemented in depth $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{polylog}(N))$ without ancillas, achieving sublinear simulation depth and total gate count $N^{5/3 + o(1)}$.
fields.question: Can quantum simulation of electronic structure using atomic orbital bases match the low circuit depth and gate count scalings achieved by plane-wave and real-space representations?
fields.prior: Atomic orbital Trotter steps typically required deep circuits due to up to $\mathcal{O}(N^4)$ interaction terms with irregular spatial structure, trailing plane-wave and grid basis scalings.
fields.limits: Assumes a constant number of orbitals per atom, fixed minimum interatomic separation, and asymptotic regime in orbital number $N$.

fields.result: Single hole box (SHB) assisted gate-dispersive readout enhances the $(1,1)$ to $(2,0)$ interdot power signal-to-noise ratio twenty-fold over direct gate-dispersive sensing (from $18.5\pm 3$ to $372\pm 12$ at integration time $t_{m}=50\text{ ms}$), cutting unity-SNR integration time from $2.7\text{ ms}$ to $135\text{ }\mu\text{s}$.
fields.question: Can compact RF gate-dispersive readout detect charge and interdot transitions in planar Ge/SiGe quantum dots?
fields.limits: SNR is constrained by substrate/dielectric dissipative loss degrading resonator impedance matching; optimal drive power is $-95\text{ dBm}$; SHB in this device is an unintentional auxiliary dot.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Comparison of the RF-GD and RF-GD-SHB response. (a),(b) RF-GD amplitude and phase response near the $(1,1)$ – $(2,0)$ interdot charge transition with SHB off-resonance. (c) Phase response (average of 3 traces) along the detuning axis in (b), with the characteristic quantum-capacitance dip used to extract the interdot tunnel coupling. (d),(e) Same as (a),(b) but with the RF-GD-SHB on-resonance, and operating as a charge sensor (f) Phase response (average of 3 traces) along the detuning axis in (e), with the broadened step response for the SHB. The SHB improves the SNR by a factor of approximately 20, from 18.5 to 372. We verified the noise in panels (c) and (f) to be the amplifier white noise.

fields.result: Orbital flux and gauge-invariant tunnel parity $\mathcal{P}=\pm 1$ control singlet, triplet, and doublet many-body branch competition in a parallel double-dot Josephson junction in the strong-coupling regime $U/\Delta \gg 1$, producing nonreciprocal diode efficiencies approaching $\eta=40\%$ near charge boundaries and $10\text{--}15\%$ within the triplet sector.
fields.question: How do orbital magnetic flux and tunnel-sign parity control nonreciprocal Josephson currents across many-body spin and charge crossovers in a strongly interacting parallel double quantum dot?
fields.limits: Zero-bandwidth superconducting leads, interdot direct tunneling $\tau_{12}=0$, interdot Coulomb repulsion $U_{12}=0$, single-level quantum dots.
tools: Fourth-order perturbation theory of non-local cotunneling and exchange
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3 : Josephson-diode efficiency as a function of the first-dot energy $\epsilon_{1}$ and magnetic flux $\Phi/\Phi_{0}$ for (a) even ( $\mathcal{P}=1$ ) and (b) odd ( $\mathcal{P}=-1$ ) tunnel parity at $U=8\Delta_{b}$ . Dashed curves mark boundaries between singlet- and triplet-dominated ground-state envelopes within the $(1,1)$ charge sector. Panels (c) and (d) show $I_{c}^{+}$ (blue) and $I_{c}^{-}$ (red) for even and odd tunnel parity, respectively, along the line cuts shown by the arrows at $\epsilon_{1}=-5\Delta_{b}$ (dashed) and $\epsilon_{1}=-7.7\Delta_{b}$ (solid).
fields.figure_gloss: Diode efficiency $\eta$ plotted as a function of quantum dot level energy $\epsilon_1$ and loop flux $\Phi/\Phi_0$ for even ($\mathcal{P}=1$) and odd ($\mathcal{P}=-1$) tunnel parity. Nonreciprocity emerges around phase-shifted crossings of singlet, triplet, and doublet spectral branches.

fields.result: Real-space lattice-wave interference driven by defect pairs can be quantitatively described using the local Huang-Rhys factor $S$, yielding interference geometry tunable into Dirac-like and nodal-line states via defect spacing, depth, and localization.
fields.question: How can single-mode coherent phonon interference launched by localized electron-phonon coupling at defects be described and mapped in real space?
fields.limits: Theoretical model assuming monoclinic $\text{HfO}_2$ parameters, a single selected optical phonon mode ($\omega_k = 76\text{ THz}$, $k = 7.8\text{ nm}^{-1}$), and negligible multi-mode mixing over the coherence duration.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: The evolution of phonon coherent patterns induced by neutral defect pairs with the ratios of energy-level depth ( $E_{2}/E_{1}$ ) and the localization strength parameter ( $\beta_{1}/\beta_{2}$ ) for defect pairs and the spatial distance between two defects. Huang-Rhys factors that arising from the contribution of the selective phonon mode ( $\omega_{k}=76$ THz) via the spatial integral around defect pairs as function of the ratio of $E_{2}/E_{1}$ and $\beta_{1}/\beta_{2}$ in the right-hand and left-hand insets, respectively. The energy-level depth $E_{1}$ =0.1 eV among the bandgap for defect I is adopted.
fields.figure_gloss: Spatial maps of phonon interference fringes and integrated Huang-Rhys factors $S$ as functions of energy-level depth ratio $E_2/E_1$, localization ratio $\beta_1/\beta_2$, and defect spacing $D$, showing transitions into Dirac-like and nodal-line destructive interference patterns.

fields.result: InAs/GaAs quantum dots with a 10 nm GaAs capping layer achieve emission linewidths down to 0.13 nm and exciton lifetimes of 0.9-1.1 ns, matching 95 nm capped baselines.
fields.question: Can epitaxial InAs/GaAs quantum dots maintain high optical coherence and lifetime when placed within 10-20 nm of the surface for near-field coupling?
fields.prior: Wang et al. (2017) reported 65 ps lifetime and 0.65 nm extrapolated linewidth for 10 nm capping layers; Guimaraes et al. (2018) reported 0.14 nm for 20 nm capping layers.
fields.limits: Measured at $\sim 17$ K under non-resonant 880 nm pulsed excitation; system spectral resolution limit is 0.04 nm.
tools: two-step capping layer growth with thermal interrupt
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Collection of InAs/GaAs QD narrowest emission linewidths, plotted as a function of capping layer thickness (colored solid circles), compared with linewidth values from previous reports [ 33 , 28 ] . The black dashed line is an exponential fit to Wang et al.’s data [ 28 ] . The red dashed line shows the exponential fit to our data.
fields.figure_gloss: Narrowest emission linewidth versus GaAs capping layer thickness compared against prior published data. Linewidth scales down to 0.13 nm at 10 nm thickness, up to 5 times narrower than previous extrapolations.

fields.result: Introduced dissipative nutational damping term $\alpha_{\eta}\eta\bm{m}\times(\bm{m}\times\ddot{\bm{m}})$ to inertial LLG theory. It generates a dc nutational spin-pumping current $J_{s,z}^{\text{nsp}}\propto\omega^2$ and broadens the nutational linewidth to $\alpha+\alpha_{\eta}$ while leaving FMR linewidth at $\alpha$.
fields.question: Does a novel form of nutational damping and spin pumping emerge in the ultrafast THz magnetization dynamics regime?
fields.limits: Linearized small-angle precession regime, norm-preserving magnetization, lowest evanescent FM modes.
tools: scattering matrix formulation beyond frozen-in approximation
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : The precessing magnetization pumps spin currents into the normal metal with two contributions, the conventional contribution $J_{s,z}^{\text{sp}}$ linear in the driving frequency $\omega$ and the nutational contribution $J_{s,z}^{\text{nsp}}$ quadratic in $\omega$ . Both contributions exhibit resonance peaks for right-handed driving fields at the FMR frequency, and for left-handed driving fields at the NR frequency.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of spin pumping into an adjacent normal metal, showing linear conventional spin current $J_{s,z}^{\text{sp}}\propto\omega$ alongside the quadratic nutational spin current $J_{s,z}^{\text{nsp}}\propto\omega^2$.

fields.result: Realized kinetic inductance broadside cavities with $\sim 10^7$ volume compression and slow plasmons ($v_{\text{p}}\approx c/100$), observing underdamped cavity-plasmon polaritons down to 0.04 THz and avoided crossings with $\sim 15\text{ ps}$ graphene plasmon lifetime.
fields.question: Can sub-terahertz cavity-matter polaritonic modes in van der Waals heterostructures be probed with high frequency resolution at millikelvin temperatures?
fields.prior: was 30 to 40 times lower plasmon lifetime using normal metal counter-plates
fields.limits: Measurements restricted to $T_{\text{base}}\approx 10\text{ mK}$ under frequency limit $4\Delta/h\approx 190\text{ GHz}$ set by Al Josephson junction gap; plasmon lifetime appears limited by cavity length via edge scattering.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 4 : Hybrid graphene-superconducting confined plasmons and strong cavity coupling. (a) Schematic of NbN-graphene-NbN plasmonic trilayer structure. fields.result: Secret key distribution implemented using entanglement-swapped photons from a GaAs quantum dot, yielding an estimated secure key rate of $1\times 10^{-3}\text{ bit}$ at optimal $30\text{ ps}$ BSM temporal post-selection.
fields.question: Can correlated photons generated from a deterministic quantum emitter and distributed via all-photonic entanglement swapping support secure quantum key distribution?
fields.limits: Asymptotic limit. Employs single-emitter temporal multiplexing rather than independent remote quantum dots; requires high temporal filtering ($30\text{ ps}$) to overcome distinguishability limits.
tools: strain-tuned GaAs/AlGaAs quantum dot in circular Bragg resonator
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4 : QKD performance as a function of BSM coincidence time window. (a) QBER as a function of the BSM coincidence time window. (b) Bell parameter $S$ as a function of the BSM coincidence time window. The threshold $S=2$ for classical correlation is highlighted by a dashed grey line.
fields.figure_gloss: Quantum bit error rate (QBER) and Bell parameter $S$ plotted against BSM coincidence time window. Shows the trade-off where narrower time windows reduce error and push $S$ above the classical limit of 2.

fields.result: Adding local $\mathfrak{su}(D)$ exchange interactions restores Heisenberg-limited spin squeezing $\xi^2 \propto 1/N$ in multi-level spin arrays across spatial dimensions $d=1,2,3$ for any power-law interaction exponent $\alpha$.
fields.question: Can gap protection enable Heisenberg-limited spin squeezing in multi-level qudit arrays with finite-range interactions?
fields.prior:
Without protection, squeezing scales as $\xi^2_{\min} \propto N^{-
u}$ with $
u \approx 1$ only for $\alpha \lesssim d/2$, degrading to $
u \approx 1/2$ at $\alpha=d$ and $
u \lesssim 0.05$ for $\alpha \gtrsim 3d/2$.
fields.limits: Valid during early-time exponential growth regime before depletion ($n_{i,\pm 1} \ll 1$). Assumes periodic boundary conditions and gap-protection strength above critical threshold $\chi \gtrsim \chi_c(L)$.

The collective phase is defined by $\nu$ reaching 1.

fields.result: 2D qubit cluster states generated from 5-qudit 1D cluster states using pairwise fusion gates and adaptive single-qudit measurements, achieving fusion success probability $1-1/d$ without ancilla photons.
fields.question: Whether universal quantum computation can be performed using pairwise fusion gates on qudits while maintaining the boosted fusion success probability $1-1/d$.
fields.prior: Standard linear-optical fusion success probability was 50% without ancillae, or up to 75% requiring Bell state or single-photon ancillae.
fields.limits: Loss tolerance saturates at large $d$ because pairwise fusion gates boost fusion probability but require successful single-qudit measurements; loss of photons representing graph vertices neglected in percolation model.

The numerical estimates are obtained from crossings of the percolation probabilities for different lattice sizes.

fields.result: Collinear type-II PDC enables mode-selective single-photon addition in $5\%$ MgO:LN at $1556\text{ nm}$ for temperatures between $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $15^\circ\text{C}$ ($K=1.003$ at $15^\circ\text{C}$), whereas noncollinear type-I PDC enables single-photon addition with Schmidt number $K=1.00002$ in $2\%$ ZnO:LN.
fields.question: Which phase-matching and group-velocity matching conditions allow spectro-temporal single-photon addition and mode-selective addition to multimode quantum fields at telecom wavelengths using lithium niobate and its doped variants?
fields.prior: Mode-selective addition was known to be impossible in congruently grown bulk lithium niobate at room temperature because phase-matching and group-velocity matching cannot coincide.
fields.limits: Numerical simulations based on bulk crystal Sellmeier fits; requires cryogenic/sub-ambient cooling down to $0^\circ\text{C}$ to $15^\circ\text{C}$ for type-II mode selectivity.
tools: Sellmeier equations for LN, MgO:LN, and ZnO:LN
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : Phase-matching and group-velocity-matching curves for degenerate collinear type-II PDC in $5\%$ MgO:LN at a crystal temperature of $15^{\circ}$ C, as a function of pump wavelength.
