fields.result: Gray code quantum read-only memory (GQROM) and an automated EDA flow reduce state transition complexity and gate-induced errors for loading classical data into quantum circuits.
fields.question: How to design a scalable, low-overhead programmable quantum read-only memory to load classical data into quantum circuits?
fields.limits: Simulated and validated on Qiskit framework.

fields.result: Two-level error-correcting encoding combines embedded dephasing correction in $S-\mathscr{s}$ molecular spin dimers with an outer multi-qubit code, bypassing the loss of transferred coherence in anharmonic qudits.
fields.question: How can fault-tolerant quantum error correction handle both diagonal dephasing and off-diagonal relaxation errors in single-molecule spin architectures?
fields.limits: Simulated under Markovian secular spin-bath dynamics at $B_z=0.35$ T; assumes ideal syndrome measurement and two-qubit gates on the outer code; inter-molecule entanglement mechanisms not implemented.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Average error of a logical rotation followed by syndrome extraction and recovery, as a function of the dephasing time $T_{2}$ . The error is quantified by the entanglement infidelity $P_{\rm err}=1-F_{e}$ of the logical channel with respect to the target unitary and is averaged over the universal set of planar logical rotations $R_{L}^{p}(\theta,\phi)=\exp[-i(\cos\phi\,Y_{L}-\sin\phi\,X_{L})\theta/2]$ , with $(\theta,\phi)=(\pi/4,\pi)$ , $(\pi/2,\pi)$ , $(\pi/2,-\pi/2)$ , $(\pi/2,-\pi/4)$ , and $(\pi/2,-\pi/8)$ . Red and blue curves correspond to the $S=3/2$ Cr complex [ 31 ] and to the $S=7/2$ Gd complex [ 32 ] , respectively. Solid, dashed, and dotted curves correspond to $T_{1}\rightarrow\infty$ , $T_{1}=1$ s, and $T_{1}=100$ ms, respectively. For each qudit, the duration of each operation is set by the smallest dipole matrix element among the transitions involved in the logical gate, syndrome extraction, and recovery, taking $10$ ns as the reference duration for a $\pi$ pulse on a spin 1/2 [ 37 ] . This yields total gate–syndrome–recovery sequence durations of $250$ ns and $551$ ns, for $S=3/2$ and $S=7/2$ , respectively. The black curves show an uncorrected $S=1/2$ subject to the same dephasing (no relaxation) for the time required by a logical gate on the spin 3/2 ( $\sim 83$ ns, dashed) or by the manipulation of a bare spin 1/2 (10 ns, solid). In the absence of relaxation, increasing the spin size leads to a progressively stronger suppression of dephasing errors, whereas for finite $T_{1}$ the curves eventually saturate to a $T_{2}$ -independent plateau set by residual relaxation.
fields.figure_gloss: Entanglement infidelity $P_{\rm err}$ of planar logical rotations versus dephasing time $T_2$ for embedded $S=3/2$ and $S=7/2$ units at different relaxation times $T_1$, compared against bare spin-1/2 qubits.

fields.result: Coupling a 2DEG to a chiral cavity isolates resonant from antiresonant vacuum interactions, yielding a handedness-dependent correction to Hall resistivity $\rho_{xy}^{(s)} = h/(\nu e^2) - s\,m^*\gamma^2 D / (n_{\mathrm{2D}} e^2 \omega_{\mathrm{cav}}^2)$ and an unsqueezed or two-mode squeezed ground state for co- or counter-rotating modes.
fields.question: How does a circularly polarized, time-reversal-symmetry-breaking chiral cavity vacuum modify the polariton spectrum, ground state, and DC magnetotransport of a two-dimensional electron gas?
fields.prior: In achiral or linearly polarized cavities, Hall resistivity is immune to polariton broadening and light-matter coupling at zero temperature, satisfying $\rho_{xy}^{\mathrm{ach}} = h/(\nu e^2)$.
fields.limits: Spatially uniform cavity field (Kohn's theorem center-of-mass coupling), leading order in polariton broadening $\gamma$, zero temperature.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: (a),(e) A 2DEG in a chiral cavity confining right- and left-circularly polarized light, respectively. (b) Eigenspectrum of the CRI Hamiltonian: the two chiral-vacuum-dressed modes cross, with the cavity-like branch renormalized to $\Omega=\omega_{\mathrm{cav}}+g^{2}/\omega_{\mathrm{cav}}$ by the diamagnetic term and the cyclotron-like branch by the vacuum Bloch–Siegert shift. (f) Eigenspectrum of the CRA Hamiltonian: two polariton branches with avoided crossing. (c), (g) Longitudinal resistivity vs. magnetic field $B$ for various coupling strengths, for the CRI and CRA systems, respectively, normalized by the Drude resistivity $\rho_{\mathrm{D}}=m^{*}\gamma/(n_{\mathrm{2D}}e^{2})$ , where $n_{\mathrm{2D}}=2\times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ . We observe Shubnikov de Haas (SdH) oscillations as a function of $B$ . The SdH oscillations are modeled through a field-dependent broadening parameter $\gamma_{r}(B)$ . The CRA system exhibits damped SdH oscillations, due to strong light–matter hybridization, whereas the CRI system shows undamped SdH oscillations, owing to its chiral-vacuum-dressed modes. (d),(h) Hall resistivity $\rho_{xy}$ , normalized by the classical Hall resistivity $(B/e\,n_{\rm 2D})$ , at fixed $g/\omega_{\mathrm{cav}}=0.42$ and $\gamma/2\pi=5$ GHz. The achiral cavity case shows no cavity-induced correction, coinciding with the bare 2DEG case. In the cases of chiral cavities, there is a handedness-dependent correction; see Eq. ( 10 ). Here, $\omega_{\rm cav}/2\pi=0.35$ THz, $g/\omega_{\mathrm{cav}}=0.42$ , $\Omega/2\pi=0.412$ THz, and $\gamma/2\pi=5$ GHz, fixed for panels (b),(d),(f),(h). Dashed line marks the cavity frequency, dotted marks the renormalized cavity frequency $\Omega$ , dash-dot marks the cyclotron frequency.
fields.figure_gloss: Polariton eigenspectra, longitudinal resistivity, and Hall resistivity versus magnetic field $B$ for counter-rotating (CRI) and co-rotating (CRA) chiral cavity modes, showing mode crossing versus anticrossing and handedness-dependent Hall corrections.

fields.result: Constructing modular hyperbolic surface and color codes by wiring static boundary connections between Euclidean planar modules reduces physical qubit overhead by $\ge 10\times$ compared to planar surface codes under circuit-level noise. Larger modular codes reach encoding rate $k/n=1/16$ with distance $d\ge 22$, exceeding the $[[288,12,18]]$ bivariate bicycle code.
fields.question: Can low-overhead quantum error-correcting codes be implemented using mostly nearest-neighbor connectivity on flat planar modules connected only via sparse boundary links?
fields.prior: Planar surface codes require high physical qubit overhead; standard high-rate LDPC codes like the $[[288,12,18]]$ bivariate bicycle code require non-planar 2D routing across all qubits.
fields.limits: Circuit-level numerical simulations, assumes static inter-module links restricted to module boundaries and standard depolarizing noise models.
tools: Neural network and minimum-weight perfect matching decoders

fields.result: Constructs fault-tolerant CSS state preparation circuits via polynomial-time ZX-calculus rewrites, lowering logical error rate by an average of 33.7%, raising acceptance rate by 9.5%, and cutting CNOT count by up to 53.8% across codes up to distance 15.
fields.question: How can fault-tolerant CSS state preparation circuits be synthesized scalably with reduced circuit depth and qubit overhead?
fields.prior: Flag at Origin (FaO) modular flagged gadgets (Khesin et al. 2024), limited by offline gadget generation and large depth.
fields.limits: Restricted to CSS states and CSS noise (standard unidealization rules fail for non-CSS stabilizer codes); evaluated under circuit-level depolarizing noise ($p=10^{-3}$ and $p=10^{-4}$); post-selection discards states with $\ge d/2$ syndrome faults.
fields.figure_caption: (a) Compare the logical error rate and acceptance rate of SpiderCSS and FaO.
fields.figure_gloss: Scatter plots of percentage improvements of SpiderCSS over the FaO baseline for CSS states up to distance 15. The left panel shows logical error rate reduction vs. acceptance rate increase; the right panel shows circuit depth reduction vs. active qubit count reduction under footprint- and depth-optimizing reuse.

fields.result: Round-robin circuits sparsified via stabilizer deformations implement fully addressable, fault-tolerant transversal CZ gates with circuit depth independent of code distance for 2D translationally invariant qLDPC codes. On a 288-qubit gross code ($d=12$), the addressable tCZ achieves ${\sim}4\times$ lower spacetime overhead and ${\sim}5\times$ lower logical error impact than code surgery.
fields.question: How can fully addressable, fault-tolerant, low-depth transversal logical two-qubit Clifford gates be realized on quantum low-density parity check codes without multi-round code surgery?
fields.prior: Addressable logical operations on qLDPC codes relied primarily on lattice surgery taking $O(d)$ measurement rounds, or on transversal constructions limited in code distance or stabilizer structure.
fields.limits: Restricted to 2D translationally invariant qLDPC codes, evaluated primarily on periodic boundary conditions; complex codes with incomplete disjoint representative sets require either an intermediate stabilizer round to restore full distance $d$ or accept distance reduction to $d/2$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 9: An inter-gross addressable tCZ . We simulate the 288-qubit gross code with code capacity distance $d=12$ . While there is a marked difference in the LER magnitudes for the tCZ and memory experiments, the tCZ displays fault-tolerant LER scaling.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate versus physical error rate for the 288-qubit $d=12$ gross code comparing an addressable transversal CZ against code surgery ($XX$ measurement) and quantum memory baselines, showing fault-tolerant error suppression.

fields.result: Encoded quantum memory achieves optimal spacetime cost $C = O(S(K + \log(S/\varepsilon)))$ using an explicit noisy syndrome extraction circuit and $O(N)$ classical decoding work per cycle. Relative spacetime overhead $C/(KS) = O(1 + \log(S/\varepsilon)/K)$ is constant for $K = \Omega(\log(S/\varepsilon))$.
fields.question: Can the optimal spacetime cost $\Omega(S(K+\log(S/\varepsilon)))$ for storing $K$ logical qubits for $S$ steps with error at most $\varepsilon$ be attained using realistic, noisy quantum error correction circuits and efficient decoding?
fields.prior: Lower bound $\Omega(S(K+\log(S/\varepsilon)))$ was matched only under idealized error correction (Bharti et al. 2024); independent surface code patches require $O(KS\log^2(KS/\varepsilon))$.
fields.limits: Requires long-range qubit connectivity, fast and reliable parallel classical processing, error strength below threshold $p < p_*$, and input/output remaining encoded in the code blocks.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Optimal quantum memory through repeated partial recovery. a) Each cycle measures every stabilizer check once, runs a fixed number of parallel decoder iterations, and applies a Pauli correction or updates the Pauli frame. Orange symbols indicate faults in the quantum circuit; we assume that classical processing is reliable. b) New faults increase the error bound, while recovery reduces it without removing every error. The curve is schematic and assumes that every cycle stays within the allowed fault count. Exceeding that count in one cycle is exponentially unlikely in the block length. c) The bar’s height represents the physical width and its horizontal extent represents the storage duration. The two shades show the capacity and reliability contributions to the required width. Each cycle has linear physical cost, giving $O(S(K+\log(S/\varepsilon)))$ total locations.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of optimal memory protocol: single-round check measurements and fixed-iteration decoding maintain residual error below the correctable threshold, sharing the $O(\log(S/\varepsilon))$ reliability overhead across $K$ logical qubits over $S$ cycles.

fields.result: Establishes operator-algebraic necessary and sufficient conditions for quantum circuit fault tolerance under general noise, yielding closed-form detection and logical-effect matrices for stabilizer circuits and linear-programming upper bounds on circuit distance.
fields.question: How can fault tolerance and circuit distance be certified and bounded algebraically across general and stabilizer quantum circuits under arbitrary noise models?
fields.limits: Non-adaptive stabilizer circuits for closed-form matrices; independent and identically distributed depolarizing noise for weight-enumerator pseudothreshold bounds.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: An adaptive circuit interacting with temporally correlated noise, shown for two rounds. The circuit implements the quantum instruments $\{C_{o_{1}}\}_{o_{1}}$ and $\{C_{o_{2}\mid o_{1}}\}_{o_{2}}$ where the instrument at round $2$ depends on the observed outcome $o_{1}$ . Double blue lines carry classical information. A copy of $o_{1}$ selects the second instrument before noise acts on its retained record. The orange maps $E_{e_{r}}$ act on the displayed data, record, and memory ports; $N_{1},N_{2}$ carry information between noise interactions. Summing over the circuit outcomes and noise Kraus operator indices gives the physical channel. This representation is a generalization of the strategic code scenario [ 61 ] , where the goal is only to protect an encoded initial state. The recovery is assumed to be noiseless.
fields.figure_gloss: A two-round adaptive quantum circuit interacting with causally correlated noise via instrument modules, classical measurement records, and noise memory systems before a final noiseless recovery operation.

fields.result: Proves dressed distance is $D=2^L$ for any $L$-dimensional rectangular subsystem code with even side lengths $q_i \geq 4$, data qubits $N=\prod_i q_i$, and logical qubits $K=\prod_i (q_i-2)$, with max gauge measurement weight $w=\max_i q_i$.
fields.question: How many logical qubits can a finite quantum memory protect under low-weight gauge measurements on rectangular coordinate grids?
fields.prior: Uniform side-four and side-six subsystem many-hypercube codes (Nakai and Goto), plus standard subsystem products like SHYPS(6) which achieves $[\[3969,36,3249,32\]]$ with rate $0.91\%$ vs $13.17\%$ ($6^5$ line-gauge code) at distance 32.
fields.limits: Static code distance; does not evaluate fault-tolerant circuit distance, noise thresholds, decoder performance, or geometric locality constraints.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Exact rate–weight frontiers at fixed distance under $10{,}000$ data qubits. The points are the discrete choices in Table 1 ; line segments guide the eye and do not represent intermediate codes. Increasing the number of axes raises distance and reduces the maximum achievable rate under this budget.
fields.figure_gloss: Protected encoding rate $K/N$ plotted against maximum gauge measurement weight $w$ for code distances $D=16, 32, 64$ under a cap of at most $10{,}000$ data qubits.

fields.result: Monte Carlo sampling of syndrome statistics, logical fidelity, and Pauli expectation values for noisy circuits with $X$, CNOT, and level-3 Clifford-hierarchy diagonal gates runs in $\mathcal{O}(n^3 T)$ time per sample, with zero scaling dependence on the number of logical qubits.
fields.question: How can one efficiently benchmark the fault-tolerant logical performance and syndrome distributions of quantum circuits containing non-Clifford gates under stochastic Pauli noise?
fields.prior: Generic exact classical benchmarking incurred a cost exponential in the number of non-Clifford gates or magic measures, or depended separately on the number of logical qubits.
fields.limits: Circuit components restricted to $X$, CNOT, and level-3 diagonal gates (plus Clifford pre/post-processing); syndrome checks must be affected by faults from a constant number of layers; restricted to circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : (a) Protocol E: three [[27,3,3]] data blocks are prepared in $|+\rangle_{L}$ , a depth-2 transversal CCZ circuit builds the encoded hypergraph state, and one shared ancilla block $A_{\rm sh}$ extracts the post-CCZ $Z$ syndrome. (b) Infidelity of the 9-qubit hypergraph state versus total acceptance rate for five treatments of the Z syndrome — A: none. B: noiseless (lower bound). C: bare ancillas. D: one Steane block per data block. E: one shared block, circled, as drawn in (a) — with the prep metachecks repaired (filled circle) or postselected (hollow). The diamond data points correspond to results with the approximation using twirling [ 12 ] . The double arrow marks the A–B gap. Simulations were performed with two-qubit depolarizing noise at a total error rate of $10^{-3}$ and CCZ gate noise at a total error rate of $2\times 10^{-3}$ with a $10{:}1$ bias toward $Z$ -type errors, following the noise model of Ref. [ 12 ] .
fields.figure_gloss: Plots total physical ancilla overhead against logical infidelity of a 9-qubit hypergraph state prepared via a depth-2 CCZ circuit on three [[27,3,3]] tricycle code blocks across syndrome extraction protocols.

fields.result: Constructs an exact, deterministic quantum recovery unitary that moves errors onto ancillas to be projected out for topological surface codes based on the quantum double $D(G)$ of any finite group $G$.
fields.question: How can exact, deterministic error recovery be realized on 2D non-Abelian quantum double surface codes $D(G)$ given non-invertible anyon fusion and non-Abelian stabilizers?
fields.prior: Thresholds and existence proofs were known, along with explicit recovery for Abelian $G$, repeated-round anyon decoders, or restricted setups like $D(D_4)$ via just-in-time decoding; general explicit recovery unitaries were missing.
fields.limits: Requires predetermined neutral correctable error clusters and perfect syndrome measurements as input; decoder/syndrome extraction circuit construction is left to future work.
tools: group algebra irreducible representation error basis
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: The circuit ( 3.14 ) for the charge transfer at a vertex $v$ of the square lattice, with the irrep error $E_{i}^{\mu}$ for an edge $i$ entering $v$ (left) and for an edge $i$ exiting $v$ (right). A dot on a control qudit in the group basis state $\ket{x}$ , connected to boxes $L$ or $R$ , applies $L^{x}$ or $R^{x}$ to the target qudits, as in ( 3.4 ). The first gate is the controlled vertex operator $U_{v}$ of ( 3.3 ), with the ancilla as control, and the second is $CL_{i,\mathrm{va}}$ or $CL_{i,\mathrm{va}}^{\dagger}$ (depending on the orientation of $i$ ), with $i$ as control. Afterwards the data qudits are in $\ket{\psi}$ and the ancilla is in $\ket{\Gamma_{ab}}$ , which the Fourier transform $F$ maps to the group basis state $\ket{\Gamma,a,b}$ before the measurement in the group basis.
fields.figure_gloss: Charge transfer circuits that map the irreducible representation error on a direct-lattice edge entering or exiting vertex $v$ onto an ancilla qudit via controlled operations.

fields.result: Quantum discrete simulation optimization has minimax expected optimality gap $\Omega(|\mathcal{X}|/T)$, achieved up to logarithmic factors by the \textsc{QUEST} algorithm ($O(|\mathcal{X}|\log T/T)$). Convergence rate improves quadratically over budget $T$ compared to classical bound $\Omega(\sqrt{|\mathcal{X}|/T})$, with worse scaling in decision count $|\mathcal{X}|$.
fields.question: How does quantum computing affect the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization in the fixed-budget setting, and can a provably rate-optimal algorithm be designed?
fields.prior: Classical discrete simulation optimization has minimax expected optimality gap lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{|\mathcal{X}|/T})$.
fields.limits: Fixed-budget setting with discrete candidate decisions $|\mathcal{X}|$. Continuous observation outputs require finite support discretization onto grid qubits.
tools: sequential quantum phase-testing lower bound reduction
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Expected Optimality Gap under Bernoulli Distribution
fields.figure_gloss: Expected optimality gap as a function of simulation budget $T$ under Bernoulli outcomes with $|\mathcal{X}|=20$. Compares the faster decay of the quantum \textsc{QUEST} algorithm against the classical \textsc{MC-EST} baseline.

fields.result: ASPIRE compiles approximate state-preparation circuits by greedily removing entanglement across hardware-native qubit connectivity. Yields shallower circuits and higher state fidelity than standard sequential staircase circuits, especially for states with long-range entanglement.
fields.question: How to compile shallow, hardware-native state preparation circuits for matrix product states without relying on sequential nearest-neighbour gate staircases?
fields.prior: Approximate matrix product state preparation relies on layered sequential staircases of nearest-neighbour gates.
fields.limits: Heuristic greedy compilation. Evaluated on empirical simulations of Hamiltonian ground states and amplitude-encoded functions under NISQ noise and early fault-tolerant settings.

fields.result: Constructs quantum orthogonal polynomial transforms (QOPT) running in $O(\text{polylog}(N, 1/\epsilon))$ time for discrete Charlier, Meixner, and Krawtchouk transforms, and for continuous Laguerre transforms. Achieves an $O(N\operatorname{polylog}((N+\alpha+\beta+1)/\epsilon))$ runtime for the discrete Hahn transform.
fields.question: Which orthogonal polynomial transforms admit efficient quantum circuit implementations with exponential speedups over classical transforms?
fields.prior: Hermite transform runs in poly-logarithmic time (Jain et al. STOC'26); naive Hahn transform is $O(N^{2})$.
fields.limits: Preserves orthogonality approximately up to an energy cutoff; assumes integer parameters for Jacobi-to-Hahn reduction; Wilson, Racah, continuous Hahn, and continuous dual Hahn families not solved.
tools: Gaussian optical gates on Cartesian grids
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: The Askey scheme of hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials, organized top-to-bottom by decreasing level; arrows denote limit transitions between families. Blue families admit poly-logarithmic QOPTs with exponential speedups (Charlier, Krawtchouk, Meixner, Laguerre). Orange families are realized here but are not poly-logarithmic: the Hahn transform attains a quadratic speedup over the naive $O(N^{2})$ implementation, and the Jacobi transform can be implemented using the Hahn in a restricted setting. The Hermite transform at the base is the foundational QOPT of [ 14 ] on which the digital implementations are built.
fields.figure_gloss: Hierarchical chart of the Askey scheme of hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials showing the limit transitions between polynomial families and their achieved quantum transform complexities.

fields.result: Every unitary $\mathcal{U} \in \mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$ satisfies either $\mathcal{U} \not\in \mathsf{unitaryP}^{\mathsf{ALL}}$ or $\mathcal{U} \in \mathsf{unitaryP}^{\mathsf{FNEXP}}$. Consequently, existence of quantum commitments implies either no polynomial-time unitary synthesis or $\mathsf{BPP} \neq \mathsf{NEXP}$.
fields.question: Does the hardness underlying quantum cryptography imply breakthrough classical complexity lower bounds?
fields.limits: Garbage-allowed implementations vs. garbage-free implementations coincide up to tensoring with the adjoint.
tools: projective unitary dilations and garbage-state tracking

fields.result: Fermionic Gaussian rank of $\lvert M\rangle^{\otimes k}$ is lower bounded by $\frac{8}{9(k+1)}\left(\frac{27(8+2\sqrt{7})}{256}\right)^k > \frac{8}{9(k+1)} 1.4018^k$, with $\delta$-approximate rank bounded by $(1-\delta^2)$ times this value. Coherent state border rank of $n$-mode bosonic Fock state $\lvert m\rangle$ is exactly $\prod_{j=1}^n(1+m_j)$.
fields.question: What are the exact and approximate rank lower bounds for decomposing magic states into fermionic Gaussian states and Fock states into bosonic coherent states?
fields.prior: For fermionic Gaussian rank of $\lvert M\rangle^{\otimes k}$, only trivial lower bound of 2 was known for $k \geq 2$. For coherent-state border rank of $\lvert 1\rangle^{\otimes n}$, superpolynomial but sub-exponential lower bounds were proved by prior work.
fields.limits: Pure states of fixed parity. Fermionic rank bound established for the four-qubit magic state $\lvert M\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\lvert 0000\rangle + \lvert 1111\rangle)$ and products thereof. Bosonic lower bound applies to coherent states, not the full set of bosonic Gaussian states.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: A summary of our results and the now known bounds on the exact fermionic Gaussian rank of the state $\left\lvert{M}\right\rangle^{\otimes k}$ . The trivial upper bound and the lower bound from theorem 1 apply to and are plotted from $k=1$ , whereas the bound from theorem 3 applies only to $k\geq 2$ . We improve on the prior state of the art knowledge for every $k>1$ , since the rank for $k=1$ is trivially $2$ . The “optimized” lower bound corresponds to directly evaluating the matrix ranks on the right hand side of equation ( 34 ). The script producing the data is available at Ref. [ 26 ] and the exact numbers are in table 1 .
fields.figure_gloss: Exact fermionic Gaussian rank of $\lvert M\rangle^{\otimes k}$ plotted against number of copies $k$, comparing the asymptotic analytical lower bound, the small-$k$ optimized lower bound, the $k=2$ bound, and the $2^k$ upper bound.

fields.result: Streaming Yamakawa–Zhandry Code Intersection in random order takes $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ qubits versus $\exp(n^{\Omega(1)})$ classical bits. Streaming Optimal Polynomial Intersection to target value $\lceil n/2+\sqrt{dn}/8\rceil$ takes $O(d\log n)$ qubits versus $\Omega(n)$ classical bits.
fields.question: Can quantum algorithms achieve exponential advantage for space complexity in the streaming model when inputs are presented in a uniformly random order?
fields.limits: Asymptotic regime with $d = \omega(\log n)$ and $d = o(n/\log n)$ for Optimal Polynomial Intersection; random oracle setting; applies to streaming memory constraints, not general query complexity.
tools: convex potential functions on read-once branching programs

fields.result: Simulates $s$-sparse Hamiltonians in $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{s}\tau+\sqrt{s\tau\log(1/\varepsilon)}+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ queries for $\tau=\eta|t|$, dissipative linear ODEs in $\mathcal{O}(\bar{g}\sqrt{s}\tau\log(C\bar{g}/\varepsilon))$, and linear systems in $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{s}\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon))$.
fields.question: Can quantum algorithms achieve exact square-root sparsity scaling for general sparse Hamiltonian simulation, linear ODEs, and linear system solvers without subpolynomial overheads?
fields.prior: Linear-in-$s$ scaling for standard block encodings; previous general $\sqrt{s}$ Hamiltonian simulation required subpolynomial factors from an iterated interaction picture (Low 2019) or conditional norm assumptions (Berry and Childs 2012).
fields.limits: Requires sparse oracle access with row/column Euclidean norm bounds $\eta$, certified time discretisation for time-dependent cases, and efficient entry decoding circuits for gate implementations.

fields.result: Measurement-assisted and LCU Clifford+$T$ compilation synthesizes continuous time evolution while preserving exact continuous symmetries such as $SU(2)$, reducing the required $T$-count by approximately a factor of five compared to standard symmetry-agnostic compilation for estimating 1D Heisenberg transport exponents.
fields.question: How can continuous symmetry-preserving time evolutions be compiled into fault-tolerant discrete gate sets without introducing symmetry-breaking synthesis errors?
fields.prior: Standard symmetry-agnostic synthesis (such as gridsynth/Solovay-Kitaev) introduces off-axis transverse errors that break continuous conservation laws and yielded incorrect transport exponents at 54 T gates per two-site Trotter step.
fields.limits: Demonstrated for spin-1/2 systems with exact $SU(2)$ symmetry, 1D lattice gauge theories, and fermionic models (Fermi-Hubbard, electronic structure); higher-spin systems remain unexplored.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Similar exponents, different $T$ -count (a) Independent matched-accuracy simulations give $1/z=0.672\pm 0.002$ for the default method at $\epsilon_{\mathrm{def}}=2\times 10^{-3}$ , $0.667\pm 0.002$ for BRS 2015 at $\epsilon_{\mathrm{BRS}}=2\times 10^{-2}$ , and $0.663\pm 0.002$ for LCU at requested $\epsilon_{\mathrm{LCU}}=2\times 10^{-2}$ , where the exponent is plotted using a power law fit on the log-log plot. (b) At these precisions, BRS 2015 has roughly $60$ percent $T$ count compared to default, and LCU has $20$ percent $T$ count compared to the default method. Note that these numbers are obtained for the desired $\delta t$ , and $T$ cost may depend on the chosen step size. The simulations use $N=100$ , $\delta t=0.08$ , and total evolution time $T=15$ . We plot time on a log scale.
fields.figure_gloss: Transport scaling comparison showing transferred magnetization versus time steps. For matched dynamical transport exponent accuracy ($1/z \approx 2/3$), the symmetry-preserving LCU compilation reduces the cumulative $T$-count compared to standard synthesis and BRS axial synthesis.

fields.result: Dynamic spin structure factor and quantum Fisher information density of 36-site $\text{Cs}_2\text{CoCl}_4$ chain simulated on 36-qubit quantum processor with 420 two-qubit gates per state. Error-mitigated spectra achieve Pearson correlation and structural similarity $> 0.9$ against DMRG-CV and Pearson correlation $> 0.85$ against inelastic neutron scattering.
fields.question: How much reliable magnetic spectral information and field evolution can be recovered from noisy quantum processors under aggressive circuit compression?
fields.limits: Zero temperature target, open boundary conditions on 36 sites with evolution restricted to 20 Trotter steps ($Jt = 12$). State preparation fidelity averaged over spin channels is $> 0.6$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Total dynamical spin structure factor $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(q,\omega)=S^{xx}+S^{yy}+S^{zz}$ of the $L=36$ XXZ chain ( $\Delta=0.25$ , $J=0.23$ meV), measured on IonQ Forte Enterprise. Rows show the longitudinal channel $S^{zz}$ , one transverse channel $S^{xx}$ , and the total $S_{\mathrm{tot}}=S^{xx}+S^{yy}+S^{zz}$ , at $h_{x}=0$ (upper three) and $h_{x}=0.764J$ (lower three). The field mapping is $h_{x}[J]=0.764\times B[T]$ , so these correspond to 0 T and 1 T. The colorbars for each row are set by the DMRG-CV $L=100$ result peak value being one. Columns: 1) Inelastic neutron scattering from [ 26 ] ( $70$ mK, inferred channel resolution) ii) DMRG-CV ( $L=100$ , $\eta=0.1\,J$ ) iii) DMRG+Trotter (L = 36) iv) QPU results with the full EM stack v) Constant- $q$ cuts at $q=\pi$ through columns (i)-(iv).
fields.figure_gloss: Longitudinal ($S^{zz}$), transverse ($S^{xx}$), and total ($S_{\text{tot}}$) dynamical structure factors plotted as frequency $\omega/J$ against momentum $q/\pi$ across four transverse fields $h_x/J \in \{0, 0.764, 1.146, 1.604\}$, comparing DMRG-CV, DMRG+Trotter, and error-mitigated hardware measurements.

fields.result: Compiling multi-excitonic Bethe-Salpeter equation Hamiltonians into first-quantized block encodings requires $\widetilde{O}(N)$ Toffolis and $O(\log N)$ logical qubits, or $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ Toffolis and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ qubits. Triexciton eigenvalue estimation in $\sim 10^3$-atom semiconductors reduces Toffoli counts by $10^6\text{--}10^7$ relative to full-Hamiltonian quantum simulation.
fields.question: Can quantum simulation of material excited states be made computationally practical on fault-tolerant hardware by operating within a classical quasiparticle Bethe-Salpeter equation framework rather than simulating the full electronic Hamiltonian?
fields.prior: Full-Hamiltonian quantum simulation of a $10\times 10\times 10$ diamond mesh required $3.7\times 10^{17}$ Toffolis in second quantization (THC) and $4.2\times 10^{18}$ Toffolis in first quantization (plane waves).
fields.limits: Heuristic GW/Bethe-Salpeter equation framework with static screened interaction and Tamm-Dancoff approximation; fixed quasiparticle count $m_{\mathrm{tot}}=2m$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Quantum and classical resource estimates for diamond. The BSE calculations use $m=3$ , a THC fitting tolerance of $0.1\,\mathrm{m}E_{h}$ MP2 error per unit cell, and no space-group adaptation. All quantum methods target $0.1\,\mathrm{eV}$ QPE error per eigenvalue estimate: an excitation energy for BSE and a total supercell energy for the full-Hamiltonian methods. Constant overheads for combining ground- and excited-state estimates are omitted. (a) Quantum Toffoli counts and classical BSE FLOPs. (b) Logical qubits and classical BSE storage, counted in floating-point values. Open markers denote extrapolated data.
fields.figure_gloss: Toffoli and logical qubit counts vs $k$-point mesh size $N_k$ for diamond triexciton ($m=3$) eigenvalue estimation at $0.1\text{ eV}$ precision, comparing full-Hamiltonian simulation methods with BSE implementations.

fields.result: Constructed efficiently computable, ordering-sensitive finite-step Trotter error bounds for arbitrarily high-order product formulas on geometrically local Hamiltonians. For product formulas of order $p > 2$, bounds improve on previous analytical bounds by several orders of magnitude and overestimate actual error by only $40\%-50\%$.
fields.question: How can term ordering be accounted for to accurately bound Trotter error and efficiently find the optimal gate sequence in product-formula simulations?
fields.prior: Commutator-norm bounds overestimated 4th-order Trotter steps by $5$–$7\times$ (Childs et al. 2021) and single-step errors by $1$ order of magnitude at 2nd order and $3$ orders at 4th order (Schubert & Mendl 2016).
fields.limits: Demonstrated primarily on 1D nearest-neighbor translation-invariant chains. Evaluates error for a specific step size $\tau$ rather than providing an analytic $\tau^{p+1}$ scaling prefactor.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 11: Performance of unrestricted Karp optimization, depth-three Karp optimization, and fixed even–odd brickwall for $500$ random translation-invariant $8$ -qubit chains at $\tau=0.1$ . Panels (a) and (b) show fourth and sixth order. The optimality ratio is the actual error of the selected circuit divided by the minimum over all $64$ ordering patterns; the empirical CDF gives the fraction of samples at or below each ratio. Both Karp strategies use the local weights in Eq. 24 .
fields.figure_gloss: Empirical cumulative distribution of the optimality ratio (actual circuit error divided by minimum error among all $64$ ordering patterns) for 4th- and 6th-order product formulas on $500$ random $8$-qubit chains. Unrestricted Karp optimization selects sequential circuits within $3.5\%$ and $4.2\%$ of optimal on average, while depth-3 Karp optimization selects wave-like circuits that strongly outperform fixed even-odd brickwall circuits.

fields.result: Momentum-basis sampling reaches $0.47\%$ relative energy error using $1.4\%$ of the fixed particle-number sector at $U/t=1$, compared to $9.5\%$ error using $33\%$ of the sector in position basis under identical Krylov constructions.
fields.question: To what extent can one-body orbital basis rotations improve the sampling efficiency and ground-state compressibility of sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization on the Fermi-Hubbard ladder?
fields.prior: Position-basis sample-based quantum diagonalization (was $9.5\%$ relative error at $33\%$ sector size for $U/t=1$).
fields.limits: At intermediate coupling $U/t_{\rm leg}=5$ and isotropic hopping $t_{\rm rung}/t_{\rm leg}=1$, compressibility remains poor, requiring $k_{0.99}\propto 3.106^{N}/N$ states to capture $99\%$ ground-state weight; hardware simulations face significant particle-number leakage at large sizes.
tools: IBM Quantum hardware (ibm_miami up to 120 qubits)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4 : Statevector reconstruction performance as a function of retained subspace fraction for the half-filled 10-site Fermi-Hubbard ladder. Panels (a-c) and (e-g) show position- and momentum-basis sampling, respectively, while varying $U/t$ (a,e), Trotter step size $\Delta t$ (b,f), and the number of initial particle-number-conserving $XX+YY$ mixing layers (c,g). Panels (d,h) compare both sampling bases as a function of maximum Trotter-step count $K$ at $U/t=1$ and $10$ , respectively. Solid curves denote exact-diagonalization references and dashed curves denote statevector-sampled reconstructions; stars mark the terminal reconstructed subspaces. Unless varied, $K=7$ , $\Delta t=0.025$ , and three $XX+YY$ mixing layers are used. Sampling uses 200 samples per Krylov circuit for the layer sweep and 2,000 for the remaining studies.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots relative energy error $\lvert E-E_0\rvert/\lvert E_0\rvert$ against retained subspace fraction for a 10-site Fermi-Hubbard ladder under position- and momentum-basis sampling across various interaction strengths $U/t$, Trotter step sizes $\Delta t$, and mixing layer counts $L$.

fields.result: Adjacent exchanges and one singlet-projector interaction between fundamental and dual qutrits generate all special unitary gates independently across all noiseless subsystems for any $r,s\ge 1$. For four-qutrit encoded teleportation under correlated Weyl noise, logical fidelity exceeds the classical bound $1/2$ while unencoded teleportation is entanglement breaking.
fields.question: Can two-body symmetry-preserving interactions provide independent logical control across a mixed register of fundamental and dual qutrits without extra initialized ancillas?
fields.prior: Fundamental-qutrit registers required three-body interactions for semi-universality, or two-body interactions using six ancillas (Hulse et al. 2021).
fields.limits: Pure and mixed tensor $SU(3)$ collective noise only; gate sequence synthesis algorithm not provided; requires retaining trials where all 4 (or 5) qutrits arrive; diamond-norm perturbation bounds assume input-independent survival probabilities.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Recovery of entanglement transmission through encoding. In the darker interval $[3/4,55/64)$ , the unencoded teleportation channel is entanglement breaking, while the encoded channel exceeds the classical fidelity bound and can preserve entanglement. The curves use $F_{\rm u}^{(0)}=29/30$ , $F_{\rm enc}^{(0)}=13/15$ , and $\mu=0.20$ . The lighter shading begins at $14/19$ , where the unencoded fidelity reaches $1/2$ . Fidelities are averaged over accepted trials under the assumptions of Sec. IV.3 .
fields.figure_gloss: Teleportation fidelity plotted against transmission noise parameter. Identifies the noise interval where unencoded teleportation drops below the entanglement-breaking threshold while encoded teleportation stays above the classical fidelity bound of $1/2$.

fields.result: Modular companion front-end for AMD ZCU216 RFSoC provides up to 16 outputs, 8 inputs, and 8 20-bit DC biases, achieving $(91.7\pm 0.4)\%$ single-shot readout fidelity and SNR of $4.4\pm 0.1$ without a quantum amplifier.
fields.question: Can an integrated, modular RF/DC companion board for the ZCU216 eliminate external room-temperature signal conditioning while maintaining high-fidelity qubit readout?
fields.limits: Readout fidelity limited by $T_1 = 58.3\pm 4.1\,\mu$s relaxation during the $5.6\,\mu$s readout pulse (causing $(4.7\pm 0.3)\%$ error); residual $\approx 3.6\%$ error from $44\text{ mK}$ effective qubit thermal population and state overlap.
tools: Modular RF and DC input/output daughtercards
fields.figure_caption: Figure 14: Single-shot qubit readout and state discrimination using the QICK Box at QUIET. (a) Rotated I-Q scatter plot showing the ground (blue) and excited (red) state clusters for 3000 single-shot measurements per state. The data are rotated to align the axis of maximum state separation with the I-quadrature. Black markers indicate the median of each distribution. (b) Projected histogram along the I-quadrature after rotation. Dashed curves show Gaussian core fits obtained from the clean (outer) side of each distribution, isolating the electronics noise contribution from T 1 decay tails. The state separation is $\Delta\mu=28\pm 0.2$ a.u., with clean-side widths $\sigma_{g}=6.4\pm 0.1$ a.u. and $\sigma_{e}=6.5\pm 0.1$ a.u., yielding a readout electronics SNR of $4.4\pm 0.1$ and a readout fidelity of $(91.7\pm 0.4)\%$ . fields.result: Heating corrections to the QPC Fano factor scale as $O(\mathcal{T}^{-1/2})$ for auto-correlation and $O(\mathcal{T}^{1/2})$ for cross-correlation, while a combined clean Fano factor $F_{\text{clean}}$ eliminates outer-arm heating to achieve $O(\mathcal{T}^{3/2})$ scaling and extract the anyon charge $e^{*}/e=1/3$.
fields.question: How can the intrinsic quasiparticle charge be extracted from shot noise in multichannel fractional quantum Hall edges where intermode equilibration and heating obscure quantum point contact partition noise?
fields.limits: Analyzed for the $\nu=2/3$ fractional quantum Hall state in the strong charge-equilibration regime ($\ell_{\text{ch}}\ll L$) and weak-transmission limit ($\mathcal{T}\ll 1$).
tools: continuum charge and thermal transport equations
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Bias dependence of the excess current noises and the corresponding Fano factors, calculated from the full expressions without expanding in $\mathcal{T}$ . The calculations are performed in the strong charge-equilibration regime, $\ell_{\rm ch}\ll L$ . (a) Excess auto-correlation $\Delta S_{\rm auto}$ and negative cross-correlation $-\Delta S_{\rm cross}$ , normalized by the equilibrium Johnson–Nyquist noise $2k_{B}T_{0}G(L)$ , as functions of the dimensionless bias $e^{*}V_{0}/(k_{B}T_{0})$ , where $G(L)\equiv 2G_{0}/3$ is the two terminal conductance of the fully equilibrated $\nu=2/3$ edge. (b) Fano factors $F_{\rm auto}$ , $F_{\rm cross}$ , and $F_{\rm clean}$ as functions of the same dimensionless bias as in (a). The horizontal dashed line indicates the quasiparticle charge $e^{*}/e=1/3$ . This plot shows that $F_{\rm clean}$ provides a more reliable extraction of the quasiparticle charge than $F_{\rm auto}$ and $F_{\rm cross}$ for FQH edges with upstream modes. For the plots, we use $L=3\ell_{\rm th}$ , and $\mathcal{T}=0.1$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Excess current noises $\Delta S_{\text{auto}}$, $-\Delta S_{\text{cross}}$, and resulting Fano factors plotted against dimensionless bias $e^{*}V_{0}/(k_{B}T_{0})$. Shows $F_{\text{clean}}$ staying close to $e^{*}/e=1/3$ while $F_{\text{auto}}$ diverges and $F_{\text{cross}}$ underestimates the charge.

fields.result: Monolithic GaAs circuit simultaneously operates two individually tunable p-i-n InAs quantum dots and a cryogenic NEMS optical router, achieving $g^{(2)}(0) = (0.62\pm 0.07)\%$ and raw two-photon interference visibility of $V_{\mathrm{HOM}} = (62.2\pm 6.7)\%$.
fields.question: Can coherent, individually tunable quantum-dot emitters be monolithically integrated with programmable, cryogenic-compatible photonic routing elements on a single chip?
fields.limits: Measurements performed at approximately 5 K in a closed-cycle cryostat. Laser leakage and finite frequency scan steps degraded resonance fluorescence HOM visibility and scattering extinction.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Quantum dot single photon source integrated with nanomechanical router. (a.) Upper panel: Resonance fluorescence spectrum of a single quantum-dot exciton transition measured under resonant continuous-wave excitation. A Voigt profile fit (orange) yields a full width at half maximum of $\Gamma_{\mathrm{RF}}=(351.8\pm 28.0)~\mathrm{MHz}$ . Lower panel: Time-resolved fluorescence under resonant $\pi$ -pulse excitation. A single-exponential model convolved with the instrument response function (IRF) yields a decay rate of $\gamma=(1.55\pm 0.08)~\mathrm{ns}^{-1}$ , corresponding to a transform-limited linewidth of $246.2\pm 13.3~\mathrm{MHz}$ . (b.) Schematic of the two photon interference setup, in which NEMS serve as the first beam splitter. (c.) Hong–Ou–Mandel (HOM) measurement for parallel (indistinguishable) and perpendicular (fully distinguishable) configurations, controlled by a half-wave plate (HWP) in the delay arm. The NEMS is tuned to a $50:50$ splitting ratio. Raw interference visibility of $V_{\mathrm{HOM}}=(A_{\perp}-A_{\parallel})/A_{\perp}=(62.2\pm 6.7)\%$ using an integration window of $4\gamma$ . (d.) Hanbury Brown–Twiss autocorrelation measurement recorded from one output of the NEMS at the $50:50$ configuration. Extracted second-order correlation, $g^{(2)}(0)=A_{\mathrm{center}}/A_{\mathrm{side}}=(12.3\pm 3.2)\%$ .
